en: In the Vimalaprabhā, yoga consists of wisdom and means; it is the attainment of the miraculous power of the body of form, [manifesting as] Vajrasattva, Mahāsattva, Bodhisattva, and Tathāgata.
Having prostrated to that Bodhicitta— the Samayasattva who is all-pervading, the exhaustion of both existence and non-existence, without beginning or end, and peaceful— [I shall explain].
The single yoga-vow of the emanation body, speech, mind, and gnosis;

the single yoga-vow of the enjoyment body, speech, mind, and gnosis of the world-realms; the single yoga-vow of the glorious dharma body, speech, mind, and gnosis; and the single yoga-vow of the innate body, speech, mind, and gnosis.
The restraint of yoga, the restraint of yoga!
It is neither waking, nor dreaming, nor deep sleep, nor the pleasure born of two sense organs;
it is not knowledge, mind, speech, or body—it does not abide within these four states.
Abandoning the action seal (karmamudrā) and devoid of the knowledge seal (jñānamudrā), that which arises from the great seal (mahāmudrā) is the innate (sahaja); it is not with another.

Having prostrated to that *evaṃkāra*, the yoga whose nature is wisdom and means—the immutable bliss of Mahāmudrā which transcends the cultivation of conceptual construction, which is free from the forms of subject and object and from the chatter of mental fabrication, which has the appearance of a city of Gandharvas and the nature of a reflected image— *Note: The term "grāhyagrāhakasaṃsthāna" is interpreted here as "the established state of subject and object. The phrase "kalpajalpavivarjitam" is translated as "free from the chatter of mental fabrication," with "kalpa" understood in its sense of conceptual thought or imagination.*
Having prostrated to that Mahāmudrā, who transcends the nature of atoms, whose form is like a reflected image, and who is endowed with the excellence of all aspects;
Having prostrated before her, the mother of all Buddhas, who is free from arising and ceasing, the conduct of Samantabhadra, and the Mother of the Universe;
Having prostrated to that Kālacakra, the body arisen from syllables, which is devoid of the vowels, consonants, the *samāpatti*, the *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* syllables, and so forth.
The omniscient one, known as the Body of Wisdom, the pervasive lord with the form of the sun, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals— that is the reality consisting of sixteen divisions.
Having bowed to the Buddha, who consists of the four bodies and is seated upon the vajra lion-throne, and who was formerly entreated by Sucandra after being praised by gods and asuras;

Having prostrated to the Vajrayoga which is fourfold as Vajrasattva— the single yoga of pure gnosis, the instruction on the discipline of the true path, the speech which is the yoga of the saṃbhogakāya honored by the three worlds, and the excellent commitment of the Jina which is the single yoga of mind and phenomena, and the yoga of the nirmāṇakāya— [I shall explain] the *Śrīparamādya*.

Having bowed my head to that single state— the non-duality of knowledge and the object of knowledge, which has transcended the power of worldly existence, whose nature is wisdom and skillful means, and which is the son of men and gods— I pay homage to the Lord who is honored by the three worlds, who is always desired as indestructible and indivisible, and who is placed within the *vajramaṇi* (the jewel at the crown) as *rajas* and the sun, and in the *uṣṇīṣa* (the crown of the head) as *śukra* (semen) and the moon.

Having bowed my head to the Lord of the gods, whose foot is placed upon the wind, fire, water, earth, the mandala of Mount Meru, the lotus, the moon, and the sun, and above which stands Īśvara and Māra, together with the foot of the Mother of the World; ||| 1 ||

Desiring to speak of that Yoga of Vajra—the supreme bliss of the syllables—which has been practiced, taught, and chanted by all the infinite Sugatas, as well as by the Bodhisattvas who are holders of the excellent thunderbolt and knowers of mantra, I, though dull-witted, shall explain it in the Kālacakra. Does not the lord of birds (the eagle) travel swiftly through the sky, while other birds do not?

In that body wherein the Lord of Jinas has proclaimed the entire universe as manifest, along with the mantras, the vowels, the bindus, and the dhāraṇīs—having entered that great ocean to swim therein, may I reach the further shore through the power of the Jinas.

That concise *laghutantra* which was previously prophesied by the One Endowed with the Ten Powers from the *Paramādibuddha* spoken by the Lord of Secrets—that very *Kālacakra-laghutantra* has been proclaimed in its entirety by Mañjuśrī within the *Kalāpa* for all the Munis.
The commentary written by Sucandra, which was sixty thousand [verses] long and indicated the meaning of all vehicles, was [abridged] by me, Puṇḍarīka.
The twelve-thousand-verse text of the *Laghutantra*, which follows the *Mūlatantra* and elucidates the vajra words, is now being written.

Having heard this tantra and received the supreme consecration according to the procedure taught by the Victor, the yogi— having mastered the entire *Laghutantrarāja* and remaining on the path of gnosis, having abandoned pride along with manifold enjoyments and power, and having dedicated his mind to the state of Buddhahood— engages in conduct for the benefit of others and listens to the commentary of the Lord.

He who, though established in the glorious Vajrayāna, is devoid of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), yet composes a commentary while possessing a heart of various scriptural fictions and endowed with the pride of scholarship—he, like a reckless blind man touching an elephant, would destroy his own tantra. For that which exists for the sake of conquering the enemy's tantra is always the work of Māra’s kinsman.

In the Vimalaprabhā, one who is conceited due to his learning, whose nature is ignorance regarding the words of the Lord of Jinas, and who is perpetually blind, enters hell after composing a commentary on the Supreme Vehicle (Agrayāna), having caused others—who are likewise blind—to fall there; with a mind drawn by the pleasure of women onto the path of unwholesome actions such as regret, killing, and so forth, he is deprived of the bliss of glorious wisdom, struck down by the state of the Vajra, and overwhelmed by external enjoyments.

Those who have been prophesied by the Teacher in the Vajrayāna that bestows the bliss of the Lord of Jinas—all those commentators and compilers of the *saṅgīti*, holders of the supreme *vajra* like myself—they speak here of the Buddha’s power for the sake of maturing gods, *bhujaṅgas*, and humans. Those who possess the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) do not speak untruth; we are those very Bodhisattvas of the world-systems whom the Lords of Jinas have declared.

Indeed, in the future time, the various intellects of the Buddhists—always devoted to treatises such as *Tarka* and the like—will become false due to the influence of their attachment to logic (*tarkasaṅgama*), even though they are directed toward their desired objects by means of that logic. Therefore, I am composing this commentary (*ṭīkā*) to crush the defects of the evil intellects of those very persons who provide misleading instructions regarding the path.

In the ocean of existence—whose infinite waters are passion; which is infested with crocodiles such as hatred devoid of discernment; which is turbulent with the waves of delusion; whose coastal shores are the greed for wealth and fortune through constant coming and going; where the submarine fire is the karma of regret, killing, and so forth; and where the roar is harsh like the sound of a whirlpool—the commentary on the glorious Vajrayāna is always the helmsman.

That Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) of the Vajra-holder is the sole bestower of the bliss of omniscience; she is the swift-moving wind-sail for great beings to cross over the six miseries via the path of liberation; she is the powerful cloth that destroys the host of Māras and afflictions for those seeking the shore of Nirvāṇa; she is the wish-fulfilling jewel of perfect cognition, the subduer of enemies who rule the three worlds, and the one who reveals all things everywhere. Having abandoned the objects of obscuration such as the aggregates, she is like the sun whose light has been attained.

He who abandons her and would serve one whose heart is crooked with greed for wealth, or who serves her with a mind conceptualized for the sake of Buddhahood, is led by her to a fall. Sin arises from the destruction of passion (*rāga*), for hatred (*dveṣa*) is born from that which is most dear; from hatred comes delusion (*moha*), and from this, the falling of one’s own *vajra* results in the constant fainting of the mind. In another chapter, the instruction on the discipline of the true path: all engagement with sense objects, such as improper food and drink, mocks the mind and destroys its happiness; thus, it wanders through six births after six births.

For those seeking the path of the Omniscient One, the investigation of words and non-words is not of great importance; for the Great Ones always proceed upon the path even through various local dialects.

The language of the Omniscient One is supreme, according to the power of the inclinations of sentient beings, whereas other grammars composed by gods and serpents are intended for those who seek disputation over words and the like.
A yogi grasps the meaning even from corrupt words, and a yogi grasps it from regional dialects;
just as swans drink the milk that is mixed in water by extracting it.

Regarding the subject of ultimate reality, the great ones never resort to the arrangement of syllables; once the meaning is known through local designations, what is the use of the words of scripture?
That alone is true knowledge which arises when even the words of corrupt speech are [recognized as such];
for the Omniscient One, there is no speech that is merely local in this world.
The supreme syllable is the fourth, the gnosis of wisdom; that indeed is what is called the Buddhas' own Great Seal by the Victor.

For one whose white [garment] leaks through attachment to wisdom, by what means can there be an increase in happiness? When spring arrives, how could the bud of the mango tree fall away without bearing fruit?
He who has not attained the Imperishable seeks perishable pleasure; such a person is miserable, like a thirsty deer that, though parched, does not drink the water standing upon the ground.

The great fool, though not yet possessing it, yearns for the impermanent pleasure of worldly existence which is subject to decay; the wise man, having attained the bliss of sovereignty, renounces it for the sake of liberation.
Sometimes during the rainy season, the female deer seeks pleasure with the lord of beasts, while the pigeon constantly subsists on grains of stone.
But for both, there is no supreme bliss simultaneously and eternally, just as it does not exist due to the emission of semen;
likewise, it is so for the ascetic and the lustful, and for those in sleep and waking, because of its perishability.

Just as one who is bitten by a snake while asleep does not live because of the absence of the collection of remedies, so too one who is bitten by that [ignorance] through the womb of a weak woman perishes;
yet, just as a stone, bark, thread, or silk garment becomes pure when burnt by fire, so too one who is bitten by that [ignorance] through the womb of a [wise] woman becomes purified.
Just as mercury, when touched by fire, runs away and does not remain steady, so too the true mind of men, through the wisdom of insight, flees and does not become stable.
For by the touch of that source, semen is indeed constantly emitted by her as well; even though it is mobile, it becomes bound through contact with fire by the power of medicinal herbs and the like.
Just as that [fire], even when situated within wood, is never seen by means of cutting or splitting, so too the fire of wisdom is not perceived through the application of pure intellect.
Just as a particle of gold is seen [within ore] through the churning [of the rock], so too the appearance of the mind is not seen by means of the methods of conceptual cultivation.
In that very place, he is seen through the singular union with the taste of the woman; yet, being devoid of the path, he does not attain the reality which was proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

The generation stage, which consists of sixteen and fourfold divisions and various conceptual paths, has been explained as being free from the mental construction of syllables such as *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*.
The yoga of the stage of generation is reality; there is no other means for accomplishing reality than through the signs such as smoke, breath control, and the central flow.
By means of this path—the vow of knowledge, the vajra-fall, and the upward-moving semen—the yogi attains the bliss of all the Buddhas.

Whether it is designated as the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*) or as the innate (*sahaja*), the mundane accomplishment of all female messengers (*dūtī*) is achieved through the conceptualizations of form and so forth, and through the practice of meditating on the mandala circle and other such [visualizations]. How much more so, then, the desired great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*)?
The path becomes pure for those disciples who, through the grace of a true guru, possess compassion for sentient beings and a constant, noble exertion toward the welfare of others.

The summary of the rules for the true path: This jewel of the excellent path, once given to another heedless being, is stolen by the thieves of evil sense-objects as he enters the forest of his own home.
For one who has entered the dense thicket of a wretched household, the jewel of the excellent path is carried away by the thieves of doubt, remorse, sleep, indolence, and restlessness.

By the thieves of killing, false speech, taking what is not given, adultery, harshness, slander, frivolous talk, covetousness, malice, and wrong view—and by these five groups of five thieves, the Jewel is constantly stolen. Furthermore, by the thieves of minor sins, heinous crimes, slaughter, violence, and addiction to the senses, the Jewel is likewise perpetually carried away.
By excessive food and drink, by various enjoyments, and by those many thieves, even one who possesses vigor is carried away when he has fallen into the stupor of negligence.

An examiner should not himself show a jewel to another, a common man, so that he might know whether it is of great value or not; for one would release the gem from his grasp based on that person's words.
One should indeed recognize one's own jewel by means of the pure words of those experts in fine gems, from whom one has it appraised as a great jewel.
Māra creates obstacles by means of the forms of fully enlightened Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
as well as [the forms of] fathers, mothers, daughters, sisters, sons, brothers, beloved wives,
and so forth; therefore, disciples must with great effort protect the jewel of the excellent path bestowed by the true guru.
Having abandoned the family of rags, one must act with extreme secrecy.
The Vīrakrama path and the Svādhiṣṭhānakrama are not for liberation;
only the Suviśuddhakrama has been shown by the Buddha as the means to liberation.

Because those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution are not gathered [into the path] by means of ordinary pleasure, the Lord of Jinas [teaches] in the tantra consisting of wisdom and method for the sake of consecration (*sekārtha*).
This "heroic conduct" (*vīrakrama*) is not external; rather, it is said to be the exhaustion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the body.

Self-consecration is called "the vision of the three realms within emptiness. In this essence-less saṃsāra, Buddhahood is the fruit; it arises for men from the exhaustion of that [saṃsāra], just as a ripe plantain fruit comes into being through the destruction of the plantain tree.
8. Kha.
0na | In the Vimalaprabhā: those beings who are scorpions or crabs belong to her who is subject to destruction;
likewise, the mind of union with Māyā becomes subject to destruction.
Non-dual, stainless, blissful, and continuous, it is the desired supreme immutable (*paramākṣara*) within great passion (*mahārāga*).
It is the gnosis (*jñāna*) that transcends existence and non-existence, the Being (*sattva*), and Samantabhadra.
It is the passionless (*araṇa*) and yet the great passion (*mahāraṇa*), the innate (*sahaja*), the glorious bearer of the drop of the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicittabindudhara*).

The glorious Kālacakra-vajra is the yoga consisting of wisdom and method. Kāla is the embodiment of compassion and emptiness, while the wheel of emptiness (śūnyatā-cakra) is said to be conventional form; thus, Kālacakra is considered non-dual.
For the sake of swiftly attaining the glory of this world-system, the yogi who constantly meditates upon the feet of the Yoginī every day shall experience the destruction of all obstacles.

Enemies, lions, lordly elephants, fire, the king of serpents, thieves, nooses, horses, the agitated ocean, Piśācas who cause fear of death, disease, and the afflictions of Indra— all these are overcome.
Poverty, separation from one's wife, fear of an agitated king, a thunderbolt strike, and loss of wealth—
these clearly come to an end for one who remembers the feet of the Yoginīs.

Even when being struck by enemies in battle with elephants as their mounts, amidst a multitude of excellent men with all their bodies armored, and with hands holding spears, discuses, swords, bows, and arrows;

Having conquered all those enemies— who grant death, possess fierce forms, and have gone in every direction and intermediate quarter— with his own weapons, he who remembers the Yoginīs obtains fame of victory on all sides. Making a lion’s roar, with a face of great transformation, terrifying with sharp fangs, lashing his tail, with curved and firm claws, having dug into the temples of rutting elephants, roaring, with eyes like the rising sun and a dangling tongue, the lion is intent on killing.

Whoever remembers the feet of the Yoginīs, fear departs far from him. [Imagine] an excellent lordly elephant, blue-black in hue with tawny eyes, his two temples overflowing with abundant rut-fluid; uprooting and crushing various choice trees, trumpeting like a thundercloud, he breaks the bonds with the tips of his tusks. Whoever remembers the feet of the Yoginīs, which remove fear, releases his body.
