10–11. Uprooting and crushing [them], Śakra— emitting sparks like falling stars, spreading a great darkness of smoke in all directions and intermediate points, and burning villages, cities, and forests— releases [this] as if from a mass of fire.

The fire that at all times causes fear of death for sentient beings and pervades all directions— [that fire] becomes cool for one who remembers the feet of the Yoginīs, which remove fear. The furious lord of serpents, resembling blue collyrium, with a coiled body, joined by fierce hissing, crooked-eyed, double-tongued, causing fear of death, possessing the speed of the wind, violent,
having arrived with a cruel gaze, manifesting his hoods and biting— [that lord of serpents] goes to destruction for one who remembers the feet of the Yoginīs, which remove fear.

In the forest, there are robbers with evil minds, bows in their palms and arrows drawn back to their ears; blocking the path of the true way, they go in every direction, armed with spears, discs, and swords, with fierce eyes, plundering the best of travelers. But for him who remembers the feet of the Yoginīs, which remove all fear, these [robbers] stay far away.

[The traveler] is afflicted by hunger, bound with many snares, his pair of lotus-feet filled with chains; his tongue, throat, and lips are parched, and his body is withered from the lack of pure water.
He who, while guarding [the gates] day and night by the command of his master’s wrath, remembers the feet of the Yoginīs that remove fear, he too attains liberation from this [danger].

Even one who has boarded a ship upon the ocean when the sea is agitated by endless fierce winds, being whirled in whirlpools by swarms of crocodiles and fish, hemmed in by wicked sea-thieves with fire and oil released [upon them], and rained upon from all sides by a great, incessant fire— whosoever remembers the feet of the Yoginīs that remove fear, he too reaches the further shore of that [ocean].

With hands like *kattika* scimitars, uttering shrieks and terrifying roars, their mouths blazing with fire, these Vetālas— cruel-minded, flesh-eaters, tormented by hunger, delighting in human blood, emaciated in body, and naked— stand stationed within the circle of the ten directions;
yet they provide protection for whoever remembers the feet of the Yoginīs, which dispel all fear.

One whose fingertips have perished, who daily loses his nose, lips, and ears, from whose pus-soaked wounds much [pus] flows repeatedly from his face, mouth, feet, and hands, and who has been abandoned by his circle of kinsmen like a corpse due to the power of a foul stench— he becomes free of disease and possesses beautiful feet if he should remember the Yoginīs.

20 20 25 30 10. In the *Vimalaprabhā*: With blazing tongues and sharp fangs, having the faces of hooded serpents, lions, śarabhas, tigers, and elephants, and holding in their hands wheels, swords, tridents, goads, and vajras—all the messengers of the lords of the gods—threaten the practitioner who is solely intent on enlightenment and established in supreme bliss; yet they meet with destruction if he has placed his feet within the minds of the Yogīśvarīs.
In the rainy season, he carries a burden even from the forest to the city through paths filled with mud; in the winter, devoid of clothing, he travels along snowy paths and journeys to foreign lands;

and in the summer, he traverses the waterless desert paths, scorched by the sun's rays and fraught with danger—all these sufferings are endured by the poor man who meditates on the feet of the Yoginīs, thereby becoming free from desire.

A pungent odor emanates from their armpits, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, and body; they suffer perpetual misfortune due to being deprived of sexual union with all women; and by the power of such inauspicious results, they are always loathed by women. However, for those who meditate upon the Yoginīs—who bestow the boon of happiness and possess excellent complexion, form, and beauty—all good fortune shall belong to them.

Agitated by treachery, the king—like the Yama of universal destruction, solely intent on total slaughter—swiftly dispatched his army, which struck fear of death into those servants; yet even he becomes pacified toward them through gifts of honor and respect, for he meditates in his own mind upon the feet of the Yoginīs, the sovereigns of the three worlds.

For those [yoginīs] for whom the fall of the thunderbolt from the sky anywhere at all constantly brings about death, fainting, and detachment throughout successive births and lifetimes—that very [thunderbolt] becomes pacified and reaches its end; they are no longer subject to birth when they meditate upon the lotus-thunderbolt feet of Śrī Karmajñāna.

For those who, through detachment from attachment to women, experience the destruction of all worldly objects day and night, that [destruction] arises repeatedly through many future births because their minds are clung to latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

But for those yoginīs who meditate upon the form of the universe—the wisdom (*prajñā*) which is honored and praised by the supreme Victors, the peerless state equal to the unequalled—that [wisdom] becomes an indestructible object for them all.

The Yoginīs—Piṅgalā, Iḍā, and Avadhūtī—traverse the three paths of the Sun, Moon, and Rāhu; their gnosis-body (jñānakāya) is the destruction of existence and non-existence, those two feet of equal movement. He who meditates upon that one, which is the imperishable state of innate bliss (sahajasukha), for him the fruit described here will swiftly come to pass in this very life, removing all fear.

The abode of the glorious Yoginīs is the House of the Vajra-Jewel; for the sake of entering it, the path free from afflictions and with its Māras destroyed has been proclaimed here by me, preceded by a hymn as spoken by the Jina. [Chapter 11: The Instruction on the Rules of the True Path] For those whose path is ruined, who have always gone into the darkness of falsehood and the company of Māras, they shall reach the House of the Vajra-Jewel without difficulty by means of this [path]. Through the man who has attained the path, the Guru here possesses a body endowed with the thirty-two marks for the sake of the world.
Established upon the wheel of Dharma, his lotus feet are kissed by the multitude of rays from the crest-jewels of the crowns of the gods;
showing the true path like the sun that has destroyed all darkness, he who meditates through the stages of smoke and so forth shall become Kālacakra, the state of innate bliss.

He whose lotus-feet are gloriously sounded by the crowns of the lords of gods, nāgas, humans, and asuras; who is the sun of perfect knowledge for the three worlds, established upon the glorious Wheel of Dharma;

the fierce slayer of the beasts of Māra and the afflictions—may the glorious Lion of the Śākyas always [protect me]. Impelled by his wisdom and through his grace, I write this commentary for the sake of the world.
From the letter *ka*, the cause is stilled; from the letter *la*, there is indeed dissolution (*laya*) here.
From the letter *ca*, the flickering mind [is stilled]; from the letter *ṛ*, time, the knowledge of imperishable bliss, and the means [are attained] through the sequential binding.
His nature is compassion;
the wheel of the world, which has the aspect of the knowable, is Śrī Prajñā, whose nature is emptiness.
For this Śrī Kālacakra, the vajra-yoga which abides entirely within the two truths, there shall be a designation that serves as its expression.
In this tantra, a commentary is indeed being written by me, the Lord of the World, who has been prophesied by the Sugata and impelled by Mañjuśrī.
This illuminator of secrets in the tantra is beneficial for the ignorant, the learned, and the foolish,
like a mother to her sons, for the sake of the happiness of all embodied beings.
Because by means of this [work] yogins find the true path of Vajrasattva,
therefore this commentary, the *Vimalaprabhā*, is quickly written.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Rule of the Supreme Deity and the True Path," from the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja* following the root tantra, for the purpose of destroying all obstacles caused by Māra. 2 5 10 15 a. First.

1 || 20 20 Having thoroughly considered the subject matter, the connection, the purpose, and the ultimate purpose of the *Vimalaprabhā*, [this work] bestows the fruit of Buddhahood in this very life through the intention of one's own mind for those beings to be trained who are free from restrictive observances.

In the abode of great bliss, within the supreme primordial Buddha’s Great Vajra-Dhātu Maṇḍala, seated upon the vajra lion-throne, surrounded by a host of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, wrathful kings, gods, nāgas, deities, and goddesses, whose lotus feet are saluted by the inhabitants of the three realms, the sovereign wheel-turner of the single realm, the Supreme Primordial Buddha, the Blessed Śrī Kālacakra, who is without lineage [of transmission], being requested by Sucandra—

The *Paramādibuddha*, the *Kālacakra* King of Tantras in twelve thousand [verses], which is without lineage (*niranvaya*), is embraced by the *Nāmasaṅgīti*—which serves as the witness to the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) of Vajradhara—and is the witness to the vajra-words in all tantras. It opens the jewel-casket of the Buddhas, relies upon both mundane and supramundane truths, and is purified by the four enlightenments and the four vajras. It expresses through words its subject matter consisting of the four bodies, the six families, the twelve truths, the sixteen realities, the sixteen emptinesses, and the sixteen compassions. It reveals the ten mundane and eleven supramundane empowerments, and elucidates the worldly and supramundane accomplishments (*siddhi*) of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*), and great seal (*mahāmudrā*). Comprising five chapters on the world-system, the internal [body], empowerment, means for achievement (*sādhana*), and gnosis—or alternatively, comprising five sections—it was taught for the sake of all beings, from humans upward, attaining the state of perfect buddhahood.

Therefore, there is the prophecy of the Tathāgata for Mañjuśrī regarding the compilation of this *Laghutantra*, for the sake of training the Brahmin sages in a future time, for my own composition of a commentary, for the purpose of teaching the tantra to others such as Yamāntaka and the rest, and so that all sentient beings dwelling in the ninety-six million villages of the realm of Sambhala and elsewhere may attain the path.

In this context, the world-system is preceded by an aggregation of atoms; sentient beings are preceded by the world-system; worldly and supramundane consecration is preceded by sentient beings; the accumulation of merit, the practice of meditating on the maṇḍala circle, and the accomplishment of worldly siddhis up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven are preceded by consecration; and the accomplishment of the Great Wisdom Seal (mahājñānamudrā-siddhi)—which transcends the aggregation of atoms and is free from the conceptual meditation on maṇḍalas and so forth—is preceded by worldly siddhis, through the power of the latencies of emptiness, compassion, the conventional, and the objectless, cultivated in previous births via the accumulations of merit and wisdom.

Therefore, first is the *Lokadhātu-kalpa*, then the *Adhyātma-kalpa*, then the *Abhiṣeka-kalpa*, then the *Laukikasiddhisādhana-kalpa*, and then the *Paramākṣarajñānasādhana-kalpa*. Thus, the *Tantrarāja* consists of five *kalpas* or five chapters (*paṭalas*) in this sequential order.
Herein, the subject matter (*abhidheya*) is the Vajrayoga consisting of Wisdom and Means—the *Ādibuddha*, the *Kālacakra Bhagavān* who is without lineage (*niranvaya*).
And this [tantra], established as having the nature of five chapters (*pañcapaṭalasvabhāvatā*), begins first with the "Chapter on the World-Sphere" (*lokadhātupaṭala*).

This Chapter on the World-Sphere is established through the nature of the teacher, beginning with the words "Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*) and so forth; it is established through the nature of the indication of the location; it is established through the nature of the perfection of the great assembly (*mahāparṣatsampat*); it is established through the nature of the requester; and it is established through the nature of the inquiry into the subject matter (*abhidheya*), the expression (*abhidhāna*), the purpose (*prayojana*), and the ultimate purpose (*prayojanaprayojana*) of the Vajra Yoga. [The mantras are] without interruption.
Having gazed at Kha-ca-0; Ka.
Having awakened [them], for the sake of attaining perfect enlightenment, he acted without hesitation.
O, [requested by Sucandra, the Paramādibuddha, the Kālacakra-tantrarāja in twelve thousand verses, which is without succession— ]

In this chapter, the summary of the teaching of the Tantra is established as follows: it is established by way of its nature as the arising of the universal image (*viśvabimba*) from the great void of the five syllables and so forth, and as the mandala, consecration, and supplication; it is established by way of its nature as the speech of the teacher and the response [of the disciple]; it is established by way of its nature as the collection of the arising of the world-system, mantras, planets, constellations, sentient beings, vital breaths, and so forth; it is established by way of its nature as the enumeration of the mandalas of wind and the rest, the oceans, islands, and mountains; it is established by way of its nature as the prophecy of Mañjuśrī; it is established by way of its nature as the thirty-one states of existence (*bhava*); it is established by way of its nature as the arising of the Great Wheel-turning King (*mahācakravartin*); it is established by way of its nature as the measurement of days and so forth, and the very subtle breaths and so forth; it is established by way of its nature as the calculation of the luminaries and the establishment of the tenets (*siddhānta*); it is established by way of its nature as the movement of the planets and the rising of the constellations from the breaths of the central channel; it is established by way of its nature as the twelve-fold zodiac signs and the terrestrial globe; it is established by way of its nature as the *svarodaya* and so forth; it is established by way of its nature as the strength of the earth and Rāhu and the rest; it is established by way of its nature as the machines for breaking and protecting fortresses; it is established by way of its nature as the wandering through the twelve divisions of the earth of the Wheel-turning Kings; it is established by way of its nature as the uprooting of the Mleccha religion and the establishment of the Buddha-dharma; it is established by way of its nature as the bestowing of the path to mundane and supramundane accomplishments upon all sentient beings; it is established by way of its nature as the teacher standing behind and in front of Mañjuśrī and Lokeśvara; and it is established by way of its nature as the maximum lifespan of humans from the Great Wheel-turning King down to Kalkin. Thus ends the chapter on the World System (*lokadhātu*). Next, in the chapter on the Inner (*adhyātma*), it is first established by way of its nature as the collection of the entry into the womb (*garbhādhāna*); it is established by way of its nature as the union of semen, blood, the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), and primordial wisdom (*jñāna*); it is established by way of its nature as the arising of the embryo month by month; it is established by way of its nature as the ten stages beginning with the fish; it is established by way of its nature as the four bodies and the four purities; it is established by way of its nature as the arising of the embryo through the four types of awakening (*sambodhi*); it is established by way of its nature as the twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths, the one thousand channels, the three hundred and sixty joints, the six elements, the six tastes, the six sense organs, the six objects, the six organs of action and their objects, the six consciousnesses, the six formations, the six feelings, the six perceptions, the six forms, the six cognitions, the six wheels, and the six mandalas above and below; it is established by way of its nature as the flow of the five aggregates and the five elements through the petals of the navel-lotus and the two nostrils via the left and right mandalas; it is established by way of its nature as the emergence of the entire Tantra through the central channel (*madhyamā*); it is established by way of its nature as the winds beginning with the life-force (*prāṇa*); it is established by way of its nature as the arising of the symbols of the deities from the elements; it is established by way of its nature as the omens of death (*ariṣṭa*) of the moon, sun, and fire; it is established by way of its nature as the arising in the six realms of rebirth through the ripening of karma; and it is established by way of its nature as the seizing, moving, and cutting of the channels and so forth by the planets.

Thus, he abides by way of having the nature of deceiving death and misfortune through the bliss of entering the middle way and so forth; he abides by way of having the nature of accomplishing external worldly activities; he abides by way of having the nature of examining all philosophical systems and inference; and he abides by way of having the nature of establishing the Dharma according to the inclinations of various sentient beings. Thus, in the chapter on the Inner [Practice].

Then, in the Chapter on Consecration (*Abhiṣeka-paṭala*), there occurs a repetition of the following passage: "It abides by way of the nature of the examination of the guru first; it abides by way of the nature of the summary of the examination of superior, inferior, and middling disciples; it abides by way of the nature of the characteristics of the ground and so forth, including the division of directions such as the villages for the accomplishment of the expansion of activities (*karmaprasara*); and it abides by way of the nature of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the substances for the fire offering (*homa-dravya*), the rosary beads (*akṣa*), the thread, the seat, the ritual stake (*kīlaka*), the water-jar (*kalaśa*), the powder-line (*rajaḥ-sūtra*), the placement of the machine (*yantra-nyāsa*), and the glorious prophecy (*śrī-vyākaraṇa*). Indeed, that [passage] does not exist in the Tibetan [translation]. Regarding *rajaṃ*, it is *rajaḥ* in Sanskrit.
This is not apprehended; this is not apprehended.

He abides by way of having the nature of the characteristics of the world-system (*diguvi kra*); he abides by way of having the nature of the complete knowledge of the ten principles (*tattva*) through the drawing of the mandala for the acquisition of the stages (*bhūmi*); he abides by way of having the nature of bestowing mundane and supramundane consecrations (*abhiṣeka*); he abides by way of having the nature of all foundations and meditative absorptions (*samādhi*); he abides by way of having the nature of the assembly, the pledges, and the worship in the pledge-circle (*samayacakra*); he abides by way of having the nature of the mudrās, gazes, signs, pledges, conventions, castes, and so forth of the thirty-six family goddesses; he abides by way of having the nature of the dismissal of the mandala circle; he abides by way of having the nature of the worship and dismissal of the dust-mandala circle in great rivers and so forth, or in one's own respective home; he abides by way of having the nature of satisfying the glorious Guru with all kinds of gifts. Thus ends the Chapter on Consecration.

Then, in the *Sādhanā-paṭala*, he first abides as the nature of the emanation of the Tathāgatas by means of the rays from the seed-syllable on the moon at his heart, beginning with the protection wheel (*rakṣā-cakra*) and the purification of the faces; he abides as the nature of the unsurpassed worship, confession of sins, rejoicing in merit, taking refuge in the Three Jewels, self-dedication, the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), resorting to the path, and the focus on emptiness (*śūnyatā*); he abides as the nature of the practice of the King of Mandalas (*maṇḍalarāja*), the Supreme King of Karmas (*karmarāja*), the yoga of the drop (*bindu-yoga*), and the subtle yoga (*sūkṣma-yoga*) according to the stage of generation (*utpatti-krama*); he abides as the nature of the practice for attaining worldly accomplishments (*laukika-siddhi*); he abides as the nature of the practice of the knowledge of the secret reality of the Vedānta, sacrifices (*yajña*), and the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅga-yoga*); he abides as the nature of the accumulation of merit through generosity and so forth; he abides as the nature of the cultivation of the mind, both manifest and unmanifest. Thus ends the *Sādhanā-paṭala*. Then, in the *Jñāna-paṭala*, he first abides as the nature of the mandala of the purification of the elements, such as the bones of the body; he abides as the nature of the deities of the six families of body, speech, and mind; he abides as the nature of the six mantra-families beginning with *Ā* and *Ka*; he abides as the nature of the thirty-six tantras of wisdom and method (*prajñopāya*); he abides as the nature of the emanation of the Great Sovereign of the Six Wheels (*ṣaṭcakravartin*), which is permeated by the yoga of wisdom, method, and action; he abides as the nature of the practice for attaining the accomplishment of the knowledge of the supreme immutable (*paramākṣara*) through the fourth consecration and the great seal (*mahāmudrā*); he abides as the nature of the emanation of the knowledge-mandala (*jñāna-maṇḍala*); he abides as the nature of the practice of serving the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); he abides as the nature of the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), which consists of all aspects of knowledge and the knowable; he abides as the nature of the examination of all activities of body, speech, and mind; he abides as the nature of the teaching of the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharma-skandha*); he abides as the nature of the vajra-consecration in the Buddha-field; he abides as the nature of teaching the Dharma according to the inclinations and dispositions of beings with various interests; he abides as the nature of the practice for attaining bodily accomplishments such as alchemy (*rasāyana*); he abides as the nature of performing the welfare of all beings through supreme immutable bliss (*paramākṣara-sukha*); he abides as the nature of the collection of phenomena, calculation, and the inclusion of designations; he abides as the nature of the praise of the five syllables, the six syllables, the great emptiness, and the drop-emptiness (*bindu-śūnya*). Thus ends the *Jñāna-paṭala*. [End of section] *Ṅa*

[In the section on the King of Mandalas and the King of Rituals: This is the summary of the teaching of the Tantra. Therefore, by this sequence, the Blessed One Kālacakra, who exists as the nature of the five chapters, is the subject matter (*abhidheya*) here;
and the collection of chapters that explains him is the title of the *Tantrarāja*.
Between these two—the signified (*abhidheya*) and the signifier (*abhidhāna*)—there exists a mutual relationship characterized as that of the signified and the signifier.

The Blessed One Kālacakra, who is the signified, abides as the intrinsic nature of the five chapters; the signifier is the designation "Kālacakra," which consists of the five chapters. Furthermore, the Blessed One Ādibuddha is the signified.
The relationship between the signifier and the signified is characterized by the designation "the Vācakamādi Buddha" as the signifier and [the reality] as the signified;
this is the connection between the expression and the expressed.

Therefore, the purpose of entering the mandala through the bestowal of the worldly consecrations is to accomplish the accumulation of merit. Furthermore, the purpose of the fourth [consecration], the Great Wisdom, through the bestowal of the supramundane consecration for the sake of attaining the accomplishment of the Mahāmudrā free from all traces, is to accomplish the accumulations of both merit and gnosis. This is the purpose.

Having thoroughly observed these very characteristics of the subject matter, for those people to be trained who are devoid of restrictive rules (*niyama*), there is the following intention of their own minds:

"The restriction (*niyama*) is the vow of the Śrāvaka level, which is the restraint of morality (*śīlasaṃvara*) devoid of the enjoyment of the five objects of desire. Those who are devoid of that are "devoid of restrictive rules" (*niyamarahitāḥ*). Their own mental inclination is the longing for the enjoyment of the five objects of desire, as well as the longing for great bliss (*mahāsukha*) through the two sexual organs; this is the "intention of their own minds" for those devoid of restrictive rules.
By this [intention of their own minds], it bestows the fruit of Buddhahood in this very life.

In this birth—that is, in a human birth—the King of Tantras bestows the fruit of Buddhahood, but not in births within the five destinies such as those of the gods and so forth. Why is that? Because [those other states] are not born from a land of karma (*akarmabhūmi*).

Here, even for gods and others, because they obtain a human birth, it will bestow the fruit of Buddhahood; this is the rule established by the Blessed One, the Great Being, the preeminent among men, through his accumulations of merit and wisdom consisting of the six elements.

Furthermore, it is not the case that in this human birth, which is otherwise characterized by evil karma, there can be no fixed rule for the Tathāgata regarding the bestowing of the fruit of Buddhahood;

for in this Mantra Vehicle, the Blessed Buddha has declared as follows: "Even those such as outcasts and bamboo-workers, even those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution, shall become Buddhas in this very life if they practice the conduct of mantra. Thus, the word of the Blessed One is true.

In this life, whatever fierce karma—such as the five acts of immediate retribution—was previously committed, that is destroyed in this Mantra Vehicle by means of the samādhi of the immutable bliss of Mahāmudrā. Then, so that no further adventitious unwholesome states may enter, one places the door-panels of the factors conducive to enlightenment—namely, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—at the gates through which the four Māras and other obstacles would otherwise enter the abode of the Vajra-Dharmodaya. Having accomplished Vajrasattva therein together with the Mahāmudrā, even those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution become attainers of the fruit of Buddhahood in this very life; such is the decree of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, it is not the consensus of the Tathāgata that those who have entered the Mantra Vehicle—even while committing fierce deeds such as the five acts of immediate retribution—shall obtain the fruit of Buddhahood in this very life.

Regarding this, the word of the Blessed One in all three vehicles is: "It is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end. Therefore, according to the Blessed One’s statement, it is the fixed rule of the Tathāgata that those who have entered the Mantra Vehicle do not obtain the fruit of Buddhahood even while committing sinful actions.
Thus it is said in the Vimalaprabhā: "Now, regarding this Mantra Vehicle, the Blessed One has spoken of the consumption of meat by yogins; that very act always constitutes the taking of life."
Sometimes destruction occurs through the taking of life;
if there were no consumer and no killer, then the taking of life would not exist for either the consumer or the killer.
Therefore, the taking of life occurs because of both the consumer and the killer.
In this regard, it is the command of the Tathāgata that the practitioner must perform the four equalities daily;

that is true. For what reason? Because [otherwise] one becomes guilty of taking life through the fault of signs (*nimitta-sāvadya*). Therefore, for that reason, the Blessed One has declared that for yogins, the signless (*animitta*) and blameless (*niravadya*) cow-pen meat (*gokula*) and so forth are edible.

In this world, in whatever place there is anything unedible or unsaleable to people—such as cow-pen meat and so forth—that which has died by its own karma, or was killed in battle, or was slain by its own fault through evil deeds such as being a thief—all that is edible for yogins.

The Tathāgata has said: "Meat that is not purchased with wealth, nor killed for sacrificial rites such as those for one's father and so forth, and which is done with a specific motive—that meat is to be eaten. Thus the Tathāgata has spoken. Now, regarding that which must be performed four times every day: one should daily prepare pills of mustard-seed size from five blameless cow-products and five [substances] such as *vairocana* for the purpose of observing the commitments (*samaya*). Alcohol and women are always blameless for meditation; they are taught according to the principle of non-attachment.
In the *Mūlatantra* as well, the Blessed One said: "For the sake of the gods' fear, protection, and the attainment of the threefold success, and for the purpose of sale,
a non-offending being was killed by the wicked and evil-doing ones who were difficult to subdue."
That meat of his is blameworthy when it is purchased, eaten, or sought after; however,
that very same meat is blameless when it has fallen into one's bowl without being requested.
It is better for the meat of a single living being to be eaten by many, than for the meat of many living beings to be eaten by a single person.
One who is engaged in yoga should eat, having truly generated compassion with a non-conceptual mind; for it must indeed be blameless and nothing else.
For the destruction of those who seize families, the Vajrī, the seer of reality, has declared that food, drink, and association with the unwholesome should always be provided.

Thus, according to the sequence thus stated, this King of Tantras bestows the fruit of Buddhahood upon those who are free from restrictive observances (*niyama*). "Bestowing the fruit of Buddhahood" means that it grants Buddhahood—namely, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), knowledge of the aspects of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the majestic qualities such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). It is so called because it gives these.
Regarding "the abode of great bliss" (*mahāsukhāvāsa*):

the abode of great bliss is the *dharmadhātu*, characterized by space, unmixed, the source of phenomena, transcending worldly analogies, and all-pervadingly auspicious. This abode of great bliss exists within the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajra Realm of the Supreme Primordial Buddha; it is without parts, where knowledge and the object of knowledge have become a single unified mass; it is indivisible, impenetrable, and characterized as the realm of all aspects, comparable to a mirror and a prognostic image.

In that great maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu, one situated upon the vajra-siṃhāsana— the vajra-siṃhāsana which consists of the maṇḍalas of moon, sun, and fire, which is indestructible and indivisible, or which is the letter *E* or the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*)— is established upon that vajra-siṃhāsana.

[In the section on] the *Tantraniyamoddeśa* [in the chapter on] the *āsana*: the syllable *vaṃ* consists of the nature of body, speech, mind, and gnosis; by him who is seated upon the vajra-lion throne, surrounded by a host of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Krodharājas, gods, nāgas, deities, and goddesses—thus [it is said].

The Buddhas are Akṣobhya and others; the Bodhisattvas are Samantabhadra and others; the Wrathful Kings are Ullīṣa (Uṣṇīṣa) and others; the Gods are Īśvara and others; the Nāgas are Ananta and others; the Goddesses are Vajradhātvīśvarī and others, Dharmadhātu and others, Atinīlā and others, Carcikā and others, Gaurī and others, Śvānāsyā and others. A "host" (*gaṇa*) is a collection of these; surrounded by that is "surrounded by a host of gods and goddesses. By that [phrase] "surrounded by a host of gods and goddesses," it is meant "by him whose lotus-feet are worshipped by the three realms."

The triple world consists of the realms of desire, form, and formlessness; he whose lotus-feet are saluted by that [triple world] is "he whose lotus-feet are saluted by the triple world. By that "one whose lotus-feet are saluted by the triple world," it is meant "the universal monarch of the triple world"—that is, he who simultaneously turns the wheel of Dharma within the triple world is the universal monarch of the triple world; by him, the universal monarch of the triple world.
"By the Paramādibuddha" means:

the Paramādibuddha is characterized by the complete awakening through the net of illusion consisting of the five aspects and twenty aspects in a single moment, which is supreme immutable bliss; he is the *ādi-buddha* (primordial Buddha) because he is supreme (*parama*), thus [he is] the Paramādibuddha. "By that Paramādibuddha" refers to him who is without lineage (*niranvaya*).

The *anvaya* is the phenomenon (*dharma*) consisting of wisdom and method, characterized by the apprehended and the apprehender; that *anvaya* has been discarded by him, thus he is "without *anvaya*" (*niranvaya*).

By means of that "one without *anvaya," namely the Blessed One Kālacakra—"Kāla" being the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*) protection of great bliss (*mahāsukha*)—he is Kālacakra, whose body is the wheel (*cakra*) of the aggregates, elements, and so forth, which has been uprooted and rendered free from obscurations.
Furthermore: by each individual syllable—by the letter *ka* [is meant] the cause in tranquility; from the letter *la* comes dissolution (*laya*) here indeed;
from the letter *ca* [comes the restraint] of the flickering mind; and from the letter *ṛ* through the binding of the sequence.
The sequential order (*krama*) consists of the emission of the drops (*bindu*) of the body and so forth; their binding through innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) is the Blessed One Kālacakra.

He is "Blessed" (*bhagavān*) because he has shattered the Māras and the afflictions (*kleśa*), and because he possesses the collection of qualities such as omniscience and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). Since he possesses this *bhaga*, he is the Blessed One; thus, [he is called] the Blessed One Kālacakra.
Regarding the phrase "requested by Sucandra":

he is *Sucandra* because he is both beautiful (*su*) and like the moon (*candra*). He has become the listener for all the Tathāgatas; being Vajrendu-vimalaprabha (Stainless Radiance of the Vajra-Moon), he is the ear of all the Tathāgatas because he collects the dharmas spoken by the Tathāgatas through the various languages of all sentient beings;
he is the Lord of Secrets (*Guhyādhipati*).

The *Guhyaka* is the Vajrayāna, which is superior to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; he is the Lord of Secrets (*Guhyādhipati*) as the presiding compiler of that [Yāna]. Likewise, according to external worldly convention, by the word "secret" (*guhya*) are meant the *yakṣas*, and he is their lord, the Lord of the Secret Ones (*Guhyakādhipati*). In the external world, the word "Aḍaka" refers to a multitude of corpses whose life-force has perished; because that [multitude] exists in this place, it is called Aḍakavatī, the cremation ground. In that place, there are great *yakṣas* who harass sentient beings and create manifold obstacles; he is the slayer of them.
"A resident of Aḍakavatī" means that, like a lord of deer in a forest, he is a great lord of yakṣas residing in Aḍakavatī.

Internally, "aḍaka" refers to the cessation of twenty-one thousand six hundred and thirty-six inhalations and exhalations; since this [cessation] exists in her, she is the Dharmameghā stage. One who resides on that stage is a "resident of Aḍakavatī."

The slayer of the yakṣas— the obstacles of Māra, the afflictions, the knowable, and the meditative attainments— and the lord of yakṣas who sets forth the Dharma for all sentient beings through the individual languages [of each] by means of the lion’s roar of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; by him, Vajrapāṇi, in his emanation body,
having been requested by King Sucandra— thus it is said.
Oṣṇīṣa Carcikā is called by the secret name Vajrendu; O Sucandra, at the request of the Yakṣīs,
it is known as the Paramādibuddha.

"Twelve thousand" refers to a collection of three hundred and eighty-four thousand syllables; because it consists of thirty-two-syllable *anuṣṭubh* verses, it is called "the twelve-thousand [verse]" and is "without remainder.
Thus, in this chapter on the teaching and summary of the *tantra*, it is stated that the Mantrayāna was taught by all the Tathāgatas through these words of request for the *Nāmasaṅgīti*.
Regarding the statement, "In this assembly, in the presence of Dīpaṅkara and Śākyamuni, the mantra vehicle was not taught by any Tathāgata," this means that at that time and on that occasion—

that is, during the period of teaching the Dharma in the Noble Land— it was not taught to the assembly in the Noble Land because of the disposition of sentient beings who were unfit due to their pride in the four castes;
it does not mean, however, that it was not taught at another time, in another land, or to another assembly in a world-system.

Therefore, according to the word of the Tathāgata, all Tathāgatas are the teachers of the three vehicles; otherwise, there would be an absence of omniscience because they would not be the teachers of the Vajrayāna.

Thus, all Tathāgatas are the teachers of the three vehicles and the teachers of the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma, according to the dispositions of sentient beings. Therefore, [this work] is embraced by the *Nāmasaṅgīti*, which serves as a witness to the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) of Vajradhara.
Regarding the statement "it is the witness of the vajra-word in all the kings of tantras":

here, in this Vajrayāna, the vajra-word is concealed within all the kings of tantras according to the dispositions of sentient beings. This is because of the Tathāgata’s own words: "That fourth is again likewise.
Thus, the fourth is not the third; for it is called "the fourth" and it is called "that again is likewise."
That very thing is the wisdom-knowledge (prajñājñāna), which is therefore the fourth [empowerment] according to the word of the Blessed One.
Regarding the "vajra-word" being secret: in all the kings of tantras, the vajra-word is not made manifest; it is to be understood through the sequence of the guru's oral lineage.
"A tantra is to be understood by means of another tantra," according to the word of the Tathāgata.
Here, in the Mantra system, the vajra-word is twofold: one is by way of worldly convention (*saṃvṛti*), and the second is from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

Of these two, the vajra-word by way of worldly convention bestows the accomplishment of the *samaya* in rites such as killing; whereas the vajra-word by way of ultimate truth is that fourth [empowerment], which furthermore bestows the fruit of the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā.
Therefore, in this *Ādibuddha*, the Vajra-word has been revealed by the Blessed One through brief statements, detailed explanations, and further elucidations.
For the very purpose of its realization, the path of the signs beginning with smoke—the meditation on Mahāmudrā—has been revealed.
"Having made the mind one-pointed upon the void, one should examine it for one day."

Therefore, according to the word of the Blessed One, in the *Paramādibuddha*, the vajra-word regarding the path of meditating on Mahāmudrā—beginning with smoke and so forth—is manifest; it has not come down through the lineage of the gurus, nor is it established by the command of a guru.
There is direct evidence for this path, because of the Blessed One’s statement: "One should examine [it] for one day, even if one is an Arhat.
In this context, there is no other means of accomplishment, such as mantras and the like, apart from the signs beginning with smoke, which must be examined by the yogin within a single day.
The sign (*nimitta*) is also threefold: the initial sign, the intermediate sign, and the final sign.
The initial sign is the path of smoke and so forth; it is the attainment of the protection of the manifestation of the universe through the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*).

The intermediate sign is the attainment of the first stage (*bhūmi*) through eighteen hundred moments of the supreme immutable (*paramākṣara*), the perception of the objects not previously seen by means of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), and the acquisition of worldly accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*).

The signless (*animitta*)—which is the inner sign (*antanimitta*)—is Buddhahood and the state of holding the Vajra; it is the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā through the attainment of the twelve and ten stages (*bhūmi*) by means of twenty-one thousand six hundred supreme unchanging moments (*paramākṣarakṣaṇa*). This, beginning with the "Vajra Word" (*vajrapada*), was taught by the Blessed One in the *Paramādibuddha*, the King of Tantras, preceded by signs and made manifest.
Therefore, among all the Kings of Tantras, this Tantra is the witness to the Vajra Words for those who seek other tantras.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it says: "The opening of the jewel-casket of the Buddha" means that the jewel of the Buddha is the supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*), and the casket is the lotus of the vajra-jewel; thus, it is the "opening of the jewel-casket of the Buddha. That by which this is opened is the King of Tantras; therefore, it is called "the opening of the jewel-casket of the Buddha.
It is said to be "based on the mundane and supramundane truths":
the mundane truth consists of the meditation on the conceptualized maṇḍala-circle and the accomplishment of mundane siddhis through the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*).

The supramundane truth is the accomplishment of the *mahāmudrā* siddhi through the signs of smoke and so forth, by means of non-conceptual mind in the stage of completion (*utpannakrama*). This stage of completion is the innate (*sahaja*), non-conceptual, and omniform, being devoid of conceptualization regarding faces, arms, colors, and shapes.
"Based on these two truths" means based on the mundane and supramundane truths, because of the vision of the two paths.
"Purified by the four vajras" refers to the fourfold perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*).

The single-moment awakening (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodhi*), the five-aspect awakening (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*), the twenty-aspect awakening (*viṃśatyākārābhisambodhi*), and the illusion-net awakening (*māyājālābhisambodhi*). Purified by these four awakenings—through the process of birth from a womb and the process of generating the images of smoke and so forth—it is thus purified by the four awakenings. It reveals the path to the accomplishment of the four bodies (*catuḥkāya*), the six families (*ṣaṭkula*), the twelve truths (*dvādaśasatya*), the sixteen realities (*ṣoḍaśatattva*), the sixteen emptinesses (*ṣoḍaśaśūnyatā*), the sixteen compassions (*ṣoḍaśakaruṇā*), and the mundane, supramundane, consecration (*abhiṣeka*), action (*karman*), wisdom (*jñāna*), and great seal (*mahāmudrā*) siddhis. These are the four bodies.
The pure, enjoyment, and emanation [bodies] are characterized by the states of deep sleep, dream, and waking for one born from a womb;
and these are free from obscurations for the Buddhas.
These are the six families.

Imperishable bliss is the gnosis element (*jñānadhātu*); consciousness is the space element (*ākāśadhātu*); mental formations are the wind element (*vāyudhātu*); sensation is the fire element (*tejodhātu*); perception is the water element (*toyadhātu*); and form is the earth element (*pṛthvīdhātu*). These are with obscuration for those born from a womb, but without obscuration for Buddhas. The twelve truths are as follows:

ignorance, mental formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death. These twelve truths are with obscuration for those born from a womb, but without obscuration for Buddhas.

Due to the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) through the division of the twelve transits (*saṃkrānti*), those of those born from a womb possess veils (*sāvaraṇa*); for the Buddhas, they are without veils (*nirāvaraṇa*), because of the cessation of the twelve links [of dependent origination].
Thus, there are sixteen principles (*tattva*).

The Emanation Body (nirmāṇakāya), Emanation Speech (nirmāṇavāk), Emanation Mind (nirmāṇacitta), and Emanation Wisdom (nirmāṇajñāna); the Enjoyment [Body] (sambhoga), Enjoyment Speech (sambhogavāk), Enjoyment Mind (sambhogacitta), and Enjoyment Wisdom (sambhogajñāna); the Dharma Body (dharmakāya), Dharma Speech (dharmavāk), Dharma Mind (dharmacitta), and Dharma Wisdom (dharmajñāna); and the Innate Body (sahajakāya), Innate Speech (sahajavāk), Innate Mind (sahajacitta), and Innate Wisdom (sahajajñāna)—this is the summary of the teaching on the *Ānanda*, *Parama*, and *Virama* tantras. These are the sixteen realities according to the divisions of the Innate (*sahaja*). For those born from a womb, these sixteen are with obscurations because they involve the emission of half-and-half drops; for Buddhas, they are without obscurations because they hold the sixteen half-and-half drops.
The sixteenfold emptiness is the dark fortnight, the sun, and wisdom; the sixteenfold compassion is—
The white fortnight and the moon are skillful means (*upāya*).
There are three divisions of emptiness (*śūnyatā*): emptiness, great emptiness, and ultimate emptiness.
Among these, emptiness is the emptiness of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), corresponding to the five lunar dates beginning with the first day of the dark fortnight.
Great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) is the emptiness of the five elements (*dhātu*); these are the five lunar days beginning with the sixth.
Ultimate emptiness (*paramārthaśūnyatā*) is the emptiness of the five sense faculties (*indriya*); these are the five lunar days beginning with the eleventh.
Thus, the fifteen lunar days constitute the fifteen emptinesses, ending with the new moon (*amā*).
Between the entry into the first day of the waxing moon that ends in the new moon and the [subsequent] entry, there is the sixteenth, which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*) in all its aspects.

Likewise, compassion (*karuṇā*) is threefold: that which has sentient beings as its object (*sattvālambanī*), that which has phenomena as its object (*dharmālambanī*), and that which is objectless (*anālambanī*).
Among these, that which has sentient beings as its object consists of the five lunar days beginning with the first day of the waxing moon.
The five lunar days beginning with the sixth are *dharmāvalambinī* (supported by phenomena).
The five lunar days beginning with the eleventh, up to the full moon (*pūrṇimā*), are *anāvalambinī* (unsupported).
Between the end of the full moon and the entry into the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapratipat*), there is the sixteenth [day], which is *karuṇā* (compassion).
The non-duality (*akaitva*) of these two is the subject matter, consisting of the sixteen emptinesses and the sixteen compassions; it is that which is expressed by the [following] designations.
Regarding the "worldly and supramundane consecrations" (*laukikalokottarābhiṣeka*):
first, the worldly ones are water, crown, ribbon, vajra-bell, great vow, name, permission, vase, secret, wisdom, and gnosis.

For those born from a womb, according to worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*), there are ten initiations (*abhiṣeka*); the eleventh, which is supramundane (*lokottara*), is for the sake of purifying the body, speech, mind, gnosis, elements, aggregates, sense bases, the organs of action, and so forth. Fourthly, because it is established by the rule that "that again is such," the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*)—characterized by the supreme unchanging gnosis (*paramākṣarajñāna*)—is the mouth of the Guru, the purifier through the removal of the obscurations of body, speech, and so on.
This is the accomplishment of the Action Seal (*karmamudrā*), the Gnosis Seal (*jñānamudrā*), and the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*).
The Action Seal possesses breasts and hair.

The wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*) is that imagined by one’s own mind; the great seal (*mahāmudrā*) is free from conceptual construction and has the nature of a reflection. Their accomplishment is threefold: the accomplishment of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) belongs to the desire realm; the accomplishment of the wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*) belongs to the form realm and is characterized by the existence of the state of form; and the accomplishment of the great seal (*mahāmudrā*) is devoid of both existence and non-existence and is endowed with the excellence of all aspects. This *Paramādibuddha* is the illuminator of the mundane and supramundane paths for these four bodies and so forth.

In the manner thus described, [this teaching], consisting of five chapters on the world-system, the inner self, consecration, means of achievement, and gnosis—or alternatively, consisting of five kalpas—was taught for the sake of all beings, such as humans and others, to attain the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha. "Sam" means in the correct manner, and not in the hidden manner of the *vajrapada*. Following this, from the *Paramādibuddha*, there was the prophecy of Mañjuśrī by the Tathāgata to compile the *Laghutantra*, as well as my own prophecy to compose the commentary (*ṭīkā*), and the prophecy for Yamāntaka and the others to teach the tantra.

And in the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is stated: "In the future time, for the sake of those to be converted among the Brahmin seers (*brahmarṣi*), and so that all sentient beings dwelling in the sixty million villages beginning with the realm of Sambhala may attain the path of the Mahāyāna, Mañjuśrī was prophesied by the Tathāgata to compile the *Laghutantra* from the twelve-thousand-verse *Paramādibuddha*, for the sake of those to be converted among the three hundred and fifty million Brahmin seers dwelling in the village of Kalāpa in the future time."

I, Lokeśvara, have also been prophesied to compose a commentary on the *Laghutantra*; furthermore, twenty-three other Krodharāja Bodhisattvas have been prophesied to teach the *Laghutantra* through their emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) for the sake of all sentient beings dwelling in the ninety-six million villages, so that they may attain the path of the Mahāyāna.

"The path of the Mahāyāna" refers to the vase, secret, wisdom, and gnosis initiations within the Vajra family of Mañjuśrī; "for the attainment of that" means "for the attainment of the path of the Great Vajrayāna."
Therefore, through the vase, secret, and wisdom-knowledge empowerments (*kalaśa-guhya-prajñājñānābhiṣeka*), all castes become a single *kalka*.
One who possesses that *kalka* is a *kalkī*; his lineage is the *kalkigotra*.
Through the empowerment of the Vajra family, this applies to all practitioners of mantra (*mantrin*); such is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Thus, Mañjuśrī, this Kalkī Yaśas has been prophesied; in the lineage of this Yaśas, I, Lokeśvara, have been prophesied as the second Kalkī in the world.

Thus, in this sequential order, there are the ten wrathful kings beginning with Yamāntaka, and the thirteen bodhisattvas beginning with Kṣitigarbha; these thirteen bodhisattvas are prophesied to appear in the intervals between the wrathful kings such as Yamāntaka. As emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), they shall be kings residing in ninety-six million villages, promoters of the Tathāgata’s Dharma for all sentient beings, destroyers of the evil laws of barbarians and others, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, and perfected in the qualities of sovereignty such as the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*).

Henceforth, from the *Ādibuddha*, [the topics] are the prophecy for Mañjuśrī regarding the compilation of the *Laghutantra*, the commissioning of me to compose the commentary (*ṭīkā*), and the teaching of the Dharma by Yamāntaka and the others. Thus ends the second section, which is the summary of the Blessed One’s teaching of the tantra after having examined the subject matter (*abhidheya*), the expression (*abhidhāna*), the relationship (*sambandha*), and the purpose (*prayojana*) and the purpose of the purpose (*prayojanaprayojana*), in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja* following the *Mūlatantra*. 2.

The introduction concerning the purpose, the teacher, the requester, and the relationship between the Root Tantra and the Condensed Tantra has been stated. Now, however, the relationship between the teacher and the requester is explained here.
At some point, there may be a statement from one who has not heard the commentaries on the preceding and subsequent tantras.

Here, in this Vajrayāna, it is indeed well known that the great Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the great yakṣas and resident of Aḍakavatī, was the one who requested [the teachings] from the Tathāgata and the compiler of the scriptures. How is it, then, that King Sucandra—the sovereign of the village of Kalāpa in the land of Sambhala, born from the womb of Queen Vijayā—becomes the requester? It is not heard in some other tantras, nor has he been prophesied [therein]. Is there not a contradiction regarding the mutual relationship between the teacher and the requester? To this, it is said:
For in this case, whatever someone might say—that in the Mantra system there is no one born from the womb who acts as the requester of the Tathāgata—is not so;
[as stated in] the chapter on "The Description of the Connection between the Teacher and the Requester in the Root Tantra and the Abridged Tantra": Why?
Because even the Blessed One was born from a womb.

In this system of Mantra, if one born from a womb were not the requester of the Tathāgata nor the compiler [of his teachings], then Śākyamuni—the omniscient teacher born from the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā in the womb of King Śuddhodana of the Śākya clan—would not exist; for he was born from a womb.

Now, as for the statement that "first he performed the destruction of Māra, then enlightenment was produced, and thereafter he became the omniscient teacher of Dharma; subsequently, once he had passed into *parinirvāṇa*, there was no further entry into a womb"—this is a supreme contradiction, because that which is not established by itself cannot serve as a proof for another.
Here, at the beginning, since there is no state of being old, no one among gods, asuras, or humans performs the destruction of Māra.
Even the one who has attained initial perfect enlightenment does not perform it, because of the absence of all obscurations.
And he does not act simultaneously; for at the moment when Māra exists, at that very moment there would be no Buddhahood, because the mind is still possessed of obscurations.
At the moment when Buddhahood exists, at that very moment Māra is absent, because the mind is free from obscurations.

Furthermore, in this land of action (*karmabhūmi*), apart from the Blessed One, no one else born from a woman’s womb possesses the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*), the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), the thirty-two circles of the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft, or the six superknowledges (*abhijñā*). Therefore, that which is called "Māra" is the mind of cyclic existence (*saṃsāracitta*) of sentient beings, defiled by habitual tendencies (*vāsanāmala*); whereas that which is called "Buddhahood" (*buddhatva*) is the mind free from the habitual tendencies of cyclic existence.
And so the Blessed One said in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: "There is that mind which is a non-mind" (*asti tac cittaṃ yac cittam acittam*) (Aṣṭasāhasrikā, p. 3).
That very [mind] is naturally luminous when free from the latencies of saṃsāra; therefore, Māra is the defiled mind, and the Buddha is the stainless mind.
Here, the defeat of Māra externally by the Buddha is, for sentient beings, a manifestation of their own minds, like a dream.
In ultimate reality, the heart of the Tathāgata will be explained in detail in the fifth chapter.

In this saṃsāra, the entry of noble Buddhas and Bodhisattvas into saṃsāra for the sake of sentient beings is inexpressible [to those still wandering]. It was said by the messengers of Yama and King Yama at the time of my, Lokeśvara’s, entering hell for the sake of sentient beings: “We bow to those Buddhas who, though liberated from the bonds of existence, take up existence for the sake of sentient beings; who, out of compassion, do not abandon the fruit of karma even when its time has come, being the ones who deliver the message of the meaning of emptiness; whose mental impurities have been burnt away by the fire of right perception, who are always moist with perfect compassion, and who delight in the welfare of sentient beings while acting beyond the reach of discursive thought. Thus it is said.
Therefore, regarding the welfare of sentient beings, the entry into a womb or the descent into hell by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas cannot be conceptualized by ordinary people.

Even a single Bodhisattva—who has emerged through the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), is a master of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and has attained the ten masteries (*vaśitā*)—teaches the Dharma of a Bodhisattva to those beings who are to be disciplined by a Bodhisattva through manifold emanation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) throughout a thousandfold great thousandfold world-system (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*); yet that Great Bodhisattva is not manifold.

Thus, the Buddha, the Blessed One—by the power of his former vows, having fulfilled the accumulations of merit and wisdom, and being endowed with the qualities of sovereignty such as the four fearlessnesses—resides in his buddha-field within the thousand-millionfold world-systems. Through infinite and boundless activities of illusory emanations that are free from obscuration, and through infinite and boundless voices produced by infinite and boundless sentient beings who request them, he teaches the mundane and supramundane Dharma in the language of the Omniscient One, which proceeds according to the sounds of all sentient beings.
It is not the case that there are many omniscient ones.

Just as a certain illusory person (*māyāpuruṣa*) manifests many illusory forms, and by means of those manifested forms uproots trees and even shakes the peaks of mountains, and like Mahādeva or Viṣṇu, binds beings such as Devadatta and others—for that illusory person is not manifold—so too, through the illusory emanation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, there is the welfare of sentient beings within the three realms of existence.

Therefore, for the sake of teaching the mundane and supramundane Dharma to all sentient beings, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was previously born as Prince Siddhārtha in the Śākya clan of the noble land of Lumbinī from the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā, the consort of King Śuddhodana; he was a master of the twelve stages, a holder of the Great Māyā, a learned one, and a great magician of Māyā-indrajāla.
Furthermore, in the land of Sambhala, in the village of Kalāpa, he was born from the womb of Queen Vijayā as Vajrapāṇi Sucandra, a master of the ten stages.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, was born in the Buddha-field for the purpose of teaching the mundane and supramundane Dharma; he is one who has directly realized the twelve stages (*bhūmi*).

To the north of the Śītā River, for the sake of those to be converted by Sucandra who dwell in ninety-six million villages, there was King Sucandra, who was the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, so that they might attain the path of the Perfectly Awakened One through the *Paramādibuddha-tantrarāja*.

The relationship between these two—the Buddha as teacher and the Bodhisattva as petitioner—is established through emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) or enjoyment bodies (*sambhogakāya*), without contradiction between earlier and later [teachings].
By that emanated body, Vajrapāṇi, for the sake of accomplishing the mundane and supramundane siddhis of all sentient beings, King Sucandra requested the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata, too, having perceived the imminent fitness and purity of mind of the inhabitants of the ninety-six million villages in the lands of Śambhala and elsewhere north of the Śītā River, taught the Paramādibuddha in twelve thousand verses, which reveals the vajra-word while being free from the concealment of the vajra-word.

From this King of Tantras consisting of twelve thousand verses, for the purpose of composing a shorter tantra and for the teaching of the Root King of Tantras, the Tathāgata—having seen the ripening of one and a half koṭis of Brahmin seers in a future time, as well as those dwelling in ninety-six koṭis of villages—prophesied Mañjuśrī as Yaśaḥ Kalkī by means of the Vajra-family initiation, for the sake of making all castes into a single mass (*ekakalka*).
I too, the commentator Puṇḍarīka, have been prophesied as the second Kalkī.
Therefore, after me, Yamāntaka and the others were prophesied.
Regarding this, the Blessed One said: "Six hundred years from the first year, there will be one named Sambhala;
for the sake of maturing the sages, Mañjughoṣa shall become King Yaśas."
His consort is the Great Goddess Tārā, and his son is Lokeśvara, who holds a lotus.

O Sucandra, in your lineage there shall be one eloquent in speech born of the Vajra family; by him, through the single *kalka* (mixture) of the four castes, he shall be a Kalkin of the Vajra clan, yet not by means of the Brahmin caste. Thus was this teaching of the Dharma heard by me from this sage.
There will be the claim that he is not omniscient because of what has been heard from others.
In whatever manner the maturation of sentient beings may be achieved,
in that very manner one should perform the teaching of the Dharma.
A practitioner of yoga diligently grasps the Dharma through both correct words and corrupt words.

When the subject matter has already been obtained through the word "region" (*deśa*), what is the purpose of the word "treatise" (*śāstra*) therein? [The answer is: It is that which is devoid of the non-elucidation of the vajra-words. Bho: From this year (*adyābdāt*). Gha: That (*tat*). Ka, Ca, Bho: Not (*na*). Kha: By name (*nāma*). Bho: The summary of the relationship between the teacher, the requester, the root-tantra, and the abbreviated tantra. Just as for a jewel in the earth there are various distinct names spoken according to region after region, yet there is no difference in the jewel itself anywhere.
Thus, for my pure Dharma, various compilers have proclaimed various designations individually, according to the inclinations of sentient beings.

Therefore, this [work] of mine, consisting of one hundred and thirty verses in the *sragdharā* meter, is considered by me to be the *Śrītantra*, which contains the essential meaning in a concise form, beginning with the words "O Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*).
The King of Speakers will teach this work, complete in five chapters;
he is the compiler and the commentator, the bearer of the white lotus.
In this tantra, Candra is the illuminator of the path of the Buddhas for the lineages of the sages and others;
he is Sureśvara, Tejī, Somadatta, and Sureśvara.
Viśvamūrti, Sureśāna, Yaśas, Puṇḍarīka, and Sūryaprabha were the kings in succession; Vighnaśakra was created as the last.
Vajrapāṇi, you are Sucandra, Kṣitigarbha, Yamāntaka,
Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, Jambhaka, and Mānaka, in sequence.
Khagarbha and Mañjughoṣa are the Lords of the World in their respective order;
between them are the ten wrathful deities, beginning with Yamāntaka, as well as the bodhisattvas.
In the Kalki lineage, thirteen others will arise in succession:
Yaśas, Kalkī, Gotra, and then Kalkī Puṇḍarīka.
Bhadrakalkī is the third, and Vijaya is the fourth;
Sumindra (or Sumitra) and Raktapāṇi, and Viṣṇugupta is the seventh.
Arkakīrti, Subhadra, Samudravijaya, Aja, Kalkī as the twelfth sun, Viśvarūpa, and Śaśiprabha.
Ananta, Mahīpāla, Śrīpāla, Harivikrama,
Mahābala, Aniruddha, Narasiṃha, and Maheśvara.

— Puṇḍarīka [is] white-bodied (kha). The Tibetan reading for this is somewhat different: "The King of the White [Clan] is Mahīprabha; he is an emanation of the obstructing enemy. 4. ka. *saprabhaḥ*; bho. *bdun pa* (*saptamaḥ*).
5. ka. *dhvajaḥ*; bho. *rgyal dka'* (*aja*). In the *Vimalaprabhā* commentary on the verse of the first chapter, *ajakalkī* appears, whose Tibetan translation is *rig ldan rgyal dka'* (*vidvān aja*).
6. Kha. Malo;
in the *Vimalaprabhā*, Anantavijaya will be the Kalkī Yaśas, and after him, his son, the Great Wheel-turner Raudrakalkī, will come to be.
An eloquent speaker who brought an end to the barbarian religion through his supreme meditative absorption.
Because you will be the eloquent teacher for Sūryaratha and the others,
therefore, Sucandra, you shall be the compiler of the Root Tantra.
In this regard, you alone are the commentator and the ripener of sentient beings;
in the *Laghu-tantra*, Mañjughoṣa himself is the commentator, bearing the lotus.

Thus, in the *Lokadhātu-mūlatantra*, according to the stated sequence, the Bodhisattvas and the Wrathful Kings were prophesied; likewise, the Tathāgata prophesied that the universal monarchs would be the teachers of the mantra for the ninety-six million villages.

Therefore, by the decree of the Tathāgata, King Sucandra had the twelve-thousand-verse *Mūlatantrarāja* and its sixty-thousand-verse commentary written in books using the various local languages of regions such as Sambhala, and he revealed them to the inhabitants of the ninety-six million villages.
Those beings who were devoted to this very [teaching] heard it, recited it, and retained it in their own minds, and they also revealed it extensively to others.

Therefore, in the second year after the time of the Tantra’s teaching, having displayed the miraculous power of the maṇḍala-circle, he departed from that place with his emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) and went to the realm of enjoyment (saṃbhoga), for the sake of the accomplishment of sentient beings. After that, the teaching of the Tantra was performed by Sureśvara for a hundred years; likewise by Tejin, Somadatta, Sureśvara, Viśvamūrti, and Sureśāna.

Within the womb of Viśvamātādevī, Mañjuśrī Yaśorāja became the emanation-body (*nirmitakāya*) of this Lord of Gods, Khagarbha, and he remained as a teacher of the Dharma upon that lion-throne of the Bodhisattva for a hundred years.

Then, when those hundred years were complete, through the power of the Tathāgata’s prophecy and empowerment, and perceiving that the time had come to ripen the sages, King Yaśas—knowing by the power of his five super-knowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) that they had attained the true path and desiring to grant them the ascetic observances (*niyama*)—issued an invitation to them all.

To the south of Kalāpagrāma is the Malaya garden, twelve yojanas in length and equal in size to Kalāpagrāma. To its east is the Upamānasaras lake, twelve yojanas in length; to the west is the Puṇḍarīkasaras lake, of the same dimensions. Between these two lies the Malaya garden.

In the center of the Malayodyāna park, King Sucandra constructed the mandala-circle of the Blessed One Kālacakra, consisting of deities and goddesses fashioned from the five precious gems; it was square, measuring four hundred cubits in length.
On the exterior, the Body Mandala was square, with four gates, four archways, adorned with eight cremation grounds, and surrounded by five walls.
On the outside, it was adorned with the four circles of earth and the other elements and a vajra-fence; extending to the edge of the vajra-fence, it measured eight hundred cubits in length.
In the center, measuring half the size of the body-maṇḍala, is the speech-maṇḍala; it is square, with four gates, adorned with four archways, and surrounded by five walls.
Measuring half the size of the speech-maṇḍala is the mind-maṇḍala; it is square, with four gates and four archways.

[In this] chapter: The summary of the relationship between the Teacher, the requester, the Root Tantra, and the Abridged Tantra; [the mandala] is adorned and encircled three times by walls.
The wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*) is half of that, adorned with sixteen pillars;
half of that again is the eight-petaled lotus, and the pericarp is one-third of the lotus.
Thus, the maṇḍalas of body, speech, and mind are complete in all their characteristics and endowed with necklaces and half-necklaces.
[The pavilion] is adorned with jeweled bands, railings, and *vakulī* trees, and is resplendent with mirrors, half-moons, and bells.

In this maṇḍala-hall consisting of three circles, on the full moon day of the month of Phālguna, King Yaśas gave a command to three and a half crores of Brahmanical seers (*brahmarṣi*), headed by Sūryaratha: "O Sūryaratha and other Brahmanical seers, listen! My word brings about the wealth of omniscience.
On the full moon day of Caitra, I shall bestow instruction upon you who observe the rules of the Vedas and the Smṛtis."
"Therefore, you must set aside those Brahmins of noble lineage from various other lands and present them to me.

Following these words, as they were being scrutinized according to their conduct in various regions, they were all found to have fallen away due to mutual contradictions regarding their local customs: namely, the consumption of the flesh of goats and buffaloes by followers of the Kāpālikas, the drinking of intoxicants, and the taking of [sexual relations with] mothers and other [forbidden kin].
Seeing their opposition in this way, King Yaśas said: "I must enter here into this maṇḍala-hall of the Blessed One Kālacakra, and I shall bestow upon you the mundane and supramundane initiations.
Furthermore, by my command, you must partake of food and drink together with my family, and there must be matrimonial alliances.
Now, if you do not carry out my command, then leaving our ninety-six million villages, go wherever it pleases you."

Otherwise, when eight hundred years have passed, your sons, grandsons, and others will engage in the Mleccha religion and will teach the Mleccha religion in the ninety-six great regions, such as Sambhala and others.

Having killed the animal at the neck with a knife while reciting the *mleccha* deity-mantra "Viṣmillāha," they will then eat the meat of those slaughtered animals according to their own deity-mantras. They will declare the meat of animals that have died through their own [natural] actions to be unfit for consumption; yet even that practice shall be authoritative for you, based on the Smṛti statement: "Animals were created for sacrifice" (*yāgārthāḥ paśavaḥ*). Thus, there is no difference between the dharma of the *mlecchas* and the Vedic dharma regarding the taking of life.

Therefore, in your lineage, sons, grandsons, and others, having witnessed the power of those Mlecchas, will themselves become Mlecchas when eight hundred years have passed in the future—at which time they will appear as an incarnation of the god Māra in battle.

Once those Mlecchas have arisen, even all the four castes and others residing in the ninety-six crores of villages will become Mlecchas, according to the words of the Brahmanical Rishis: "The path is that by which the great men have gone" (*Mahābhārata*, *Vanaparva*, *Anuśāsana-parva*, Chapter on Brahmā).

In this regard, even in the Mleccha dharma and the Vedic dharma, the taking of life must be performed for the sake of the deities and ancestors; and likewise in the Kṣatriya dharma, it is said [in the Yājñavalkya-smṛti, Ācārādhyāya]: "Having gratified the ancestors and the gods, one who eats meat does not partake in fault," according to the words of the Brāhmaṇas; and likewise: "I see no fault therein for one who, being wicked, should act wickedly.

In this very world-realm (*lokadhātu*), having taken the Vedic Dharma as their authority, they will embrace the Mleccha Dharma;
for that reason, I have given you this injunction so that the Mleccha Dharma does not enter [this land] in the future. Therefore, you must carry out my command.

When these words were spoken by Yaśas, together with the royal command and the accompanying order for punishment, the Brahman-sages spoke to Sūryaratha as if lightning had struck their heads: "O Sūryaratha, inform King Yaśas that we shall not abandon the Vedic dharma of our caste for the sake of engaging in the religious practices of the consecration of the Vajra lineage.
Therefore, by your command, we shall go to the excellent land of the Āryas, to the region south of the Śītā and Himavat mountains, within the island of Laṅkā."

By the word of those brahmin seers, Sūryaratha makes this request to you, O King of Men: "O Great King of Kings, Supreme Lord, you who are fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics, the ornament of the Śākya clan, O Most Compassionate One, show us mercy! Since we are engaged in wholesome deeds, we must certainly carry out your command; therefore, we shall not proceed with the consecration of the Vajra family."
"By your command, we shall go to the noble land situated to the south of the Śītā River, on the Himavat mountains, in the midst of the island of Laṅkā.

Then, at the words of Sūryaratha, King Yaśas said: "May you depart quickly from the region of Sambhala, so that all beings dwelling in the ninety-six million villages to the north of the Śītā River may abandon the unwholesome paths of action, such as taking life, and through the empowerment of the Blessed Kālacakra, become attainers of the path of perfect knowledge."
By the command of King Yaśas, all these brahmin seers departed from Kalāpa village; on the tenth day, they entered the depths of the forest.

When they had entered the midst of the forest, King Yaśas, by means of his power of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), understood that through these brahmin seers (*brahmarṣi*) traveling to the Noble Land (*āryaviṣaya*), all the beings dwelling in the ninety-six million villages would develop hostile thoughts. He realized that for this reason—the fact that the path of perfect knowledge taught in the Vajrayāna was not present here—these seers, out of fear of King Śrī-Yaśas, had abandoned their own abodes and taken their families and belongings to go to the Noble Land.
Thinking that "all [people] desire liberation," people such as Kṣatriyas and others will become unfortunate, for they lack the capacity for the profound and vast Dharma due to their unworthy minds.
Thus, having understood the intentions within the minds of all people, Yaśonarendra entered the meditative absorption named "Deluding the Families of All Viṣṇus, Brahmās, and Rudras."

By that meditative absorption and through the power of the deities' empowerment, all those sages became deluded in that very forest; they were bound by the inhabitants of the forest, such as the *sara* and others, and brought back once more to the great maṇḍala house. Having been cast at the feet of King Yaśonarendra, they regained their senses and beheld King Yaśonarendra.

Seeing that very maṇḍala-hall in the Malaya garden, they were filled with wonder and spoke these words: "Aha! This is a great marvel! While we were unawakened in the great forest, by whom have we been brought to this great maṇḍala-hall? Upon hearing these words from the Brahman seers, Sāgaramati, who had assumed a manifested body as a minister of King Yaśas, said: "O Sūryaratha and you other Brahman seers, do not be filled with wonder."

This King Yaśorāja, from the *Dvīpāntarapaṭala*, is not some mere local person, but a certain great bodhisattva who, seeking to favor you, appeared through the empowerment of the Buddha. Therefore, having gone for refuge at his feet, make your request for the path to accomplish mundane and supramundane siddhis, as well as for the empowerment, in this *Ādibuddha-tantrarāja*.

Then, by virtue of those words of Sāgaramati and through the empowerment of the Buddha, the brahmin seers Sūryaratha and the others were awakened and spoke these words: “Excellent, excellent, Sāgaramati! Since our minds have been awakened by your speech, you should now go for refuge to the Three Jewels and make a request for the empowerments and the path for attaining mundane and supramundane accomplishments in the *Kālacakra-tantra-rāja*, so that all sentient beings may attain perfect buddhahood in this very life.”

Having spoken thus, those sages addressed King Sūryaratha in the Brahma-family: "O Sūryaratha, you are one whose heart grasps the meaning of all mundane and supramundane treatises, from the Vedas down to the single volumes of the scriptures; therefore, at our request, carry out the entreaty of King Yaśas.
We too, having first gone for refuge to the Maṇḍala, shall all perform the entreaty."

Then, at the word of that Brahmā-ṛṣi, Sūryaratha fashioned a mandala with flowers made of jewels and gold, and having cast a handful of jewel-flowers at the feet of King Yaśonarendra, he prostrated at the feet of Yaśas together with the Brahmā-ṛṣis—his two knees touching the ground, his two hands raised to his head—and placing his right knee upon the earth and joining his palms to his forehead, he entreated King Yaśonarendra: "May the Blessed One teach the *Ādibuddha*, the King of Tantras, in which even those who have committed the five deeds of immediate retribution are prophesied for Buddhahood in this very life; where they are gathered by the Blessed Vajradhara through supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*) and are prophesied as attainers of Mahāmudrā."
"This *Ādibuddha* consisting of six and twelve thousand [verses] was taught by the Tathāgata to King Sucandra.
Therefore, having condensed that very *Ādibuddha* into a short tantra-king with few words, please teach it for the sake of the disciples of the Brahmanical sages.

Then, having heard this request from Sūryaratha, and by the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment and through the force of the resolute intention (*adhimukti-citta*) of the Brahmanical sages, he—acting as the compiler of the brief summary—teaches the Tantra-king in the *Sragdharā* meter, which summarizes the Teacher, the time, and all other [factors] of the Omniscient One.

And for those who advocate for beautiful words, in order to destroy their attachment to beautiful sounds, [the author] has relied on taking the meaning as the refuge: in some instances there is an ungrammatical word (*apaśabda*) within a verse; in some instances there is a break in the caesura (*yatibhaṅga*); and in some instances there is a word lacking a case-ending (*avibhaktika*).
