In some places there is the elision of a letter or a vowel; in some places a long vowel becomes short in a meter, and a short vowel likewise becomes long; in some places the locative case is used in the sense of the ablative, and the genitive in the sense of the dative; in some cases an *ātmanepada* ending occurs for a root that takes *parasmaipada*, and a *parasmaipada* ending for one that takes *ātmanepada*; in some places the plural is used for the singular, and the singular for the plural; the neuter for the masculine, and the masculine for the neuter; in some places the dental *śa* occurs where the palatal is expected, and the dental or palatal where the retroflex is expected; and in some places the palatal or retroflex occurs where the dental is expected.
In this way, others should also be followed by the teacher who instructs the tantra;
likewise, the Blessed One said in the *Mūlatantra*: "O Sucandra, the beloved objects of all Buddhas should always be given to the disciples and to the gurus—namely, wife, daughter, and son."
Smell exists in the earth, form in water, taste in fire, touch in air, and sound in the imperishable; [these are] the great principles of the elements.
In the sky of the Vimalaprabhā, having worshipped with perfumes, incense, lamps, food, drink, garments, and so forth, the true son offers the Mahāmudrā to the Guru.
"World-systems" (*lokadhātu*) and other such terms—these and others should also be understood by the yogi from the readings of the scriptures (*āgama*).

Thus, even in this commentary, I have written [this] relying on the refuge in the meaning (*arthaśaraṇatā*), for the sake of destroying the pride of those who take fine words (*suśabda*) as the primary concern.

Now, in whatever manner the destruction of the pride of fine words regarding family-mantras (*kulavidyā*) occurs, in that very manner, relying on the refuge in the meaning, the teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is given for the sake of liberation, whether through the languages of various regions or through the languages of grammatical treatises (*śabdaśāstra*).

Thus ends the third chapter, the exposition on the relationship between the Root Tantra and the Abridged Tantra concerning the Teacher, the Time, and the Petitioner, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghu-kālacakra-tantra-rāja* following the Root Tantra. || 3 ||

There is no [separate] section on the teacher, the requester, and the means of accomplishment. Now, through the connection with the teacher, the requester, and others—namely Śrī Narendrasūryaratha, who was emanated by Mañjuśrī—I shall expand upon this *Laghutantrarāja*.

Here, in this glorious Kālacakra maṇḍala palace, at the conclusion of the eastern gate, in the great jewel pavilion, Yaśonarendra—seated upon a great jewel lion-throne, his lotus feet saluted by millions upon millions of village lords who were born into the lineages of the ninety-six great royal families of gods, asuras, and nāgas, and who wore crowns of great jewels; he who is the embodiment of the wisdom of all Tathāgatas and was requested by Sūryaratha—spoke thus to Sūryaratha: "Excellent, excellent, Sūryaratha! It is well that you have exerted yourself to hear from me the true essence of the Supreme Primordial Buddha Tantra King (*paramādibuddhatantrarāja*), so that all beings, beginning with the Brahmin seers, may attain the path to perfect enlightenment."

Therefore, since you have asked about this *Kālacakra-vajrayoga*—the true essence (*sadbhāva*) of the supreme *Paramādibuddha-tantra-rāja*, which accomplishes both mundane and supramundane attainments—I shall teach it all to you. As the compiler (*saṅgītikāraka*), you too should listen with a one-pointed mind; by the power of the empowerment of the Tathāgata previously prophesied, I shall extract from the great *Tantra-rāja* this Yoga, which consists of wisdom and method, the essence of the *Laghu-tantra-rāja*, through a compilation in verse on the earth.
Through the connection of the relationship between the Perfectly Awakened One, the teacher Sucandra, and the requester, I [have composed] this for King Yaśas.

Then the Blessed Mañjuśrī, in his emanation-body as King Yaśas, spoke the first chapter on the collection of the teacher and others, which had been prophesied by the Tathāgata from the *Paramādibuddha*: "Having bowed my head to the Omniscient One, whose body is the embodiment of gnosis (*jñānakāya*), whose form is like the sun, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals, who is seated upon a lion throne, and who is saluted with the heads of the best of gods."
King Sucandra, having placed his joined palms upon his head, questioned [the Lord] regarding the Yoga in the Śrī Kālacakra for the sake of the liberation of men during the time of the Kali age. (1)
From "māśritya" onwards, the manuscript *gha* is fragmentary.
In manuscript *kha*, [the word] "sadā mudrām" does not exist.
[End of] the section on the summary of the means for the teacher and the petitioner in the first chapter.
In this *Tantrarāja*, for the purpose of summarizing the teacher and other [factors], this opening verse was recited by the Blessed One.

Here, the "teacher and others" refers to: the teacher (*deśaka*), the place (*sthāna*), the great assembly (*mahāparṣad*), the requester (*adhyeṣaka*), the teaching of the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*), and the purpose, the purpose of the purpose, and the purpose of that purpose.

Among these, first, the summary of the teacher is accomplished by the Blessed One through these twenty-three syllables: "the omniscient one, the body of gnosis, whose form is like the sun, with eyes as broad as lotus petals, the Buddha."
With these five syllables, "siṃhāsanastham," the setting [of the teaching] is established;
with these seven syllables, "suravaranamitam," the great assembly is established;
and with these twenty-eight syllables, "mastakena praṇamya pṛcched rājā sucandraḥ karakamalapuṭaṃ sthāpayitvottamāṅge," the requester is established.
By these fourteen syllables—"yogaṃ śrīkālacakre kaliyugasamaye"—the summary of the teaching of the True Dharma (*saddharmadeśanā*) has been made.

By these seven syllables—"muktihetornarāṇām"—the summary of the purpose, the purpose of the purpose, and the purpose of that purpose has been made. Thus, by these eighty-four syllables in this sequence, the summary of the teacher, the place, the great assembly, the requester, the teaching of the Dharma, and the purpose, the purpose of the purpose, and the purpose of that purpose has been extracted from the Root King of Tantras (*mūlatantrarāja*) by the Blessed Mañjuśrī, who was prophesied by the Tathāgata.

"Since it was prophesied by the Tathāgata," one might ask, "In all the *tantrarājas*, the Blessed Lord Vajradhara’s place of residence is indicated by the Tathāgata through such phrases as ‘Thus have I heard’ (*evam mayā śrutam*) and so forth; how then can this *tantrarāja* be said to have been taught by the Buddha, the Blessed One, without the phrase ‘Thus have I heard’ and the like?

Because of the absence of the indication of the place of residence and the phrase ‘Thus have I heard,’ the statement that this *tantrarāja* was not taught by the Buddha, the Blessed One, will be the speech of someone who relies on the refuge of mere names and letters."

Therefore, that which is to be said here regarding the future time by foolish people who rely on the designation of "phonemes" (vyañjana) is as follows: the Blessed Tathāgata’s teaching on the location where the Lord Vajradhara dwelt—beginning with the words “Thus have I heard” (*evam mayā śrutam*) and so forth—in all the King of Tantras, is not [correct]. Why?

Because the teacher of the Dharma relies on the refuge of meaning rather than [specific] words, and because the compilers also perform the compilation by means of various local languages, if the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma here were expressed through the Sanskrit language—produced by the effort of the throat, palate, and so forth—and were merely regional, then the Tathāgata would be unable to teach the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma even over many periods of time; nor could the compiler write them down, due to that single, regional Sanskrit language.

In this regard, because there would be no infinite emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), one who teaches the Dharma simultaneously through the voices of infinite, infinite sentient beings across infinite, infinite world-systems would not exist; and due to the absence of teaching the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*), he would not be omniscient.

But it is not so. Here, the Buddha is immeasurable, the Dharma is immeasurable, and the Saṅgha is immeasurable. Therefore, according to the word of the Tathāgata, there is not just one omniscient teacher, nor is there just one omniscient language that conveys meaning through the voices of all sentient beings, nor is there just one description of the place where he dwelt.
The community of Śrāvakas is not the sole requester of the Tathāgata;

rather, here, by virtue of the diverse inclinations (*adhimukti*) of sentient beings, there are many omniscient ones, many languages of the omniscient one, many places of residence, many requesters, and many teachings of the Dharma.

Therefore, the teaching of all the Tantras is not [delivered] by the Tathāgata through a single divine language—such as "Thus have I heard"—produced from the throat, palate, and other articulatory organs.

In this regard, first of all, in the Śrāvaka system, the teaching of the Dharma in the Magadha language at the beginning of the Tripiṭaka and other works is as follows: "Thus indeed (Itipi) that Blessed One is the Perfectly Awakened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One," and so forth. Likewise, to the north of the Śītā River in the region of Campaka, the teaching of the Dharma in the Koṭigrāma language is as follows:
"Akarṣu, ṣaka, gagalku, jirāmaka, vijirikā, dudurūpaka," and so forth.
O friend,
you are indeed a fool!
O Jigamaka Vijirita,
you who have seen the true form!
(arā ṣṇaka; ṅa ṣṇaka; ṅa tvakhaṣṭaka; bho)
O monk Khaṣṇukegagaṇaka, this is the teaching of the Dharma from the Jinamaṇa world-system.

Likewise, in the very beautiful region of Uttara-Rukma, there was the teaching of the Dharma in the Koṭigrāma dialect; for example, the teaching of the Dharma through such names as Akamaya-satra (da), Baladatta, Viraṭa, Manika, Akuṭa, Varadatta, Jigita (ti)-Varadatta, and so forth.
In this way, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the three vehicles occurred in many regions and dialects, and not solely in the Sanskrit language beginning with "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*).

Now, even among the *tantrarājas* written by the compilers (*saṅgītikārakas*) in the Sanskrit language, in some cases there is an indication of the place of residence beginning with "Thus have I heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*), while in other cases there is no such indication of the place of residence at the outset beginning with "Thus have I heard. This is the case in many *tantrarājas*, such as the *Śrī-samāja* in twenty-five thousand [stanzas], the *Māyājāla* in sixteen thousand [stanzas], and so forth. However, in some cases, such as the *Paramādibuddha* in twelve thousand [stanzas], the *Yogānuviddha* in thirty-six thousand [stanzas], and the *Mahālakṣābhidhāna*, there is no such indication at the outset.

Thus, while in some instances in various *tantrarājas*, as well as in the *mūlatantrarājas* and the minor *laghutantras* extracted from them, the teaching begins with "Thus have I [heard]," in other cases it might not;

therefore, here in the *Śrīsamāja*, the Blessed One said: "Thus have I heard at one time: the Blessed One was dwelling in the wombs (*bhaga*) of the vajra-women of the body, speech, and mind of all the Tathāgatas."

The description of the location where [the Buddha] dwelt is as follows: likewise, in the *Māyājāla*, the description of the location where he dwelt begins with "Thus have I heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*).
Similarly, in other Root Tantras and Kings of Abridged Tantras, there is a description of the location where he dwelt.
Here, in the *Paramādibuddha*, the Blessed One said: "The glorious Buddha, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals, is seated upon a lion throne."

The Omniscient One, the Body of Gnosis, whose nature is the passion of body, speech, and mind, who through the passion of body, speech, and mind possesses the imperishable solar form— He is Vajrasattva, the presiding deity. In the mandala of body, speech, and mind, He is the indestructible Vajrayoga, Kālacakra, the immutable bliss.
The Buddha is without beginning or end, the primordial Buddha, free from causal succession;
he is the universal auspiciousness of the vajra and the universal vow of the universe;
he possesses the meaning of reality in twelve aspects and upholds the truth in sixteen aspects.

Such is the description of the places of residence and so forth. Likewise, in the *Paramādibuddha*, which consists of thirty-six thousand verses and is permeated by yoga, the Blessed One said: “Abiding in the vajra-lotus of the ḍākinīs, in the form of innate bliss (sahajānanda), that one supreme deity is established within the nature of the three worlds.”

With these words, the instruction on the places of wandering was given. Furthermore, in the *Yogānuviddha* and the *Lakṣābhidhāna*, the Blessed One said: "The teaching of the Dharma" is an addition; "Akamayasat" means "given by force" (*baladdatta*). [In the chapter titled] *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittarahasyo Guhyasamāja-nāma-mahākalparāja*, there is the summary of the teacher, the petitioner, and the practice: "In the secret [reality], he abides within the self of all female messengers and all sentient beings."
"The being consisting of all female messengers is Vajrasattva, the Great Bliss.
With these words, the location of the dwelling is indicated;
and that is to be understood from the oral instructions of the Guru.

Likewise, regarding the requester in the *Śrī-samāja*: "Then Vajrapāṇi, being empowered by the Blessed One Vajradhara, spoke thus: 'May the Blessed One teach the Great King of Tantras, the unsurpassed among all tantras, the *Śrī-samāja* of all Buddhas, which is the designation of all Buddhas.
Thus.
With these and other such words, there is the entreaty of Vajrapāṇi. Likewise, in the *Māyājāla*, Vajrapāṇi is well known as the petitioner;

however, here in the *Paramādibuddha*, it is the [deity] Sattvānāṃ Kleśanāśāya who, having been exhorted by the Blessed One, acts as the petitioner. Through the yoga of body, speech, and mind, having worshipped the two lotus-feet of the Teacher with jewel-flowers, and again with a handful of flowers joined in reverence (*puṣpāñjali*):
Then, having placed both knees upon the ground with the head [also touching],
and having prostrated with the right side toward the earth, [one should perform] the circle of prostration (*jānmaṇḍala*).
Placing his palms together at his forehead, the King makes this request:
"O Teacher, please teach the entirety of the unsurpassed tantra of all vehicles."
In this Śrī Kālacakra, which is endowed with Ālikāli, the primordial Buddha is always characterized by the mass of all accomplishments; [this is] the yoga.
The reality realized in a single moment, bearing the four drops, is divided into sixteen parts through its differentiation into four moments.
Emptiness, gnosis, and the drop (bindu) are the supreme and great Vajradhara;
the five-syllabled is the Great Emptiness, and the six-syllabled is the Emptiness of the Drop.
One should likewise contemplate the twenty-five principles— the Buddhas, gods, and asuras externally, within the body, and in others— as well as the Puruṣa and the Prakṛtis.
The measure of the universe within the body, which is the cause of the origin of the three worlds and the experience of gods, asuras, and others— all this is clearly explained [herein].
"Please teach," and so forth—thus was the request made by King Sucandra in the *Paramādibuddha*.
Likewise, in the *Yogānuviddha*, Viśvarūpiṇī said: "Having bowed to the illustrious Viśvarūpiṇī, she asks Vajrabhairava."
What is the tantra permeated by yoga? It is Vajrasattva, the supreme bliss.

After such an exhortation regarding the *Yogānuviddha*, Vajravārāhī spoke concerning the *Lakṣābhidhāna*: "Having prostrated to Heruka, who is the essence of the three realms of existence, [I ask]: O Vajrasattva, what is the supreme bliss of the *Lakṣābhidhāna* Tantra?"
Thus, the request [for teaching] is described in the *Lakṣābhidhāna*;
in this same way, the request by the yogi should be understood in other royal tantras as well.

Therefore, because the Blessed One is the teacher of infinite dharmas, one should not state at the beginning of all the royal tantras, "Thus have I heard," and so forth, as a description of the location where he dwelt.

By means of this limited Sanskrit expression, even the Buddha becomes limited; for, in this noble land, having observed the pride of the learned non-Buddhist outsiders who maintain that words are ultimate, there arose the intention of those Buddhists of immature intellect, namely: "Just as Brahmā, Hari, Hara, and others who speak in Sanskrit are the chosen deities (*iṣṭadevatā*) of the Brāhmaṇas, Vaiṣṇavas, Śaivas, and so forth, so too our own chosen deities—the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—must be speakers of Sanskrit."

In this context, it is not by means of this limited refined (saṃskṛta) speech that the compilers of the Dharma become preachers of the Dharma through the voices of all sentient beings; for without the language of the omniscient ones, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would be bound to the birth-status of gods and thus limited. Therefore, because they preach the Dharma through the various voices of sentient beings, in this Mantra system there is no single fixed designation for an entity; even for a single entity there are multiple designations, owing to the multiplicity of designations.
Nor can any single designation be primary, because it serves to indicate the absence of all designations.

For example, among the terms *strī*, *nārī*, *yuvatī*, and so forth, no single designation "woman" (*strī*) could be primary, because all of them indicate the state of possessing breasts and hips. Likewise, among the designations *ekāra*, *rahasya*, *padma*, *dharmodaya*, *khadhātu*, *mahāsukhāvāsa*, *siṃhāsana*, *bhaga*, and *guhya*, no single designation *ekāra* is primary, because all of them indicate emptiness in all its aspects.

Likewise, among the designations of *vaṃ* (the syllable *vaṃ*), great passion (*mahāsukha*), great desire (*mahārāga*), the innate (*sahaja*), the supreme immutable (*paramākṣara*), the drop (*bindu*), reality (*tattva*), primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), and the purified mind (*viśuddhacitta*), not even one single designation, such as *vaṃ*, is primary; for all of them serve to establish the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), and the immutable happiness (*akṣarasukha*).

In this way, the syllables *e* and *vaṃ* represent emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects (*sarvākāravaropetā śūnyatā*) and the non-dual bodhicitta consisting of compassion that is non-referential toward all phenomena (*sarvadharmanirālambakaruṇā*), because they establish the nature of these realities.

The syllable *Evaṃ*, Vajrasattva, Bodhicitta, Kālacakra, Ādibuddha, Yoga whose nature is wisdom and means, that which consists of the object of knowledge and knowledge, non-dual, without beginning or end, peaceful, Saṃāja, and Saṃvara—by such various names, the non-dual yoga whose nature is wisdom and means, which is without substrate (*niranvaya*), is to be understood by the yogi.

In this regard, as for the syllable *E* and the syllable *Vaṃ* which were taught by the Blessed One at the beginning of the *Samāja* and other *Tantrarāja*s in the form of an etymological definition (*nirukti*), they were likewise written at the beginning of the tantras by the compiler (*saṅgītikāra*) for the sake of maturing the gods through divine speech. Therefore, the elision of these two syllables at the beginning of the *Samāja* and other *Tantrarāja*s is not intended;
for it is not the case that the Blessed One taught these two syllables via the palate and so forth [without speaking them], nor did the compiler write them down without having heard them.

Therefore, the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of these two syllables is stated: the first *a* is the space-element (*khadhātu*), the secret lotus; from that comes the *visarga*, the sun, which is the female passion (*rajas*); then the *a*, the consciousness of Rāhu, presided over by bliss; then the *anusvāra*, the moon, which is the semen.
Between these two *a*s—the space-element and the consciousness of Rāhu—the *visarga*, the sun, which is the female passion, undergoes the change to *i*.

When the *visarga*, the sun, has thus attained the state of *u* (in the form *au*), there is an absence of the *guṇa* vowel in ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*); due to the absence of the *guṇa*, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs.

The letter *vaṃ* consists of the subsequent vowel *i* (the letter *i*) joined with the preceding vowel *a* (the letter *a*), which is the space-element (*khadhātu*), the secret lotus, ending in the locative case; this *a* undergoes *guṇa* (vowel strengthening) with the subsequent *i*, thus forming *e*. Within this *ekāra*—the space-element as the support—the letter *vaṃ* is the supported. It should be understood that in the center, externally, in the body, and in the supreme [state], it consists of the visarga, the form of the letter *a*, the anusvāra, the sun, Rāhu, the moon, the *rajas*, the *ālayavijñāna*, and the semen (*śukra*).

In this Root Tantra, the Blessed One said: "Within the syllable E is the central syllable VAṂ, the abode of the bliss of all Buddhas; in the element of space (khadhātu), this Vajrasattva exists through the union of body, speech, and mind."

The body is the drop (bindu), the moon, and the semen; speech is emission (visarga), the dust (rajas), and the sun; and the mind is their form—these are said to be established within the single element.

"By means of the yoga of body, speech, and mind, abiding within the maṇḍala of body, speech, and mind through passion for body, speech, and mind, situated within the nature of the three realms of existence"—

for this reason, in the *Samāja* and other sovereign tantras, the Tathāgata spoke the description of the place of residence beginning with "Thus have I heard," for the sake of maturing the gods and for the attainment of perfect buddhahood.

Thus, by this designation, whatever state (*bhāva*) was taught in the *Śrī-samāja* and other [tantras], that very same state was taught by the Tathāgata in the *Tantrarāja* such as the *Lakṣābhidhāna* under terms like "the secret" (*rahasya*). And that [state] is to be understood through the oral instruction of the Guru within various tantras and through the various types of intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣā*). Regarding this, the Blessed One said in the Root Tantra: "The tantra characterized by the six points consists of intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣa*), likewise not literal speech (*ruta*), and likewise neither of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) nor of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*)."
Therefore, according to the word of the Blessed One, no single perception alone can be predominant.

In this Mantra system, the Blessed One has taught a threefold conviction (*pratyaya*): first, conviction in the tantra; second, conviction in the guru; and third, conviction in oneself. Through these three convictions, the path to perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambuddha*) becomes completely pure. Otherwise, a path that is taught by a guru in the absence of these three convictions does not bestow the fruit of perfect enlightenment upon the disciple, because of the disciple’s dullness of faith (*śraddhājaḍatva*).

"The worldly fruit exists by way of conventional truth"—this is the proposition made here by the Blessed One in another tantra: "Having rendered the mind free from conceptual construction, one should examine the sign for one day; if, according to the procedure taught in the tantra and through the guru's instruction, no conviction arises in the disciple, then the word of the Blessed One would be false."

Now, if the guru does not become the bestower of the path to the disciple according to the procedure taught in the *Gurutamtra*, then the promise of the Blessed One does not become false; this is because the guru lacks knowledge of the path and because he teaches a cultivation of a perverted and impure path.
In this regard, one should examine for one day no other sign than that of the *maṇḍala-cakra* sādhana, setting aside signs such as smoke, according to the word of the Blessed One.

In this *Tantrarāja* consisting of three families (*trikulātman*), the subject matter (*abhidheya*) consists of body, speech, and mind, and thus has three faces. In that which consists of four families (*catuḥkulātman*), the subject matter consists of body, speech, mind, and gnosis, and thus has four faces. When combined with the single family of gnosis, the tantra becomes four families in nature, and the subject matter likewise becomes five families in nature. Together with the single essence, it becomes six families in nature.

Here, in this tantra consisting of four families, the subject matter consists of the four families—the union of the sun, moon, Rāhu, and fire [which correspond to *rajas*, semen, mind, and gnosis]—in a single yoga.

In this *Nāmasaṅgīti*, the Vajrayoga has been clearly proclaimed by the Tathāgata through three verses beginning with the thirty-third in the Praise of Discriminating Wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*); namely: "Vajra-sun of great light, vajra-moon of stainless radiance, Great passion beyond passion, blazing with light of every color."
The Perfectly Awakened One, seated in the vajra posture, upholder of the Dharma of the Buddhas' assembly, born from the lotus of the Buddha, glorious, and bearer of the treasury of omniscient wisdom.
The King who holds the universal illusion, the great master of the knowledge of the Buddhas,
the diamond-sharp, the great sword, the utterly pure, the supreme syllable.

Thus, from these words of the Blessed One, it follows that the subject matter consists of four families; the Blessed Lord Kālacakra is the essence of the establishment of the pure Dharma-mantras of Vajrasattva.
Likewise, he consists of five families through the division of the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*). Thus...

In the *Māyājāla*, the Blessed One said: “He has five faces, five topknots, and a crest of five locks of hair; he bears the great vows, wears the girdle of muñja grass, is a celibate student, and is the supreme among those who observe vows.”

Thus, he is to be designated by way of the division of aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*) as consisting of six families; yet, it has been stated that he also consists of one hundred families according to the differentiation of his faces, as expressed in the first verse of the *Ādarśajñānastava* together with the final quarter-verse of the *Viśuddhadharmadhātu*: "Terrifying as Vajrabhairava, the King of Wrath, six-faced and formidable, six-eyed and six-armed, powerful, a skeleton with fangs bared, possessing a hundred faces like the Halāhala poison. From this word of the Blessed One, it should be understood that in various tantras and other scriptures, the subject matter is to be known as three-faced, four-faced, five-faced, six-faced, or even hundred-faced. Here, in the *Samāja* and other tantras, that very place which was spoken of by the Blessed One by means of the syllable *E* is described by the Blessed One in the *Lakṣābhidhāna* and other texts using words such as "the secret" (*rahasya*). That which was said to be denoted by the syllable *Vaṃ* is the same as what is called Vajrasattva by the term "Great Bliss" (*mahāsukha*). In this manner, according to the stated sequence, in the *Paramādibuddha*, which consists of four families, the subject matter consists of both four families and six families. By the twenty-three syllables beginning with "Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*), the Blessed One has indicated that Great Bliss is the Vajra of Bodhicitta, inseparable from emptiness and compassion. Here, by the term "lion-throne" (*siṃhāsana*), the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) in all its forms is meant; the Buddha who resides upon that lion-throne is Vajrasattva. "Yoga" refers to the great purpose, the supreme immutable (*paramākṣara*). This Yoga is celebrated in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*, in the *Vajradhātumaṇḍalastava*, by fourteen verses, as follows: "The Blessed One, the Buddha, the Perfectly Awakened One, born from the syllable *A*; the syllable *A* is the foremost of all letters, of great purpose, and the supreme immutable. He is the Great Breath, indeed the Unborn, devoid of verbal expression. He is the foremost cause of all speech, the radiant clarity of all speech. He is the Lord, the highest of great sciences, the Guru, the highest of great mantras. He is established in the system of the Mahāyāna, the supreme of the Mahāyāna systems. Up to this point, this subject matter is celebrated throughout all other tantras, according to the dispositions of middling and superior beings. Likewise, by the fourteen syllables beginning with "Emptiness and Gnosis" (*śūnyaṃ jñānaṃ ca*), the subject matter consisting of six families is expressed. That very same subject is also celebrated in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*, in the second verse of the *Kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñānastava*: "The generator of the meaning of all mantras, the Great Bindu, without letters; the Great Emptiness of five letters, the Void of Bindus, of six letters. [End of excerpt from] the *Vimalaprabhā* [on the World Realm].

Therefore, because it is taught through infinite designations, the King of Tantras (*tantrarāja*) beginning with "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) is indeed taught by the Tathāgata. However, one must not say that what is taught through [terms such as] "the secret" (*rahasya*) and "the omniscient one" (*sarvajña*) is not taught by the Tathāgata; for by finding fault in one's own tenets (*svasiddhānta*) or the tenets of others (*parasiddhānta*), the sixth root downfall (*mūlāpatti*) occurs. Therefore, having understood the connection between the preceding and following parts in other tantras, one should discern their virtues and faults. Otherwise, by finding fault in what has not been seen, those wicked and ignoble ones who are outside the heart of the Tathāgata, who are attached to the enjoyment of sense objects and faculties, and who engage in false speech, will go to the Avīci hell. Thus, according to the sequence stated above and through the reasoning of the supreme scripture (*paramāgama*), the Lord has taught the *Paramādibuddha*, the King of Tantras, which is free from contradiction between its earlier and later parts, beginning with "the omniscient one. Now, someone might think: "He who is omniscient is the Buddha, the Blessed One, because two designations express a single state of being. Why then is there this redundant statement of the Lord as 'Buddha'? To this it is said: It is true that he who is omniscient is the Buddha, the Blessed One. However, others such as Hari and Hara are also imagined to be omniscient by the common folk. In order to refute their omniscience, it is said: "The omniscient one is the Buddha, the Blessed One. Here, there is no other omniscient one in the triple world; among Hari, Hara, and others, he is the one who teaches all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) through the languages of all sentient beings. Why is it said here that among them none is omniscient and a teacher of all phenomena through the languages of all beings? Because Hari, Hara, and others are born within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) of the six realms as gods, whereas the Buddha, the Blessed One, is established at the far limit of the shore beyond cyclic existence. In this regard, the Tathāgata spoke in the *Nāmasaṅgīti* in the thirteenth verse of the *Suviśuddhadharmadhātustava*: "Standing at the far limit of the shore of cyclic existence, having accomplished what was to be done, standing on firm ground, established in the knowledge of isolation (*kaivalya*), and tearing asunder with the weapon of wisdom (*prajñā*). Therefore, the statement "the omniscient one is the Buddha, the Blessed One" is not redundant. Now, one might ask: "He who is omniscient is the Knowledge-Body (*jñānakāya*); why is there this redundant statement of the Blessed One as 'Knowledge-Body'? To this it is said: It is true that he who is omniscient is the Knowledge-Body. However, there are also other Buddhas—the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—and in order to refute their status as Perfectly Complete Buddhas (*samyaksambuddha*), the redundant statement "the omniscient one is the Knowledge-Body, the Perfectly Complete Buddha, the Blessed One, the Knowledge-Body" is made. Here, among the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, none has ever been a Knowledge-Body or a Perfectly Complete Buddha. Why is it said here that among the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas none has ever been a Perfectly Complete Buddha? Because the Śrāvakas and Buddhas abide in a Nirvāṇa with remainder (*sopadhinirvāṇa*), whereas the Perfectly Complete Buddha is liberated from all remainders. And so the Blessed One spoke in the *Nāmasaṅgīti* in the eleventh verse of the *Pratyavekṣaṇājñānastava*: "Liberated from all remainders, well-established in the path of space, bearing the great wish-fulfilling gem, the all-pervading Lord, the best of all jewels. Therefore, the statement "the omniscient one is the Knowledge-Body, the Perfectly Complete Buddha, the Blessed One, the Knowledge-Body" is not redundant. Now, one might ask: "He who is the Knowledge-Body has a body like the sun because he destroys the darkness of ignorance; why then is there this redundant statement of the Blessed One as 'having a body like the sun'? To this it is said: It is true that he who is the Knowledge-Body has a body like the sun because he destroys the darkness of ignorance. However, there are also other Buddhists who are proponents of consciousness (*vijñānavādin*). In order to refute their doctrine of the nature of consciousness (*vijñānadharmatā*), the redundant statement "the Knowledge-Body has a body like the sun, transcending the nature of consciousness, the Perfectly Complete Buddha" is made. Among the proponents of consciousness, none has ever been a Knowledge-Body, a sun-bodied Perfectly Complete Buddha. Why is it said here that among the proponents of consciousness none has ever been a Knowledge-Body, a sun-bodied Perfectly Complete Buddha? Because the proponents of consciousness abide in the phenomenon of consciousness, whereas the Perfectly Complete Buddha has transcended the nature of consciousness. And so the Tathāgata spoke in the *Nāmasaṅgīti* in the twenty-third verse of the *Pratyavekṣaṇājñānastava*: "Transcending the nature of consciousness, bearing non-dual knowledge, free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), effortless (*nirābhoga*), and bearing the bodies of the Buddhas of the three times. Therefore, the statement "the Knowledge-Body has a body like the sun, the Perfectly Complete Buddha" is not redundant. Now, one might think: "That which is the subject matter (*abhidheya*) in the Tantra is the formless Knowledge-Body, while he who has eyes as broad as lotus petals is possessed of form; why then is there this statement of the Blessed One as 'having eyes as broad as lotus petals'? To this it is said: What is to be said here by the ignorant—that the subject matter in the Tantra is the Blessed One possessed of form with eyes as broad as lotus petals—is not so. Here, by the word "lotus" (*padma*) in its definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) is meant. In that lotus, in the space-element, sentient beings are situated as having the nature of the hundred families (*śatakula*) and long [dimensions], like the petals of a lotus; thus they are "lotus petals," and as far as their end extends—those whose hundred eyes are broad belong to the Blessed One, hence he is "one with eyes as broad as lotus petals. This was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Nāmasaṅgīti* in the sixth verse of the *Ādarśajñānastava*: "With eyes formidable with vajra-flames, with hair like vajra-flames, the vajra-penetration, the great penetration, the hundred-eyed one, the vajra-eyed one. Therefore, according to the word of the Blessed One, the Perfectly Complete Buddha, the Blessed One, has eyes as broad as lotus petals and is devoid of form. That Buddha is seated upon a lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*); the lion-throne is the space-element. Alternatively, the moon, sun, and fire mandalas are the lion-throne, and he who is situated upon that is "seated upon the lion-throne. Regarding this, the Blessed One said in the Root Tantra:
In another tantra, I have stated that the Vajrin resides upon a lion-throne within the secret place, the space-element, the bhaga, the source of phenomena (dharmodaya), or the lotus.
He is known by such names as Vaṃ-vajrī, Vajrasattva, Vajrabhairava, Īśvara, Heruka, Kālacakra, and Ādibuddha.
I have explained that the locus is characterized by its basis through various perceptions of objects, and that which is supported is likewise [defined] by the diverse dispositions of sentient beings.
The omniscient Vajradhara, the Teacher, the Buddha seated upon the lion throne,
is the expounder of Kālacakra, having been entreated by you, Sucandra.

Therefore, the Buddha, the Blessed One, is omniscient, the teacher of mundane and supramundane dharmas, the instructor of gods, asuras, and humans, supremely compassionate, affectionate without cause, and liberated from all obscurations.
Consequently, even among those such as Hari and Hara, the Buddha, the Blessed One, alone is the teacher and the omniscient one.

There is no other who, within the triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems, can simultaneously teach the mundane and supramundane dharmas through infinite and limitless sounds for infinite and limitless sentient beings.
Why?
Because it arose from a limited, single divine species—that is, because it was produced by a limited, single refined language (*saṃskṛta*).

That [language] is not the speech of the Omniscient One, for it does not teach the mundane and supramundane Dharma to sentient beings of various inclinations through their respective individual languages.
In this world of mortals, it is directly perceived that the Gītā taught by them, as well as all the established doctrines, Purāṇas, Dharmas, and the four Vedas, are regional in nature.
Why? Because of the study of the Vedas restricted to Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas.
Here, the study of the Vedas must be performed by Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, and certainly not by Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and the like.

Likewise, the teachings on the dharma of the *Gītā*, the *Siddhāntas*, and the *Purāṇas* are to be heard from the mouth of a Brahmin by the four castes—Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—and the taking of ordination (*pravrajyā*) is not for fishermen and the like.
Therefore, because they are taught with words that exclude certain groups from the dharma, these dharmas are merely local and do not benefit all sentient beings.

In this mortal world, because they are unable to teach the mundane and supramundane Dharma to beings of various inclinations through various sounds using a limited Sanskrit language for that reason, they impose prohibitions upon the *viṭas*, *śūdras*, and others.
In this mortal world, it is declared that those born of inferior lineages, such as the *viṭas* and *śūdras*, must not study the Vedas, nor may they take up the staff of renunciation (*pravrajyā*).

The intention behind Pāṇini’s statement in the *Mahābhāṣya*, “A single word well-employed [is] a cow of plenty in heaven,” is based on false pride; for there is no such thing as a language spoken by an omniscient being.

In this mortal world, if all men—even Śūdras and others—were knowers of the Vedas, the Gītā, the Siddhāntas, and the treatises on logic, then who would show respect to the Brāhmaṇas? This is because knowledge, dharma, and wisdom would be common to all, and since all householders are attached to worldly enjoyments, they would lack any special excellence.

Knowing this, wicked sages greedy for wealth wrote down religious texts such as the *Gītā*, the established doctrines (*siddhāntas*), and the *Purāṇas* in the Sanskrit language; they then established the rule that the Vedas must be studied through oral recitation, which creates great delusion for childish people—this is the intended meaning behind the teaching of those who are not omniscient.

In former times, the Vedas, Gītās, Siddhāntas, Purāṇas, and Dharmas did not exist written in books; they resided in the mouths of ascetics (*yatis*). However, due to the power of the age of the five corruptions (*pañcakaṣāya-kāla*), they have now been written in books by the ascetics because of their lack of wisdom. Here, the partial teaching of Dharma by Hari, Hara, and others is not to be approved by Buddhists, as it is devoid of compassion for all sentient beings, causes the suffering of *saṃsāra*, produces false pride, and is characterized by arrogance regarding caste.

In this world-system, those teachings which were taught by the Omniscient One in the language of the Omniscient, recorded in books by the compilers in various languages of sentient beings—teachings that explain worldly matters such as the Vedas, that explain the meaning of the three vehicles, and that were taught through both conventional truth and ultimate truth—those beings who are devoted to them listen to, study, read, recite, preserve, and extensively proclaim and establish for others those eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma taught by the Omniscient One, which explain both worldly and supramundane meanings. Having honored them with various flowers, various perfumes, various incenses, various powders, various garments, various bells, various banners, various yak-tail whisks, various parasols, various canopies, various pearl necklaces, various jewels, various lamps, and various jeweled ornaments, they prostrate before them with the five limbs.

Thus, these teachings taught by the Omniscient One are beneficial to others; by virtue of one's inclination (*adhimukti*), they serve for the benefit of others. They were neither enjoined nor prohibited by the Tathāgata on account of anyone’s caste or lack of caste, and thus even today they have not vanished.
Let it be so for now regarding other regions.

In this noble land where the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, when the Blessed One had passed into parinirvāṇa, the compilers recorded the three vehicles in books according to the Tathāgata’s own injunction (*nayena*): the Tripiṭaka in the Māgadha language; the Sūtrāntas in the Sindhu language; the Pāramitā-naya and Mantra-naya in the Sanskrit language; and the Tantras and other Tantras in Sanskrit, Prākṛt, Apabhraṃśa, and the unrefined languages of the barbarians such as Śaba and others—in this manner, the Dharma taught by the Omniscient One was recorded by the compilers.

The Three Vehicles have been written in the language of Bhoṭa for the land of Bhoṭa; in China, in the Chinese language; in Mahācīna, in the Mahācīna language; in the land of Pārasika, in the Pārasika language; to the north of the Śītā River, in the language of the Campaka region, the Vānara region, and the region called Suvarṇa; likewise, to the north of the Nīla River, in the language of the Ruhaya (Ruhma) region and the Surasmā region. Thus, they have been written in the ninety-six regional languages for the ninety-six regions consisting of millions upon millions of villages.

Thus, within the twelve sections—namely, the heavens, the mortal realm, and the subterranean regions—the three vehicles (*yānatraya*) have been inscribed through the various cries of diverse beings by the compilers of the scriptures (*saṅgītikāraka*). The Śrāvakas [inscribed] the Śrāvaka vehicle; the Pratyekabuddhas, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; and the Bodhisattvas, the Pāramitā Mahāyāna and the Mantra Mahāyāna. This [teaching], consisting of cause and fruit, has been written down by various compilers in various regional languages, according to the scriptures and reasoning. When examined in this way, it is clear that the Blessed Buddha is the omniscient one who teaches the Dharma in the language of the omniscient; no other, such as Hari, Hara, and so forth, is so.

Now, if there were anyone among Hari, Hara, and the others who was fully endowed with these qualities, he too would be worthy of our salutation, worship, and honor—in every respect, for worldly purposes and for the sake of all sentient beings. Here, in the manuscript, the reading "nānādaśaḥ" is an addition; it also appears as "Me Lon sNa Tshogs" (nānādaśaiḥ) in the Tibetan manuscript.
Let them remain. By necessity.
Ṅa. rukma; Bho. Rugma (rugma).
Ṅa. *surammā*; Bho. *Suramma* (*suramma*). Regarding the phrase "of Hari, Hara, and others," this usage is intended to mean that [the names] were written in the manuscript.
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is said: "The devotion of the virtuous is toward qualities, not toward the Buddha, Īśvara, or others.
That devotion which is directed even toward those devoid of qualities is inert and born of inauspicious karma."
Dharmas that benefit sentient beings have been taught even by commoners;
yet those that harm sentient beings, though taught by the wise, are not dear to me.
Even a mother in this world is a rākṣasī with the intent to devour her own son;
since she has no compassion for her offspring, how could she have it for any other person?

Where even the killing of father and mother is declared to be dharma when caused by sacrifices and the like— what need is there to mention other [acts] by those brahmins intent on their own self-interest?
Thus:

"Therefore, in the world-system, the omniscient Buddha, the Blessed One, who is compassionate toward all sentient beings, is the omniscient teacher of Dharma through all sounds; likewise, Sucandra, Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the ten stages, is renowned in the Paramādibuddha as the requester and the compiler."

Thus ends the fourth chapter, the summary of the means for the Teacher and the Petitioner of the King of Tantras, beginning with the words "Omniscient One," etc., in the *Vimalaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja* following the *Mūlatantra*. Now, the summary of the Vajra-yoga is stated, beginning with the words "Yoga is Śrī Kālacakra," etc.

Here, in the Mantra system, relying upon both mundane and supramundane truths, the Blessed Buddha has indicated the meaning in two ways within the various tantras: one according to worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*), and the second according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

In this regard, that which is taught according to worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*) is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), while that which is [taught] from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
These two meanings are to be understood by disciples through the instructions of the Guru.
Thus, in all other tantras as well, the subject matter is twofold: one according to worldly convention, and the second from the perspective of ultimate reality.

That which exists by way of worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*) possesses color, arms, emblems, and shape; that which exists from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is devoid of color, arms, emblems, and shape.

Of these two, that which is taught by way of worldly convention is a phenomenon produced by the conceptualization of one's own mind for the sake of accomplishing mundane siddhis, both externally and internally, and it bestows the fruit of mundane siddhis.

That which is taught by means of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)—for the sake of accomplishing the supramundane Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) siddhi endowed with all excellent aspects—is free from the phenomena of one's own mental construction; it is directly perceived as a manifestation of one’s own mind appearing in the sky for yogins, like a prognostic image (*pratisenā*) in a mirror for a young girl.
It bestows the fruit of desired objects; the fruit is imperishable bliss, the gnosis-mind (*jñānacitta*).
The oneness of these two minds is the Dharma whose nature is wisdom and method (*prajñopāya*).
And in the manuscript, the reading is "apriyā me 'priyā me" (in the ṅa and ca recensions);
in the Hetuka [recension], it is "kāraṇekaḥ."
In the manuscript, the term "reciter" (*saṅgītikāraka*) does not appear in this chapter.

This is the summary of the teaching on the teacher and so forth: the Vajrayoga of great significance, the supreme immutable, the primordial Buddha, the partless, the Blessed One Kālacakra, the Vajrasattva renowned throughout all other tantras;
that very Blessed One is said to be the "svābhāvikakāya" of the Prajñāpāramitā within the causal system of the Pāramitānaya.

Likewise, in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-kārikā*, regarding the determination of the four activities, Maitreya said: "The essential body (*svābhāvika-kāya*), the body of perfect enjoyment (*sambhoga-kāya*), and another, the emanation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), as well as the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*) together with its activity—thus it is proclaimed as fourfold.

That very Blessed One, in the Mantra system characterized by the fruit, is called the Innate Joy (*sahajānanda*) and the Innate Body (*sahaja-kāya*). Free from subject and object, transcending the nature of consciousness, and non-abiding in either cyclic existence or nirvana, he is the assembly (*samāja*) of the Buddhas and the enclosure (*saṃvara*) of the Goddesses.
By this body of gnosis, there is innate equality of flavor; such is the definitive meaning.

In this regard, for this vajra-yoga—which is without causal succession (*niranvaya*), free from the extremes of eternalism and nihilism, transcending worldly analogies, abandoned by the notions of "is" and "is not," perceived directly as an object of realization, non-conceptualized by one's own mind like the reflection in a maiden’s mirror, possessing all aspects, arisen from space, being Samantabhadra, present in all sense faculties, abiding within the self of all sentient beings, innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), and devoid of cause and example—there exists an analogy for the destruction of all partisan grasping by yogins, due to its dissimilarity to the unity of existence and non-existence.

Just as in a worldly example: "Because of its dissimilarity to a jar, a sky-flower does not exist due to the absence of all existence," and likewise, "Because of its dissimilarity to a sky-flower, a jar exists due to the presence of all existence"—
these two serve as examples by virtue of their mutual dissimilarity.
Thus, because of the dissimilarity with annihilation, existence exists in every respect; because of the dissimilarity with existence, annihilation does not exist in the absence of everything.
By the word "annihilation," Nirvana is characterized as non-existence;

likewise, the world views these two—the jar and the sky-flower—as having a dissimilarity in their oneness. In conventional worldly truth, there is no oneness between this jar and this sky-flower, because they are mutually contradictory.
That which is existent does not become non-existent, and that which is non-existent does not become existent, by virtue of their respective natures as being and non-being.

For that reason by which the mind possesses the characteristic of existence, it does not possess the characteristic of non-existence; and for that reason by which the mind possesses the characteristic of non-existence, it does not possess the characteristic of existence, because of their mutual contradiction.

Furthermore, here, the form (*bimba*) consisting of emptiness and compassion—the pure mind, comparable to a young maiden’s reflection in a mirror—possesses no characteristic of form, because atoms do not exist; nor does it possess the characteristic of non-form, because it exists within emptiness.

Therefore, conventional reality has the nature of emptiness, and emptiness has the nature of conventional reality. Because it transcends worldly analogies, that mind exists which is a mind that is no-mind, free from the characteristics of the phenomena of permanence and annihilation, and inseparable from emptiness and compassion.

Because of the difference between the two minds from the perspective of ultimate truth, it is said in the words of the Tathāgata: "The non-dual Vajrayoga is that which transcends existence and non-existence, and is the exhaustion of being and non-being," because it is without causal continuity (*niranvaya*).
Regarding this, the Blessed One said in the Root Tantra: "And the Svabhāvakāya is in the self of all."
And because of all their modes of being, there is a single flavor between the sky-flower and [the other],
not by way of intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, the word "citta" does not appear here in the manuscript; however, between "viśvasya bimbasya" and "viśuddhacitta," a certain two-syllable word is seen in all the manuscripts, which is indeed indistinct.
The portion marked by square brackets is not present in the two Bhutanese manuscripts,
but it is present in the *Vimalaprabhā*. It is non-dual, having transcended existence and non-existence and being the exhaustion of both.

Vajrayoga is the great bliss inseparable from emptiness and compassion, transcending the nature of even the subtlest atom. It is devoid of empty phenomena and does not abide in formless nirvāṇa, because it is non-abiding in both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. Nor does it abide in both, because they are mutually contradictory;
there is no unity of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, just as there is none between shadow and sunlight.

Just as fire resides in the fire-drill wood (*nariṇī*), but does not reside in the wooden shaft (*sarakāṇḍa*), nor in the exertion of a man’s hands; so too, the Vajrayoga is to be understood by the yogin everywhere—in the external, the internal, and the supreme.
Here, that which is called "enlightenment in a single moment" (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodhi*) is the moment of supreme immutable bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*);
this one who is enlightened in a single moment becomes the manifester of all moments until the end of the count of breaths.
Then, at that moment, he became fully awakened as a *samyaksaṃbuddha*.

Here, in that very moment of fullness (*pūrṇakṣaṇa*) in which all Tathāgatas have attained perfect awakening, there is for all phenomena neither arising, nor abiding, nor cessation, because they are without continuity (*niranvayatvāt*).
In the moment in which the arising of phenomena occurs, in that same moment there is no abiding or cessation.

In this context, at the very moment in which stability (*sthiti*) occurs, there is neither disintegration (*bhaṅga*) nor arising (*utpāda*). And at the very moment in which the disintegration of all phenomena occurs, there is neither arising nor stability. Thus, in this sequential manner, it would follow that for all phenomena there could be no momentary arising, momentary stability, and momentary disintegration; yet these cannot occur simultaneously. For all phenomena, at one and the same time, the moments of arising, stability, and disintegration cannot be identical.

Now, as for the claim that from the moment of arising comes the moment of duration, from the moment of duration comes the moment of destruction, and from the moment of destruction arises the moment of arising—

this very thing is not tenable by way of ultimate reasoning; for here, a subsequent moment does not arise from a preceding moment that has not ceased, nor does it arise from one that has already ceased.

Just as a sprout does not arise from a destroyed seed, nor does it arise from a non-destroyed seed, so too, due to the absence of ultimate existence (*paramārthasattā*), there is no single moment (*ekakṣaṇa*); for unity and plurality are mutually exclusive.

Thus, regarding the statement that "he who is enlightened in a single moment is the manifestor of all moments": first, having become enlightened in the moment of supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*), he becomes the manifestor of twenty-one thousand six hundred moments of supreme unchanging bliss.

Beyond that, the absence of all moments—devoid of both unity and plurality—is the supreme non-dual yoga (*paramādvayayoga*), the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the Buddhas, because existence is devoid of existence.

As long as there is worldly existence (*laukika-sattā*), so long does the investigation into the one and the many persist, because phenomena (*dharmas*) are merely appearances within momentary consciousness (*kṣaṇika-citta*). When consciousness is said to be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) because it is free from momentary phenomena, then the "position of no-intrinsic-nature" (*niḥsvabhāva-pakṣa*) is declared by the Blessed One to be no position at all. For a "position" (*pakṣa*) is indeed an entity (*bhāva*) or a non-entity (*abhāva*); it is existence or non-existence, being or not-being, existent or non-existent, one or many, permanence or annihilation, saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, form or formlessness, sound or silence, the momentary or the non-momentary, passion or the absence of passion, hatred or the absence of hatred. [Note: The text from "in the full moment" (*pūrṇakṣaṇe*) up to "in which" (*yasmin*) is not present in the manuscript.]
In the chapter on sentient beings, the summary of the teaching and so forth begins with "delusion" and "non-delusion," and so on; because these are mutually dependent,
that which is devoid of such positions is the non-abiding nirvāṇa of the Buddhas, which is without intrinsic nature.
The Victors declare that reality (*tattva*) is knowledge devoid of single or multiple moments.

That very [reality] appears in four ways to sentient beings by the power of their own mental dispositions, and it also appears in sixteen aspects through the fourfold divisions of *ānanda*, *parama*, *virama*, and *sahaja*.
Then there is the bliss of body, the bliss of speech, the bliss of mind, and the bliss of gnosis;
likewise, the supreme bliss of body, the supreme bliss of speech, the supreme bliss of mind, and the supreme bliss of gnosis;
and likewise, the cessation-bliss of body, the cessation-bliss of speech, the cessation-bliss of mind, and the cessation-bliss of gnosis.
Thus, there is the innate bliss of body, the innate bliss of speech, the innate bliss of mind, and the innate bliss of gnosis.
When the yogi knows reality in these sixteen aspects, he is called by the Blessed One "one who knows the sixteen-aspected reality.
That very reality is called the Sahajakāya (Innate Body).
From that arises the *dharmakāya*, from that the *saṃbhogakāya*, and from that the *nirmāṇakāya*.

Likewise, there are the innate speech, innate mind, and innate gnosis; the *dharma*-speech, *dharma*-mind, and *dharma*-gnosis; the *saṃbhoga*-speech, *saṃbhoga*-mind, and *saṃbhoga*-gnosis; and the *nirmāṇa*-speech, *nirmāṇa*-mind, and *nirmāṇa*-gnosis. Thus, by the power of the mental dispositions (*cittādhimukti*) of sentient beings, reality appears in sixteen aspects. That very [reality] is the Innate Body (*sahajakāya*), purified by the liberation of emptiness, the Gnosis-Vajra, the Omniscient One, whose nature is both Wisdom and Means—the Purified Yoga.
That very *dharmakāya* is called the *dharmayoga*, which is the *jñānakāya* consisting of wisdom and means, the adamantine mind purified by the signless liberation (*animittavimokṣa*).

That very same [body] is the *sambhogakāya*, which is called the *mantrayoga*, consisting of wisdom and means, the adamantine speech with the form of the sun, purified by the wishless liberation (*apraṇihitavimokṣa*).

That very same [body] is the *nirmāṇakāya*, which is called the *saṃsthānayoga*, consisting of wisdom and means, the adamantine body with eyes as broad as lotus petals, purified by the unconditioned liberation (*anabhisaṃskāravimokṣa*).
Thus, Vajrapāṇi asked the Buddha regarding this fourfold Vajrayoga:

the Wisdom-Vajra, purified by the liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*), whose nature is wisdom and means, is the Sahajakāya, having attained omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and being all-knowing because of his all-seeing nature;

the Mind-Vajra, purified by the liberation of the signless (*animitta-vimokṣa*), whose nature is wisdom and means, is the Dharmakāya; and the Knowledge-Body (*jñānakāya*), having attained the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), because it abides in supreme immutable bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*).

The Speech-Vajra, whose nature is wisdom and skillful means, is the Sambhogakāya, purified by the liberation of the wishless (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa*), having attained the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*); it possesses a body like the sun because it simultaneously teaches the mundane and supramundane Dharma through the voices of infinite, infinite sentient beings. Thus, the Body-Vajra, whose nature is wisdom and skillful means, is the Nirmāṇakāya, purified by the liberation of non-activity (*anabhisaṃskāra-vimokṣa*), having attained the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); its eyes are as broad as lotus petals because it simultaneously manifests the miraculous display of an array of bodies in all their aspects through infinite, infinite emanation-bodies.

Thus, he who is enlightened in a single moment is the Wisdom-Vajra (*jñānavajra*), the seer of all objects, enlightened through the five aspects, the Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*), and the supreme immutable bliss; or, he who is perfectly enlightened in twenty aspects is the Speech-Vajra (*vāgvajra*), whose reality-meaning consists of twelve aspects, and who teaches the Dharma through the voices of all sentient beings;

he who is enlightened through the Net of Illusion (*māyājālābhisambuddha*) is the Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*), the knower of reality in sixteen aspects, whose body is emanated through infinite nets of illusion.

In this context, the fourfold vajra-mind, when purified, possesses the characteristics of the four bodies (*catur-kāya*); it is the non-existent mind that is the fourth mind, consisting of the two sense organs smeared with the stains of irresistible passion, which is the yoga of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
(The *bhaga*-organ.)
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is stated that the fourth mind (*turyacitta*) is the mind of non-existence (*abhāvacitta*); the Svābhāvikakāya is the Omniscient One,
and the mind of non-existence— which is the state of deep sleep overcome by darkness— is the Dharmakāya, the Gnosis Body (*jñānakāya*).
The mind that is the non-existence of the dream-mind, wherein existence and non-existence are produced by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is the *saṃbhogakāya*, whose body is like the sun.
The mind that is the non-existence of the waking-mind, characterized by the perception of various conceptual entities, is the *nirmāṇakāya*, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals.
This *vajrayoga* is to be explained in detail in the *Jñānapaṭala*; in this *Lokadhātupaṭala*, it is presented merely by way of summary.
One should inquire about this yoga, consisting of gnosis, mind, speech, and body, in the *Śrī Kālacakra*, the king of tantras;
at what time? At the time of the Kali age.
What is "kali"? It is the letter *ka*; it is the series of consonants beginning with the letter *ka*.
The letter *ka* is the mouth of all consonants because it is indicated at the beginning; or alternatively, it should be understood as being of the nature of *rajas*.
Now, the summary of the purpose, the purpose of the purpose, and the purpose of that purpose is stated: "for the sake of liberation for men."

For the sake of liberation for human beings, first of all, the purpose is to act for the benefit of sentient beings through such means as entering the maṇḍala; then, by the power of meditating on the form of the maṇḍala-circle through the accumulation of merit, and by the power of meditating on the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the purpose is the accomplishment of mundane siddhis through the sequence of heroism (*vīrakrama*) and the sequence of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhānakrama*). Thus, there is the "purpose of the purpose" (*prayojana-prayojana*), which is the purpose of each subsequent purpose.

In this realm of space, through the cultivation of the non-conceptual mind by means of signs such as smoke and so forth—by means of the Mahāmudrā which possesses all aspects and universal form, and which is the means for achieving supreme unchanging bliss—one attains Buddhahood and Vajrasattva. Through the two accumulations of merit and wisdom, beings attain the state of a *sattva* in this very life; this is the summary of the purpose and the purpose of the purpose. This Yoga of the Supreme Primordial Buddha (*Paramādibuddha*) was taught by Buddhas of the past, is being taught by those of the present, and will be taught by those of the future.

By means of the past, present, and future times; by means of the past, present, and future moments; and by means of infinite, infinite Tathāgatas, for the sake of infinite, infinite sentient beings in infinite, infinite Buddha-fields, this has been taught, is being taught, and will be taught for the attainment of Buddhahood by the assemblies.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Summary of the Teacher and Other Elements, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the commentary on the *Laghu-kālacakra-tantra-rāja* following the *Mūla-tantra*.
The reading [is as follows]. It does not exist in the Ś manuscript;
it does not exist in the Bho manuscript;
it does not exist in the Bho manuscript.
d.
Regarding that, in the manuscript designated as Ṅa, there is an additional reading here: "in the *Dvādaśasāhasrikā*."

[In the chapter on] the summary of the mandala initiation and so forth: the summary of the mandala initiation and so forth. Now, having been requested by Sūryaratha, the Blessed Mañjuśrī, in his emanation-body as Yaśonarendra, spoke with a second verse regarding the request of Sucandra, which had been prophesied by the Tathāgata in the Paramādibuddha: "Emptiness and gnosis, the drop, the bearer of the supreme vajra, the Buddhas, gods, and asuras; externally in the body and internally in the [subtle] elements, the Puruṣa consisting of twenty-five principles."

Explain correctly this measurement of the universe within the body, the construction of the three worlds, the bestower of enjoyment upon gods and asuras, as well as the mandala and the consecration of the Teacher of gods and men.

Here, the Blessed One spoke of the "Great Void of Five Syllables," the "Void of the Bindu," and the "Six Syllables" for the purpose of requesting [the teaching] and for the sake of summarizing the Six Families and so forth. I shall now explain this with the words beginning "The Void," and so on.

Here, first, by means of the verse of request, the hidden meaning of the Tantra is revealed; once revealed, it becomes easy to understand for those of immature intellect as it is explained below. Therefore, it must be stated briefly at the outset of the commentary.

Here, through these designations beginning with "The Void," entities that are both unseen and seen are revealed—those which are beyond the range of the individual sense faculties and yet are within the range of the individual sense faculties.
In all cases, whether an entity exists or does not exist, linguistic convention is preceded by conceptual designation (*saṃjñā*). This is as in the case of "sky-flower" and "jar.

Just as non-existence designated by the term "sky-flower" does not become existence, so too existence designated by the term "jar" does not become non-existence; it is expressed by its own specific designation.

Thus, those entities which have been taught by the Tathāgata in various tantras and other scriptures through technical designations, regional designations, mantra-syllable designations, and individual syllable designations, and which have been recorded by the compilers of the teachings—all of these are to be understood by yogins according to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) and not the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*);
for in this context, even a single non-entity or entity has various designations.

Therefore, yogis should not form conceptual constructions regarding the designations of even a single entity that has been described through various names; for they must rely on the reality of the object as it is pointed out by a true guru and thoroughly examined like gold.

Here, this great person (*mahāpuruṣapudgala*) consisting of the six elements is subsumed by the designations of "void" (*śūnya*) and so forth, through these fourteen syllables: "void," "knowledge" (*jñāna*), "drop" (*bindu*), and "holder of the supreme vajra. They are as follows: the aggregate of knowledge (*jñānaskandha*), the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), the element of knowledge (*jñānadhātu*), the space element (*ākāśadhātu*), mind (*manas*), ear (*śrotra*), sound (*śabda*), the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), the divine faculty (*divyendriya*), the bhaga, the emission of urine, and the emission of semen. The state of being free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇatā*), their state of having a single flavor (*samarasatva*), and their state of being unified into one (*ekalolībhūtatva*) are called "void"; it is not a total non-existence, because it is to be personally realized (*saṃvedyatva*) by the yogi. That very [state] is called the "unstruck" (*anāhata*) by the Victors.

The sign of this Unstruck (*anāhata*) is a mere line in the shape of a knife-blade located in the middle between the left and right, front and back, which is unutterable and is called the "Great Void of the First Syllable.
Then there is "Knowledge" (*jñāna*). Here, the word "and" (*ca*) is indicated for the purpose of conjunction, because it conveys the sense of a combination.
By this designation "Knowledge," the third void is to be understood; namely: the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*), the eye, taste, the hand, and movement.

The state of these [elements] being without obscuration, their state of equal flavor (*samarasatva*), and their state of having become a single fusion is "knowledge" (*jñāna*), the third syllable, the "Great Void" (*mahāśūnya*).
Its symbolic sign is two dots (*bindu*) to the right of the central unstruck sign (*anāhatacinha*), which are not to be pronounced;
this is the verse of the request (*adhyeṣaṇāvṛtta*).

a. In the manuscript Ka, the phrase "by means of the designations of single syllables for the preceding flowers and so forth" does not appear in the *Vimalaprabhā*. By this designation "bindu," the fourth void is to be understood from the preceding letter *ca*; namely: the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the water element (*toyadhātu*), the tongue, form (*rūpa*), feet, and grasping (*ādāna*).

The state of these [elements] being free from obscuration, their state of equal flavor (*samarasatva*), and their state of having become a single fusion is the "Bindu," the fourth syllable, the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*). Its symbolic sign is a single Bindu to the left of the central sign, which is not to be uttered; it is the "Bearer of the Supreme Vajra."

*Varaś ca varaś ca kuliśadharaś ca varakuliśadharam*: due to the single *ca* at the beginning of the *dvandva* compound, these three are to be understood as having the designation "empty" (*śūnya*), while the first *vara* has the designation "excellent" (*vara*) as stated in the second [section] on emptiness. Namely: the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), the wind element (*vāyudhātu*), olfactory contact (*ghrāṇasaṃsparśa*), the faculty of speech (*vāgindriya*), and the excretion of feces (*viṭsrāva*).

The state of these being without obscuration (*nirāvaraṇatā*), their state of having a single flavor (*samarasatva*), and their state of being unified into one (*ekalolībhūtatva*) is the "excellent" (*vara*); thus, the second syllable is empty, its sign of designation being a mere line in the shape of a staff to the east of the sign of the central *anāhata*, which is unpronounceable.

By the designation "second excellent," it is called the fifth emptiness. It is as follows: the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*), the body faculty (*kāyendriya*), odor (*gandha*), the anus (*apāyu*), and speech (*ālāpa*).
The state of these [five] being unobstructed, having a single flavor (*samarasatva*), and having become one mass is the "excellent five-syllable void.
Its symbolic sign (*saṃjñācihna*) is the shape of the letter *ha* (halākṛti) located to the west of the central unstruck sign (*anāhataciṅga*), which is not to be articulated.

Thus, by this aforementioned sequence, through the five [elements] having become one mass, the five-syllable great void is the syllable *vaṃ*, Vajrasattva, called the Great Bliss Vajra (*mahāsukhakuliśa*).
In this context, the five syllables designated as vowels are not to be uttered; they are as follows: in the center, the void of the letter *a* in the form of a curved knife (*karttikā*);
on the right, the void of the letter *ṛ* as two dots (*bindu*);
and on the left, the void of the letter *u* as a single dot (*bindu*).
In the east, there is the form of a staff (daṇḍa) devoid of the vowel *i*;
in the west, there is the shape of a plow (hala) devoid of the vowel *lṛ*.
In this manner, the modifications consisting of long vowels, guṇa, vṛddhi, and yaṇ-adeśa are to be understood.

Thus, the syllable *vaṃ* consists of five vowels, is the great emptiness (*mahāśūnya*), has the nature of non-referential compassion, transcends the reality of atoms, resembles a reflected image (*pratisenā*), and is accessible only to yogins.

Herein lie the vowels for the aggregates of gnosis (*jñāna-skandha*) and consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), and so forth; namely: the aggregate of gnosis is *aṃ*, and the aggregate of consciousness is *a*.
The element of consciousness is *aḥ*,
the element of space is *ā*,
and the faculty of mind is *aṃ*.
The ear,
sound, and the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu) are A.
Bhaga is indeed the emission of urine; Haḥ is the divine organ. Haṃ.
The emission of semen—alas!
these [channels], being struck in the middle and free from obscuration, are to be understood by the mark known as the "crow-sign" (kākākāra);
such is the aggregate of mental formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
The wind element is *ī*,
the nose faculty is *e*,
and touch is *ai*.
The faculty of speech, the emission of semen,
and these aforementioned unobstructed [states] are to be understood as having the form of a staff.
In the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha): the fire element (tejo-dhātu),
the eye faculty (cakṣur-indriya).
Rasa is taste; the sense organ is the tongue (pāṇīndriya); Ra is movement; Rā is speech.
These are to be understood by the sign of two unobscured *bindu*s on the right; thus,
in the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*),
there is the water element (*toyadhātu*), which is *ū*.
The tongue-faculty has form as its object,
the foot-faculty is for movement, and the hand-faculty is for grasping; these are to be understood as unobscured by means of the drop-mark (bindu) to the north of the central sign.
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is *lṛ*; the earth element (pṛthivīdhātu) is *lū*;
the body faculty (kāyendriya) is *al*.
The object of smell is *āl*,
the anus-faculty is *la*,
the speech is *ālāpa*, and the [anus] is *lā*.
These [consonants] in the western [group] are to be understood as being without coverings (nirāvaraṇa), characterized by the mark of the plow (halākṛti).

These are the thirty-six divisions consisting of the modifications of vowels (*svara*), qualities (*guṇa*), increments (*vṛddhi*), and *yaṇ*-substitutions (*yaṇādeśa*). Where the aggregates (*skandha*) are separately divided into thirty-six types, there the six tastes (*rasa*) are taken in place of the aggregates: sour (*amla*), astringent (*kaṣāya*), bitter (*tikta*), pungent (*kaṭu*), sweet (*madhura*), and salty (*lavaṇa*).
This is the agent (*kartṛ*).
O, Reg bya (spa) ka!
[In the chapter on the middle sign, following the north, is] the summary of the initiation of the mandala and so forth; and [there are] salts.
Aṃ, a, i, ṛ, u, lṛ—these are the six tastes; the remainder is according to the previously stated rule.
This very Great Void of five syllables, consisting of thirty-six principles, is called the Vajra by the Victors.
He who holds that is the Vajradhara;

he is the drop (bindu), the void, the six-syllabled, the letter E, the source of phenomena (dharmodaya), whose form is the emptiness of all aspects. For example: the aggregate of consciousness, the element of space, and the ear.
The *dharmadhātu* is the emission of the seminal essence (*bhaga-śukra*).

Its unobscured emptiness (*nirāvaraṇa-śūnyatā*) is omniform. Above the one who does not rely on the middle [channel], its symbolic sign (*saṃjñā-cihna*) consists of the letter *ka*, which is the first consonant of the *ka*-group; it is the first [syllable] without vocalization, the "drop-emptiness" (*bindu-śūnya*).
The aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha),
the wind element (vāyudhātu), and the sense-base of smell (ghrāṇasparśa).

The emission of speech for these is unobscured emptiness (*nirāvaraṇa-śūnyatā*), which is the prior sign of all aspects. Its preceding conceptual sign consists of the *ca*-group; having not uttered the consonant *ca*, there is the second [element], the "bindu-emptiness."
The aggregate of sensation, the fire element, and the eye faculty.

The movement of their hands is unobstructed emptiness in all its aspects; on the right of the right-hand symbol is its symbolic sign, consisting of the *ṭa*-group, the consonant *ṭa*, which is unutterable and is the third, the "bindu-emptiness."
The aggregate of perception, the water element, and the form of the tongue.

The unobstructed emptiness of their faculty of feet and grasping is of all aspects; in the north of the northern [direction], its symbolic sign consists of the *p*-group (*pavarga*), specifically the consonant *pa*, which is not to be articulated, and the fourth [vowel], the drop-emptiness (*binduśūnya*).
The aggregate of form consists of the earth element,
the body faculty, and odor.

The anus is their unobscured emptiness in all its aspects; it is the sign of the final [letter] following the last sign, consisting of the *tavarga* class, the consonant *ta*, which is not to be pronounced, and is the fifth, the drop-emptiness (*binduśūnya*).
The aggregate of gnosis,
the element of gnosis,
the mind, sound, the divine faculty, and the emission of urine.

The unobscured emptiness (*nirāvaraṇa-śūnyatā*) of these [syllables] is in all its aspects beneath the central unstruck sign (*anāhata-cihna*). Its conceptual sign is the letter *sa*, consisting of the entire group of vowels, the syllable *sa* which is inexpressible, the sixth, the "drop-emptiness" (*binduśūnya*).
