Thus, the six-syllabled Dharma-source (*dharmodaya*), the wielder of the vajra, is the letter *e*; this is emptiness with an object (*sālambā*), having the nature of a reflected image (*pratisenā*).

Here, the consonants of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and so forth are: k, kh, g, gh, ṅ; c, ch, j, jh, ñ; ṭ, ṭh, ḍ, ḍh, ṇ; p, ph, b, bh, m; t, th, d, dh, n; s, ṣ, ś, ka, ha, ya, va, la, kṣ.
Furthermore, the differentiation of the aggregates, elements, and so forth is to be understood through the division of these vowels and consonants into short and long [quantities].

By way of bodily division, the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense faculties (*indriya*) consist of short vowels and consonants as their phenomena (*dharma*); the elements (*dhātu*) and objects (*viṣaya*) consist of long vowels and consonants as their phenomena. Through the division of the modifications of the elements, there are thirty-six elements: six aggregates, and by way of the division of the six sense faculties and so forth, there are thirty-six aggregates. Namely: the six tastes, the six elements, the six sense faculties, the six objects, the six organs of action (*karmendriya*), and the six objects of the organs of action—these are the six modifications of the taste-elements;
and the six consciousnesses, such as auditory consciousness and the rest.

Thus, the six formations (*saṃskāra*), the six feelings (*vedanā*), the six perceptions (*saṃjñā*), the six aggregates of form (*rūpaskandha*), and the six aggregates of gnosis (*jñānaskandha*)—these transformations of the aggregates are to be explained in detail as they will be stated later; here they are merely indicated by way of summary.

In this context, the group of vowels consisting of five syllables, which is the great void (*mahāśūnya*), the semen, and the moon, is called "the drop-void" (*binduśūnya*). The group of consonants consisting of six syllables, which is the passion (*rajas*) and the sun, is called "the drop-void."

In this context, semen is the moon, represented by the syllable *vaṃ*, which is the vajra; passion is the sun, represented by the syllable *e*, which is the lotus. The unification of these two—the vajra and the lotus—is Vajrasattva.
Thus, the vajra is supreme bliss, gnosis, and semen.
Sattva is the arising of the letter E; it does not exist in manuscript Ka. It exists in manuscript Śrāva.
O! In manuscript *ka*, it appears that "va" follows "sa";
in manuscript *kha*, "jñāna" is absent.
In the *Vimalaprabhā*: "The reflection of wisdom in all its aspects is the object of knowledge; it is the sun."

The reality (*tattva*), which is free from obscuration and unified as a single essence through the empowerment of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), brings about the welfare of the world.
This very state constitutes the single yoga of body, speech, mind, and wisdom, and serves as the cause for the four faces:
wisdom is the western face, yellow; consciousness is the eastern face, black; the moon is the body-face, white in the north; and the sun is the speech-face, red in the south.
In these two, the moon and the sun, six elements each are to be understood according to their secondary and primary distinctions;
they are the constituents of earth, water, fire, air, taste, and great taste.
Among these, in the case of semen (*śukra*), three are manifest and three are unmanifest.

The water element, the wind element, and the taste element— these elements are manifested in the semen; in the menstrual blood (rajas), the designation of the space element arises from the taste element,
and thus three are manifested while three remain unmanifested.
The earth element, the fire element, and the great flavor element— these elements arise in the *rajas*;
here, the "great flavor" is designated as the knowledge element (*jñānadhātu*),
while the remaining [elements] do not arise in the semen or the *rajas*.
Thus, for those born from a womb, the three elements produced from the moon and sun become respectively body,
speech, and mind; that is to say, the elements of the moon are the body, speech, and mind of method (upāya),
while the elements of the sun are the body, speech, and mind of wisdom (prajñā), due to their arising from semen and ovum.
These elements are the six families of the six sense organs and so forth.
Thus, the families of body, speech, and mind, together with the family of essential nature (*svabhāva*), become four families;

the three bodies become four bodies; and the three states become four states. Likewise, the five element-families together with the gnosis-element become six families; similarly, for those born from a womb, the five aggregate-families together with the gnosis-aggregate become six families.

For a girl, up until the age of twelve, and for a man, up until the age of sixteen; for a girl, up until the time of her menses, the triad of families (trikula) or pentad of families (pañcakula) is to be understood;
for a man, up until the time of the emission of semen, the triad of families or pentad of families is to be understood;
at the time when the element of gnosis (jñānadhātu) arises, both possess the tetrad of families (catuḥkula) or hexad of families (ṣaṭkula) until death.
Likewise, the Blessed One said in the *Mūlatantra*: "The three families, the five families, and indeed the hundred families are of one single nature.
Now, those belonging to these families are described as "Buddhas" and so forth.

Here, "Buddhas" refers to the six aggregates, such as gnosis (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*); and by the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "gods and asuras," the six [faculties] beginning with the mental faculty (*manas*) and the sense organs are included. Thus, there are the six elements (*dhātu*) and the six objects (*viṣaya*).
Likewise, the six wrathful deities (krodhas) are the six organs of action (karmendriyas),
and the six wrathful goddesses (krodhadevis) are the six functions of the organs of action; these deities will be described as being located at the twelve joints of the hands and feet.

Thus, there are eight Yoginīs beginning with Śvacikā; the Asuras are the Nāga kings; and the goddesses begin with Śvānāsyā. Now, for the purpose of leading in the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthikas*), "Prakṛti" and "Puruṣa" are discussed. Thus the Blessed One said in another Tantra: "Mahāmāyā is the great fierce one who effects the destruction of beings; she herself is the creator, she herself is the destroyer, she herself is the king, she herself is the lord. This is false. In the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no creator or destroyer, nor any other phenomenon (*dharma*) imagined by the non-Buddhist outsiders, such as *prakṛti*, *puruṣa*, and so forth.
The nature of the non-Buddhist schools consists of twenty-four principles, with the *puruṣa* as the twenty-fifth;
therein, "the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is unchanging" (*Sāṃkhyakārikā* 3).
This fourth state (*turyāvasthā*) is the progenitor of sentient beings, O Bhagavan. (Cha Ses = *aṃśa*)
kha. [She who] brings about the withdrawal of her own [nature], and kha. [she who is] the agent of withdrawal;
[this is] the summary of the initiation in the mandala and so forth, in the section on the space-element.
"The seven beginning with the Mahat are both evolvents and evolutes" (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 3);
thus, earth, water, fire, air, mind, intellect, and ego— these sixteen are the evolutes.

The twenty-four principles consist of the five sense organs, the five objects of the senses, the five organs of action, and the divine organ (the mind). The *puruṣa* is neither a principle (*prakṛti*) nor a modification (*vikṛti*).
Here, because the *puruṣa* is all-pervasive, it is neither a principle nor a modification; it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
It is established that [the universe] consists of twenty-five principles, both externally and within the body.

Externally, there are the five elements; Rāhu, Sūrya (Sun), and Candra (Moon) make eight, which constitute *prakṛti* (primordial nature). Then there are the five planets beginning with Maṅgala (Mars), the five sense organs, the five objects of the senses, and the six tastes of earth and the other elements—these sixteen are the *vikāras* (evolutes).

Now, some say that the six living bodies (jīvakāya), beginning with the sense faculties (indriya), constitute the measure of the universe within the body; this "construction of the three worlds" is to be explained in the chapter on the inner self (adhyātmapaṭala).

Here, "the three worlds" refers to the external world-system (*lokadhātu*); "in the internal" refers to the body; "its construction" is to be explained according to the sequence that will be described—this is the rule of action—and it "bestows enjoyment upon the gods and asuras."
In this system, for the gods it is a meal by day, and for the asuras it is a meal by night;
likewise, there is the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) and the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana).
Explain this correctly: the maṇḍala and the empowerment of the Teacher of gods and men.
Here, according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), explain the powder maṇḍala by means of the casting of powders and the laying of lines;

however, according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is again devoid of the laying of lines and devoid of the casting of powders—devoid of the mind that conceptualizes the forms, colors, arms, and postures of the deities, and devoid of meditative cultivation—and is in every respect like a reflection in a mirror within the expanse of space.
Likewise, the worldly consecrations are seven: water, crown, ribbon, vajra-bell, great vow, name, and authorization;
likewise the higher ones are the vase, secret, and wisdom-knowledge; and the eleventh is the supramundane consecration, which is the fourth—explain all this correctly.
For what reason?

In this noble land, in the future time, Vajrācāryas will become plunderers of wealth; for the sake of wealth, they will go to the houses of wealthy men who are conceited about their riches and sell the Dharma;
out of greed for wealth, they will bestow supramundane consecrations upon those who are unworthy.
First they will become servants to kings and others, and later they will become gurus;
yet they will not grant the supramundane empowerment even to other noble-minded individuals who are devoid of wealth but have abandoned the ten paths of unwholesome action;
instead, they will cause them to experience affliction.
Driven by material gain, they will proclaim the Vajra-word to wicked beings;
others, likewise ignorant of the Vajra-word, will engage in mutual disputes.
Out of pride in their own scholarship, even while failing to understand the meaning of the Tantra, they will compose commentaries on the Tantra.
The beings belonging to the host of Māra, acting as teachers for sentient beings, will teach the vajra-word perversely;
they will reveal to those of childish intellect that the Buddha-knowledge is the bliss born of the two organs.

They will claim that the third is the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*), and that the fourth is that very same thing again, using the word "thus" (*tathā*) to say that the third knowledge is the Buddha-knowledge—asserting, as it were, that there is no distinction between cause and fruit, in accordance with what was spoken by the Blessed One.

Thus, having seen that in the future time corrupt teachers will prevail, the Blessed Buddha did not reveal the fourth initiation of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*) in any of the other tantras;
for in the Noble Land [India], people, out of pride in their scholarship, will see the books and become teachers of the Vajrayāna without having received the initiation.

Therefore, in all the *laghutantras* and *mūlatantras*, the fourth wisdom-knowledge—the cultivation of Mahāmudrā and the path of smoke and so forth—is well-guarded, though it is revealed in some *mūlatantras*.
Furthermore, in this *Paramādibuddha*, both the root tantra (*mūlatantra*) and the concise tantra (*laghutantra*), the fourth [empowerment], the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*), is manifest;

likewise, the cultivation of Mahāmudrā and the path beginning with smoke (*dhūmādimārga*) are manifest. Yet, these have not come down through the lineage of the Vajrācāryas, unlike the means for achieving external accomplishments through mantra-deities and the *Vīrakrama* and *Svādhiṣṭhānakrama*, which have come down through the lineage of the gurus.
In the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*, the reading is: "The seven, beginning with the Great One (*mahat*), are both nature (*prakṛti*) and transformation (*vikṛti*)."

In the *kārikā*, the reading is "the sixteenfold is the transformation" (*ṣoḍaśakastu vikāraḥ*). In the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*, the reading is "the Puruṣa is neither the primordial nature nor the transformation" (*na prakṛtir na vikṛtiḥ puruṣaḥ*).

Regarding the phrase "not come" (*nāgatam*), in the *Vimalaprabhā*: this sequence of purification, which bestows the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, is clearly set forth in the book of the *Paramādibuddha*. Having understood the mental dispositions of worthy beings to the north of the Śītā River, it was taught by the Blessed One and written down in a book by Vajrapāṇi, taking the *Nāmasaṅgīti* as his authority, so that beings would become free from doubt. Therefore, the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the entire system of Mantras was indicated by the Blessed One to Vajrapāṇi within the *Nāmasaṅgīti* regarding the Mantra Vehicle.

Therefore, those who do not know the Paramādibuddha do not know the Nāmasaṅgīti; those who do not know the Nāmasaṅgīti do not know the Jñānakāya of Vajradhara; those who do not know the Jñānakāya of Vajradhara do not know the Mantrayāna; and those who do not know the Mantrayāna are all transmigrators, devoid of the path of the Blessed Lord Vajrasattva. Thus, the Paramādibuddha should be heard by true disciples seeking liberation, and it should be taught by a genuine guru.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, the summary of the initiation into the mandala and so forth, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja* following the *Mūlatantra*. 6.

(7) Summary of the Compendium of World Systems (ka) Summary of the Response: Now, the response of the Blessed One from the *Paramādibuddha* has been compiled by Mañjuśrī, the compiler, in the third verse; that very [verse] I shall expand upon, beginning with "I am pleased," etc.: "I am pleased with you, O Sucandra, preeminent among gods, humans, rākṣasas, daityas, and nāgas! This which was asked by you has been understood by those free from passion within the lineage of the supreme sages."

O Lord of Men, listen as I explain the entire yoga within the body, beginning with Nirvāṇa and ending with the Earth, together with the movement of the stages, as well as the maṇḍala and the consecration. 3.
"I am pleased with you, Sucandra"—this is the address.
O Sucandra, I am pleased with you.
Why?
"Because this *Kālacakra-yoga* which you have asked about has not been known by the most excellent gods, humans, and others, therefore I am pleased.

Here, "the most excellent gods" refers to those beginning with the Cāturmahārājakāyikas and ending with those who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*);
"humans" refers to universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) and so forth.
The *rākṣasas* are those such as Nairṛta and others; the *daityas* are those such as Aparājita and others; the *nāgas* are those such as Ananta and others.

The noble Ānanda and others who are free from passion, as well as the supreme sages such as Nārada and others—by these lineages, including the preeminent gods, humans, and so forth, the Kālacakra yoga, beginning with Nirvāṇa and ending with Earth, has not been known.

Nirvāṇa is the element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*) which is its beginning; at the end is Earth (*dharā*), the ground; and since they are not explicitly mentioned in the middle, [it includes] the elements of space, wind, fire, and water.
These elements, beginning with space, are the pervaded, while the gnosis-element (jñānadhātu) is the pervader.

Thus, the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader is yoga—as the Blessed One has said: "Earth, water, fire, air, the element of space, and consciousness—this is called the sixfold element, the Great Person (mahāpuruṣapudgala)."
"Accompanied by the movement of the phonemes (*padagatisahita*).
The phoneme (*pada*) is twofold, consisting of vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*).
The "movement of the phonemes" (*padagati*) is the articulation of vowels and consonants at the places of production—the throat, palate, head, lips, and teeth.
"Accompanied by that movement" refers to verbal expression through the convention of mantra.
In this context, the convention is twofold: first, the convention of mantra; second, the convention of suchness (*tathatā*).
Therein, the convention of mantra is verbal expression, which is worldly; the convention of suchness is ultimate, being devoid of the utterance of speech.
Where there is a convention for verbal expression, there the designations of mantras such as *oṃ*, *āḥ*, and *hūṃ* apply;
where there is a convention for suchness (*tathatā*), there [the letter] *a* is the gateway to all phenomena because they are unarisen from the beginning.

Likewise, in the *Māyājāla* in sixteen thousand [stanzas], the Blessed One said: "For example: The Blessed Buddha, the Perfectly Awakened One, is born from the syllable *A*. The syllable *A* is the foremost of all phonemes, of great significance, and the supreme syllable. It is indeed the Great Breath (*mahāprāṇa*), unarisen, the foremost cause of all verbal expression, yet devoid of vocal utterance; it is the perfect luminosity of all speech."

Furthermore, in that very same *Samādhijālapaṭala*, it is said: "The syllableless, the source of mantra, the three great mantra families, the five-syllabled, the great void, the void of the bindu, and the six-syllabled—this is suchness, the ultimate convention taught by the Blessed One in the Mantra Vehicle. Likewise, [it is] nirvāṇa, the element of gnosis, the unstruck (*anāhata*)."
"Not uttered" means it does not possess the characteristics of uttered vowels and consonants.

Thus, the Blessed One has stated that the nature of the mantra-convention, beginning with the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), is characterized by verbal expression, which is the quality of being uttered from the throat and other vocal organs.
In this regard, the letters *a*, *kuha*, and the visarga (*visarjanīya*) are gutturals (*kaṇṭhya*).
The *icuyaśa* sounds are palatals (*tālavya*); the *ṛṭuraṣa* sounds are retroflexes (*mūrddhanya*); the *upūpadhmānīya* sounds are labials (*oṣṭhya*).
The letters *ḷ*, *tula*, and *sā* are dental; thus, there are those belonging to two places of articulation, three places, four places, and five places.
It should be understood that there are both mantras and *kūṭa*-mantras, by means of the convention of uttered mantras (*pravyāhāra-mantra*).
And all of those are conceptual in form, serving as indicators for things possessing conceptualization in order to achieve worldly accomplishments;

however, that which is free from the utterance of speech, the conventional signifier of suchness, the ultimate Mahāmudrā devoid of the accomplishments of Karmamudrā and Jñānamudrā, has been taught by the Blessed One in all the King of Tantras for the sake of achieving accomplishment.

"O Lord of Men, listen as I explain this entire yoga within the body; and [I shall explain] the mandala and the consecration according to the sequence to be described, for the sake of all sentient beings attaining the state free from obscurations"—this is the summary of the Blessed One’s reply.

The Summary of the Compendium of World-Spheres: Now, I shall explain the compendium of world-spheres taught by the Blessed One through the fourth verse of the *Paramādibuddha*, as compiled by Mañjuśrī, beginning with "From time, in the voids..."—from time, in the voids, arise wind, fire, water, the continents, mountains, oceans, the constellations, the moon, sun, stars, planets, sages, and nāgas.

And those who have become gods in the world-system of Vimalaprabhā, as well as those born from the animal womb, humans of four kinds upon the various surfaces of the earth, and hell-beings, have arisen within the void like salt in water; and the egg-born have arisen within the egg. || 4 ||
In this Mantra system, the Blessed One has stated that the practitioner (*mantrin*) is one who has emerged from the three vehicles and is established in the fruit of the single vehicle.
However, he who does not understand the intentional terminology (*abhisandhi*) of the three vehicles becomes, over time, lost to the path of omniscience.

Not understanding the various types of intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*) within the Mantra vehicle, he commits acts such as the taking of life and the consumption of the property of monasteries and temples; by adhering to the positions of eternalism and nihilism, and being attached to the enjoyment of external objects, he goes to hell after having defiled the Three Jewels under the pretext of being a teacher (*ācārya*).
In this regard, four elders are to be propitiated by sentient beings for the sake of the next world and this world.

Among these, the one advanced in knowledge— a Vajrācārya who has attained the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), reached the stage of *muditā*, and may be either a monk or a householder— is declared by the Blessed One to be equal to ten monks and worthy of worship.

In his absence, one who is advanced in asceticism (*tapovṛddha*) and wears the saffron robe (*kāṣāyadhārī*) is always to be venerated by householders and teachers, even by ministers with many years of consecration (*varṣāgra*), because of his seniority in asceticism and because householders lack such specialized knowledge.

A scholar (*paṇḍita*) who is senior in learning (*śrutavṛddha*) is worthy of honor; he illuminates the Teaching (*śāsana*), subdues opponents and the hosts of Māra, and these are to be propitiated by sentient beings for the sake of the next world.
Just as a king who has grown wealthy must be propitiated by those seeking enjoyments in this world, so too these four types of elders are to be propitiated by sentient beings.

Therefore, one who knows the three vehicles is an elder in asceticism (*tapovṛddha*). For a householder, there is no authority for the *prātimokṣa* or for study within the Śrāvaka vehicle until he becomes an ascetic.

Therefore, a householder does not become an elder without supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), nor has the Blessed One stated anywhere in the *Yānas* that there is the enjoyment of monasteries and temples for householders who lack the life of renunciation (*pravrajyā*).

Consequently, for the sake of fully understanding the three vehicles (*yānatraya*), one first relies upon the Vaibhāṣika system [stating] that the world-system (*lokadhātu*) exists as a collection of atoms (*paramāṇu*).

For it is said: "The person exists; the person is the bearer of the burden; I say he is neither eternal nor non-eternal. From these words of the Blessed One, the arising and cessation of world-systems, as well as the periods of dissolution (*saṃvarta*) and evolution (*vivarta*), are to be understood.
Therefore, due to the power of the time of arising following dissolution, [beings arise] in empty [worlds].

"Empty" means, according to worldly convention, that the sense organs such as the eye are beyond their own range; they are composed of the substances of earth, water, fire, wind, and space, which exist in the form of atoms (paramāṇu) having natures consisting of five, four, three, two, and one quality respectively, while the sixth quality, the *dharmadhātu*, is all-pervasive. Thus they are empty. Within those empty atoms, by the power of the time of production, there arises what is called "wind."

Among those atoms, first of all, the atoms of wind become mutually conjoined; because of that conjunction, and due to their lightness, mobility, and movement, it is called "wind. Likewise, when the atoms of fire become conjoined, being united with the wind, it is called "electric fire" (*vidyudagni*).
In this way, water atoms, being closely joined together and conjoined with wind and fire, are called rainwater;
likewise, earth atoms, being closely joined, manifest as the rainbow in the sky and are called "the earth.
Tastes, in their atomic form, are all-pervasive everywhere.
Thus, within the five voids, there arise wind, fire, water, and earth; by the power of the winds that sustain, churn, and shape, there come to be the continents, mountains, and oceans—
seven continents, seven mountains, and seven oceans.

In the chapter on the summary of the world-system (*lokadhātu-saṃgraha-uddeśa*): "The constellations, the moon, the sun, the hosts of stars and planets, and the sages"—the constellations (*ṛkṣāṇi*) are twenty-seven; those associated with them are infinite.
[The moon] has the form of Indra’s mandala; likewise, the stars and planets have the form of stars; [and] Mars and the others [are as described].
The seven sages are the stars; the gods are the nāgas;
and the deities are those belonging to the Four Great Kings and so forth. The spirits (bhūtas) are the unconquerable pretas and so forth; the nāgas are Ananta and so forth.
The animal realm (tiryagyoni) is fourfold:

those born from eggs, such as Garuḍas and others, have wind as their source; those born from a womb, such as lordly elephants and others, have fire as their source; those born from moisture, such as insects, moths, worms, and others, have water as their source; and those of spontaneous birth, such as trees and others, have earth as their source. Likewise, the great beings of spontaneous birth have taste (rasa) as their source.
The scriptural reading is *vividhamahitale*.

That which is both "various" (*vividhā*) and "earth" (*mahī*) is "various earth" (*vividhamahī*). Its surface—consisting of the nature of the seven continents and the nature of the twelve regions—is the "surface of various earth" (*vividhamahitala*), which is the world of the *nāgas* and the world of the seven hells. In that [world], there are humans upon the various earths, and hell-beings in the surface, that is, in the hells.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Thus, the meaning is:

"Just as salt arises in the midst of water, so do egg-born beings arise within the egg. This is the illustration here: salt for the production of stationary beings (*sthāvara*), and the egg for the production of moving beings (*jaṅgama*). The word "ca" indicates conjunction; just as through contact with heat the water-atoms of salt attain the solid state of salt, so too do Meru and other such stationary beings [arise].
Just as the atoms of semen and fluid within the egg attain the state of being limbs such as the mouth and body, so too should mobile beings be understood;
the detailed arising of this world-system shall be explained in the fifth chapter.
This concludes the summary of the collection of world-systems.

The Summary of the Vajra Body. Now, I shall expand upon the fifth chapter, the *Vajrakāyasaṃgrahavṛtta*, taught by Mañjuśrī according to the previous sequence, beginning with the words "In the body," and so forth: "In the body, in gnosis, in space, in wind, fire, water, and earth; in their union, in divine vision, and in emanation—within the tenfold world thus described, O King, the birth of the mantra-source occurs within the Vajra Body. Liberation likewise occurs right here. He who knows this correctly does not become a bound beast; his mind is liberated from conceptual construction. (5)
"Body" refers to the moon as unobscured;
"gnosis" refers to the sun as unobscured; and "space" refers to the element of form as unobscured.
Thus, the wind element, fire element, water element, and earth element— being stable— constitute the fivefold stable realm (sthāvaradhātu) free from obscuration;
"mobile" refers to the sixfold realm of the person (puṅgaladhātu), which is free from obscuration.
Regarding "and in the divine, unseen creation":

it is both divine and unseen, and that is the creation; in that divine, unseen creation—within the formless existence (*arūpabhava*) consisting of mere consciousness and ego, in the fourfold [realms] such as the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), and likewise in the tenfold worlds beginning with the body, which are described by the Tathāgatas as the support of Vajra-knowledge—in the Vajra-body, there occurs birth from the mantra-source (*mantrayoni*) within the drops (*bindu*) and so forth, O Lord of Men; herein lies the mantra-source.

From the moon comes the bindu; from the sun, the visarga; from the space element, *a*; from the wind element, *ka*. In the Kha manuscript, the reading here is "other tantras related to that" (*tatsambandhānyatantrāṇi*); however, according to the Tibetan [translation], the reading "infinite [tantras] connected to that" (*tatsambaddhānyanantāni*) appears more correct. (Kha: 0 in the Mantra Vehicle).

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the syllables: *kṣā* for the fire element (*tejodhātu*), *ṛ* for the water element (*udakadhātu*), *u* for the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*), the semi-vowel *ma* for the stationary element (*sthāvaradhātu*), the semi-vowel *kṣa* for the moving element (*jaṅgamadhātu*), and the semi-vowel *ha* for the formless element (*arūpadhātu*)—one should arrange these mantra-syllables in counter-clockwise order.
Then, the subsequent semi-vowel moves above the preceding semi-vowel; for the vowels beginning with *ḷ*, there is the substitution of *yaṇ* according to the rule *iko yaṇaci*;
at the end, there is conjunction with the vowel *a*, followed by the *visarga*, the crescent moon-shaped *bindu*, the circular *jñāna-bindu*, and the flame-shaped *visarga*.

The source of the mantras refers to those mantras characterized by the qualities of *vṛddhi* and so forth; for example: *ha kṣa mū la*. Here, the body of the world-system (*lokadhātukāya*) is the vajra-body.
Within the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), there is the letter *ya*, which is the mandala of wind;
above that is the letter *ra*, which is the mandala of fire.
Above that is the syllable VA, the water mandala;
above that is the syllable LA, the earth mandala;
and above that is the syllable MA, Mount Meru, consisting of five aspects.
Above that is the letter *kṣa*, representing the mobile body under the designation of a lotus;
above that is the formless body, consisting of the letter *ha* and the *visarga*, which is the sun.
The moon, the drop,
the resonance (nāda), and the single-pronged vajra symbol—
thus the vajra-body, the world-realm in the form of a maṇḍala, is to be described by means of what is about to be said.
Thus, for those who possess the mantra of manifestation (*sambhūtimantra*), liberation occurs right here repeatedly;
furthermore, at the time of withdrawal (*saṃhārakāla*), liberation—meaning dissolution—occurs right here. He who knows this correctly [attains it].
Thus, by this sequence of statements, whoever understands the vajra-body as being without obscuration does not become a beast (*paśu*); a "beast" is one who lacks knowledge.
"Free from mental conceptualization" (*cittasaṃkalpamukta*) means that conceptualization is the nature of imagining a mandala; being free from that is "free from mental conceptualization.

The summary of this tenfold form was spoken by the Tathāgata in the *Suviśuddhadharmadhātustava* as follows: "The Lord of Sages, the all-pervading one possessing the ten powers, is tenfold and seeks the ten goals."

The Great One who accomplishes the welfare of the entire world without exception, who has mastery over the ten aspects; whose self is beginningless and free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), whose self is pure, and whose nature is suchness (*tathatā*);
who speaks the truth, who acts according to his word, and whose speech is never otherwise; who is non-dual and proclaims non-duality, abiding at the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);
who roars the lion’s roar of selflessness (*nairātmya*) and strikes terror into the deer-like followers of false paths. (Nāmasaṃgīti 64.5–6). Thus ends the summary of the Vajra Body (*vajrakāya*).

Herein is the expansion of the mantra (*mantraprastāra*) according to the Devanāgarī order: *haṃ kṣa ma la va ra ya ka*. It occurs [in] 3. kha. kha. [as] the elemental self (*bhūtātmā*). [End of] the chapter on the assembly of the world-realms (*lokadhātusaṃgraha*). Now I shall expand the sixth verse concerning the summary of the arising of Rāhu and the others, beginning with "vāmāṅge" and so forth: "In the left limb is the white radiance, the digit of the nectar of the world; in the right is the red-colored [radiance]."

Rāhu, Kālāgni, Candra, Ravi, Śaśitanaya (Budha), Bhauma, Śukra, Guru, Ketu, and Mandas—these seven pairs exist in the world as luminaries situated in water, fire, and air; however, there is one pair devoid of darkness at the end of darkness.
"In the left limb, white radiance" means:

in the left limb, within the previously mentioned *anāhata* [cakra] situated at the center and designated by the symbol of the half-vajra, there is a single drop (*bindu*); and that white radiance is the white ray of gnosis (*jñānaraśmi*), which is the very digit of the nectar of the world (*jagadamṛtakalā*). That same [digit] is red-colored on the right.
To the right of that unstruck (*anāhata*) sound is the red radiance known as the sign of emission (*visarga*), which is the red ray of gnosis (*jñāna-raśmi*).
Outside of those two, on the left and the right respectively, there are Rāhu and Kālāgni;
thereafter, there are the Moon and the Sun.
Thus, Mercury, Mars, Venus, Jupiter,
Ketu, Saturn, rain, lightning, water, and fire— these seven pairs existing in the world, within the realm of the universe, are for the sake of that discipline.
In these, the mantra-syllables are, respectively, for the left and the right:
*aṃ aḥ*, *u ṛ*, *ū ṛ*, *o ar*, *au ār*, *va ra*, *vā rā*. These seven *yuma*s are the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*) of the seven days;
thus, there is one pair free from darkness at the end of darkness.

Free from darkness (*tamas*), having the form of white and red rays of knowledge, it is the limb of the Unstruck (*anāhata*) on the left and right of the Unstruck, and nothing else. Behind it is yellow *Tārā*, whose ground is the rainbow; she is fourfold and divided into two. Vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the single wind that becomes tenfold at the crown and the base.

In the front, in the middle, is the Vajra with its seed-syllable above, situated below together with its own power (*śakti*) and a multitude of qualities. Knowledge (*jñāna*) is everywhere empty (*śūnya*), conjoined with the state of Śiva, and liberated from all phenomenal existents (*bhāva*). || 7 ||
"And yellow on the back"—by the word "and" (ca), the meaning is that there is a yellow ray of gnosis (*jñānaraśmi*).
On the back of the *anāhata* [cakra], there is a sign known as the shape of a plow (*halākṛti*); outside of that, in the west, is the yellow radiance with form (*sākārā*);
beyond that, the subtle star (*sūkṣmatārā*), the great star (*bṛhattārā*), and likewise the rainbow (*suradhanuḥ*).

The earth is of two kinds, consisting of clay and stone; likewise, that yellow light is fourfold. The vital air (prāṇa) is of two kinds, becoming tenfold as the single wind located at the head, the base, and the front. Above that unstruck sound (anāhata) is the dark blue ray; externally, it is the prāṇa-vāyu arising from the seed-syllable of emptiness (śūnya). Below is the dark blue ray; externally, it is the apāna-vāyu produced from the seed-syllable of gnosis (jñāna).
In the east is Kṛṣṇaraśmi; outside is the wind named Samāna, followed by Udāna; likewise, Vyāna, Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—these are the ten winds.
Of these, one pair is below and above, and another pair is in the front and back, belonging respectively to air and earth.
Dhanañjaya has seven pairs; he is neuter because he does not abandon a dead body.
Regarding these, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the mantra-syllables of the world-system are: *ha* and *hā* above and below.
Then, according to their respective order, the seven pairs of preceding and following [vowels] are:
a-ā-i-ḷ; ī-la; e-al; ai-āl; ya-la-yā-lā; and kṣa. Thus are the seven pairs, preceding and following.
Above and below there is one pair;
at the end of darkness are seven pairs, which are the presiding deities of the seven days, according to the division of the four twilights.
On Sunday at midnight, [the syllable] *a* arises in the east;
*a:* arises in the south;
*ā* arises in the west.
In the rising of the north, Aṃ is for the Moon;
Ī, Ṛ,
LṚ, and Ū are for Mars.
For Mercury: e, ar, al, o;
for Jupiter: ai, ār, āl, au;
for Venus: ya, ra, la, va.
The seed-syllables for the twilight periods (*sandhyā*) of the seven days of the week, beginning with Saturday (*śanaiścara*), are as follows in sequence;
in the center is the upward-pointing seed-syllable of the Vajra.

In the center of the seed-syllables of the upper, lower, eastern, southern, western, and northern directions is the unstruck (*anāhata*) vajra in the form of a curved knife (*kartṛkā*). Above it is its seed-syllable, the *anusvāra*; that which is situated on the left side is above it, accompanied by a multitude of qualities. Its own power (*svaśakti*) is established below; the power of that *anusvāra* is the *visarga*.
Its qualities are these red rays;
together with them is the Śakti. Accompanied by the multitude of qualities, one's own Śakti stands below the Anusvāra in the form of a half-moon.

The anterior-posterior mark is at the feet and the head; because the *anāhata* is not mentioned [elsewhere], thus the five-syllabled *vaṃ* is in the domain of Vajrasattva, and the syllable *haṃ* is in the practice of Vajrānaṅga.

Outside of that, the six-syllabled *bindu-śūnya* is called the support (*ādhāra*). In the case of the *vaṃ*-syllable and the *haṃ*-syllable, the syllable *kṣa* is the womb (*yoni*), which is the vajra and the lotus.

The word "knowledge" (jñāna) refers to the emission (visarga), which is empty everywhere; above the unstruck sound (anāhata), it has the form of a half-moon and exists as emptiness everywhere within every external phoneme.
The word "bindu" refers to the point (bindu), which is empty everywhere.

"Accompanied by the state of Śiva and liberated from all states"—this refers to Śiva as the Unstruck (anāhata). His "state" (pada) is the mark of the preceding and succeeding [sounds]. Accompanied by that, Śiva is liberated from all states. That very [Śiva] is everywhere—in all external phonemes, qualities, feet, or heads, and in air and earth respectively; above the head is the digit (kalā), above the digit is the point (bindu), and above the point is the resonance (nāda) known as the Unstruck.
Its mantra syllables are: *e~ va~ śa~ ha~ a~ a~:*; *ā~ ā~ i~ ī ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ u~ oṃ e~ aiṃ ara~ āi~ a ā au~ ha~ hā~ ya~ yā~ ra~ rā~ va~ vā~ la~ lā~*; *kṣa*.
Thus, it should be understood that among all mantra syllables, the five-syllabled Great Void (*pañcākṣaro mahāśūnya*) is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) within those to be pervaded (*vyāpyeṣu*).

This was stated by the Blessed One in this King of Explanatory Tantras, the *Māyājāla*: "Likewise, the Great King who holds the universal illusion (*viśvamāyādharo rājā*), the great holder of the Buddhas' vidyā."
“Vajra-sharp, the great sword, pure, the supreme syllable;
partless, all-pervading, omnipresent, subtle, the seed-syllable, untainted;
dustless, free from dust, stainless, with faults cast out, free from disease. Thus is the summary teaching on the arising of Rāhu and the others.

Thus ends the section on the summary of the world-system (*lokadhātu-saṃgrahoddeśa*). Now, I shall expand upon the eighth chapter, the summary of the increase and decrease of the digits of the moon (*candrakalā*), the increase and decrease of days and nights during the solar transits (*sūryāyana*), and so forth, beginning with the verse starting "The first thirty," etc.: "The first thirty vowels, joined with *ha*, *ya*, *ra*, *va*, and *la*, [constitute] the lunar days; and by means of those lunar days, the Sun moves through the consonant groups (*varga*) together with their measures (*mātra*), for a duration measured by zero, six, and fire (thirty-six). [37b] The first thirty vowels are those joined with *ha*, *ya*, *ra*, *va*, and *la*; these are the lunar days (*kalā-dina*). By means of those lunar days, the Sun moves through the consonant groups (*kādyān vargān*) along with their measures (*samātrān*), for a duration measured by zero, six, and fire (thirty-six). The meaning is as follows: the Sun moves through the thirty consonant groups, each consisting of five letters and accompanied by the five vowel-measures (*mātrā*), for a period of thirty-six days. Thus, he moves through the consonants *ka* to *ma* in fifteen days, and through *ya* to *kṣa* in another twenty-one days. This is the movement of the Sun through the consonants. Furthermore, the Sun moves through the vowels *a* to *au* in fifteen days, and through *a* to *au* again in another fifteen days. This is the movement of the Sun through the vowels. Thus, the Sun moves through the consonants and vowels for a total of thirty-six days. This is the summary of the increase and decrease of the digits of the moon and the increase and decrease of days and nights during the solar transits. The rest is to be understood from the commentary. Thus ends the summary of the increase and decrease of the digits of the moon and the increase and decrease of days and nights during the solar transits. Here ends the fifth chapter, the summary of the world-system, within the *Vimalaprabhā*, the commentary on the *Kālacakra Tantra*. Chapter Five. The vowels beginning with *ha*, the channels (*nāḍī*), the gods, humans, and serpents, the source of beings, and the mantras beginning with *ka*—when these are joined, the birth of a king indeed occurs from the three elements in this manner. (8)

The first thirty vowels, joined with *ha*, *ya*, *ra*, *va*, and *la*, belong to the Moon. Those beginning with *a*—namely *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, and *lṛ*—along with their short, long, *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and *yaṇ*-substitute forms, divided by the distinctions of short and long, become thirty;
these are the "Moons" (*candras*), which serve as the cause for the increase and decrease of the lunar digits (*kalās*).

The five divisions beginning with *pratipad* are of three kinds; they are threefold by way of the *nandā* and other divisions: threefold is *nandā*, threefold is *bhadrā*, threefold is *jayā*, threefold is *riktā*, and threefold is *pūrṇā*.

These fifteen digits of increase (*vṛddhikalā*) in the bright fortnight are further divided according to the qualities of *tamas*, *rajas*, and *sattva*, and according to the distinctions of weak, medium, and intense.
Established here as the threefold path by way of the intrinsic nature of the elements beginning with space:

the second is *i*, the third is *ṛ*, the fourth is *u*, and the fifth is *la*. [The days] Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā correspond respectively to the elements of space, wind, fire, water, and earth. In the first stage, which is the measure of softness (*mṛdu-mātra*), there is the opening of darkness;
thereafter, the second stage is the differentiation of qualities (*guṇa-bheda*).
The sixth is *a*, the seventh is *e*, the eighth is *ar*, the ninth is *o*, and the tenth is *al*;
these are the Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā tithis, corresponding to the elements of space, wind, fire, water, and earth.

Darkness (*tamas*) is the first soft measure (*mṛdumātrā*) of the opening (*udghāṭana*); that which is the middle measure (*madhyamātrā*) of the first section (*pūrvakāṇḍa*) has become manifest (*bhūtā*).
The *raja-udghāṭana* is gentle;

therefore, in the third section (*kāṇḍa*), the *yaṇ*-substitutions beginning with *ha* occur: the eleventh is *ha*, the twelfth is *ya*, the thirteenth is *ra*, the fourteenth is *va*, and the full moon (*pūrṇamāsī*) is *la*.

Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, and the elements of space, wind, fire, water, and earth; [the states of] being, opening, soft, dusty, middling, intense in the first section, empty, and full in the second section; this is its fivefold division. *Bhotamaḥ* [is] *sūnala*. Of this, there is a fivefold division.

On the eleventh day, by the differentiation of the quality of *sattva*, the first digit (*kalā*) of the waxing moon is "the Child" (*bālā*) when it is in its highest degree; on the twelfth day, it is "the Maiden" (*kumārī*); on the thirteenth day, "the Youthful Woman" (*yuvatī*); on the fourteenth day, "the Aged" (*vṛddhā*); and on the fifteenth day, it has reached full maturity.

Thus, the digit of the waxing moon, having matured on the fifteenth day, is designated as "Full. In this way, the increase of the lunar digits in the bright fortnight is divided into fifteen distinct stages.

At the end of that [sixteenth day], at the beginning of the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapratipad*), the time of entry into darkness is called the sixteenth digit (*ṣoḍaśī kalā*). At the end of that, during the digit of the first day of the bright fortnight (*śuklapratipatkalā*), there occurs an entry into darkness on the first day of the dark fortnight, and the second digit of the bright fortnight becomes fully ripened. Then, on the second day, the second digit also enters into darkness; the third digit becomes fully ripened, and in this manner, on the third day of the dark fortnight, it too enters into darkness.
In this way, from the fourth lunar day until the fifteenth digit has fully matured, they enter into darkness;

then, at the end of the new moon, at the juncture when the first digit begins to rise—in the portion where the sixteenth part emerges—there occurs the entry of Rāhu. Thus, the eclipse of the moon is of two kinds: on the full moon, Rāhu swallows it up to the end of the full digit; on the new moon, Rāhu [swallows it] beginning from the rise of the first digit.
In this context, within the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), there is an entry into darkness (*tamas*) by way of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) starting from earth and the other elements;
subsequently, there is the dissolution of those [elements] arisen in the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*).

On the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapratipad*), the earth enters into the darkness of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu-kalā*), becoming veiled by darkness; on the second day, the portion of air (*vāyu-kalā*) becomes veiled by the darkness of water.
The third, the fire-element (vahnikalā), becomes covered by the darkness of fire;
the fourth, the water-element (udakakalā), becomes covered by the darkness of wind; the fifth, the earth-element (pṛthivīkalā), becomes covered by the darkness of the space-element (ākāśadhātu).
Thus, in the first section, the mere entry of darkness is gentle.
Then, in the second section (*kāṇḍa*) as well, there is the activity of veiling by darkness according to the stated sequence.
In that second section, darkness is of a mild degree (*mṛdu-mātrā*), whereas in the preceding section it was of a moderate degree (*madhya-mātrā*).
Likewise, in the third section too, there is the activity of veiling by darkness.
In that [first] section it is of mild degree; in the second section it is of middling degree; in the third, it is of intense degree.

Therein, the intense degree is divided into five parts: on the eleventh day it is "infant" (*bāla*); by the division of intense darkness (*tamas*) on the twelfth day it is "child" (*kumāra*); on the thirteenth day it is "youth" (*yuvan*); on the fourteenth day it is "old" (*vṛddha*); and on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) it becomes fully matured (*paripakva*).
Thus, in the second stage (*kāṇḍa*), there is the medium degree of *mātrā*; in the third stage, there is the dull (*mṛdu*) degree of darkness (*tamas*).
Then, upon the arrival of the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*), there occurs the departure of the ripened darkness characterized by the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*).

On the second day, there is the departure of the darkness of water; on the third, the darkness of fire; on the fourth, the darkness of wind; and on the fifth, the darkness of the space element (*ākāśa-dhātu*).

Thus, the first digit (*kalā*) is of the soft degree (*mṛdu-mātrā*); the earth becomes full and ripened. The second is the grown (*vṛddhā*); the third is the young woman (*yuvatī*); the fourth is the maiden (*kumārī*); the fifth is the child (*bālā*); and from the sixth onwards, they remain set (*astaṅgata*). Thus, during the soft stage of the digit and the soft ripening, there would be no entry of darkness, until the third [digit] of the dark fortnight reaches intense ripening (*adhimātra-pāka*). Of these fifteen digits each, those that have set rise on the sixteenth day, and those that have risen set on the sixteenth day.

Thus, the thirty vowels beginning with the digit of the moon (*candrakalā*) are the designations for the lunar digits (*kalā*). Those that have entered into darkness are the white [digits], while those that are black are designated by metaphorical usage (*upacāreṇa*).
The vowels belonging to these white and black digits, starting from the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), are the words of the mantra.

The term *varga* refers to a collection of five syllables; it is recited according to the divisions of the five elements, beginning with space (*ākāśa*) and ending with earth (*pṛthivī*). The collection of vowels (*svara*) is recited at all times according to the divisions of space and so forth.
In this regard, the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated formula) serves as the indicator for the entire recitation of consonants.
In this context, the thirty pure consonants beginning with *ya* are modifications of the vowels;

elsewhere, they are included within the recitation of the consonants beginning with *ka*, as they are read in the section on the initial vowels (*ādisvarakāṇḍa*). They are as follows: *a, i, ṝ, u, ḷ, k*.

Therefore, the six groups (varga) beginning with *ka*, consisting of thirty consonants—namely *ka, ca, ṭa, pa, ta,* and *sa*—have the nature of the elements of space, wind, fire, water, earth, and consciousness, due to their being articulated from the throat, palate, head, teeth, and lips respectively.
The sixth group consists of five elements through its individual articulation. These groups, beginning with *ka*, are accompanied by the vowels (*samātra*).
The measures (*mātrā*) consist of the five short vowels beginning with *a* and the five long vowels; these ten combined constitute the [first] set.

At the end of the short vowels, the nasalization (*anusvāra*) constitutes the sixth measure, and at the end of the long vowels, the spirant (*visarga*) constitutes the sixth measure; these two are to be pronounced in conjunction with consonants and vowels.
Those [vowels] joined with these measures are called "with their measures" (*samātra*).
The sun moves for a measure of zero, six, and fire (360), that is, for a measure of three hundred and sixty.
By those measures of zero, six, and fire—namely, twelve months—there are two solstices (*ayana*).
In each individual solstice, whether southern or northern, there are one hundred and eighty days.

In the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*), beginning from Kakaṇṭha and so forth, the Sun moves for six months through the six groups of consonants (*ṣaḍvarga*) accompanied by the six short vowels, according to the sequence of creation starting from space (*ākāśa*) and distinguished by the transition (*saṃkrānti*) months.

Thereafter, in the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*), it moves for six months through the six groups of consonants accompanied by the long vowels, according to the sequence starting from earth (*pṛthivī*).
Wherever it moves accompanied by the short vowels, there is an increase in the night; wherever it moves accompanied by the long vowels, there is an increase in the day.
In this context, the moon represents the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) and the sun represents the northern course (uttarāyaṇa).
A single consonant represents the moon;
two consonants joined together represent the sun.

Likewise, during the six months of the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*), it moves through the six groups of consonants, each with its vowel, numbering one hundred and eighty, by way of the nature of the moon and according to the differentiation of the increase of the night.

The division into three hundred and sixty parts, resulting from the flow of the five mandalas beginning with space, is to be explained in what follows; its summary was stated by the Blessed One in the *Māyājāla*, the King of Tantras, within the *Pratyavekṣaṇā-stava*: "He who is the great mind of all Buddhas, the movement of the minds of all Buddhas, the great body of all Buddhas, and the Sarasvatī (eloquence) of all Buddhas; he is the Vajra-Sun, the great light, possessing the stainless radiance of the Vajra-Moon."
"Great passion beginning with dispassion, with a radiant luster of all colors"—

this refers to *anurāga* (attachment/passion) on the fifth, tenth, and full moon days of the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), and *virāga* (dispassion) on the fifth, tenth, and new moon days of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).

Between these two, at the end of the three full moons, at the conclusion of the *virāma*, there is the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*), the five-syllabled yoga that has become a single fusion, the heart of the Tathāgatas.
Therefore, the Moon, which is the great mind of all Buddhas, is the Great Void at the end of the sixteen digits;

the Sun, which is the movement of the minds of all Buddhas, is darkness at the junction of the arising of the first digit at the end of the new moon; and at the end of the sixteenth, the Bindu-Void is the six-syllabled [yoga].
Thus, the great body of all Buddhas is the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*); the Sarasvatī of all Buddhas is the Point-Void (*binduśūnya*).

The Vajra-Sun is the Great Light, the Point-Void, the six-syllabled [mantra]; the Vajra-Moon is the Stainless Radiance, the five-syllabled Great Void. This Dharma of Wisdom and Means shall be explained in detail below.
The Syllableless, the Source of Mantras, the Great Mantra of the Three Families, shall be explained in detail.
Now, the nadīs of each day and night are described;
"hādyāmātrāśca nāḍyaḥ" means those which are both beginning with 'ha' (hādyāḥ) and are measures (mātrāḥ), thus "hādyāmātrāḥ."

By virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), the consonants are included; these twelve [vowels], together with their measures (*mātrā*), constitute sixty measures. Among them, those joined with short measures (*hrasva-mātrā*) from midday until midnight consist of thirty measures during the increase of the night;
those joined with long measures (*dīrgha-mātrā*) from midnight until midday consist of thirty measures during the increase of the day.
In this manner, the increase of night and day should be understood for each successive day.

Here, the mantra-syllables follow the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) during the increase of night, and the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) during the increase of day. They are as follows: *ha hi hṛ hu haḷ haṃ*, *yayi yṛ yu yuḷ yaṃ*, *ra ri ṝ ru ḷ raṃ*, *va vi vṛ vu vūḷ vaṃ*, *lali lu lu lūḷ laṃ*. Thus, night is differentiated by the aspect of wisdom (*prajñā*), while means (*upāya*) is differentiated by the body (*kāya*).

the first syllable becomes the seed-syllable of gnosis (*jñānabīja*), and the entire name becomes the recitation-mantra (*jāpamantra*) for accomplishing the welfare of the universe. It should be understood that there are infinite mantras, distinguished by the names of infinite sentient beings.

Just as a heap [of letters] is determined for the sake of auspicious or inauspicious results by the first letter of a name, and likewise by all the letters of the name— whether deficient in measure or otherwise— as well as by the first letter and the entire name, so too is the accomplishment of the practice of meditation and recitation achieved. There is no delusion regarding dependent origination, for the power of jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs is inconceivable, and it arises from the transformation of one’s own mind.

In such cases, when preceded by the *ka*-group—that is, when preceded by a collection of vowels beginning with *a* and joined with consonants beginning with *ka*—there indeed occurs the address to the King (*nṛpa*), which is the "origination. (ca) The Indication of the Places of Birth of the Vowels: Now I shall explain the ninth summary verse concerning the places of birth and so forth of the vowels, beginning with the words "the place of birth. This is the place of birth of the vowels associated with *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, and *ya*—that is, those joined with the *ka*-group [consonants]—in the throat, the upper part of the palate, the space (*kha*), wind, fire, and water, and in the teeth, earth, and the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣacakra*).

[The vowels] beginning with *a* are in the heart, the neck, the head, the navel-cakra, and the secret place; they are in the universal (*viśva*), the black (*kṛṣṇa*), and the red, resembling the moon and gold, and reside in the deities of the elements, the shoulders, and so forth. 9. *Haḥ*.
Regarding the statement, "The birthplaces of the vowels joined with *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa*, together with *kā* and so forth":
here, the vowels previously mentioned—*a*, *i*, *ṛ*, *u*, and *ḷ*—are five;
their fivefold birthplaces correspond respectively [to the aforementioned consonant groups].

Of what kind [are they]? "Endowed with *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa*" means joined with the letters beginning with *ka* and so forth, respectively—that is, joined with the groups of letters starting with *ka*. Wherever "beginning with *ka*" (*kādi*) is written, or where the seed-syllable *ka* is written, an empty space is seen there. In the Tibetan version (*bho.
pāṭhe*), "ka" appears in sequence: [in the chapter on] the summary of the mental world-system (*lokadhātumānasaṃgrahoddeśa*).
"65. Not thus"—meaning those joined with each individual letter beginning with *ka*, such as *ka*, *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and so forth;
by the inclusion of the word "beginning," it is understood that they are accompanied by *ha*, *ya*, *va*, *ra*, *la*, *sa*, and *ha*.

And so it has been said: "The vowels *a*, *u*, *ṛ*, *ḷ*, the visarga, and the *ka*-group are guttural (*kaṇṭhya*); *i*, *e*, *ca*, *ya*, *śa* are palatal (*tālavya*); *ṛ*, *ṭ*, *u*, *ra*, *ṣa* are retroflex (*mūrdhanya*); *u*, *o*, *pa*, and the *upadhmānīya* are labial (*oṣṭhya*); *ḷ*, *t*, *u*, *la*, *sa* are dental (*dantya*). Thus, the places of origin (*janmasthāna*) are: the throat for the gutturals; the upper part of the palate for the palatals; the root of the tongue for the retroflexes; the lips for the labials; and the teeth for the dentals—these being the places of origin for air (*pavana*), fire (*havija*), earth (*ambubhūmi*), and water (*ambubhūmi*) respectively. This is the "birth" (*janma*) of the letters beginning with *a* and so forth, in their respective order. Through these places of articulation, there occurs the comprehension of the meaning of the word (*śabdārthapratipatti*). Here, the phrase "comprehension of the meaning of the word" refers to this process.
In this context, the place of birth should be understood as the basis for the procedure of mantra recitation;

furthermore, it is described according to the division of wheels within the body for the purpose of the place of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā): "from the beginning" refers to the crown wheel (uṣṇīṣacakra), the heart, the throat and head, and the navel wheel, respectively.

"From the beginning" means from the vowel *a* and so forth, according to the classification of the elements such as space (*ākāśa*) and the rest; these should be understood as the places of birth for the purpose of meditating on the wheels starting with the crown, respectively.
Here, in the crown wheel (*uṣṇīṣacakra*), the vowels *a*, *u*, *ṛ*, and the visarga are to be meditated upon;

in the heart wheel (*hṛccakra*), *i*, *e*, *ya*, and *śa*; in the throat wheel (*kaṇṭhacakra*), *ṛ*, *ṭu*, *ra*, and *ṣa*; and in the forehead wheel (*lalāṭacakra*), *u*, *pū*, and the upadhmānīya are to be meditated upon; while in the navel wheel (*nābhicakra*), *lṛ*, *tu*, and *la* are to be meditated upon. Thus, all [the letters] are to be visualized: in the green crown wheel as all colors, in the black heart wheel, in the red throat wheel, in the moon-colored forehead wheel, and in the gold-like navel wheel.

Regarding the deities of the aggregates (skandha) and elements (dhātu) and so forth, one should understand that the placement of limbs (aṅganyāsa) and so forth is to be applied as follows: in the crown wheel (uṣṇīṣacakra), which has the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) and the space element (ākāśadhātu) as its presiding deities; in the heart wheel (hṛccakre), which has the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra) and the wind element (vāyudhātu) as its presiding deities; likewise, in the throat wheel (kaṇṭhacakre), which has the aggregate of feeling (vedanā) and the fire element (tejodhātu) as its presiding deities; in the forehead wheel (lalāṭacakre), which has the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā) and the water element (udakadhātu) as its presiding deities; and in the navel wheel (nābhicakre), which has the aggregate of form (rūpa) and the earth element (pṛthivīdhātu) as its presiding deities. This is the instruction on the birthplaces of the vowels.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, the Summary of the World-Sphere (*lokadhātusaṃgraha*), in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Śrī Kālacakra Tantra-rāja*, which is extracted from the *Śrī Paramādibuddha*. 7.

(8) Summary of the Measurement of the World System: Now, the measurement of the world system as taught by the Blessed One according to the dispositions of sentient beings has been compiled by Mañjuśrī, the compiler, from the *Paramādibuddha* in verses beginning with the tenth; that very [teaching] I shall now expand upon. "From the limit of the wind to the boundary of Meru"—meaning from the limit of the wind up to the boundary of Meru, including the hells and the city of the Nāgas, there are two hundred thousand *yojanas*. The measure of Meru is one hundred thousand [yojanas], and from the abode of the hosts of planets, it is twenty-five thousand.
The neck is fifty [units], and the mouth, the firm foundation, is twenty-five; likewise, outside that is one void, devoid of the three worlds, without qualities, and lacking all principles. ||10||
99. In the *Vimalaprabhā*: From the wind-circle up to the limit of Meru, including the hells and the city of the serpents (*phaṇi*), it is two hundred thousand *yojanas*.

Here, according to worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*) and by virtue of the various inclinations and dispositions of sentient beings, the measurement of the world-system and its inhabitants appears as taught.

However, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), no measurement or dimension of the world-system is possible, because it is solely through the power of the merit and demerit of sentient beings that such measurements appear.

In this world, in whatever cave measuring five cubits a Bodhisattva free from passion dwells, by the power of his merit and knowledge and through the force of his supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*), a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) accompanied by his army enters that cave; yet it is not expanded by anyone, nor does any crowding occur for the universal monarch and his army once they have entered that cave. In this same way, the measurement of the world-system (*lokadhātu*) is to be understood from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

In this context, whatever is the measure of the world-system (*lokadhātu*) is as it is in the body; for it is said, "What is that? and because it is stated that "the measure of the world-system is for the sake of the world-system mandala, and the measure of the body-element (*kāyadhātu*) is for the sake of the body-mandala," just as Mount Meru is one hundred thousand *yojanas* in height according to worldly measurement, so too the skeleton of the body is one cubit (*hasta*) in height, and by that measure of a cubit, the body is four cubits.

The world-system consists of four hundred thousand *yojanas*, with Mount Meru measuring one hundred thousand *yojanas*. Otherwise, [it might be argued]: "As it is externally, so it is not in the body, because of the disparity;

thus, let the measurement of the world-system be as it is according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*). In this regard, there would be no thesis for the Blessed One, because of [the criteria of] 'scorching' and 'cutting'.
Furthermore, what kind of thesis would there be regarding the accumulation of merit and wisdom?

Since there are various opinions regarding the measurement of the world-system (*lokadhātu*) according to the intent of the Vedic systems— such as the false claim that a single Brahmā-egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) measures ten million *yojanas*—

the measurement of the world-system has been established here through the logic of the planetary mathematics, the zodiacal signs, and the celestial sphere, in order to mature the Sun, the Chariot, and so forth, and for the sake of destroying that [Vedic] notion of the Brahmā-egg.
Therefore, having seen this Buddhist system of measurement, one should not entertain such delusions.

If the Blessed One has stated that the measurement of a world-system (*lokadhātu*) is thirty-six hundred thousand [yojanas], how is it that the measurement of a world-system is four hundred thousand *yojanas*?

Regarding this, the thought might arise in someone's mind: "Is the Blessed One a speaker of falsehood? That statement should not be accepted by the wise; rather, it is due to the influence of the inclinations (*āśaya*) of sentient beings.
Thus it has been said: "Sentient beings have diverse inclinations and perceive diverse tenets."
Those who have ascended various paths and are conceited with the pride of knowledge;
As long as their own and others' tenets are not demonstrated through reasoning,
even those who pride themselves on being omniscient fall under the sway of that [false system].

Untruth [is that which arises] from benefiting sentient beings; truth, which is the cause for the accumulation of merit, [arises] from harming others, even if it results in rebirth in the Avīci hell and other such realms.
Those who did not give shelter in their homes, being evildoers, see as preta-s a mountain shaped like a needle-point as their dwelling.

The perfected ones (siddhas), having attained mastery over the netherworld (pātāla) and proceeding toward the city of the Apsarases, perceive from all sides the earth as both possessing fissures and being perfectly firm.
Therefore, the measure of the world-system was spoken by the Tathāgata according to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the minds of sentient beings;
it is a mere reflection and no Tathāgata, out of dogmatic attachment, perceives a world-system and describes the measure of a thing in terms of subject and object.
Having thus fully understood all this, the Blessed One spoke of the measure of the world-system for the sake of maturing the sages and for the purpose of the body-mandala.
"Kha ṅa [is] for sentient beings;
kha ṅa [is] for a watch (yāma).
Thus ends the summary of the measurement of the world-system in this chapter. Here, from the limit of Vāyu up to the summit of Meru, [are the measurements] of the mandalas of earth, water, and fire.
Below, the wind-mandala is situated within the space-element;
from that [wind-mandala] down to Meru, there are seven hells, and the eighth is the City of the Serpents (phaṇipuram),
which constitutes the hell of the serpents measuring two hundred thousand yojanas.

Here, the wind-maṇḍala is fifty thousand [yojanas] in extent. Within that great, harsh wind and great darkness, there are two hells, each twenty-five thousand yojanas in vertical dimension; in horizontal measurement, they are equal to the circumference of the earth-circle. Likewise, within the fire-maṇḍala there are two hells: one is the Fire Hell, and above it is the Intense Smoke Hell.
Similarly, within the water-sphere (*udakavalaya*) are two hells: Paṅkāmbhas, which is joined with mud and water, and Vālukāmbhas, which is joined with sand and water, both being extremely cold.
Within the earth-sphere (*pṛthvīvalaya*) is the hell Śarkarāmbhas, twenty-five thousand *yojanas* in extent;
above that is Phaṇipura, also twenty-five thousand *yojanas*, extending both downwards and upwards.
That same measure is twofold: one half is the world of the Asuras, and the other half is the world of the Nāgas.

Likewise, from the soles of the feet to the waist in the body is two cubits; having divided those same two cubits into eight parts, the hells, the hoods, and the cities should be understood to exist respectively in each single part.
The measure of Meru is one hundred thousand [yojanas].
From that terrestrial sphere, the measurement from the base of Meru to its summit is one hundred thousand yojanas;
this constitutes the body from the waist to below the throat, measuring one cubit, wherein the host of planets revolves.
Therefore, from that abode of the host of planets, there are twenty-five thousand [yojanas]; the neck of Meru is six finger-breadths within the body;
then the mouth of Meru is fifty [yojanas], from the neck to the end of the forehead being twelve finger-breadths within the body.
Therefore, the firm and immovable *uṣṇīṣa* consists of twenty-five thousand [breaths];
in the body, this measures six finger-breadths from the forehead to the location of the crest (*śikhā*).
That is external emptiness, solitary, devoid of the three worlds, without qualities, and devoid of principles (*tattva*).
The external void between the lower wind-mandala and the upper uṣṇīṣa consists of individual atoms in the form of elements such as the material and immaterial;
thus, it should be understood through "single-void" that space is not all-pervasive.
Such is the measurement of the four-lakṣa world-system.

In the body, there are four cubits (*hasta*), and a cubit consists of twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Now, the horizontal measurement is stated here: from the wind-sphere up to the limit of the wind, on the stable surface of the earth, there are the continents, mountains, and oceans—four hundred thousand, fifty thousand, and two hundred thousand *yojanas* respectively; and the circle of fire and wind is two hundred thousand *yojanas*.

Above the center of Meru, the stellar wheel of zodiac signs revolves day and night; divided into six parts, each measuring two hundred thousand [yojanas], the entire triple world has arisen through the conjunction of time.
From the end of the wind to the limit of the wind: four hundred thousand [yojanas] extend from the wind to the edge of the wind, reaching from the eastern wind-circle to the western wind-circle;
likewise from south to north. Thus, upon the stable surface of the earth, there are the continents, mountains, and oceans.

Then, within the wind-mandala, there is the fire-mandala in the shape of a circle; likewise, in the middle of the fire-circle is the water-circle, and in the middle of the water-circle is the earth-circle, which is that very stable ground. Upon it are the six continents and the six mountains; the six oceans, together with the seventh water-circle, constitute the seven oceans; together with the seventh, Jambūdvīpa, are the seven continents; and together with the Vajra mountain are the seven mountains—the Vajra mountain being the Vāḍava fire.

The Salt Ocean (*kṣārasamudra*) is situated at the end of the circle of water; it stands below, extending horizontally in all directions to the edge of the Great Jambūdvīpa and beneath the earth. From the edge of the Salt Ocean, there is the Salt Ocean [itself]. Space (*kha*), wind (*vāyu*), space (*kha*), and below [space] (*adhasi*). Space (*kha*) extends to the edge of the ocean, which is four hundred thousand [yojanas]; in the *Vimalaprabhā*, half of the four hundred thousand [is mentioned].
Four hundred thousand [yojanas] means two hundred thousand from the center of Meru to the edge of the salt-water ocean ring on both the right and left sides; specifically,
one hundred thousand on the right and one hundred thousand on the left.

Thus, the east-west, northwest-southeast, and southwest-northeast [axes] consist of a circle of fire and a circle of wind measuring two hundred thousand *yojanas*. From that circle of salt water, to the right and to the left, there is a circle of fire and a circle of wind measuring two hundred thousand [yojanas]; specifically, one hundred thousand to the right and one hundred thousand to the left, and likewise one hundred thousand to the north—in this way, it is so in all directions.
"In the center is Meru; above it, the wheel of the zodiacs together with the stars revolves day and night"—what is the meaning of this statement?
What kind of thing is Meru in the center? It is that above which the twelve-spoked wheel of the zodiacs, accompanied by the multitude of infinite stars (*satāra*), revolves day and night.
Here, what is the logic of these words? Is there some other Meru as well, on account of which such a statement is made?
Here, even the Mandāra tree is included under the designation "Meru"; therefore, this statement is intended to distinguish it from the Mandāra.
Thus, in the sixfold division, there are two hundred thousand [yojanas] each.

According to the sequence stated here—downward and upward, east and west, south and north—in these six divisions from the center of the terrestrial circle, the entire triple world (tribhuvana)—namely, the realms of heaven, earth, and the netherworld—is produced through the conjunction of time (*kālayoga*), by virtue of the power of the cycles of dissolution and origination (*saṃvarta-utpatti*).

[This world] has arisen from the conjunction of time, wind, and the configuration of the sustaining churning [wind], for the purpose of sentient beings experiencing the fruits of their virtuous and non-virtuous karma. Now, the measurement of its circumference is stated here: The circumference of the horizontal extent of the world-system all around is threefold [the diameter]. The circumference of the earth is three hundred thousand [yojanas]; that of water, fire, and wind follows the sequence of six, nine, and twelve [hundred thousand].

O King, when there is one hundred thousand yojanas externally in the abode of the three worlds, that corresponds correctly to one cubit in the body of a human being at the level of the earth, according to their respective measures. (12)
"The circumference of the horizontal measurement of the world-system is threefold all around.

This means that here, in every case, the circular measurement of the horizontal extent of the world-system—of all things from Mount Meru up to the wind-circle, including the continents, mountains, oceans, and so forth—is threefold.

Thus, the circle of the earth is three hundred thousand [yojanas]; the horizontal measurement of the earth's own perimeter is one hundred thousand, while its circular measurement is three hundred thousand.
Thus, regarding water, fire, and wind:

for the circles of water, fire, and wind, the horizontal measurement from the end of each respective circle to the end of the next is two hundred thousand and three hundred thousand [yojanas] respectively;
the circular measurement follows the sequence of six, nine, and twelve.

O Lord of Men, it should be understood that in the abode of the three worlds, there are six hundred thousand *yojanas* for the water-circle, nine hundred thousand for the fire-circle, and twelve hundred thousand for the wind-circle respectively; thus, what is one hundred thousand *yojanas* on the outside is correctly one cubit in the body, according to its own respective measure, within the abode of the earth-surface.

That which is one hundred thousand *yojanas* in the external world-system becomes the measure of a single cubit in one's own body by means of one's own hand, according to the sequence previously described.

Now, the measurement starting from the atom (*paramāṇu*) and so forth is explained by the verse beginning with "by the subtle" (*sūkṣmaiḥ*): Eight subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) indeed make one minute atom (*aṇu*). By these [minute] atoms, there is the tip of a hair; by these [hair-tips], a louse-egg (*rājī*); by lice (*yūkā*), barley-corns (*yava*); and by barley-corns, finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Eight finger-breadths make a cubit (*hasta*); four cubits here make a bow (*dhanus*). Two thousand bows make a *krośa*; and by four *krośas*, there is a *yojana* for measuring [distances] in heaven, on earth, and in the sky. (13)
[In the chapter on] the summary of the measurement of the world-system: "Indeed, one atom (*aṇu*) is formed by eight subtle [particles].
Here, one atom is formed by eight subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) arranged in a row; this is the measure of an atom.
By these eight atoms of human children, [one *likṣā*] is formed.
The measure of a *rājī* (line) is formed by these eight *vālāgra*s (hair-tips) standing in a row;
by those [lines] is the measure of a *yūkā*, and by those [yūkās] is the measure of a *yava*. By eight such *uraga-yavas* (serpent-yavas), one *aṅgula* is produced;
and by twelve *aṅgulas* [is a *vitasti*].

Twelve *arka*s make one *yugma*, and two kinds of *yugma* make twenty-four; thus, by twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) arranged in a row, the measure of a cubit (*hasta*) is obtained. Four of those make a bow (*dhanus*). Here, by two thousand [bows] there is a *krośa*. Four of those make a *yojana*.

By that *yojana* is measured the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) of the gods, the terrestrial chariots of humans and others, and the measurement in the sky for the purpose of the revolution of the moon, sun, and so forth.

Now, thirty-one states of formless existence (*arūpabhava*) are described: first, the *Saudharma* heaven; then two pairs of ages (*yuga-yugayugala*); the *Brahmaloka-uttara*; the *Śrīkalpa*; the *Śvetakalpa*; from the world of *Suvasita*, the eleven [heavens] of desire (*kāma*); and four initial forms devoid of the *ha*-pair.
There are sixteen beginning with *ya*, those beginning with *ha*, and those ending with *la*, which are the desires (*kāma*). The ten manifest types of consonants are each one. (14)

"At first, the Saudharma-kalpa": "at first" means initially; by the word *saudharma*, the formless realm (*arūpabhava*) is expressed. "Kalpa" refers to that place where gods with a lifespan of a kalpa reside; thus, the celestial region is called the Saudharma-kalpa.
"Yuga-yuga-yugalami" [means] a pair of pairs of ages.

Two *yugas* constitute a pair (*yugala*), which makes four; the meaning is that the station of the formless realm (*ārūpyabhava*) consists of four types of *yuga-yuga-yugala*. The intention is that their lifespan is one, two, three, or four *kalpas*.
