Below the crown of Mount Meru is the station of the hair, consisting of the fourfold emptiness-totality (*ākāśakṛtsna*) for those who have cultivated it. Likewise, the forehead station consists of the fourfold wind-totality (*vāyukṛtsna*) for those who have cultivated it, corresponding to the Brahma-kalpa.

Thus, for those who have meditated upon it, the fourfold fire-totality (*agni-kṛtsna*) consists of two pairs of *yugas* in the region of the nose, which transcends the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*). Likewise, for those who have meditated upon it, the fourfold water-totality (*udaka-kṛtsna*) consists of two pairs of *yugas* in the Śrī-kalpa, from below the nose down to the chin.
Similarly, for those who have meditated upon it, the fourfold earth-totality (*pṛthivī-kṛtsna*) consists of two pairs of *yugas* in the region of the throat, belonging to the Śveta-kalpa.
Thus, for the sixteen [deities] possessing form, there are sixteen kalpas; starting from sixteen kalpas down to one kalpa is their lifespan.

From that point, beginning two finger-breadths below the throat down to the limit of the wind-circle below, are the eleven realms of desire (*kāmabhava*); the world of *Suvasita* is called the eleventh realm of desire, meaning that the realm of desire is divided into eleven types. Furthermore, the first four forms are devoid of the pair *ha*.

Here, the seed-syllables of form and the other [sensory objects] are the four vowels beginning with *a*; these, excluding the two *ha*s, are spoken of as the six voids (*ṣaṭśūnya*). Regarding the phrase "the sixteen are of the nature of *ya* and so forth" (*yādirūpa*), here the sixteen vowels have *i* as their first; they are called "those beginning with *ya*" (*yādi*), thus "the sixteen are of the nature of *ya* and so forth."

The desires beginning with *ha* and ending with *la* are manifest as tenfold; from the letter *ha* to the letter *la*, these ten modifications of the vowels constitute the tenfold desires beginning with *ha* and ending with *la*. They are manifest, existing, and declared in the *Āgama* of the *Vimalaprabhā*: "The consonants are each six," whereby all the consonants beginning with *ka* are included by way of abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*).
Which single phoneme becomes *ka* and *ṣa*; the conjunction of *ka* and *ṣa* is the letter *kṣa*, and that is the eleventh, the existence of desire (*kāma-bhava*).

Through these thirty-one existences, the threefold existence (*tribhava*) occurs here; through the division of the elements, there are the three realms (*tridhātu*), and this would be the triple-vajra (*vajratraya*), comprising the entirety of the three worlds through the divisions beginning with *A* and *Ka*.
The hell of Śarkarāmbhas is said to be [named] Ratnābha; the second is Vālukāmbhas; then Paṅkāmbhas, Tīvradhūma, and Havir; then Tamas, and Raurava is the seventh.

"By thirty-one existences, there shall be three existences here"—by these thirty-one existences beginning with the letter *a*, there are the three existences: existence in the desire realm (*kāma-bhava*), existence in the form realm (*rūpa-bhava*), and existence in the formless realm (*arūpa-bhava*).

Here, "thirty-one existences" refers to the four formless [realms]: those who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), those who have reached the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*), those who have reached the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), and those who have reached the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*); these are the four formless [existences].

The sixteen levels of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are: the Akaniṣṭhas, Sudarśanas, Atapas, Abṛhas, Bṛhatphalas, Puṇyaprasavas, Anabhras, Śubhakṛtsnas, Apramāṇaśubhas, Parīttaśubhas, Ābhāsvaras, Apramāṇābhas, Parīttābhas, Mahābrahmans, Brahmapurohitas, and Brahmakāyikas—these are the sixteen levels of the form realm. The eleven levels beginning with the Paranirmitavaśavartins are those of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Here, the six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—namely, the Paranirmitavaśavartins, the Nirmāṇaratis, the Tuṣitas, the Yāmas, the Trāyastriṃśas, and the Cāturmahārājakāyikas—are of inferior eons; their lifespans last for six, five, four, three, two, and one eon respectively. Included here are the asuras, who dwell within those [heavens], as well as humans, animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings;
thus, there are thirty-one states of existence (*bhava*) in the desire realm.

The vowels beginning with *a* are the designatory mantras (*saṃjñāmantra*) for formlessness (*arūpa*) and the others, respectively, according to the order previously stated. That is to say: *a, ā, aṃ, aḥ* are the [bases of] the totality of formlessness and space (*ākāśakṛtsna*); *i, ī, e, ai* are the totality of wind (*vāyukṛtsna*); *ṛ, ṝ, ar, ār* are the totality of fire (*agnikṛtsna*); *u, ū, o, au* are the totality of water (*udakakṛtsna*); *ḷ, ḹ, al, āl* are the totality of earth (*pṛthivīkṛtsna*). Thus, by the power of their ethical discipline (*śīlabala*), these sixteen forms became the [deities] of Akaniṣṭha and the other realms through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhibala*) upon the totalities of wind and the rest.

By the syllables *ha*, *hā*, *ya*, *yā*, *ra*, and *rā*, the six classes of beings belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) came into being through the power of generosity and the power of mantra-recitation: *va* and *vā* represent the asuras; humans came into being through the power of generosity, and among them, [specific types] through the power of wholesome and unwholesome karma; *la* and *lā* represent animals and hungry ghosts—animals through inferior evil and hungry ghosts through middling evil; and by the syllable *kṣa*, hell-beings came into being through supreme evil.

In the first nāga-world, by the power of merit, and in the first hell, by the power of evil, there is a lifespan of an *adharma-kalpa*; in the second and third hells, a lifespan of a *madhyama-kalpa*; in the fourth and fifth hells, a lifespan of an *utkṛṣṭa-kalpa*; in the sixth and seventh hells, a lifespan of a *mahākalpa*;
and in the eighth hell, a lifespan until the dissolution of the world-system (*lokadhātūpasaṃhāra*).
Thus, by means of these thirty-one existences, the meaning is "the three realms of existence" (*tribhava*).
The division of the elements is threefold, namely the three realms;
this is the triple vajra, which is body, speech, and mind.
It should be understood that the entirety of the three worlds—celestial, terrestrial, and subterranean—is [subsumed] through the divisions beginning with *ā* and *ka*.

Just as the letter *kṣa* arises through the combination of a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) *ṣa* with the vowel *a*, so too is the retroflex taken in place of the dental; thus, by the removal of the *tra*, it becomes *tra*, O [friend], there is no [other]. 9. [In the chapter on the half-moon: The summary of the measure of the world-system: one *yojana* is the measure of the lowest eon to travel across in length and breadth.

And when that [space] is filled with fine tips of hair, and each single tip of hair is removed once every hundred years until it becomes empty, then that is one day of the lowest *kalpa*. Thirty such days make a month; twelve months make a year; and a hundred years are called a *kalpa*.
Thus, the square of that—the multiplication by the number of lowest *kalpas*—is the middle *kalpa*; and the square of the middle *kalpa* is the supreme *kalpa*.
In this way, due to the power of their sins, sentient beings experience the sufferings of hell and so forth for many countless *kalpas*.
By the power of merit, the happiness of the gods in the heavens and other realms lasts for many eons;
now, the designations of the abodes of the nāgas and so forth are being stated,
regarding which there is no dispute with the non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthikas) and others as to their names.
Regarding the statement that "Śarkarāmbhas is said to be a hell": here, *ratnābha* refers to a dwelling (*āvāsa*) where there is radiance (*ābhā*) from jewels (*ratna*);
from that world of asuras and nāgas, it is twenty-five thousand *yojanas* below in measure.
Therefore, from that Ratnābha hell, Śarkarāmbhas is declared—that is, it is said to be a hell;
Bālukāmbhas by name is the second, and Paṅkāmbhas is the third—these are the two cold hells.
Then, Tāmradhūma is the fourth hell, and Havya is the fifth—these are the two hot hells.

Below that is the sixth, Tamas; the seventh is Mahātamas; and the two hells of Khara and Vāta together with Vajrārcis constitute the eighth, Vajrasūcyagrabhūmāga, which is eternally blazing—thus there are eight great hells in Pātāla.
There are seven oceans of salt, wine, water, milk, curd, ghee, and honey. The mountains are Nīlābha, Mandara, Niṣadha, Maṇikara, Candra (white-shining), Varaparamakuśa, Droṇa, Sītādri, and Vajra.
The Kinnaras dwell in Bhogabhūmi, and the Krauñcas and Raudras in Jambū; the human being dwells in the seventh region, Karmabhūmi. || 16 ||

"The seven oceans are the alkaline, the wine, water, milk, curd, clarified butter, and the sweet; thus, the alkaline ocean is outside the circle of the earth, while the wine and others are the seven mountains above the earth—namely Nīlābha, Mandara, Niṣadha, Maṇikara, Droṇa, Śītādri, and Vajra. Vajra is on the outside of the alkaline ocean. The Himavat and other principal mountain ranges (kulaparvatas) are situated outside each respective ocean of wine and so forth, like the binding of a water-wheel."

The islands are Candra (Moon), Śitābha (White Light), Varaparamakuśa (Excellent Supreme Kuśa), Kinnara, Krauñca, Raudra, and Jambū; humans dwell in these. Among them, the seventh, Mahājambūdvīpa, is ring-shaped, measuring one hundred thousand yojanas in width and three hundred thousand in circumference; it should be known that where humans dwell is the land of action (*karmabhūmi*), while the other six are lands of enjoyment (*bhogabhūmi*).

Jambūdvīpa extends from the shore of the salt ocean, while the remaining continents extend from the shores of the oceans of wine and so forth. Now, the four continents within the great Jambūdvīpa are described: O Lord of Men, in the east it is semi-circular; in the south, a triangle of fire; in the north, a full moon; and in the west, a half-moon. In the center of the mandalas is Sumeru, made of excellent adamant, shaped like a zero (a dot), and consisting of the best of vajras. The mountains, nagas, planets, and directions are situated there, and the surface of the earth measures one thousand yojanas. (17)
[The reading is] "pāṭhaḥ"; however, according to the lexicon (*kośa*), the reading "niṣadha" is correct.
Regarding the circles that have emerged from the *bhaura* [wind]: in the *Vimalaprabhā* [section on the World System], it is stated: "First, the wind-circle is circular in the east;

in the east, by the nature of the wind-circle, it is circular and half-moon shaped; in the south, by the nature of the fire-circle, it is triangular; in the north, by the nature of the water-circle, it is circular and half-moon shaped; in the west, by the nature of the earth-circle, it is square. [Note: The text appears to contain a scribal error regarding the final shape description.]

In the center of the mandalas—namely the east, south, west, and north—is Meru, which has the nature of the solar mandala, appearing as a drop (bindu) and composed of the supreme vajra. Thus, Meru is situated in the middle of the mountains, the nāgas, the planets, and the directions; it measures one thousand yojanas in height from the surface of the earth.

The measurement in *yojanas* of these four mandalas is, respectively: "the earth-surface" (*bhuvitala*) as seven thousand; "the mountains" (*śailā*) as eight thousand; "the planets" (*grahā*) as nine thousand; and "the directions" (*dig*) as ten thousand *yojanas*. This is the measurement for the four continents in their respective order. Herein, that which is circular in the east and square in the west has the nature of wind and earth from front to back, and the nature of water and fire on the left and right of the body;
therefore, the characteristic of the four continents is by way of the form of the four mandalas.

Now, the measurement of the extent of Mount Meru and the others is stated: the height of Meru from the base at the surface of the earth is one thousand and fifty-one yojanas; on the excellent surface of the ground, the Cakravāḍa is correctly [situated], and above it are five peaks. At the base of the earth, there is the Cakravāḍa in all directions; outside of that are the islands, mountains, and oceans, as well as fire and wind in every direction. (18)

The extent of Meru from top to bottom, reaching as far as its eastern, western, northern, and southern parts, is fifty thousand [yojanas] at the base upon the surface of the earth; the circumference of the Cakravāḍa is sixteen thousand plus one thousand [yojanas];
five peaks extend upward, while [the rest] are submerged within the surface of the earth; and outside of that Cakravāḍa in all directions are the islands and mountains.

Outside that Cakravāḍa, within the space of the four peaks at the location of the openings, there are six continents, six oceans, and six mountains; among them, Himādri with its peak constitutes the seventh, Jambūdvīpa. Outside of that is the ring of the salt ocean, followed on all sides by the rings of fire and wind;

thus each one [of these] is one thousand [yojanas]. The six oceans are each less than the moon [in diameter] by one moon [unit]; likewise, the islands are one thousand, and the Kulaparvatas are twenty-five thousand.
Jambūdvīpa is vast, measuring half a hundred thousand [yojanas] from the salt ocean; likewise is the measure of Fire, Wind, and the final one, the Supporter of the Three Worlds.
Each of the six oceans is one thousand minus one moon and its light (i.e., 999);
the meaning is that each individual ocean is one thousand less one hundred and one.
Likewise, there are six continents and six excellent mountain ranges.
Thus, the equal measurement of these eighteen—of the continents, oceans, and mountains—is six;

that same [measurement], when divided by eighteen from sixteen thousand due to its subtlety, is the clear [result]: six hundred and eleven. This is the summary of the measurement of the world-system in the eleventh chapter.
The measurement of the moon and its reflection has been stated here briefly as being "devoid [of that].

In this context, from the central abode of Brahmā at the center of Meru, extending eight thousand *yojanas* downward in all directions, there is one [ring] belonging to the Cakravāḍa. Beyond nine thousand *yojanas*, up to sixteen thousand *yojanas*, the six continents and so forth are situated.
Therefore, the clear measurement is obtained by dividing sixteen thousand by eighteen parts.

Outside of that, the vast Jambūdvīpa, twenty-five thousand [yojanas] in extent, is ring-shaped in the eight directions around Meru; outside of that, the measure of the salt ocean is half a lakṣa in all directions,
and likewise is the measure of the fire-ring, the wind-ring, and the final one which supports the three worlds.

Thus, from Mount Meru, the abode of Brahmā, there are two hundred thousand yojanas in each direction; in the body, the earth-mandala is half the chest, the water-mandala is the upper arm, the fire-mandala is the forearm, and the wind-mandala extends from the wrist to the fingertips— such is the measurement of the world-system.

Now, the location of the Kālacakra deities, the nāga seats (pīṭhas), sub-seats (upapīṭhas), and so forth, is described starting with "In the Brahmāṇḍa, the Kālacakra... and so on: "In the Brahmāṇḍa is the Kālacakra together with the supreme Jina, praised by the hosts of gods; on Meru is the circle of the Gīrvāṇas, and that which has gone to the surface of the earth is the five-colored [mandala] of the snakes.

From all directions of glorious Meru, extending to the edge of fire and wind, is situated the entire circle of the earth consisting of all the seats (pīṭhas) and sub-seats (upapīṭhas), the fields (kṣetras), the chandohas, the melāpakas, and the cremation grounds (citibhuvana). (20)

In the external body, which is the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), there is the Kālacakra at the crown jewel (*uṣṇīṣamaṇi*). That very [deity] is praised together with the best of Jinas and accompanied by all the Buddhas as the *Samāja*, having become one with the hosts of deities such as the Bodhisattvas and Brahmā;
thus, on Mount Meru is the circle of gods (*gīrvāṇacakra*) beginning with Brahmā, while on the surface of the earth is the five-colored circle of the Nāgas.
In all directions from Śrī Meru, situated upon the circle of the earth, are all the *pīṭhas* and *upapīṭhas*.

The *pīṭha* is established in the four cardinal directions with the natures of air, fire, water, and earth as Pūrvavideha, Laghujambūdvīpa, Uttarakuru, and Aparagodānīya; the *upapīṭhas* are likewise situated in the four cardinal directions with those same natures, specifically in the southeast, southwest, northeast, and northwest.
Thus, the field (kṣetra) and sub-field (upakṣetra) are in the eastern half of the ocean;
the chandoha and upachandoha are in the western half of the ocean;
and the melāpaka and upamelāpaka are in the half-circle of the fire-girdle (agnivalaya).

The half behind the fire [mandala] consists of the Veśma and Upaveśma; the half behind the wind-circle consists of the eight great cremation grounds (mahāśmaśāna), namely Śmaśāna and Upaśmaśāna, located at the edge of the wind-circle.

In this way, the twelve stages (*bhūmi*) beginning with the *pīṭhas* are to be understood; and within the body, the twelve stages correspond to the twelve joints of the hands and feet. Now, the locations of the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*) are described: In the east is Śakra; Agni is in the southeast; Yama, Dhanada (Kubera), and Varuṇa are in the south, southwest, and west respectively; Vāyu, Yakṣa, and Hara are in the northwest, north, and northeast; and above and below are Brahmā and Viṣṇu. All these guardians of their respective directions, together with their retinues, [reside there]. In their midst is Kālacakra, the progenitor of the best of Jinas, the Unstruck One (*anāhata*), whose body is vajra. (21)
In the east is Śakra; Śakra is on the summit of Meru in the eastern direction;

Agni is in the southeast; Yama is in the south; Danu is among the Daityas; Varuṇa is in the west; Vāyu is in the northwest; Yakṣa is with the Giver of Wealth (Kubera); Hara is in the north; Brahmā is in the upper region; and Viṣṇu is below.

All these, Śakra and the others, together with their retinues, are the guardians of their respective directions; among them, Kālacakra—the progenitor of the Jinas, the Unstruck (Anāhata), the Vajra-body—is the lord of the guardians of the directions. Now, the wandering of the Great Cakravartin across the twelve divisions of the earth is described: on the ridges of Mount Meru, in all directions upon the surface of the earth, Durjaya wanders; wherever Dharma has perished and the Kali Yuga prevails, there he goes.

Having slain the Mlecchas in battle, he moves about after establishing them in their own dharma; indeed, the Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages have passed, and now the other age, Kali, prevails through the power of time.

On the ridges of Meru, he wanders through the directions for the sake of enjoyment; he is difficult for the Dānavas and Mlecchas to conquer. In whichever region of the earth the Dharma of the Tathāgata has perished and their contrary (perverted) Dharma prevails, there on that ground the Cakrin wanders during the Kali Yuga. That very Kali Yuga is characterized by unrighteousness (*adharma*); the meaning is that it carries the Kali Yuga along.
In whichever region it carries the Mleccha-dharma, to that very region he goes with great force; he proceeds.

Having slain the Mlecchas, Dānavas, and others in battle, he moves about, having established those Mlecchas and others in their own duty (*svadharma*). By the conjunction of time (*kālayoga*), the Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages have indeed ceased, and the Kali age alone prevails;
the meaning here is that this is another cycle of ages beginning with the Kṛta, and not another [cycle] beginning with a Great Kṛta (*mahākṛta*) age.
This age proceeds by the conjunction of time.
Time is the wheel of the twelve zodiac signs; through its conjunction—that is, through the conjunction of time—it proceeds by way of the division of the four *sandhyās*.
In whichever segment that powerful Wheel enters, there the Kṛta Yuga occurs; Tretā is behind the King [of the wheel], and Kali is in front, while Dvāpara is between the two.
The duration of each of the Yugas is twenty-one thousand years plus one hundred and sixty; when multiplied by the arrows [five] of the Yugas, that is the measure of one hundred human years.
In whichever region that powerful Wheel-turner (Cakrī) enters, there the Kṛta Yuga prevails; the meaning is that the Dharma of the Perfectly Awakened One (Samyaksambuddha) prevails there.

Tretā is behind the king; that is, Tretā occurs behind the king. At the end of the Kṛta, there is the absence of one quarter of the Dharma; at the end of the Tretā, there is the absence of two quarters. Kali also precedes the king; there is the absence of all four quarters of the Dharma. Regarding the measure of the four Yugas, that is their total measure; the measure of each individual one is multiplied by the number of arrows (five) in a Yuga.
"Yuga" means four, and "śara" means five; multiplied by these [makes] fifty-four, which is "multiplied by yugas and arrows.
When the hundred human years are thus multiplied, it becomes five thousand four hundred. This is because the measure of each individual yuga is equal.

In the chapter on the measurement of the world-systems, this is the summary of the measurements: now, the measurement of the breaths of those born from human bodies and others is stated— The measure for the minute-bodied beings (*aṇutanuja*), humans, spirits (*bhūta*), gods, and asuras is, respectively, twenty-one thousand six hundred times the number of subtle breaths in a day and age (*yuga*).

The Lord of Power (*Śaktibhartṛ*) passes through one day of enjoyment; the measure of power (*śaktimāna*) consists of [twelve] ages (*yuga*). In every land (*khaṇḍa*), the Wheel-turner (*Cakrī*) proceeds to the state of Śiva in a single day of twelve suns.
Regarding the passage beginning with "subtle breath" (*sūkṣmocchvāsa*):

"Subtle" refers to one part of a single human inhalation and exhalation, which consists of twenty-one thousand six hundred [breaths]; this is a subtle breath. Six of those breaths constitute one *pāṇīpala* for beings such as insects and the like. Sixty *pāṇīpalas* make one *ghaṭī*, and sixty *ghaṭīs* make one day. Thus, a "day" for beings such as insects is a count of twenty-one thousand six hundred inhalations and exhalations. By those breaths, a day passes for them; for *bhūtas* and *pretas*, a day is measured by *dhrus*. "Dhru" means their own day.

Thirty times the breath of a human being constitutes one breath for the dark fortnight (the day) of the *pretas* and the *pitṛs*, and the bright fortnight (the night) is their own day. By means of these *nāḍīs*, three hundred and sixty breaths of humans constitute one breath of the gods, which is their day.
Twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths of humans constitute one breath of the *asuras*.
A *dhrū* is a human year;
a *śakti* is a single breath of Śakti, which is the lifespan of the Akaniṣṭha class of beings;
a *yuga* is a single breath of the Sustainer (*Bhartṛ*), consisting of a total of sixty-one thousand six hundred human years.
Regarding the "Lord" (*bhartuḥ*), this refers to the class of beings who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

For those of subtle breath—the humans of minute bodies, the *bhūtas*, gods, and asuras—the measure is respectively one thousand and two hundred and twenty-one years, and six [days]. Thus, for the Lord of Power (*śakteḥ*), it is a single day.
In this manner, according to the previously stated sequence, for these beings starting from the minute-bodied ones, their own respective days amount to twenty-one thousand six hundred.
Among these measures, the measure of power (*śakti-māna*) of the Akaniṣṭha gods is carried upon the surface of the earth by the Wheel-turner (*cakrin*) as the measure of power for the *yugas*.
Thus, in each and every region (*khaṇḍa*), the Wheel-turner proceeds to the state of Śiva;
having established the Buddha-dharma in each individual region, he proceeds to the state of Great Bliss (*mahāsukha-pada*), the abode of Great Bliss.
Twelve suns [arise] in a single day;

likewise, in each individual section, there is one universal monarch (*cakravartin*) who propagates the Dharma. Thus, twelve universal monarchs exist on a single day. Each one passes away in eighteen hundred years of human beings, which correspond to eighteen hundred breaths of power (*śakti-śvāsa*).
Thus, the twelve suns are the suns of Dharma, the initiators of the path of merit and wisdom.
Externally, according to the year and the division of the twelve zodiac signs, the twelve suns move;

now, the temporal divisions for each individual day by means of the breaths of the subtle [winds] and so forth are described: O King, all fortnights, months, seasons, yugas, ages, the time of fire (the three hours), the two solstices, the entire year, as well as the days, ghaṭikās, ascendants, and pāṇīpala-measures [are contained therein].

In this manner, these very [elements] move through the bodies of gods, humans, and asuras—those who owe debts to their progenitors—just so within the body, the abode of the three worlds, during the day of the Lord of Power (Śaktibhartṛ). || 25 ||
Regarding the phrase "pakṣāḥ" and so forth:
here, in each individual day, there are twenty-four fortnights (pakṣas) for the [signs] beginning with Aries;
these constitute all the months, which are twelve months in total.
The six seasons, the four periods of the yuga,
and the three times known as the time of fire— these are the [three] times.
The two solstices (*ayanau*) constitute one year, O King; all this is to be understood according to the division of years.

Likewise, day by day, there are three hundred and sixty days, three hundred and twenty *ghaṭikās*, thirty *pāṇīpalas*, and four thousand two hundred and fifty *lagnas*. The *ghaṭikās* number twenty-one thousand six hundred, and the *pāṇīpalas* number twelve hundred and ninety-six thousand. Thus it is stated in the *Vimalaprabhā*. [End of section on] the World System (*lokadhātu*).
These very components of the year for the body-born beings and others proceed thus day by day; they proceed by way of the divisions of breath.
Therein, one fortnight passes with nine hundred breaths, and with twenty-four fortnights, a day—the year—passes.
Eighteen hundred breaths constitute a month; twelve months pass as a day, which is a year;
thirty-six hundred breaths constitute a season (*ṛtu*); six seasons pass as a day, which is a year;
and fifty-four hundred breaths constitute a yuga.
A day [of Brahmā] consists of four yugas;
seventy-two hundred breaths pass as one period of time (kāla); and a day [of Viṣṇu] consists of three kālas, which passes as a year.
A year is reached by means of ten thousand eight hundred breaths through two solstices;
thus, for the body and the other [elements], each day and year is reached by their respective measures of twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths.
Thus, by sixty breaths a day and night passes;
by three hundred and sixty days and nights a year passes;
and by five breaths a lunar mansion (lagna) passes.
A day passes as thirty-four hundred and twenty lunar mansions (*nakṣatra-lagna*); one breath passes as one *ghaṭikā*;
and sixty counts of one breath pass as one *pāṇīpala*.
One breath passes for every three hundred and sixty parts of a breath;
[one breath passes for every twenty-one thousand six hundred parts of a breath];
twenty-one thousand six hundred ghaṭikās constitute a day, which becomes a year.
A day and a year pass with twelve hundred and ninety-six thousand *pāṇipala*s;
a day and a year pass with seven hundred and seventy-six thousand breaths (*śvāsa*s);
likewise, one hundred days (or one hundred years) pass with seventy-seven hundred and sixty million breaths.
Due to the power of karma, that supreme lifespan becomes deficient or excessive;
by the power of yoga for yogins and by the power of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for ascetics, it becomes increased through their respective measures,
such that a single breath passes in the duration of one *ghaṭikā*.

Due to the power of evil beings, he becomes weakened, and for him there is no certainty through supreme scripture or reasoning. However, it is stated in the Vedas: "A person indeed has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundred faculties" (AiB 2.17.4.19).
This is a figurative statement (*prapañcavacana*) meaning that a hundred years is the maximum lifespan for humans, [given] the increase in the lifespan of men during the Kṛta Yuga.

Here, according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), the term "person" (*puruṣa*) refers to each day and each year. Through one hundred days and one hundred years, within the internal [body] and externally again, by means of the rotation of another cycle of breaths, it is said: "The person has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundred faculties.
Thus, through two hundred days, the four ages (*caturyuga*) pass within the internal [body]; externally, they correspond to forty-three lakh and twenty thousand years by means of the breaths.

Thus, by the revolution of both wheels, for both persons, two months constitute one season; on the left and right, there are ten mandalas, and the flow of the vital breath (prāṇapravāha) constitutes one mandala in four hundred and thirty-two thousand years.
In this way, with five mandalas, all the planets enter into the void at their respective places of birth.

Then, again, by the engagement of another foot, it will be said that another person has emerged from the middle [channel]; this is what must be stated in the *Śrī Kālacakra-tantrarāja*, twelve thousand verses extracted from the *Śrī Paramādibuddha*, in the commentary *Vimalaprabhā*, the eighth chapter, the summary of the measurement of the world-system (*lokadhātumāna*). [Chapter 9] The Great Summary on the Method of Astral Knowledge (*jyotirjñānavidhi*).

Now, in this great chapter on the method of the knowledge of luminosity (*jyotirjñānavidhimahoddeśa*), I shall expand upon the following: the manifestation of Mañjuśrī in the realm of Sambhala; the destruction of the astronomical Siddhāntas due to the arising of the Mleccha religion; the commencement of the *Laghukaraṇa*; and the prophecy of the Tathāgata beginning with "from the first year.

Six hundred years from the first year, King Yaśas will appear openly in the place called Sambhala. From that time, for eight hundred years, the Mleccha religion will indeed prevail in the land of Makha.

At that time, O man, it should be known that on earth the calculation of the planets will become clear and simplified, while the destruction of the established astronomical systems (siddhāntas) will occur throughout the entire surface of the world through the power of Time. || 26 ||
"Six hundred years from the first year, Yaśas will appear in the land named Sambhala.

Here, "the first year" refers to the year of the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma. Six hundred years from that year, in the region named Sambhala to the north of the Śītā River—where "Yaśas" is the reading in the scriptural tradition—the one of great fame, Mañjuśrī, will manifest; the meaning is that he will assume an emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
"From that, after eight hundred years... [continues].
Therefore, it has been determined by the Nāgas that after eight hundred years from the passing of Yaśas,
the practice of the Mleccha religion will indeed prevail in the region of Makha.
In the southern region of Makha, adorned with ten million villages, there will arise among the Mlecchas the practice of the Asura-dharma known as Tāyi.
During that time of the Mlecchas, men on earth must clearly understand the *laghukaraṇa* (abbreviated calculation); for it is said that the *siddhāntas* (astronomical treatises) will have perished.

The Siddhāntas are the Brahma, Saura, Yāma, and Romaka. Regarding the destruction of these four Siddhāntas, "the destruction of the Siddhāntas occurs on the entire surface of the earth" means that "entire" refers to where the systems of the Tīrthikas exist. There, the "entire surface of the earth" extends from Śītā to the south; it is not the case that the destruction of the Buddhist Siddhānta occurs only in regions such as Sambhala.
"Kālayoga" means that it will come into being through the conjunction of time;

"time" refers here to the Mleccha-dharma, and the "conjunction with the Siddhāntas" is *kālayoga*. From that *kālayoga* it will arise. The locative case in "kālayoge" is used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe saptamī*);

therefore, the statement that the *laghukaraṇa* (abbreviated calculation) is "clear" due to the destruction of the Siddhāntas is like the proverb of the mother and the sweetmeat. In reality, for the followers of other sects (*tīrthikas*), the *laghukaraṇa* and so forth are not clear.
Why? Because of the sarcastic statement, "the destruction of the Siddhāntas.
If the Karaṇa and other systems were accurate, then there would be no destruction of the Siddhāntas, since the planets can be established through the Karaṇa as well.
Furthermore, solar correction (*sūrya-śuddhi*) is not observed in other Karaṇas when tested by shadow on the day of the winter solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*).

During the northern transit (uttarāyaṇa), if the solar longitude is not purified by the correction for shadow (chāyā-śuddhi), it is impure; because the solar longitude is impure, the lunar longitude is likewise impure. In this same manner, even Mars and the other planets, though corrected with respect to the sun, remain impure in their own longitudes due to the impurity of the solar longitude.
Because the longitudes of the planets are thus impure, the results of the planets in horoscopes and other astrological works produced by the Tīrthikas are rendered useless.

In this Siddhānta system, the corrections and additive values for the planets are to be calculated by women and children, so that the planets may be easily understood by ordinary people and others. Because of this, envy has arisen among the wicked heretics (*duṣṭatīrthika*): "If all women, children, and the like come to know the movement of the planets, then who will show us respect? Therefore, it was written: "The naked ones (*acelaka*), the Śaivas, and those who worship Rāhu as a god shall come forth. (gCer Bu Pa Dan sGra Can bzo, hByun Bar hGur Ro).

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, having reflected thus—"Having removed the Siddhāntas, we shall compose the Tantras and so forth"—the Siddhāntas were kept secret, while the composition of the Tantras and such was made public.

In the Tantra, numerous sets of daily accumulations (*ahargaṇa*) were presented; likewise, in the Karaṇa, the fourfold operation of slow and fast [planets] was elaborated upon, so that when foolish people saw this difficulty, they fled far away and no longer even practiced what is called astrology.

Thus, due to the power of time, the constant (dhruvaka) in the astronomical manual (karaṇa) is no longer precise; because it is imprecise, the solar longitude is incorrect, and due to that incorrect solar longitude, the longitudes of all the planets became incorrect. Therefore, the manuals and other works composed by wicked-minded people for the sake of deceiving others have resulted in their own ignorance through the injury they inflicted upon others;
hence, injuring others is always reprehensible.

Since the daily additive increments for the planets are to be stated hereafter, the *laghukaraṇa* (abridged calculation) is now set forth: The well-known Mleccha year beginning from the Prabhava cycle is mixed with [the numbers] fire (3), sky (0), and ocean (4). This Mleccha year is diminished by eight (8), one (1), and moon (1). The remainder is multiplied by twelve (12) and increased by the months starting from Caitra. This sum is divided by thirty (30); the quotient is added to the top [of the original number], O King, and thus the pure accumulation of months is obtained. (27)

Regarding the statement "mixed in the ocean of nine breaths," the *dhruvaka* here is not fixed, because in the *Tantrarāja* it is stated that the *dhruvaka* is established again at the end of the sixty-year cycle;
likewise, in this system, the *mañjuśrī-kāla* becomes the fixed *dhruvaka* in the calculation after six hundred years from the time of the Tathāgata.

Therefore, the era of the Mlecchas consists of eight hundred years; from that era of the Mlecchas, diminished by one hundred and eighty-two, is the era of Aja-Kalkī, by which Aja the *laghukaraṇa* was purified.
That very era becomes the constant (*dhruvaka*) in the *karaṇa*, starting from the year of the Mlecchas, beginning with the Prabhava year.

Those sixty-year cycles of which *prabhava* is the beginning, mouth, or first are called *prabhavamukha*. Within each of these, the preceding year of the current year is included as having entered the *prabhavamukha*;
thus, mixed with that, the well-known *mleccha* year consists of four hundred and three years.
Starting from the first year up to the sixtieth year, it remains mixed as having entered the *prabhavamukha*.
That very year becomes well-known among all other systems of calculation, just like the days of the week beginning with Āditya;

it is mixed into the aggregate of four hundred and three years, and thus the Mleccha year is established. The Mleccha is Madhumatī, the incarnation of Rahmaṇa, the teacher of the Mleccha dharma, and the preceptor and lord of the Tāyis, the Mlecchas.

The year of the Mleccha lord is diminished by one hundred and eighty-two—meaning diminished by "hand, hood, and moon" (182)—which is the year of the time of Ajakalkī in the region of Sambhala; that very [remainder] is the aggregate of years in the *laghukaraṇa*. Furthermore, that same aggregate of years, multiplied by twelve for the purpose of determining the aggregate of months, becomes the aggregate of months once it has been multiplied by twelve and reduced by the remainder of one hundred and eighty-two.
"Combined with the months beginning with Caitra" means that very same aggregate of months is combined with the current months starting from Caitra for the sake of the current month;
thus it is "multiplied by the lower yuga."

That same mass of months, having placed the mass of months both above and below the heap— having made the mass of months below the heap and multiplied it by four for the purpose of determining the intercalary month—
is divided by zero-fire-moon (130). Here, an intercalary month occurs every thirty-two and a half months of the sun, due to the absence of a solar ingress (saṃkramaṇa) on the new moon day.
By that, there would be no quotient; therefore, the heap is multiplied by four to become the quotient-heap.
When the quotient-heap has been multiplied by four, according to the maxim "In the absence of the cause, there is the absence of the effect," the heap to be divided is multiplied by four.
Therefore, from the *Jyotirjñānavidhimahoddeśa*: the result obtained by dividing the heap by the quotient-heap is the quotient.

That which was obtained [from the calculation] is entered at the top; that very same accumulated excess month (*adhikamāsa-piṇḍa*) becomes entered into the heap of months at the top, O Lord of Men, for the purpose of calculating the thirty lunar days (*tithi*) in the current month so that the month-count is purified. Now, the monthly constant (*māsadhruvaka*) is stated: The months, situated in three places, are multiplied by ten and three (thirty) and placed in the middle heap; the quotient obtained from dividing the root [heap] by six becomes a debt (*ṛṇa*) which must be subtracted from the middle heap.

The upward and downward [values] multiplied by thirty and divided by sixty reveal the mixed wealth; that which is obtained enters the head, and the remaining day-count is determined by the best of sages. ||28||
"Months situated in three places, multiplied by hand and fire, are those which stand in the middle heap"— here,

having placed the pure months in three places, those months which stand in the middle heap are multiplied by "hand and fire," that is, by thirty-two, for the sake of the weekday *ghaṭikās* of each month.

"Obtained by a sixth part of the root" means that what is obtained by dividing the root-quantity (mūlarāśi) by six becomes a debt in the middle quantity; therefore, it must be subtracted from the middle quantity because it is a debt. [This is indicated by] "the upward and downward [signs] reveal thirty-two [units] as mixed wealth."

This fixed value, beginning with Maṅgala and so forth, has arrived as the calculation for setting (astamana). Therefore, for the purpose of calculating the rising of the Sun and other planets, there is an addition of two units to the upper heap (mūrdhni rāśau); there is an addition of thirty ghaṭikās to the lower heap (adho rāśau). Thus, the mixed [sum] of the upper and lower [values] is "two and thirty" (netraṃ ca triṃśat), meaning twenty-three. Divided by sixty, the quotient is added to the original heap of ghaṭikās; the quotient obtained by dividing by sixty becomes the heap of days (vārapiṇḍa), while the remainder becomes the heap of ghaṭikās for the duration of the day. This is entered at the top.

That same [sum] divided by sixty gives the quotient for the weekday-pile (*vārapiṇḍa*), which is added to the top of the weekday-heap. When this is divided by the seven excellent sages (i.e., seven), the remainder is indeed the weekday; thus, in the monthly calculation, the weekday must remain at the top. The pile of *ghaṭikās* below the weekday is placed in two positions and mixed with the sun and moon (twelve and one). Divided by six (the seasons) and increased by five (the elements), the entire sum is to be added to that top heap. When the first hand (one) has struck the heap, the resulting pile is divided by eight and two (ten).

When the middle value is multiplied by nine and divided by the product of the lower and upper values, the result is added to two; this is subtracted from the middle value. Furthermore, when the middle value is divided by six, it is added as a positive quantity to the top heap after being doubled. || 29 ||

Now the terms for the weekdays are stated: "The lunar month-pile mixed with the sun and moon" means that very same lunar month-pile, mixed with the sun and moon, and further increased by one hundred and twelve;
the phrase "sun and moon" refers to the *karaṇa* system and not to the *siddhānta*, thus it results in two places.
The accumulated months are divided by the sun’s [mean] revolutions;
the quotient obtained by dividing by one hundred and twenty-six is added as a positive quantity to the upper heap,
for the purpose of accounting for two piṇḍas per month, which must be added to the upper heap.
When the first [value] has been subtracted, the remainder is to be added;

thus, everything is mixed with the *bhūta* [five]. This is the requirement for the calculation: the quotient obtained by dividing by the sun [twelve] and the seasons [six] is the established result (*siddhānta*).

Since one *piṇḍa* becomes additional in the place of the *piṇḍas* every one hundred and twenty-six months due to the movement of the moon, the *piṇḍa* is divided by twenty-eight; because there are twenty-eight divisions for the seven-day week, the quotient obtained by that division constitutes the daily weekday-position (*vārapada*) for each month.
The remainder obtained by dividing the *vāra-ghaṭikā* by six (*ṛtu*) becomes the constituent part of the *piṇḍa*; it should be placed beneath the *piṇḍa*.
Now, the calculation for the solar asterism (*sūryanakṣatra*) is stated: "The months that have been purified, multiplied by eleven (*īśa*), exist in three places—in the head, the middle, and below."
Those months which are in the middle are multiplied by the lords (īśa), that is, multiplied by eleven; this is according to the *Karaṇa* system and not according to the *Siddhānta*.

"The quotient obtained by dividing by nine times the lower [value], increased by two" means that the quotient obtained by dividing the lower quantity by forty-nine (nine times one less than four) is increased by two; this is an additive constant (*kṣepaka*) according to the *Karaṇa* system.
If [the time] is deficient, it is subtracted from the middle heap; "deficient" means it is a debt (*ṛṇa*). Furthermore, even when divided by *ghaṭīs*, it becomes a credit (*dhana*);
that is, the quotient obtained by dividing the middle heap by sixty *ghaṭīs* is added as a credit to the heap at the top, becoming the nakṣatra-accumulation (*nakṣatrapinda*).

The remaining *ghaṭikās* of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) are divided by sixty; that same [remainder] is placed as wealth at the top of the zodiacal sign (*rāśi*). Having doubled it and added the *cakṣa*, it becomes divided [by sixty], O King; the remainder is the enjoyment of the asterism and so forth. To the day of the week (*vāra*), one day is to be added; to the mass of *ghaṭikās*, twice the number of kings (two) are to be added below, and two *nāḍīs* of Rudra (eleven). This reveals the wealth to be added to the solar enjoyment (*sūryabhoga*); this shall be the fixed [correction] for the month. Although it has been stated thus, it must be applied again month after month. ||30||
And when the conjunction is divided by twenty-seven,
it becomes the invitation to the king;
the remainder is the Sun's enjoyment of the asterism and so forth.
Here, at the top is the sum of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra-piṇḍa*), and below is the sum of the lunar mansion minutes (*ghaṭikā*).
Furthermore, this impure monthly reckoner has been composed even from the purified [result] for the sake of instructing beginners;
one *vāra* (weekday) should be added to the weekday, and one *vāra* should be added to the position of the weekday.

"Twice the king's ghaṭīs" means sixteen ghaṭīs; "twice the king's ghaṭīs" means thirty-two ghaṭīs, which are to be placed in the position of the ghaṭikās. "And two in the piṇḍaka below" means that two are to be given in the position of the piṇḍa below the ghaṭikās; and "two asterisms" refers to the position of the nakṣatras.

In the place of the *ghaṭikās* of the constellations, "Rudra" means eleven *nāḍīs* should be added; this makes it clear that [this] is wealth (*dhana*). In the solar transit (*sūryabhoga*), the constellations and so forth are to be applied.
Therefore, it should be a monthly offering; even though it has been so described, it is to be given month after month, that is, offered in each individual month.
This "monthly offering" was prophesied by the Blessed One in advance, depending on the requirements of the ritual procedure.

Now, the calculation by means of the month, lunar day (*tithi*), and so forth, is stated: The lunar days (*tithis*) are to be added, subtracted, and again added to the *vāra*, *nāḍī*, and *pada* [of the weekday]; in the *piṇḍa* [total], they are divided by four; when the result is even or odd, the factors of the *pada* are to be added or subtracted. In the case of zero, the subtraction is zero. In the *pada* of thirty-three, there is five; in those of twelve and twelve, ten; in the *pada* of forty-one, twenty less one. [Note: This verse describes the specific additive and subtractive values for the various *pada*-units (0–40) in the calculation of the weekday.]
"The lunar days (tithis) are to be added or subtracted again within the divisions of the day (vāra), nāḍīs, and padas.

Here, in the monthly constant (dhruvaka), starting from the first lunar day of the bright fortnight up until the thirtieth new moon (amāvāsī), the lunar days are to be added or subtracted. 1. ṅa. below; 2. kha. "by ninefold, ninefold"; 3. ṅa. "from the constant (dhruva)."

In the chapter on the Great Exposition of the Method for Knowing the Luminaries (*jyotirjñānavidhimahoddeśa*), it says "to be added again": they are to be added in the place of the day (*vāra*) for the sake of the daily days of the week; they are to be subtracted in the place of the *ghaṭikās* due to the loss of one *ghaṭikā* from the lunar digits (*candrakalā*); and they are to be added again in the place of the aggregate (*piṇḍa*) through the purification of the addition or subtraction of the lunar signs (*candrapada*). Thus, regarding the matter of what is to be added or subtracted when the aggregate is divided by fourteen: "fourteen" refers to the moon; when the quotient is even, the resulting value is to be added, and when it is odd, it is to be subtracted. In the place of the aggregate, when the aggregate is divided by fourteen, if the quotient is even, the resulting value becomes a credit (*dhana*); if the quotient is odd, the resulting value becomes a debit (*ṛṇa*).
In this case, when the parts are equal, one has gone by two or returned by four, so that even though not gone, it is equal;
whereas in the case of unequal parts, one has gone by one and returned by three,
for there is no further division beyond that.

Above fifty-seven, there are twenty-seven clusters (*piṇḍaka*) consisting of thirty lunar days; they do not exist [as such], and therefore four are divided by fourteen parts. By that, it should be understood that items (*padārtha*) are to be added or subtracted according to even and odd divisions.

An "item" (*padārtha*) refers to the lunar-day positions (*candracārapada*); in the fourteen places, above and below, they are distinguished by the sevenfold rotation of the earth and other elements through both direct (*anuloma*) and reverse (*viloma*) order.
And those objects may be either to be given or to be abandoned;
in the void, the void is pure.

Thus, if that which remains as the fourteenth part is zero, then the object is also zero; the principle is that it is neither to be given nor to be abandoned. This is the method of calculation (*karaṇa*).

When the remainder is seen in the thirteenth place— namely, the "place of the thirty-three moons" (tridaśaśaśipada), which is the fifteenth place— or in the single place (ekapada), there are five *ghaṭikās* as either wealth or debt. Likewise, when the remainder is in the twelfth place, which is the "place of the two eyes and suns" (netrārka), ten *ghaṭikās* are to be added, according to the increase or decrease of the lunar digits (*candrakalā*).
"Called the lunar days" refers to fifteen; "in the eleventh fire" means in the third [house];
they become ten in the fourth house, when the remainder of the portion in the square of the waters (4) has been seen, and twenty less one (19);

thirty-two in the fifth house; twenty-one in the sixth; twenty-five in the seventh by those divisions of the sun; and in that [seventh], the Ravikas are to be given as revealed by the specific solar divisions.

In the odd and even [piṇḍas], the Vedas (4), the fires (3), the rays (12), and the moon (1) are [the values] in the first part; and in the other part, the ocean-moon (14) is in the even and odd [piṇḍas]. These are the days to be added and subtracted according to whether the [piṇḍa] is even or odd. ||32||
Twenty-two in the fifth interval, nine in the ninth,
six in the eighth [interval] called *vasu*, and twenty-four *jinās* in the seventh step;
when the remainder of the division is seen, twenty-five *ghaṭikās* are to be added if it is even and subtracted if it is odd.

In that [calculation], by means of the divisions of the sun, the solar positions (sūryapada) are produced through the division of the sun during the lunar-day occupation (tithibhoga); when there is a debt for the sun, it is a debt in that [total], and when there is a credit for the sun, it is a credit in that very same [total]—this is the "division of the sun" (arkaprabheda).
Here, the lunar positions (candrapada) are five, four, three, two, and one, in the eastern and western halves respectively.

"Bhūta" refers to five; "Punarbhūta" refers to five below that; "Iṣu" refers to five below that; "Veda" refers to four below that; "Śikhin" refers to three below that; "Kara" refers to two below that; and "Śaśin" refers to one position below that—thus there are seven positions for the words.
Then, in another seven positions, in reverse order starting from one, there are five words up to the fourteenth position.

Thus is the placement of the lunar signs (*candrapada*) in fourteen positions: 1. *ṅa*: "By half of the mass (*piṇḍa*), mouth, and Indra"; 2. This does not exist in the *ṅa* manuscript; 3. *bho.*: *Cig La Sogs Pa* (*ekādinā*); *ka*: *ekodinā*; *ṅa*: *ekadināt*. "In the mass, when divided by four and one (*abdhi-candra*), the days of the week (*vāra*) are to be added or subtracted according to whether the result is even or odd.
Here too, when the remainder of the division by fourteen is seen, if it is even, five and so forth are to be added to the days; if it is odd, they are to be subtracted.

When fourteen parts remain, if one [digit] is seen, five *ghaṭikās* are to be taken; in the second [case], ten with those situated in the second place; in the third, fifteen with those situated in the third place; in the fourth, nineteen with the four situated in the fourth place; in the fifth, twenty-two with the three situated in the fifth place; in the sixth, twenty-four with the two situated in the sixth place; and in the seventh, twenty-five with the one situated in the seventh place. Thereafter, the increase of the lunar steps ceases.

When the eighth [digit] is seen, having first discarded eight places together with the seven preceding ones, the remaining six unenjoyed places are made into a single aggregate (*ekapiṇḍa*), and twenty-four *ghaṭikās* are to be added or subtracted.

In the ninth [place], there are twenty-two *ghaṭikās* for five places; in the tenth, nineteen for four places; in the eleventh, five for three places; in the twelfth, ten for two places; in the thirteenth, five for one place; and in the fourteenth, zero—such is the established conclusion (*siddhāntaniścaya*).

The remainder [of the lunar day] is multiplied by the number of seasons (six) and divided by twelve; that quotient is likewise added to the same [remainder] according to the specific solar signs. The ghaṭīs of the sun's position are thus produced.

Furthermore, the product of the true lunar day multiplied by four (the Vedas), when increased by one-third, becomes the asterism of the season; however, if it is a debt (negative), one should subtract the sun's three-quarter-asterism from the middle motion. || 33 ||
"The remainder [is found] by dividing by the seasonal sun (six), and the quotient is likewise.
Here, "saccāra" refers to the components of the total sum (*piṇḍa*) situated below the total; "by the seasonal sun" means those remainders obtained by division.

Regarding the "saccāra-total," that which is the movement-position (*cārapada*) remaining after division by four is the movement-position above it; for the components of the total, there is a hundredfold position.
In that case, the *graha* has entered;
therefore, that *grāhya* is to be given for the sake of the *deya*.
By that term, the remainder—the constituent part of the *piṇḍa*—is multiplied; then, the quotient obtained by dividing by one hundred and thirty-six is likewise to be given.
Everything is just like the previously mentioned sum of *ghaṭikās*.
In that very context, by means of the various divisions of the sun, the *ravikās* are to be added or subtracted as before; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Now, the daily motion of the sun is stated: "That which is multiplied by the Vedas and the lunar days is indeed positive; it is mixed with the quotient."
Multiplied by four and by the lunar day (*tithi*), and divided by four and by sixty, it becomes the clear positive value.
In the place of the sun’s *ghaṭikās*, that [value] multiplied by the lunar day and added to one-third of the lunar day is to be applied as a positive value in the place of the *ghaṭikās*.
However, the asterism (*ṛkṣa*) with its seasons and three-quarters should be subtracted from the middle of the revolution (*bhukti*) of the sun, even if it is negative.

Here, for the purpose of purifying the position of the sun, the sun’s natal sign (*janmarāśi*) must be subtracted, so that the daily movement of the sun in terms of days, *ghaṭīs*, *pāṇīs* (minutes), and *palas* becomes known; otherwise, there is no purification of the sun’s position day by day in the calculation.

Therefore, from the movement of the lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī, six nakṣatras plus one-quarter—that is, forty-five *ghaṭīs*—are subtracted, whereby three signs beginning with Aries are purified.
Thus, Cancer becomes the natal sign of the sun due to the purification of its degrees.
Therefore, one should subtract the seasonal asterism together with its three quarters from the sun, and then subtract fifteen [degrees];
[in some versions] fourteen; [in Tibetan: *cha sas si* (fourth part)];
[in the Ṅa manuscript: *guruḥ*].
[In the chapter on] the Great Instruction on the Method of Knowledge of Luminosity (*jyotirjñānavidhimahoddeśa*), regarding the "middle of the elapsed portion" (*bhuktimadhye*):

the "elapsed portion" (*bhukti*) is the passage through the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and so forth; in that "middle of the elapsed portion," one should subtract the lunar mansion from the place of the lunar mansions, and subtract the *ghaṭikā*s from the place of the *ghaṭikā*s. As for the remaining task: in the slow calculation (*mandakārya*), having multiplied the steps by six, four, and one, the *nāḍī*s [are obtained] by means of the passage; the quotient obtained by dividing by five, three, and one is accompanied by the passage.

What is to be added and what is to be subtracted from the Sun depends on the movement of the solstice; otherwise, there is no purity in the Sun. [The corrections for] time, taste, serpent, ten, Hara, Hara, Rudra, direction, elephant, and six [are applied]. (34)

"Having separated out the solar enjoyment (sūryabhoga), the remaining work is to be done 'as for Mars'. Here, the remaining work is to be understood as being the same for the Sun as it is for Mars; however, the *cārapadas* (walking-steps) of Mars are different.
For the Sun, the *padas* for the slow-motion correction (*mandakārya*) are [the number of] tastes, pairs, and moons.
"Rasa" means six; "yuga" means four; below that is "śaśin," meaning one; and below that is "eka," also meaning one.

In the three zodiac signs [of the first half], and in reverse order in the latter half, there is one in the fourth sign, four in the fifth sign, and six in the sixth sign. This operation of the signs (*rāśikarma*) is the slow-motion correction (*mandakārya*). In this slow-motion correction, these six values occur across the six signs beginning with Cancer (*karkaṭa*).
"Another [calculation] for Mars must be stated":

having multiplied the *nāḍīs* by the [mean] motion of Mars, one takes the quotient obtained by dividing by the "arrows, qualities, and moon" (135); this, along with its own motion, is to be added to or subtracted from the Sun according to the movement of the solstice (*ayana*), for otherwise there is no purification—this statement is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyama*). Thus, having multiplied the *nāḍīs* by the motion of Mars, one then divides by the "arrows, qualities, and moon" (135); the resulting quotient of the *ghaṭikā*-aggregate becomes a credit (*dhana*) in the *ghaṭikā* place, and it becomes a debit (*ṛṇa*) due to the movement of the solstice.

Wealth occurs starting from Capricorn (makara) and debt occurs starting from Cancer (karkaṭa) due to the movement of the solstice; thus there is a daily correction, and not otherwise, according to the method stated in the *Karaṇa*. Here, the method stated in the *Karaṇa* is described: "Time and taste" (*kālo rasa*) refers to Cancer; in the first fortnight, "time" (*kāla*) means three *ghaṭikās*, and "taste" (*rasa*) means six in the second fortnight of Cancer.
Thus, in Leo, there are eight and ten;
likewise, in Virgo, eleven Hara-s and again eleven Hara-s; then in Libra, eleven Rudra-s and ten (Dik); and thus in Scorpio, eight and six Nāga-s. ||34||

At the end of the northern and southern courses, fire and ether [respectively] become the debt and wealth [of the sun]; and for six months, the sun moves through the divisions of the fortnights according to the distinctions of the monthly transits.

Having added the lunar days to the sun and multiplied by the lower flavors (six), mixed with the duration of the weekday, and then diminished, it becomes the moon, O King; this is the conjunction of the mixed sun and moon.
ka. kha. read *kārām*; ṅa. reads *kāram*.
ṅa. [states]: "As others [say], in the case of *maṅgala*."
Ṅa. by means of enjoyment;
Ṅa. or;
according to the Tibetan reading of the root text, "wealth and debt" (dhanamṛṇam) [is used] instead; Ka. for six months.
O Siddha, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is said: "Then, on the bow [sign] is fire—thus three; 'kha' means emptiness at the end of the movement.
Likewise, in the case of Capricorn and so forth, 'dhanam' (wealth) refers to the *karaṇa* system; this is not the intended meaning in the *Siddhānta* in all cases.
Thus, for six months, the sun moves according to the divisions of the fortnights, due to the distinctions of the monthly transits (*saṃkrānti*)."

Now the lunar course (*candrabhoga*) is described: "Having added to the sun" means having added the lunar days (*tithi*) to the solar portion. The lunar days multiplied by the lower flavors (*adhararasa*, i.e., six) are those [days] multiplied by six. Mixed with the solar-course [value], meaning mixed with the minutes and so forth of the solar-course, they become diminished; in the place of the minutes, the lunar course occurs. "The mixed sum of sun and moon" means that the sum of the courses of the sun and moon becomes the mixed total.

The elapsed lunar days multiplied by twenty-seven, with the number of elapsed moons and karas subtracted, and the remainder divided by seven; the pure years mixed with eight, multiplied by four hundred, and from which eight is subtracted; divided by one thousand three hundred and seventy; multiplied by zero and six, and divided by sixty; [the result] added to thirty-two days and nāḍīs—this is the constant (dhruvaka) here for the month of the solar ingress (saṃkrānti). || 36 ||

"Multiplied by two, the lunar days, diminished by one, and divided by seven—the remainder is the *karaṇa*. That is to say, when the lunar days are multiplied by two, one is subtracted, and the result is divided by seven; the remainder is the *karaṇa*. Through the consumption of the weekdays (*vāra*), the [daily] progression occurs.
Herein, the five components (*pañcāṅga*) are: weekday (*vāra*), lunar day (*tithi*), asterism (*nakṣatra*), conjunction (*yoga*), and *karaṇa*.

Herein are the days (*vāra*): seven, namely Āditya, Soma, Maṅgala, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, and Śani. The lunar dates (*tithi*) are fifteen, beginning with the first (*pratipad*). The lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) are twenty-seven: Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśirā, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Aśleṣā, Maghā, Pūrvaphālgunī, Uttaraphālgunī, Hastā, Citrā, Svātī, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūlā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, Pūrvabhādrapadā, Uttarabhādrapadā, and Revatī.

Likewise, the *yogas* are twenty-seven: Viṣkambha, Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, Śobhana, Atigaṇḍa, Sukarmā, Dhṛti, Śūla, Gaṇḍa, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Śaṅku, Vyāghāta, Harṣaṇa, Vajra, Siddhi, Vyatipāta, Varīyān, Parigha, Śiva, Sādhya, Śubha, Śukla, Brahmā, Aindra, and Vaidhṛti. These are the twenty-seven *yogas*.

On the first half of the first day of the bright fortnight, the first *karaṇa* is *vava*; on the first and second halves of the second day, they are *vālava* and *kaulava*; on the first and second halves of the third day, they are *taitila* and *garaja*; and on the first and second halves of the fourth day, they are *vaṇija* and *viṣṭi*. Likewise, on the fifth day, they are *vava* and *vālava*; on the sixth day, *kaulava* and *taitila*; on the seventh day, *garaja* and *vaṇija*; and on the first half of the eighth day, *viṣṭi*.

On the second half of the eighth day is Vava; on the first and second halves of the ninth day are Bālava and Kaulava; on the tenth day are Taitila and Gara; and on the eleventh day, in its first and second halves, are Vaṇija and Viṣṭi.

Furthermore, regarding the first and second halves of the [lunar days], the application of the *samāsānta* suffix is made for the asterisms (*nakṣatra*) in manuscript Kha. In the manuscripts, the sequence "Vava Karaṇa" does not exist; the sequence "Kaulava" does not exist in the Garavaṇik manuscripts; and the sequence "Kaulavagara" does not exist in those two manuscripts. Beyond this, manuscript Ṅa was not obtained. one should thus fully understand everything; otherwise, the calculation of the motion in the Siddhānta will be incorrect.

"Otherwise, one should avoid impurity from this [calculation] such as the *laghukaraṇa* and so forth. Thus, the definition of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) taught in the *Paramādibuddha-tantrarāja* has been summarized in the *Laghutantrarāja* by the statement "the destruction of the established doctrines" (Kālacakra-tantra 1.26), and made perfectly clear by that tantra.
For what reason?

Here, the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthikas), having seen the *Laghutantrarāja* and having seen the purification of the solar motion, will write [their own version] within their own systems, thinking, "The purification of the solar motion exists in our system as well. For this reason, it has not been set forth here with reference to the commentary;
thus, for six months, there are two [periods of] decrease and increase respectively—namely, decrease and increase.

Regarding day and night—of both the day and the night—by means of the movements of the sun, namely its northern course (*uttaracāra*) and southern course (*dakṣiṇacāra*): "by the movements of the sun" refers to the *nāḍīs*, breaths (*prāṇa*), and *liptās* [of time]. At every daily moment, there is an increase or decrease of four breaths (*śvāsa*) and three *pāṇīpala*s per degree of the solstice (*ayanāṅga*). This measurement applies from the northern part of Kailāśa up to Himavat. Per degree of the solstice—which consists of one hundred and eighty-two and a half days—there is an increase during the night on the right (southern) side and a decrease during the day on the left (northern) side.

To the south of Kailāśa, as will be explained here regarding the measurement, on the day of the sun's transition into the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana-saṃkrānti*), the day consists of thirty-six *ghaṭikās* and the night consists of twenty-four;
likewise, during the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), the duration of night and day should be understood by reversing this order.

Now, the movement of Rāhu through the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) is described: The months, mixed with [the sum of] eyes (2) and suns (12), multiplied by two (eyes), and mixed with one moon (1) and one node (parvan), divided by zero, oceans (4), and light (1), and multiplied by seven (munis) and ten (karas)—the result is the mansion by means of the portion starting from space (0).

Whatever remains, multiplied by sixty, gives the *ghaṭikās*; those again multiplied by sixty give the *liptās*. The quotient obtained is the wheel; it is not the mouth, but for the darkness (Rāhu), it is mixed with half the tail-mansion.
Thus are the months.
The months are the *karaṇa* months; "mixed with two and twelve" refers to the dependence on the *karaṇa*, not the dependence on the *siddhānta*,
as indicated by the phrase "two and twelve."

"Combined with one hundred and twenty-two" means multiplied by two for the sake of the heap of fortnights; "combined with one lunar parvan" means one fortnight is added to the heap of fortnights for the purpose of the full-moon phase, while two fortnights are added for the purpose of the new-moon phase. Thus it becomes the heap of fortnights.
"Divided by zero-four-ocean": for the purpose of calculating Rāhu's monthly (pakṣa) consumption, there is a division by the "monthly orb," which is four hundred and sixty months;
those remaining months resulting from being divided by that "zero-four-ocean" [number] are multiplied by the "hand of the sage" (70).

For the purpose of calculating the enjoyment of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), one divides by the portion beginning with space (*kha*, i.e., zero); the result obtained by dividing by the portion beginning with space—namely, by four hundred and sixty—is the lunar mansion (*ṛkṣa*).
Furthermore, whatever remains as a residue is multiplied by sixty; the result obtained by dividing by that same divisor becomes the *ghaṭikās*.
In this way, when multiplied by sixty, they become *liptās* by that same divisor;
when multiplied by six, they become *śvāsas* by that same divisor. The quotient obtained is the *cakra*; the remainder is not the *vaktra*.

In this context, when the quotient obtained by dividing by the "withered ocean" (40) from the asterism and so forth is subtracted from the cycle consisting of twenty-seven asterisms, the "face of the cycle" (*cakravaktra*) is produced.

The "face" (*vaktra*) constitutes the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) in the calculation of the [moon's] position starting from Aśvinī; and it is called *tamī* because it possesses darkness (*tamas*), that is, Rāhu. For that *tamī*, the tail is mixed with half of the asterism.

The half-ṛkṣas consist of thirteen and a half constellations; mixed with these, it is called "the face" in the calculation of the mouth, while the "tail" constitutes the tail-portion. The months are multiplied by thirty and mixed into three places. By what are they mixed? With the mountains (seven). Then, [the result] is divided by the mountains, sky, and arrows (707); the quotient is subtracted from the product of the oceans and tastes (64). This is the uncorrected day-count, which becomes the corrected day-count when reduced by the quotient obtained from dividing by the oceans and tastes (64). That remainder is divided by the mountains, Nāgas, and seasons (687); the remainder is multiplied by the eyes (two), and then again by the khara-s (sixty), resulting in nāḍīs beginning with the mountains (707).

Now, for the purpose of determining the lunar mansions (nakṣatra) enjoyed by the planets beginning with Maṅgala, the accumulated count of days (ahargaṇa) is stated: "The months" refers to the months according to the Karaṇa system. Multiplied by thirty, they become the heap of days.
Those days, when combined with each day of the current month, constitute the total.
The remainder from the three places is multiplied by thirty-seven;

this product, divided by seven hundred and seven, is added to the middle heap. Then, the middle heap is diminished by the quotient obtained from dividing it by sixty-four (the "ocean-flavors"). This is the non-corrected day-count (*asphuṭāha*). In some cases, for the sake of accuracy, one weekday is subtracted when there is an excess of weekdays per day; thus, the corrected day-count (*sphuṭāhargaṇa*) is obtained.

Now, the calculation for Mars (Maṅgala) is stated: "Mixed with Śailava and Ka" means it is mixed with one hundred and sixty-seven, not according to the Siddhānta [system], but according to the Karaṇa [system]. "The clear day-count divided by Śaila-nāga-ṛtu" means that the aforementioned day-count is divided by six hundred and eighty-seven; thus it is "divided by Śaila-nāga-ṛtu."
Therefore, having understood the revolution of Mars, the remainder is struck by twenty-seven and then divided by seventy-four; this results in the asterism [occupied by] Mars.
It should also be multiplied by sixty—the "six tastes"—and divided by seventy-four and so forth; the result obtained in *nāḍīs* is the time occupied by Mars.

"By the previously mentioned method, [one calculates] the *pāṇīpala* and so forth. Here, there are five types of places for the experience (*bhoga*) of all the planets: the place of the zodiac sign (*rāśi*), the place of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the place of the *ghaṭikā*, the place of the *pāṇīpala*, and the place of the breath (*śvāsa*). These are situated one below the other: in the places of the breaths, the breaths do not remain above; those obtained by a division of six enter into the *pāṇīpala*s. The *pāṇīpala*s do not remain when divided by sixty; those obtained by a division of sixty enter into the *ghaṭikā*s in the zodiac sign.

In this manner, even the *ghaṭikās* enter into the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) and the zodiacal sign (*rāśi*). The lunar mansions remain in two types of actions for thirteen minus one and a half [units]. It is traditionally held that six signs remain. Now, the purification of Mars (*maṅgala-śuddhi*) is stated: If there is a debt (*ṛṇa*) greater than nine and a half in the addition of the cycle (*cakra-miśra*), it should be subtracted; if it exceeds half the cycle, the half-cycle should be discarded. Furthermore, the remainder after subtraction should be reversed (*utkrama*).

When the asterism is multiplied by sixty and increased by the [elapsed] yoga, it is divided by eighteen hundred; the quotient obtained is added or subtracted from the slow motion (mandakarma), respectively in reverse or direct order.
"Nine and a half [nakṣatras] are to be subtracted from Āra (Mars).
Here, when the Moon's consumption of the nakṣatra and so forth has been separated out, there remains one consumption belonging to Āra; thus, nine nakṣatras are to be subtracted.
"And a half" means that thirty ghaṭikās—[calculated as] thirteen and a half in the place of ghaṭikās—are to be subtracted for the purpose of determining the birth-foot (janmacaraṇa).
Regarding the passage "If, in the lunar mansion revolution beginning with Aśvinī, there is a debt that is greater, it should be subtracted from the mixed wheel":

here, in the lunar mansion revolution beginning with Aśvinī, a debt must necessarily be subtracted. If the debt—the quantity of the debt—is greater than the quantity of the revolution (the bhoga-rāśi), then it should be subtracted from the mixed wheel; the "wheel" refers to the collection of twenty-seven lunar mansions; the meaning is that the debt should be subtracted from that which is mixed with the wheel.
"It should be discarded from the wheel" means the same.
In this case, if the remainder after subtraction is equal to half the circle (180°), then it should be discarded even if it exceeds half.

Here, the remainder that exceeds half is the inverse (utkrama) of the remainder that was subtracted; by means of this inverse, there is a positive value in the slow-motion correction (mandakārya) for all planets, whereas in the direct order (krama) there is a negative value.
When the asterism (ṛkṣa) is multiplied by sixty, whatever results are the ghaṭīs for the purpose of the total ghaṭī-piṇḍa.
When the heap of asterisms is multiplied by sixty, the heap of ghaṭikās situated below becomes the "head" (mūrdhan).
Divided by one hundred fifty-five for the purpose of determining the steps of the zodiacal signs,
the quotient obtained from dividing the heap of ghaṭikās by one hundred thirty-five constitutes the step of the sign.

Furthermore, in the case of slow-moving planets (*mandakarma*), wealth and debt should be understood according to their sequence—whether in direct or reverse order—as they correspond respectively. Here are the steps for the movement through the zodiac signs (*rāśicāra*): The principles (*tattva*), eighteen, and seven [are the degrees]; there are six manifest steps (*rasapada*) in both the upper and lower halves of the half-circle (*arddhacakra*). One should multiply the *nāḍīs* by the elapsed portion [of the sign] and divide by sixty-three (*śaraguṇaśaśi*); from the quotient obtained, subtract it from the upper circle. In the first half, that which is desired is to be taken according to the steps; in the latter half, it is indeed to be discarded. Having made a single aggregate of the elapsed [portion], one should add or subtract it from the *nāḍīs* according to the planet's motion. [Verse 42]
The principles (*tattva*) for birth are twenty-five in the first zodiac sign (*rāśi*), eighteen in the second, and seven in the third; thus, there are twenty-seven in the first three signs.

Then, in the subsequent half-circle, there are seven in the fourth sign, eighteen in the fifth, and twenty-five in the sixth; thus, there are thirty-six manifest flavors (*rasapada*) in the lower and upper halves of the circle.
One should multiply the *nāḍīs* by the duration of experience; the zodiacal sign [of the time] divided by one hundred and thirty-five yields the duration of the sign's movement.

That very [number] is the step within the six steps; from that comes the second. "Bhoga" means that which is enjoyed; by that remaining *bhoga*, one should multiply the remaining *nāḍīs*. Divided by the moon multiplied by the arrows (15), the quotient is obtained from the *dur-dhacakra*.
From the heap multiplied by the *nāḍī-bhoga*, the portion obtained by dividing by one hundred and thirty-five is to be taken in the first half; it becomes the desired [value].
"By virtue of the position" means as long as the planet does not enter the latter half (aparārddha), it must indeed be subtracted from the latter half.
That same degree becomes the portion to be subtracted in the latter half.

Having made the elapsed [portion] a single aggregate—meaning having combined into one aggregate the degrees traversed by the planets according to the signs situated in the former half—and having likewise made the untraversed [portion] a single aggregate in the latter half, and having discarded the traversed [portions] of both the former and latter halves, there is an addition or subtraction in the *nāḍī* (time-unit) according to the movement of the planets.

The movement of the planets is both retrograde (*utkrama*) and direct (*krama*); depending on that, there is what is to be added and what is to be subtracted. By virtue of retrogression, it is to be added; by virtue of progression, it is to be subtracted from the *nāḍī*, while in the zodiacal sign (*rāśi*) of the *ghaṭikā*s, it is by means of the planet's longitude in the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*)—this is the rule. In all cases of slow motion (*mandakarma*), this is the procedure for the calculation of signs (*rāśikarmavidhi*) for Mars and the other planets, known as the purification of the birth-sign and its quarters (*janmacaraṇaśuddhi*).

In this chapter on the Great Exposition of the Method for Knowing the Luminaries, the procedure for the swift calculation (*śīghrakarma*) is now stated: In the swift calculation, Mars is to be subtracted from the Sun; likewise Jupiter and Saturn.
