Then, in the same way, Mercury and Venus are [subtracted] from the Sun. Indeed, in the swift operation, these become positive (*dhana*) in due order. Here, the remainder is the motion (*cāra*); having multiplied it by the *nāḍīs* of the planetary steps (*grahacaraṇapada*), one takes the portion obtained by dividing by sixty as the planetary step to be added or subtracted accordingly.
In the case of the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are likewise to be subtracted during the process of mean motion;
that is, immediately thereafter.
Furthermore, the planetary longitude as purified by the operation of signs (rāśikarma) is to be subtracted from the solar longitude.

Regarding the phrase "Mars is to be subtracted from the Sun": when the slow motion (mandabhoga) is devoid of solar influence, having set the planetary motion separately, then likewise Jupiter is also to be subtracted, and Saturn, the son of the Sun, is to be subtracted from the Sun—just as Mars is [subtracted] by the word "also" (api).
Where?
In the calculation of swift motion (śīghrakarmaṇi).

Thus, when Mercury is in its own sign (saumya) and in its own exaltation (saumyabhoga), the Sun is to be subtracted for the purpose of finding Mercury's longitude; and when Venus is in its own sign and in its own exaltation, the Sun is likewise to be subtracted for the purpose of finding Venus's longitude.
Herein lies the rule: "The planet at its exaltation is to be subtracted from the planet at its depression.
Therefore, in the case of both Mercury and Venus, the Sun is to be subtracted.
"Indeed, wealth arises gradually in a swift undertaking.
Here, in this swift action or swift undertaking, wealth arises by degrees.
"Khalu" signifies with certainty.
In the manner described, there is a debt when half a cycle (ardhacakra) has been relinquished.
The remaining asterism, purified by the transit of the exalted planet, becomes the movement of the planets through the asterisms according to their daily transit.
That very movement of the planets through the quarters consists of many ghaṭikās.

Having multiplied the remaining *nāḍīs* by those *ghaṭikās* which are the steps of the planet's movement, one should take the quotient obtained by dividing by sixty; this is to be added to or subtracted from the step of the planet's movement in the same manner as before—that is, as previously stated, it is to be added in the first half and subtracted in the latter half. Having made the elapsed [time] into a single sum, all that is to be added or subtracted according to the movement of the planet must be placed openly in the *anupada* for Mars, beginning with "the Victors" (*jinādyāḥ*). Having made the elapsed [time] into a single sum, all that is to be added or subtracted according to the movement of the planet [is applied].
In this matter of the calculation for swiftness (*śīghrakarma*), [the value] is to be added in direct order (*krama*) and subtracted in reverse order (*utkrama*).
In the first half [of the cycle], it is the elapsed group (*bhukta-piṇḍa*); in the second half, it is the unelapsed group (*abhukta-piṇḍa*), as before.

Regarding Mars (*bhauma*), "the movements begin with the Jinas" means that the Jinas are twenty-four; those fourteen groups of words beginning with the Jinas—situated at the start of the fourteen-word group, specifically at the first word—are the movements beginning with the Jinas for Mars. Thus, all of them are to be established in the clearly manifest fourteen-syllable position, which is the place of the fourteen lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).
O Lord of Men, in this manner the sequential calculation for all the planets is to be understood.
When Mercury is in its own period (*bhoga*), Venus becomes purified; [then] the Sun and Mercury, the son of Soma, become purified.
Being purified in the period of Venus, it becomes Venus; and because both Mercury and Venus are purified through their periods, there is the purification of Mars.

Now the Mercury [calculation] is stated in the *Vimalaprabhā*: The entire total of days multiplied by zero, space, and moon (1000), diminished by fire, sun, and mountain (712), is divided by mountain, void, and serpent (897). The remainder, struck by the divisions beginning with the asterisms (nakṣatras) and so forth, and further multiplied by the proclaimed divisor, yields the signs (*rāśi*), and again the minutes (*ghaṭikā*) in the portion of Mercury. O good king, having subtracted the portion of Mercury, correctly discard the sun from the middle, the king (one sign), and half an asterism. [Verse 45]
The entire total of days is multiplied by zero, space, and moon (1000);

this is the previously purified total number of days. That same total number of days, multiplied by one hundred, is multiplied by zero, space, and moon (1000), and is then diminished by fire, sun, and mountain (723). Thus, that hundredfold total of days is diminished by seven thousand two hundred and thirty-three.

"Divided by mountain, apertures, and serpents" means divided by seven, nine, eight, seven, and eight—namely, by the days of the mandala, which are eight thousand seven hundred ninety-seven (8,797)—from the "mountain" (seven) onwards. It is "divided," meaning partitioned, by these mountain-aperture-mountain-serpents. Furthermore, "the remainder is struck by the divisions of asterisms and so forth" means that even the remainder of the mandala-day portions, having been multiplied by the total number of days, is further multiplied by twenty-seven, the divisions of the asterisms and so forth.

Furthermore, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), it is meant that the remainder of the mandala-parts is multiplied by sixty; likewise, [the remainder] is multiplied by the *pāṇīpala* and then multiplied by six breaths (*śvāsa*).
By dividing this by the aforementioned days of the mandala, the resulting quotient is the lunar mansion (*ṛkṣa*). Again, in the place of the *ghaṭikā*s—

Thus, the breaths obtained by means of *pāṇīpala*s constitute the [periods of] the benefic planets in their respective movements; having subtracted the benefic from the Sun, O good king, one should correctly subtract the king [the Sun] and half a lunar mansion (*ṛkṣa*).

Having subtracted from the lunar longitude obtained by the circle of days that which was acquired for the purpose of purification in the swift calculation (*śīghrakarma*), O Good King, subtract from the mean Sun sixteen constellations (*nakṣatra*) and half a constellation (thirty *ghaṭikās*) within the solar *ghaṭikā* duration. If the debt is not cleared, then one should add the circle of constellations and subtract the debt, according to the previous rule. The remaining work is as follows: in the case of Mars, there is wealth (*dhana*) and debt (*ṛṇa*) in both slow (*manda*) and swift (*śīghra*) operations; for Mercury, in the slow operation it is ten, seven, and three, and in the swift operation it is sixteen and so forth.

Having made the day the base, divide it by sixty-four (32); the remainder is multiplied by seven and divided by twenty-seven; the resulting asterism is again multiplied by seven and [divided by twenty-seven] for the slow motion of Jupiter in the calculation of *ghaṭikās*. || 46 ||

The remaining work is as follows: wealth and debt, slow and swift action—this is easily understood. Regarding Mercury (Saumya): "Ten, mountain, and peak" refers to the slow-motion calculation (*mandakārya*).

When Mercury is in its slow-motion operation (*mandakārya*) within the six signs, there are ten in the first sign-position (*rāśipada*) of the front half, seven ("mountain") in the second sign-position, and three ("peak") in the third sign-position; this is the first half. Then, in the latter half, there are three in the fourth sign-position, seven in the fifth sign-position, and ten in the sixth sign-position; thus, "ten, mountain, and peak" are the positions (*padāni*) for the slow-motion operation.

In the work concerning the stars for swift activities, the kings and so forth—the sixteen and so on—become fourteen in the fourteenth place, and they are to be stated in what is about to be said; this is the purification of Mercury [in the chapter]. Now Jupiter is described: in the "Great Summary of the Method of Astral Knowledge," it says, "having made the mass of days diminished by zero-zero-six-two" (1260); that is, having made the mass of days—the previous count of days—diminished by zero-zero-six-two (1260). This is in view of the *karaṇa* system, not in view of the *siddhānta*.
"Divided by the nature of thirty-two and four thousand thirty-two" means divided by 4032.

"In the remainder"—that is, in what remains after the division—"multiplied by the destroyer of stars" (ṛkṣaghna), meaning multiplied by twenty-seven, [the result] becomes the asterism according to the movement through the mandala.
Furthermore, the ghaṭikās and so forth occur again according to the previously stated sequence; this applies also in the case of Jupiter's movement.

The asterism to be subtracted is zero; in the slow-motion calculation (mandakārya), there are nine steps for Rāhu, and further, the swift steps are clearly indicated by the verses. Having multiplied those days by four hundred and eight, and having subtracted the result from twenty-seven, divide by forty-eight; when multiplied by seven, it is the asterism-occupation (ṛkṣabhoga); and again, in the swift-motion calculation for Venus, the value is in ghaṭīs. || 47 ||

Regarding the statement "the asterism is to be subtracted from the Sun," here, in the calculation of Jupiter's [mean] motion, twelve asterisms are to be subtracted; the remaining operation is to be performed as with Mars.
For the slow-motion calculation of Saturn (*haranavaśikhin*), the *pada*s are as before: eleven in the *pada* of six signs, then nine, and then three for Śikhin (Rāhu).
Likewise, in the latter half [of the year], it is done in reverse order.
Thus, regarding the *śīghra-karman* (the calculation for mean motion), those *manu-padas* which were previously mentioned in the *dik-pada* should be stated here;
"dik" refers to the ten *nakṣatra-cāra-padas* that are to be explained in what follows. This concludes the purification of Jupiter (*bṛhaspati-śuddhi*).
Now Venus is described: having multiplied the number of days by ten (khendu), having subtracted eighty-four (jalanidhivasu),
and having divided by two thousand two hundred and forty-seven (abrejinākṣa).

For the purpose of purifying the fast motion (śīghra-caraṇa) by means of the days of the circle of signs (caraṇamaṇḍala), when the remaining [period] is the destroyer of the asterism (ṛkṣaghna), the planetary longitude (ṛkṣabhoga) is again [calculated] by means of the duration in ghaṭikās, just as for Mars; likewise is the duration in pāṇīpala and so forth for Venus in its fast motion. In the slow motion (manda-kārya) of Venus, the season-asterism (ṛtvṛkṣa) is to be subtracted from the Sun; in the slow motion, the steps (padāni) are five (śara-yuga-śaśinaḥ); and in the fast motion, they are clearly to be added or subtracted according to the divisions beginning with the principles (tattva), just as for Mars.

The true number of elapsed days, diminished by eighty-four thousand eight hundred and seventy-six, and divided by sixty-one thousand six hundred and fifty-seven, yields the lunar asterism; eighteen should also be subtracted from the moon’s [longitude]. (48)

"Ṛtvakṣa" refers to the six nakṣatras to be subtracted from the Sun's position (sūryabhoga); in all such cases, the locative case is to be understood as having the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe*).

Regarding "the arrows, the pair, and the moon are the *pada*s for the slow motion (*mandakārya*)," it is as before: in the place of the six signs (*ṣaḍrāśisthāna*), "arrows" (*śara*) means five, "pair" (*yuga*) means four, and "moon" (*śaśin*) means one. Thus, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is stated: "five, four, and one."
The first half [of the verse] is thus; the second half concerns *śīghra* (swift) action.

By the divisions of the principles (*tattva*) and so forth—that is, by the twenty-fivefold division and others—it is made manifest in the fourteen lunar mansion quarters (*nakṣatracaraṇapada*). Just as in the case of Mars (*maṅgala*), there is that which is to be given and that which is to be discarded; likewise, in the case of Venus (*śukra*), the position of movement (*cārapada*) becomes either to be given or discarded. This is the purification of Venus (*śukraśuddhi*). Now, Saturn (*śani*) is described:

"The clear day-count is diminished by twenty-eight thousand four hundred and sixty" means that the previous day-count is clearly reduced by 4820; this is according to the *Karaṇa* system, not according to the *Siddhānta*. Therefore, "divided by six, six, three, and one" means divided by 10766—the number of days in a [lunar] revolution.
The result obtained from the remainder when multiplied by the asterisms and divided by the days in a revolution constitutes the asterism (nakṣatra).
In this way, the movement of the Moon [Sasini] consists of palas and so forth;

eighteen [nakṣatras] are to be subtracted from the movement of Saturn, meaning eighteen lunar mansions are to be subtracted from Saturn's motion. When there is a debt (a negative remainder), the zodiacal circle (cakra) is added and then the subtraction is performed. This prior rule is for the purpose of determining the quarter of the birth asterism. In its slow motion (mandakarma), it has twenty-six days per season; in its fast operation (śīghrakārya), it begins with six [days] and so forth. Its movement is fast and slow according to the sequence of positions, while it is retrograde when moving in reverse order.

The emergence of the planets from the eastern and western halves occurs by virtue of the sun's motion; for Ketu, its swift and retrograde movements occur every thirty-seven months multiplied by twelve.

Regarding the phrase *ṣaḍ-vāviṃśad-vinartuḥ*: in the six positions of the *āśis*, there are twenty-two units in the first zodiac sign (*rāśi*), then fifteen days, and then "season" (*ṛtu*), which is six;

thus it should be understood for the latter half as well. Because of the statement "in the position of the manifest flavors" (*prakaṭa-rasa-pade*), in the matter of swift calculation (*śīghra-kārye*)—that is, in the operation of the swift lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*)—the "flavors and so forth" (*rasādyāḥ*) are to be added or subtracted in the fourteenth place; these, beginning with the six units, are to be stated in the collection of planetary movements (*graha-cāra-samūha*) in every respect. This is the purification of Saturn (*śanaiścara-śuddhi*).
Now the characteristic of motion (cāra) is stated: "Motion is swift and slow; it is the movement through the steps in sequence.

In the case of swift action (*śīghrakarma*), the enjoyment (*bhoga*) of a planet that has risen from the solar orb during the fourteen *ghaṭikās* of the first half [of the day] is called swift motion (*śīghracāra*).
Regarding "movement through the steps in sequence" (*kramapadagamana*), the enjoyment that occurs in the latter half is called slow motion (*mandacāra*).
Then, when half the circle has been traversed in reverse order, the planet enters retrograde motion;
that retrograde motion is called *vakracāra*.

In the first half and the second half [of the zodiac], due to the movement of the Sun, the emergence of the planets is called "direct motion" (*nirgamacāra*), because they have abandoned their retrograde course.

From the point of rising (*udaya*) until the end of the first half, there is an increase in wealth as they move in regular order. Then, in the second half until the midpoint of the circle (*cakrārddha*), there is a decrease in wealth. Thereafter, by abandoning the half-circle and moving in reverse order, there is an increase in debt in the first half and a decrease in debt in the second half, until the entry of the Sun into the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). When the Sun has set, the rising occurs again in that very same sequence; thus it should be understood.

"In thirty-seven months multiplied by twelve (444), there occurs the swift and retrograde [motion] of Ketu. Here, this introductory statement regarding Ketu is to be explained in detail in what follows. This concludes the section on the planets (*grahādhikāra*). [In the chapter on] the Great Introduction to the Method for Knowing Luminaries (*jyotirjñānavidhimahoddeśa*): Now, the time of the setting and rising of the planets is stated: "Whichever planet enters the solar orb certainly sets; having left the sun, it shall rise. And its path is according to the division of the movement of the solstices (*ayanagati*)."
He who stands on the left path proceeds by the north due to the movement of the sun; he who stands on the right clearly proceeds by the south, and here there is mutual combat between the two enemies.

Whosoever enters the solar orbit necessarily sets; because he is no longer visible due to the rays of the solar disc, he is said to have "set," yet it is not that the planet has ceased to exist in every respect. Having left the sun, he shall rise again; that very same planet which had set becomes risen once more by virtue of its own movement after leaving the sun, because it has been abandoned by the solar rays.

"And its path according to the division of the movement of the solstices" means that for that risen planet, there is a path according to the division of the movement of the solstices (*ayanagativibhāga*). "The division of the solstices" (*ayanavibhāga*) refers to the division between the two solstices: from the Fire-Circle (*agnivalaya*) to Kailāsa (or *Kailāśa*) in the north as far as the Himavat mountains, and from the Himavat mountains in the south as far as the Fire-Circle, divided by one hundred and eighty-two and a half days. By this, there is the division of the movement of the solstices of the Sun; by that division of the Sun's movement, the path of the planets that have arisen occurs. Thus, whichever [planet] is situated on the left path, by virtue of the Sun's motion, it travels by way of the north.

In this system of the left path (*vāmamārga*), because the gentle planets—Mercury, Venus, and Ketu—arise from the left side, they enter the solar disc at the time of setting with their left side, and likewise rise with their left side. Therefore, whichever planet is situated on the left path moves to the north of the malefic planets; just as one situated on the right (*savya*) of the Sun moves to the south.

Here, "situated on the right" refers to those who have set in the solar disc on the right path, namely Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. Being malefic, they move to the south of the gentle planets, because they arise from the right side.

Here, because Ketu arises from the left side (vāmāṅga), he is gentle (saumya) by way of bodily division; because Jupiter (Bṛhaspati) arises from the right side (dakṣiṇāṅga), he is fierce (raudra) by way of bodily division. Likewise, it is clear that there is mutual combat between enemies here; thus, there is mutual combat between these gentle and cruel ones—Mercury and Mars, Jupiter and Venus, and Saturn and Ketu—because they are enemies. If this occurs for those situated in their own signs, the combat is certain to take place in that lunar mansion (nakṣatra); indeed, no other combat occurs there, but rather a conjunction with one another.

If the entry of the moon occurs in the left [nostril] and the exit of the sun occurs through the north, there will be the rising of the left horn; however, in some cases, due to the influence of the solstice, it occurs in the right during the exit.

If there is a certain battle for those situated in their own *kṣetra*, then "own *kṣetra*" refers to the sign of Aries and the sign of Scorpio for Mars. If Mercury's transit occurs while he is situated in that *kṣetra*, then in that case, there will certainly be war.
Likewise, if Mars is in Mercury's *kṣetra*, namely Gemini or Virgo...
"In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is stated that the enjoyer of the world-system arises through the power of the feet; nevertheless, there is war.
Thus, if Venus is in Sagittarius or Pisces within the domain of Jupiter, then there is war between Venus and Jupiter."
Likewise, if Ketu is in Taurus or Libra—

the fields of Venus— or similarly in Capricorn or Aquarius— the fields of Saturn— then there is indeed war; likewise, if Saturn is in Cancer, which is the field of Saturn, then there is war with Ketu, because [Saturn] was born from Ketu.

Regarding the statement "there is no war [of planets] with another in a *nakṣatra*," it means here that the birth of the planets is again in relation to the *nakṣatras*. War does not occur only in its own *rāśi* (zodiacal sign), but war with an enemy also occurs in the *janmanakṣatra* (birth asterism). Thus, there is war between Venus and Mars in their respective *nakṣatras*: in Punarvasu (the *nakṣatra* of Venus), in Maghā (the *nakṣatra* of Mars), in Hastā (the *nakṣatra* of Jupiter), in Anurādhā (the *nakṣatra* of Mercury), in Mūla (the *nakṣatra* of Saturn), and in Uttarāṣāḍhā (the *nakṣatra* of Ketu). There is war between Mercury and Mars in their own respective *nakṣatras*.

Thus it is for Venus and Jupiter, as well as for Saturn and Ketu; indeed, it is certain that no battle occurs in a different lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) or field (*kṣetra*) except in one's own *nakṣatra*, and that there is mutual conjunction in another *nakṣatra*. Likewise, regarding the moon, if its entry (*praveśa*) occurs on the left [side] of the sun, and its exit (*nirgama*) occurs to the north, then the rising of the horn (*śṛṅgonnati*) occurs in the north.

In some cases, by the power of the solstice—during the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) due to famine or lack of rain, or by its very nature—and during the cutting of a lunar node (parvaccheda), Rāhu approaches with his face level; he swallows [the moon] directly facing it when moving to the left (vāmacāra). When moving to the right (apasavya), by the power of the sun’s movement, he is on the right side.
Thus Rāhu swallows the moon from the intermediate directions (vidikṣu), having emerged from behind. From Aśvinī up to half of Citrā is the equinoctial line (golarekhā), where night and day are equal.

Now the entry of Rāhu is described: at the "cutting of the node" (*parvacchede*), that is, at the cutting of the full moon (*pūrṇimā*)—and by the word "and" (*ca*), also at the cutting of the new moon (*amāvasyā*)—the moon enters Rāhu with its face level, meaning the eclipse occurs directly in front.

Here, "facing forward" (*sammukhaḥ*) refers to the initial eclipse; this very [direction] is to be understood through the power of Rāhu’s revolution (*valana*), as it is well-known in all other systems of calculation (*karaṇa*). Therefore, no effort was made here by the Blessed Mañjuśrī.

When Rāhu moves to the left, the eclipse of the Moon occurs on the right; when it turns to the left, the eclipse of the Moon occurs on the left. "By the power of the Sun's movement" means on the right side; that is, by the power of the Sun's movement, which refers to the movement of the Moon as it emerges from the Sun's sphere of influence.
Thus, by the power of the Sun's movement, when there is a turn to the right, the eclipse of the Moon occurs on the right.
In this way, Rāhu swallows the Moon in the intermediate directions.

In the sequence thus described, Rāhu swallows the Moon by means of its revolution (*valana*) in the intermediate directions; it also swallows it from behind when it has emerged. Because it emerges from the east due to the revolution, it swallows it from behind during the revolution toward the west; thus, the revolution and other parameters of Rāhu are to be understood from the Root Tantra (*mūlatantra*) or from other treatises. Now, the stellar sphere (*nakṣatragola*) is described: the line of the sphere passes through the middle of the night and day, starting from the half of Aśvinī up to Citrā.

From Aśvinī to the midpoint of Citrā, and from the midpoint of Citrā to the end of Revatī, is the sign of Aries; from Tula onwards is the equinox day and night. The line of the celestial sphere (golarekhā) is thirty *daṇḍas* long, serving as the cause for the sun’s rising and setting from the center of the sphere. That very sphere exists through the division of the constellations (*ṛkṣa*). In the plane of the world, the constellation is indeed situated clockwise and counter-clockwise according to the division of the zodiac signs; in the bow-shaped sign of the seasons, it is situated within the circle of fire from the center of the sphere toward the south. *Jyotirjñānavidhimahoddeśa*, Chapter on the Planets. Section on the Constellations. The constellation is situated in the position of the world, both clockwise and counter-clockwise, according to the division of the zodiac signs; in the bow-shaped sign of the seasons, it is situated within the circle of fire from the center of the sphere toward the south.

To the left is that Snowy Mountain (Himālaya), which is like the petal of a beautiful lotus; from the eastern edge of the Snowy Mountain to the western limit of the Fire mountain (Vahni), there are fifty-five thousand yojanas.
"The bear [Ursa Major] is indeed situated on the left and right in the station of the world through the divisions of the zodiac signs.

Here, in this land of action (*karmabhūmi*), due to the power of ignorance, many kinds of theories regarding the celestial sphere (*golamata*)—such as the orbits (*kakṣā*) and other distinctions—have been stated.
It is said here that in the celestial sphere, the movement of the eight planets, whether swift or slow, is equal to their passage through the zodiac signs.

Just as in the threshing of grain, the ox that wanders far from the central post is a fast-moving one and completes its circumambulation in many steps, whereas that which wanders near the post is a slow-moving one and completes its circumambulation in few steps; in this same manner, the planets are also to be understood.

The worldly view is first examined by means of reasoning: since there is no calculation-based convention here, and because of the influence of the respective intentions of their own established doctrines, there is no single consensus; therefore, it is considered as follows—regarding these planets in this celestial sphere that move faster or slower than the sun, are they situated one above the other or one below the other, or are they situated from the left side to the right side?
In either case, there is a contradiction:
if they were situated above or below the sun, then there would be no conjunction of the fast-moving and slow-moving planets, because they would not abandon their own orbits.

Then the proponent of the opposing doctrine says: "Beings situated below perceive the conjunction of the lower and upper planets as equal; that is, the equality of the upper planet being eclipsed by the lower planet. To this it is replied: Here, "equality" refers to the time of midday, not to sunrise, nor to the time of sunset.

At the time of rising, planets should be seen by sentient beings below and above [the sun] due to the influence of their distinct orbits; likewise at the time of setting, it is not otherwise. Thus, even for those situated to the right or left [of the sun], there is no conjunction with the sun because of the non-abandonment of their own orbits.
In this way, there would be neither setting nor rising of the planets within the solar disc;
therefore, in the ultimate sense, there is no difference in the orbits of the planets.
And this statement, which produces delusion for the ignorant, was composed by those lacking in knowledge;

for here, in the first [circle] is the Moon, in the second Mercury, in the third Venus, in the fourth the Sun, in the fifth Mars, in the sixth Jupiter, in the seventh Rāhu, and in the eighth Saturn—thus it occurs.

Here, in this wheel of zodiac signs (*rāśicakra*), there is an upward and downward movement for all the planets, just as the Sun has [movement] by virtue of traversing the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and by virtue of traversing the six signs.

Furthermore, when the sun moves northward or southward, no planet goes above or below the sun at the time of their conjunction. Here in the wheel of the zodiac (*rāśicakra*), by virtue of its slow motion, some planets follow behind the sun; the moon, having risen, moves ahead; and Mercury and Venus, by virtue of their swift motion and the positions of their feet, sometimes rise and move in front and sometimes behind [the sun]. Thus they are obscured.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, for the sake of fully understanding their movement, the sphere of the zodiac signs (*rāśigola*) is described: "The asterism (*ṛkṣa*) is situated in the fourteenth position on the right, and in the fourteenth position on the left, according to the divisions of the zodiac signs. The division of the zodiac signs consists of two and a quarter asterisms for each sign. By these divisions of the zodiac signs, there are thirteen and a half asterisms from the central meridian line of the sphere: starting from Aśvinī up to the midpoint of Citrā on the north, and again from the midpoint of Citrā up to Revatī, there are thirteen and a half asterisms on the south of the central meridian line of the sphere.

In the six signs beginning with Sagittarius (Dhanu), which are bow-shaped, the half-circle of constellations—the stellar wheel—is situated to the south from the center of the sphere; thus, on the equatorial line of the sphere, it is centered in the south.
To the left of that is the Snowy Mountain (Himālaya), shaped like the petal of a lotus, extending from Aries to Libra.

Just as [the zodiacal signs] are situated in six signs on the southern side, each occupying half a circle of constellations, so too are they situated in six signs on the northern side of the equatorial line of the celestial sphere (golamadhyarekhā), according to the division of each individual sign; that is, from the beginning of Aries up to the end of Virgo, and from the beginning of Libra up to the end of Pisces. Thus it proceeds from the beginning of Libra to the end of Pisces.

Herein is the arrangement of the zodiac signs (*rāśinyāsa*) upon the sphere (*gola*): in the eastern half is Aries; in the northeast (*īśāna*) is Taurus; in the northern half is Gemini; again in the northern half is Cancer; in the northwest (*vāyavya*) is Leo; in the western half is Virgo; again in the west is Libra; in the southwest (*nairṛtya*) is Scorpio; in the southern half is Sagittarius; and in the eastern half is Pisces.
Furthermore, in the southern half is Capricorn; in the southeast (*āgneyī*) is Aquarius. In this [system], when Aries rises, Libra sets; when Taurus rises, Scorpio sets.
Thus, it should be understood that for every rising sign (*udayarāśi*), the seventh sign sets, within one day and night.
Now, the measurement of the sphere according to the common worldly view is stated: from the fire [region] to the boundary of the Great Snowy Mountain (Himavat), there are eighty thousand yojanas.

Here, from the southern circle of fire to the northern Great Himavat boundary, the measurement of the sphere is seventy-five thousand yojanas; thus it is clearly to be explained in the fifth chapter regarding the east-west circumference.

The midpoint is the arrival at the meridian line; the sun moves for one night in the poison [direction], and thereafter it moves to the left and right by day and night, with a sequential change of constellations. It abandons the paths of the sky, serpents, and moon by day and night until the end of the solstice; indeed, the decrease and increase of the sun and moon occur within six finger-breadths during the sixty nāḍīs of night and day.

"From the middle of the circle, the line of the [equator]" means that the equinoctial line of the middle zodiac-circle occurs at thirty-seven and a half thousand *yojanas* out of seventy-five thousand *yojanas*. The movement upon that is the movement upon the line in the middle of the half-circle;
by the word "also," it is implied that for all planets, the movement upon the line in the middle of the half-circle occurs at their respective equinoxes, for one night, and not at all times.

"Subsequently, it moves to the left and right" means that after the equinox day (*viṣuvadina*), during the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*) it moves south, and during the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*) it moves north. "Left and right" refers to the beginning of Libra (*tulā*) and Aries (*meṣa*).

This is the division of day and night through the sequence of the paths (*mārga*), numbering one hundred and eighty according to the general system of the spheres (*gola-sāmānya-matena*); [according to] the common worldly view (*loka-sāmānya-matena*), it abandons [the path]. [The *Mahoddeśa* on the Method for Knowledge of Astronomy in the *Paṭala*]
Day and night, indeed, until the end of the solstice— from the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) to the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), and from the southern course back to the northern course—
there is decrease and increase by six parts in sixty nāḍīs for both the sun and the moon;
thus, in these six parts, there is decrease and there is increase.

A sixth part [of the day] corresponds to sixty *nāḍīs*; there is a decrease of ten *nāḍīs* during the night from Capricorn until the end of Gemini, which is the increase of the day; and there is a decrease of the day from Cancer until the end of Sagittarius, which is the increase of the night. Indeed, the decrease and increase of the sun and Saturn occur in this sixth part within the region of Kailāsa; it is not so in the Ārya country. In the Ārya country, the decrease and increase occur in a tenth part, from the summer solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) to the end of the winter solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*), and from the end of the winter solstice to the end of the summer solstice, according to the rule of shadow.

Thus, in countries such as Bhota, Līca, and Cīna, the decrease and increase [of the shadow] up to the borders of the region of Sambhala should be understood by means of the shadow, according to the ninth part, the eighth part, and the seventh part.

Now, regarding the terrestrial globe in the twelve sectors (*dvādaśakhaṇḍa*), its position at the zenith due to the revolution of the sun is described: Because the equinox occurs for the people of Śaila when the sun is in Aries and when the sun is in Libra, therefore it is indeed in the second and eighth sectors when the sun has entered Taurus and likewise Scorpio; in the sector called *randhra* (the ninth) and in the one numbered by fire (the third), when the sun has entered Gemini and Sagittarius; in the fourth sector, which is measured by the directions (the tenth), when the sun is in Cancer; and also in the fifth and eleventh sectors when the sun has entered Capricorn. // 55 //

Because for people on Mount Śaila, the equinox occurs when the sun is in Aries and the sun is in Libra—on that terrestrial sector, the half of spring is the equinox when the sun is in Aries, and the half of autumn occurs when the sun is in Libra; therefore, in this way, autumn occurs when the sun is in Aries, and the equinox of the half of spring occurs when the sun is in Libra.

Thus, through mutual dependence, because the equinox (*viṣuva*) occurs from the first land-section on Mount Śaila in the seventh section to the north of Meru’s south, and likewise in the seventh section to the south of its north; therefore, indeed, when the sun has entered Taurus (*vṛṣabha*) and Scorpio (*vṛścika*), it is so in both [sections]. Here, just as the equinox occurs when the sun is in Aries (*meṣa*) and Libra (*tulā*) in the previously mentioned southern intermediate land-section of Meru, so too it is certain that it occurs when [the sun] is situated slightly toward the southwest corner (*naiṛtyakoṇa*) and when situated in the half-part of the northeast corner (*īśānakoṇa*). When the sun has entered Taurus and Scorpio, then there is the equinox—the half of spring and the half of autumn.

Thus, when the Sun has entered Gemini or Sagittarius, there is an equinox (viśuva) in the ninth [house] called Randhra, in the third [house] numbered by fire (three), in the southwestern corner (Nairṛtya), situated in the latter half,

and in the northeastern corner (Īśāna), situated in the former half; in the tenth and fourth [houses], in the eastern and western land-sections of Meru, there is an equinox, such that there is the spring-half and the autumn-half according to the measurement of the directions.

When the Sun is in Cancer in the western land, and when it has entered Capricorn in the eastern land, the equinox occurs; thus there is half of spring and half of autumn. When [the Sun] enters Leo and Aquarius, at twenty-two thousand [yojanas], and when it has entered Pisces and Virgo, this would be the northern solstice (vāmāyana). When the Sun is in Capricorn, and the Sun is in Aquarius for the second [thousand], and in Pisces for the third land-segment, there is likewise a solstice for men. When the Sun is in Aries for the fourth, known as the "element" (bhūta), and when the Sun is in Taurus, and when the Sun has entered Gemini for the sixth thousand, and in the seventh.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, when the sun has entered the Lion [sign] in the jar [house], being situated in the fifth [sign] in the half of the northwest corner, and being in the eleventh [sign] in the half of the southeast corner, the equinox (*viṣuva*) occurs; that is, the half of spring and the half of autumn occur. Thus, in the "twelve great seasons" (*dvādaśa-rasa-mahā-vit*), when the sun is situated in the latter half of the southeast corner in the twelfth [sign], and in the sixth [sign] in the latter half of the northwest corner—this is the reading of the scriptural tradition (*āgamapāṭha*). When the sun has gone to Pisces and when it has gone to Virgo, the two equinoxes occur; that is, the half of spring and the half of autumn occur.

Thus, on the twelve levels, by the power of the twelve zodiac signs and through the division of the rising and setting of the sun, there are twelve months and six seasons. Now, regarding the twelve northern courses (uttarāyaṇas) and twelve southern courses (dakṣiṇāyanas) on the twelve levels according to the movement of the sun through the zodiac signs, it is said: "In this [place], there shall be the leftward course.
"In this" refers to the terrestrial sector to the south of Meru.

Why is it in the south? Because of the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma in the minor Jambūdvīpa, there is the southern transit (*dakṣiṇāyana*) in the southern land-mass, and the northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*) when the sun is in Capricorn;
likewise, when the sun is in Aquarius in the second land-mass, and in Pisces in the third land-mass; and for humans, the transit occurs in the fourth [land-mass] when the sun is in Aries.
In the western land-quarter, the fourth, known as Bhūta, when the fifth sun is situated in Taurus, the sixth great sun, having entered Gemini,
the northern solstice occurs in the seventh [land-quarter] to the north of Meru.

When the Sun is in Cancer in the Mārttaṇḍa region, it is the eighth solar transit (ayana) on the earth; when in Virgo in the Harigata region, it is the ninth; when in Libra in the Kanyārandhra region, it is the tenth; and when in Scorpio in the Rudrakhaṇḍa region, it is the twelfth. Thus, by the movement of the Sun through the signs beginning with Cancer, there occurs the northern transit (savyāyana) in the twelve-spoked earth. // 57 //

When the Sun is in Cancer in Mārttaṇḍa, the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) occurs in the eighth land-segment; when the Sun is in Virgo, it occurs in the ninth land-segment; when the Sun is in Libra, it occurs in the tenth land-segment; and when the Sun is in Scorpio, it occurs in the eleventh segment, O Rudra. When the Sun is in Sagittarius, the solstice for men would occur in the twelfth segment; thus, for the worlds situated upon the twelve-spoked earth, the northern solstice occurs according to the division of the twelve zodiac signs, and in this manner, the southern solstice (*savyāyana*) occurs.
According to the sequence thus described, the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*) occurs in the zodiac signs beginning with Cancer due to the movement of the sun;
in this small Jambūdvīpa region to the south of Meru, the southern solstice occurs when the sun is in Cancer.

Likewise, in the second [region] to the right, it occurs when the sun is in Leo; in the third, when the sun is in Virgo; and in the fourth, when the sun is in Libra—the southern solstice thus occurs on the western side of Meru.

In the fifth land-segment, when the Sun is in Scorpio; in the sixth, in Sagittarius; in the seventh, in Capricorn; in the eighth to the north of Meru, in Aquarius; in the ninth, in Pisces; in the tenth, in Aries; in the eleventh, in Taurus; and in the twelfth, in Gemini—thus, for the people of these land-segments, the sun’s southern course occurs according to the division of the twelve zodiac signs. Now, the measure of the Sun's northern declination above the terrestrial circle is stated: "Sixty thousand [yojanas] above is the Sun, O King; at the end of the northern course, it is diminished by eleven thousand [yojanas] on the right (southern) side."

The meridian line is eighty-one thousand [yojanas] minus one hundred arrows (five); from that point, there is an increase of two [thousand] for every fifty [yojanas] toward the north and south. // 58 //

[In the] *Jyotirjñānavidhimahoddeśa* [chapter]: "Above, the number of six nāgas" means that here, above the seventh terrestrial circle (*bhūvalaya*), the distance is eighty-six thousand *yojanas*. Furthermore, the movement of the sun occurs during the northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*) at the end [of the year], and during the southern transit (*dakṣiṇāyana*) at the beginning [of the year]. In each respective sector, starting from Cancer (*karkaṭa*) and so forth, the southern transit occurs on its own day of transition (*saṃkrānti*) across the twelve sectors in due order. Therefore, O Lord of Men, it diminishes by one thousand [yojanas] on the right [side] for each Rudra-number (eleven) of sectors.

Therefore, from the day of the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana-saṃkrānti*) until the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) in the northern course, the heat of the sun above should be known to diminish by eleven thousand and seventy-five thousand [yojanas]; thus, eighty-one thousand minus five hundred and fifty [yojanas] constitutes the central meridian line (*gola-rekhā*) in yojanas. Just as there is a double descent of the sun upon that meridian line, so it occurs.

"Khakhaśareṣu" means five thousand five hundred *yojanas*. By virtue of the movement through the zodiac signs (*rāśibhoga*), [the sun] moves within its respective sectors to the north and south of the central meridian. Now, the daily transverse declination (*tiryakkrānti*) of the sun across the twelve sectors to the right and left is described: Having crossed the salt ocean, the sun travels as far as the Fire Mountain (*Agni*) to the south; and to the north, it travels to Kailāsa; and further to the north, it reaches the Snowy Mountain (*Himagiri*). Thus, it remains situated in the northern regions.
Struck by the lunar days (tithis), the arrows travel a thousand yojanas in each solstice; diminished by five and divided by eleven, they are subtracted from all sides day by day. (59)
"Having crossed the salt ocean, the sun proceeds as far as the southern fire.

Here, on this twelve-spoked ground, in each individual continent, by the power of the zodiac signs, the sun—remaining in the southern solstice after crossing the salt ocean—proceeds as far as the circle of the southern fire, reaching the boundary of the ocean.

From that boundary, the circle of fire, he proceeds northward to Mount Kailāsa; on the northern path, situated in the northern solstice, the sun proceeds until the day of the beginning of the southern solstice.

"Bāṇāstithayāhatāḥ" means that "bāṇa" is five and "tithi" is fifteen; multiplied by those fifteen, "bāṇāstithayāhatāḥ" becomes seventy-five. The sun travels that distance of seventy-five thousand *yojanas* during its solstitial courses (*ayanāni*), from the Himālayas to the Fire-mountain (*Agni*) and from the Fire-mountain to the Himālayas; this division of the directions (*digvibhāga*) consists of seventy-five thousand *yojanas*. He traverses that division of the directions in six months according to the sequence of the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*) and the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*).
"Half an akṣa, diminished by the moon, is abandoned day by day"—

this means that the sun abandons the daily directional division of *yojanas* obtained from the quotient of one hundred and eighty-two and a half divided into seventy-five thousand. Thus, through the movement across both solstices, the number of days for the sun to traverse the mandala of the zodiac circle becomes three hundred and sixty-five.
Thus, the transverse movement of the sun across the twelve sectors (*khaṇḍa*) is to be understood.

Now, the division of the twelve months according to the sun’s revolution through the twelve sectors while situated in each individual zodiac sign (*rāśi*) is described: therefore, following the Tibetan tradition, "the increase and decrease" (*vṛddhipāta*) is the more appropriate reading.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is stated: "The Sun, situated in the zodiacal sign of Aries (*meṣa*), produces the entire collection of seasons, months, and fortnights; and on the surface of the earth, a month occurs in each sector (*khaṇḍa*) sequentially within the twelve-spoked [mandala]. Whatever measurement occurs in whichever sector by virtue of the days, that same measurement occurs at night in the seventh [sector]; thus, by the power of the three hundred thousand [leagues], there is day in front of the Sun and night behind it. (60)
"Situated in a single zodiac sign, the Sun produces the entire collection of seasons,

months, and fortnights"— here, the Sun, situated in any one sign such as Aries and so forth, produces the six seasons, twelve months, and twenty-four fortnights within the twelve sectors by virtue of his revolution through the wheel of the zodiacs.

Here, in every direction from Meru, that which touches the Dakṣiṇāgni fire by virtue of the revolution of the zodiacal wheel reaches the direction of the seventh sector and touches the peak of Meru; according to the principle that the Himavat mountain moves upward, the entire collection of seasons and so forth is to be understood for the Sun situated in each individual sign. Thus, in each sector, a month occurs in succession within the twelve-spoked [wheel] of movement.

Here, on the surface of the earth consisting of twelve spokes, there is a month for each individual region; the manner in which this occurs for the sun situated in a single zodiac sign is explained as follows: by the description of one sign here, all signs are to be understood.

In this small Jambudvīpa, it is well known that starting from Aries (Meṣa), the zodiac signs, the seasons beginning with spring (Vasanta), and the months beginning with Caitra—indeed all fortnights—are established. Therefore, it is explained how the sun, situated in that sign of Aries, produces the entire cycle of seasons and so forth across the twelve sectors (*khaṇḍa*): here, in the southern sector of Meru, the sun situated in Aries produces the season of spring and the month of Vaiśākha; in the second sector, the lower half of the southeast corner (*agni-koṇārddha*), it produces the month of Jyeṣṭha; likewise, in the sector beyond the southeast corner, it produces Āṣāḍha; in the third [sector], and similarly in the fourth, the eastern sector of Meru, Pūrvavideha, it produces the month of Śrāvaṇa; in the fifth, the upper half of the northeast corner (*īśārddha*), it produces Bhādrapada; in the sixth sector, the lower half of the northeast corner, it produces Āśvina; in the seventh sector, north of Meru, it produces Kārttika; in the eighth sector, the lower half of the northwest corner (*vāyavyakoṇārddha*), it produces Mārgaśīrṣa; in the ninth sector, the upper half of the northwest corner, it produces Pauṣa; in the tenth sector, west of Meru, it produces Māgha; in the eleventh sector, the lower half of the southwest corner (*naiṛtyakoṇāparārddha*), it produces Phālguna; and in the twelfth sector, the lower half of the southwest corner, it produces Caitra.
Thus, with two months, a season (*ṛtu*) occurs in each of the two sections; in each individual section, there are two fortnights (*pakṣa*) distinguished by the bright and dark halves.
In this way, it should be understood that the twelve months, twenty-four fortnights, and six seasons revolve in the form of a wheel within the twelve sections.

In this southern continent, whichever month occurs according to the sequence of the twelve zodiac signs at the solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), that [month] proceeds by way of clockwise rotation to the southwest corner at the next transit. From the southwest, it goes to the other half of the corner; from the other half of the corner, it goes to the western *Godānī* of Meru; situated in the western *Godānī*, it goes to the northwest half-corner; situated in the northwest half-corner, it goes to the other half of the corner; situated in the other half of the corner, it goes to *Uttarakuru*; situated in *Uttarakuru*, it goes to the northeast half-corner; situated there, it goes to the other half of the corner; situated in the other half of the corner, it goes to *Pūrvavideha*; situated in *Pūrvavideha*, it goes to the southeast half-corner of the continent; situated in the eastern half, it goes to the other half of the corner; and situated in the other half of the corner, it goes to the southern *Jambūdvīpa*. Thus, one should understand the movement through the twelve sectors according to the successive transits of the twelve months.
Whatever the measure of day is in a particular region, that same measure occurs at night in the seventh [region] from it due to the power of the solar transit (*saṃkrānti*).

Here, during the northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*), the measure of the day is diminished and the measure of the night is increased in the southern region; that very same measure occurs in the seventh terrestrial region of Uttarakuru by virtue of the sun’s rising, and by virtue of the increase of night in the south. However, that measure does not occur here [in Jambūdvīpa]; rather, in Jambūdvīpa, by virtue of the sun’s rising in the south and by virtue of the decrease of night in the seventh [region], it occurs in the south.
Thus, it should be understood in this way for every individual region everywhere.
Halfway through three hundred thousand [yojanas], there is day in front of the sun and night behind it;

thus, the measure of the sphere here is six hundred thousand [yojanas]. Due to the movement of the sun, halfway through three hundred thousand [yojanas] is day—from sunrise until sunset—and night is three hundred thousand [yojanas] from sunset until sunrise.
In this way, it should be understood for each day and night.

Now, the location of Meru within the twelve sectors is described: "O Lord of Men, the King of Mountains stands to the north of all people. The sun rises in the east, remains level with the mountain [at midday], and sets in the west.

These times—the four twilights, the watches, the day, and the night—constantly shifting, revolve around the directions of Meru; the manifest sun and earth are divided by the distinctions of the zodiacal signs. (61)
"O Lord of Men, the King of Mountains stands to the north of all [the lands], as it were;
thus, for the people situated here in the twelve regions, Mount Meru, the King of Mountains, is to the north."

"East" is that direction where the sun rises for everyone situated on Mount Meru as well as those residing in all the continents, such that "the sun shall rise in the east. For those situated in Jambūdvīpa, Pūrvavideha is the eastern direction; for those in Aparagodānī, Jambūdvīpa is the eastern direction; for those situated in Uttarakuru, Aparagodānī is the eastern direction; and for those situated in Pūrvavideha, Uttarakuru is the eastern direction—this being due to the rotation and rising of the sun. This should be understood to apply similarly to the eight continents situated at the intermediate points (koṇa). Thus, the sun rises in each individual continent with an interval of five *daṇḍas*.

Regarding the phrase "the movement of the mountain-like [sun]": in each individual division (*khaṇḍa*), the sun’s movement toward Mount Meru is equal to the mountain; it rises in the north and south, and sets in the west.

Thus, in the twelve divisions, just as there is sunrise in the east, so too should one understand that there is sunset in the west. Consequently, there are three times: dawn (*prabhāta*), midday (*madhyāhna*), and evening (*vikāla*).
There are four junctions (*saṃdhyā*): the midnight junction, the morning junction, the midday junction, and the evening junction.
There are eight watches (*prahara*): four during the day and four at night, constantly shifting throughout both day and night.
In this way, time and the other factors, transitioning through every moment of day and night, revolve from one sector to another around the directions of Mount Meru;
as stated in the *Vimalaprabhā*: "In the world-system where the sun is manifest, on the twelve-spoked wheel of the earth, they are divided according to the divisions of the zodiacal signs (*lagna*)."

There are twelve *lagnas*; differentiated by their divisions, time and the other factors revolve. Time revolves through four *lagnas* each; each individual *sandhyā* revolves through three *lagnas*; each individual watch (*prahara*) revolves through one and a half *lagnas*; thus, each individual *lagna* revolves through fifteen *daṇḍas*. A half-watch revolves through half a watch; a *muhūrta* revolves through half of a half-watch; a *ghaṭikā* revolves through sixty *pāṇīpalas*; and each individual *pāṇīpala* revolves through six breaths (*śvāsa*).

Thus, by means of the divisions of breath and the divisions of the zodiacal signs (*lagna*), time revolves and passes for embodied beings day and night. Now, the measure of the sun’s revolution in all directions around Meru is stated: In one *nāḍī* year, the sun traverses six thousand and five hundred *yojanas*; it revolves through sixty hundred thousand and three hundred thousand *yojanas* day and night; and it moves through fifty thousand and five hundred *yojanas* during the half-orbit. It carries the [shadow] through thirty *nāḍīs* day and night during the decrease and increase [of the shadow] on the globe. On the globe, there is a clockwise and counter-clockwise motion every day; from that, a pair of breaths consists of three *liptās*.

In a *nāḍī*—that is, during the period consisting of three hundred and sixty breaths—the Sun traverses six thousand and five hundred *yojanas*. Thus, while situated in a zodiacal sign (*rāśi*) within the sky, this speed of revolution belongs to the sign; it does not belong to the Sun as it remains supported by that sign. Here, the circle of signs revolves clockwise (*savyāvarta*), whereas the planets move counter-clockwise (*apasavya*) through the signs.
Just as the zodiacal circle revolves, so too Rāhu moves, circumambulating Meru while facing westward.
The planets, facing eastward, circumambulate Meru while traversing the zodiacal circle.
Thus, according to the reasoning of ultimate truth, Rāhu is meritorious, whereas the Sun and others are called malevolent, sinful planets.

"Sixty lakhs of fires" means that during the time of sixty *nāḍīs*—that is, during the period consisting of twenty thousand six hundred breaths—one traverses three lakhs [of *yojanas*]. "Five mountains" refers to a number of seventy-five thousand *yojanas* which one circles; this constitutes a day and night (*ahorātra*). Regarding the statement "the half-globe has thirty *nāḍīs* for day and night": here, on the day of the equinoxal transition (*viṣuvatsaṃkrānti*), at the aforementioned meridian line of the globe, the sun flows through thirty *nāḍīs* of day and thirty *nāḍīs* of night; the meaning is that the sun's day and night are equal.
The basis for decrease and increase (and the decrease and increase themselves) in the sphere (*gola*) is said to be "clockwise" (*savya*) and "counter-clockwise" (*apasavya*).

Therefore, from that half-sphere, in three months of the clockwise direction there is an increase of five *nāḍīs* in the night; in three months of the counter-clockwise direction there is an increase of five *nāḍīs* in the day.
Here, it should be understood that by the increase of the night there is a decrease of the day, and by the increase of the day there is a decrease of the night.
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, within the *Mahoddeśa* on the method of astrological knowledge (*jyotirjñānavidhi*) in the chapter on the *Lokadhātu*: "That pair of breaths is three *liptās*.
Here, in the right and left [channels], for the three months, there is daily—within each day and night—an increase or decrease of two breaths and three *pāṇīpala*s.
This measurement applies to the region of Kailāsa, not to the land of Ārya [India] and so forth.

In the noble land [of India], an increase or decrease of two *liptās* (i.e., *pāṇīpala*s) per day and night is to be understood; over a period of three months from the middle equinox (*viṣuva*), an increase or decrease of three *nāḍīs*—equivalent to thirty days and nights—is to be understood according to the [solar] course (*ayana*). (70b) Now, the time of rising for the twelve ascendants (*lagna*) according to the divisions of the Kailāsa region is stated: In the ascendant of Aries, there would be [29] *liptās*; in Taurus, [30]; in Gemini, [56] *ghaṭikās*; and in Cancer and Leo, [60].

In Virgo, there are indeed six and a half [periods]; and in the reverse order beginning from Libra, all six [houses] are thus declared to be set when they reach the ascendant, as well as the Sun and the lunar mansions.
"Liptyā syānmeṣalagne" means:

here, from the first rising [of the sun] until the next rising of the sign Aries, the time elapsed is ninety-two hundred and ninety liptās—that is, a mass of *pāṇīpala*s. Therefore, by dividing this by sixty, the rising time of the sign Aries is four *ghaṭikās* and fifty *pāṇīpalas*; such is the rule for the region of Kailāśa.
"Khartunetraṃ vṛṣe syāt" means [the rising time] of Taurus shall be [forty-two hundred and thirty liptās].
Thus, the duration of the Taurus ascendant (vṛṣalagna) is two hundred and sixty *pāṇīpala*s; its rising time (*udayakāla*) consists of four *nāḍīs* and twenty *pāṇīpala*s.
In the Gemini (*yugma*), that is, in the Gemini ascendant, the rising time is two hundred *liptā*s as a total, which is three *nāḍīs* and twenty *pāṇīpala*s.
"The rising times shall be five *ghaṭikās* for the arrows" means that in Cancer (*kulīra*), the rising time is five *ghaṭikās*.

Then, in Leo, "rasa" (six) is the time at the rising of the sixth house; in Virgo, "kāla" (time) refers to six and a half [ghaṭikās]. The time for the rising of the Virgo ascendant is six ghaṭikās and thirty pāṇīpala-s, which constitutes six and a half. All of this proceeds in reverse order starting from Libra. Therefore, the rule is that by this method, everything without exception is determined through the sequence of the six signs starting from Libra in reverse order, following the time-limit of the six signs.

In this regard, the rule for the region of Kailāsa is as follows: at the time of the rising of the ascendant (lagna), there are six ghaṭikās and thirty pāṇīpala-s in Libra; six in Scorpio; five in Sagittarius; three nāḍīs and twenty pāṇīpala-s in Capricorn; four nāḍīs and twenty pāṇīpala-s in Aquarius; and four ghaṭikās and fifty pāṇīpala-s in Pisces.
This is stated to be the setting by means of the six ascendants; for indeed, because it has risen by means of the six ascendants, it therefore becomes set.

Regarding the phrase "by the division of the asterisms of the Sun": at the end of thirteen and a half asterisms, there is sunset, and likewise at the end of thirteen and a half asterisms, there is sunrise. By the division of day and night, through six ascendants and thirteen and a half asterisms, the duration of the day occurs; through six ascendants and thirteen and a half asterisms, the duration of the night occurs. Day and night become shorter or longer according to the time of the rising of the ascendant, due to the movement of the sun.

Now, the number of breaths and so forth within the body for one hundred years is stated, beginning with "twenty-one thousand," and so on: Twenty-one thousand breaths, increased by sixty, have issued from the teeth; those breaths which exceed [the daily count] in the body at every moment of time are numbered as thirty-six. When the measure of a hundred-year lifespan is calculated by multiplying by thirty-six thousand, it is well known that the *ghaṭikā* arises from division by thirty, and the day (*dina*) from the sixtieth part.
It enters into two thousand six hundred and sixty-one; that is, into [the total] of two tens of thousands, one thousand, six hundreds, and sixty-one.
From this heap, it has emerged by means of the tooth-parts; it has emerged by thirty-two parts.

In the body, those breaths which exceed [the daily count] at the time of each daily transit (*saṃkrānti*)—that is, at the moment of the twelfth zodiac sign (*dvādaśalagna*)—number six hundred and seventy-five (*ṣaṭsaptatyadhikaṣaṭśata*). When multiplied by thirty-six thousand, this is the well-known measure of a hundred-year lifespan. Those breaths, multiplied by thirty-six thousand—the number of days in a hundred years—become the measure of the breaths of a hundred years.

In this context, the daily breaths of three nāḍīs, numbering two thousand one hundred and sixty, when multiplied by the number of days in a hundred years, become seventy-seven crores and six hundred and seventy lakhs.

The breaths of the central channel, *avadhūtī*, amount to two crores and forty-three lakhs, obtained by dividing those [total breaths] by thirty-two. The remainder—seventy-five crores and thirty-three lakhs—are the carriers of the five mandalas for the *lalanā* and *rasanā*; of these, by equal division, half are carried by the *lalanā* and half by the *rasanā*, from the left and right respectively, until the limit of one hundred years. A *ghaṭikā* is produced by dividing [the total breaths] by zero, seasons, and fire (360).
Then, the heap of breaths divided by three hundred and sixty yields the heap of ghaṭikās; from the sixty-fold portion, the days are obtained.

Then, the quotient obtained by dividing the heap of *ghaṭikās* by sixty becomes the *dinapiṇḍa* (the total number of days) for the *madhyamā*. From the thirty-six thousand [total *ghaṭikās*], the remainder is the *dinapiṇḍa* for the *lalanā* and *rasanā*, which should be known as three hundred thousand, forty-eight hundred, and seventy-five (*348,075*) within the limit of a hundred-year lifespan. Thus it is said: Now, the measure of a hundred years for the eight planets, through their enjoyment of the wheel [of time] together with a half [circle], as a single aggregate, is as follows: in the moon, when devoid of the *kālacakra*, there is a fortnight; in the sun, a solstice (*ayana*); in Mars, nine months; and in Jupiter, a night. There would be six years in [Saturn]; in Venus, a solstice; and in the son of the Moon (Mercury), a solstice.
O King, the years known as the lunar days (tithis) are nine in Śauri and likewise nine in Atami; that total, minus Ketu, is a single aggregate of forty-eight years and three and a half months.
Regarding "In the moon, a fortnight," and so forth:

in the moon, a fortnight (*pakṣa*) consists of one night of thirty *daṇḍas*, due to the enjoyment of half the circle of the zodiac signs (*rāśicakra*). In the sun, a solstice (*ayana*) also consists of half a day and night, due to the enjoyment of half the circle. [From the *Jyotirjñānavidhimahoddeśa* in the *Paṭala*]

In the case of Mars, nine months constitute a day and night; such is the intended meaning of the *karaṇa* system. Thus, for Jupiter, there are six years [for a day and night]. As it is for the Sun, so it is for Saturn (*bhṛgu*), whose solstice likewise lasts for six years. For Mercury, the son of the Moon, fifteen years—known as *tithis*—constitute a day and night. For the Sun’s son, Saturn, nine years constitute a day and night, arising from half the duration of the revolution of the lunar asterisms (*nakṣatra-cakra*).

All that, as a single mass, consists of eight times the years of the Yugas (2880 years), thirty-two years, and three and a half months; such is the division of the quality of *sattva* among sentient beings. In the *Kālacakra* mantra, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) flow within *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* for one hundred and fifty days. From that, gods, humans, and serpents go to their dissolution through the divisions of body, speech, and mind. Therefore, O King, this well-established and fixed number occurs in the *Kālacakra* at the half-night of the moon.

The number [of days] is half a day, due to the enjoyment of the circle of asterisms along with the [remaining] half; through the division of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, there may also be one hundred years minus the *Kālacakra*.
This aggregate of ninety-six years, increased by ten and a half months and three years and three fortnights, constitutes the single aggregate of the eight planets.
The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) flow within *sattva*.

In this [state], the life-force (*prāṇa*) and the qualities of the *sattva* element flow within beings for thirty-two years and a half-months. Thereafter, they pass away in the *rajas* state by that same measure, and then in the *tamas* state by that very same sequence. From that limit, under the influence of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, gods, humans, and animals [depart] according to their own respective lifespan of one hundred years.

"By half a night of the moon and by three fortnights of the Kālacakra"—by the word "and" (*ca*), it is meant that through the previous three years, transmigrating beings here undergo death, which is the state of fivefold dissolution. This is conventional terminology; however, according to the logic of ultimate reality, there is no fixed rule for sentient beings. Their arising and cessation must be understood by Buddhists as being under the power of their own respective karma. "A person has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundred faculties"—this is intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*).

The Puruṣa, whose nature consists of the four yugas, is characterized externally by thirty-four lakh and two thousand years of breaths; internally, he likewise consists of the four yugas according to that same measure of breaths, at which time the entry of all the planets into the void occurs—this is the reasoning of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-yukti*).

Furthermore, for sentient beings, lifespan becomes shorter or longer due to the power of their virtuous and non-virtuous actions; there is no fixed rule that it must be one hundred years, according to the word of the Tathāgata.
This number is well-established and perfectly determined in the *Kālacakra*, the King of Tantras.
"Narendra" is the address for Vajrapāṇi; "Sucandra" refers to [the interlocutor].

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the world-system (*lokadhātu*), the following is now stated concerning the aggregate of the *ghaṭikās* of the rising of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and the movement of the five planets, beginning with Mars, within the sixty parts of the central *avadhūtī*: "In the unbroken *Kālacakra*... and so forth. Having added the nine [units] of the northern and southern solstices (*ayanarṇa*) entirely to the *ghaṭikās* of the movement of the five planets, such as Mars, in their swift calculation (*śīghrakarma*).

On Mars, four and three (seven) prevail in the planetary positions according to the division of the *cāra*; they are equal in the first and second halves [of the revolution] and should be applied to the movements of debt and credit through the distinctions of their respective places. (67)

When the wheel of time is not severed—within the period of three years and three fortnights, and while the one thousand one hundred and twenty-five *ayanāṃśas* remain unexpired—one adds nine *ṛṇa* (negative) units for the nine months of gestation, and nine *ṛṇa* *ghaṭikās*. Thus, the total sum of *ghaṭikās* amounts to one thousand one hundred and thirty-four; this constitutes the *caraṇaghaṭī* for the five planets, beginning with Mars, in their swift motion (*śīghrakarman*) and in the calculation of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatrakarman*).

On Mars (Bhauma), from the [elements] fire (3) and seasons (6), there is a total of three hundred and sixty-four in Maṅgala; this is the aggregate of ghaṭikās in the house of water (14) based on the enjoyment of thirteen and a half constellations in the fourteen-footed division. By the divisions of movement (cāra), such as the twenty-fourfold divisions and so forth, the front and back are equal: one hundred and eighty-two constellations for the first half and one hundred and eighty-two for the second half, due to the halving of each constellation by its quarters.
Regarding the phrase "in the movements of debt and wealth":
according to the stated sequence, they should be applied to the movements of debt and the movements of wealth respectively through the divisions of places.

The asterism that has risen from the solar disc is the first place; from that division of places come the other fourteen places. By means of those divisions of places, those ghaṭikās are to be applied.

First, the number of Jina (twenty-four) prevails as the *ghaṭikās*; then three times the "fire-eyes" (three-twenty); then twice that with one added; then eighteen; then the lunar days (fifteen) and Hara (eleven); then from the root of fire (three), the "excellent" (nine).
Here, fifty-three is subtracted from the sun [in the zodiacal sign]; and when it is purified, there is both debt and credit in reverse and direct order respectively. 68.

First, the number of the Jaina lords (twenty-four) is in the house of the consumption of the first asterism; outside, the "eye of man" (twenty-three) arises in three ways. From the first position, it occurs in three ways in the second, third, and fourth.
In two places, it is "one with an eye" (twenty-one); then, from the fourth position, in the fifth and sixth positions, it is twenty-one in two places.
[In the seventh], it is eighteen, fifteen, and eleven.

Then, from the sixth position, there are eighteen in the seventh, fifteen (tithi) in the eighth, and eleven (harā) in the ninth position respectively. From the root outside, the "excellent" (vara) is three (vahnī), and from the ninth position, in the tenth position, there are three movements (cārā); then, from the root in the latter half, in the eleventh position, there are eleven (harā).

In the twelfth [station], there are thirty-eight; in the thirteenth, eighty; and in the fourteenth station of the abode of stability, there are fifty-three—meaning fifty together with three, thus fifty-three. This is the rule for the fourteenth station. When the sun has been purified in that half-circle of constellations (*nakṣatrārddhacakra*), debt occurs in reverse order and wealth occurs in direct order; for Mars and the others, debt is to be subtracted from the enjoyment of the constellations, and wealth is to be added.

In the chapter on the Great Exposition of the Method for Knowing the Luminaries: In the calculation of Mercury’s swift motion, the number of *ghaṭikās* arising from the Vedas (4), mountains (7), and moon (1) is sixteen; these are situated in two places. In the other [place], there are the lunar days (15), the Manus (14), Madana (3), Rudras (11), the mountain-king (8), and the void (0).

From the root, the Vedas (4), and the bearers (11), the fixed values are clearly revealed as twelve and twenty in the twelfth [position]. Furthermore, twenty-eight and thirty-four are established in the position of the Manus (14) according to the divisions of the [planetary] beginnings.
In the calculation of the swift motion (śīghrakārya) of Mercury, the number of ghaṭīs is equal to the number of Vedas (4), mountains (7), apertures (9), and moons (1);

thus, the total sum of ghaṭīs for Mercury here is one hundred and ninety-four. Just as the sum of Mercury's own ghaṭīs is placed in the fourteenth position for Mars, so it should be understood for Mercury as well. In the operation of the swift motion and the operation of the asterisms (nakṣatrakarma), there are sixteen in two places—that is, sixteen in the first place and sixteen in the second place as well.
Others say it is according to the lunar days (*tithi*): fifteen in the third, fourteen in the fourth, thirteen in the fifth;
Rudra (eleven), Śailendra (seven), and Kha (zero) in the sixth; eleven in the seventh, seven in the eighth, five in the ninth, and zero in the tenth.
"From the root, [the sequence is] 'vedā' (4) and 'dhara' (14).

Thus, from the ninth position, in the latter half of the root, four should be placed in the tenth position, eleven in the eleventh, twenty in the twelfth, twenty-eight in the thirteenth, and thirty-four in the fourteenth.
In this manner, the ghaṭikās of Mercury are to be understood as established according to their respective order through the divisions of the [planetary] movements.

This aggregate of *ghaṭikās* is indeed forty-one thousand nine hundred and sixty-four; and for the Guru (Jupiter), it is twice that amount: ten thousand eight hundred and ninety-six. From the *mūla* [of the zodiac], the movements of all the planets proceed in order:
three, six, nine, eleven, fourteen, seven, and one; this is the rule for the host of planets as they move through the divisions of the Sun, whether in direct, retrograde, or slow motion.

The aggregate of one hundred and four *ghaṭikās*, which is the number of the unassailable moon in the sky (*abadhyākāśendu*), when divided by the fourteen places of the Guru according to the division of the *cāras*,

results as follows: from that aggregate of *ghaṭikās*, there are ten in the first place and ten in the second— these being the measure of the directions (*dik*)— nine in the third, eight in the fourth, and six in the fifth— these being the seasons (*ṛtu*)—
six in the sixth, two in the seventh, and one in the eighth— these being the lunar mansions (*ṣaṭkarendra*).
From the root, in the second half, there are six outside; thus, in the ninth [pada] there are three, in the tenth six, in the eleventh nine, and in the twelfth eleven.
"Kings and sages" means sixteen in the thirteenth, and seven in the fourteenth pada; these are all the movements in sequence.
In this way, the ghaṭikās for all the feet of all the planets are to be understood according to their respective order.

In the case of swift motion (*śīghracāra*), the rule for the group of planets is that they rise in the eastern half when moving fast, and in the western half when moving slow; in retrograde motion (*vakra*), it is the reverse, rising in the eastern half and setting in the western half. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that they move according to these divisions of subtraction from the Sun (*sūryabheda*). In the calculation of the *śīghra* (fast anomaly), the number of *ghaṭikās* for Venus (*bhṛgu*) is six and four (*64*). In the three places, it is twenty-five and two Victors (*2524*); likewise, it should be two hands and two eyes (*22*) in two ways.

The defects [of the signs] are derived from the eighth root of the lunar days; the six [defects] are also [calculated as] one hundred minus three, and at the end, the duration in the station of the world is thirty-three, according to the sequence of Venus's movement.
"In the number of six moons and oceans" means four hundred and sixteen; this total belongs to Bhṛgu, that is, Śukra, in fourteen places.

From that, there are twenty-five *ghaṭikās* in three places: exactly twenty-five in the first place, likewise in the second and third; "twice the Victors" (24) in the fourth; likewise in the fifth; "hands and eyes" (22) in two ways, thus twenty-two in the sixth; and "faults, lunar days, and eight" (18) in the seventh.
In the eighth [month] there are eighteen; in the ninth, fifteen; in the eighth [again], eight; then from the latter half of the root [period], six and also fifty (the product of space and qualities).
In the eleventh, six; in the twelfth, thirty; in the thirteenth, one hundred minus one.
At the end, in the fourteenth, the number of fire and mountains—that is, seventy-three.

In the section on the cultivation of stability, the movements of Venus in the fourteen sections are to be understood in sequence. O King, the total number of *ghaṭikās* for Saturn is sixty-five; from the base, these are six, five, four, four, four, four, four, four, four, four, four, four, four, and zero. The two fortnights, the Vedas, the elements, the tastes, the Vasus, and the fires are to be established in order. Thus, the entire movement of the planets in the Kālacakra is perfectly determined. [74a]
The phrase "of Saturn, the number of the six elements" refers to a total of fifty-six *ghaṭikās* for Saturn in the fourteenth place;
from that, [the values are] "six, eight, twenty-four" in the first quarter, six in the second, and likewise in the third;
in the fourth, there are four.

Regarding the "eyes of the ocean" (*jalanidhinayana*) [two]: four are to be placed in the fifth [house], two in the sixth, a pair [two] in the seventh, and zero in the eighth. From that root [the eighth house], the latter half follows:

two in the ninth [house]—[the sequence being] "wings" (*pakṣau*) and "Vedas" (*vedāḥ*)—four in the tenth, five in the eleventh, six in the twelfth—"flavors" (*rasa*), "wealth" (*vasu*), and "peaks" (*śikhin*)—eight in the thirteenth, and three *nāḍīs* are to be established in the fourteenth place for Saturn (*śanaiścara*) in due order.

Thus, the movement of the planets is perfectly determined as a whole within the Kālacakra; that is, within the wheel of breath-days in the central channel (*madhyamā*) over a hundred years, the *Kālacakra* constitutes the enjoyment of the rising movements and *ghaṭikās* of the planets. Now, regarding the slow motion (*mandakārya*), the slow-signs (*mandapada*) and *ghaṭikās* for the birth sign are stated: "The thirty-six and a half months multiplied by eight (eighty-seven and a half) are indeed the signs in the slow motion; the number of *ghaṭikās* for the planets beginning with Mars is two, nine, and two."

The mountains for the planets are eighteen, seven, and one; the duration of Mars is on the western and eastern sides; for Mercury it is ten and nine; and for Jupiter it is eleven and thirty-three, on the eastern and western sides respectively. (73)
"Thirty-six," and so forth.

Thirty-six half-months are the thirty-six months of three years; having taken one fortnight from the three fortnights, it is indeed certain (*khalu*). "Multiplied by the eight qualities" means multiplied by the eight qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, smell, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
