By these eight qualities multiplied, the *padas* (positions) of the five planets arise for the slow-motion calculation (*mandakārya*).
From the eyes [2], the number of *rāśi*-ghaṭikās is two hundred and ninety-two (the number of apertures and eyes).
Therefore, for the manifest Mars and the others, they should be known in the six positions in reverse order in the first half and the second half.

Its own [position] is eighteen mountains (78); in the chapter on the Great Overview of the Method of Knowledge of Luminaries, the position of the Son of the Earth (Mars) is in the second half and the first part.
The principles (*tattva*) are twenty-five, eighteen, and seven—respectively, in the latter half, the former part, and [the remainder] of the son of the Earth, Maṅgala (Mars).
Thus, for Mercury (*budha*), there are ten directions, seven mountains, and three fires; likewise, nine lords...

For Khiga (Mars), there are three [aspects]: eleven, nine, and the trident (three); for Guru (Jupiter), the remainder is according to the previously stated sequence; and this applies to both the eastern and western halves.

For Venus, [the daily motion] is four hundred and one minutes; for the Moon, it is one minute; for the Sun, it is two hundred and twenty-four minutes; and for Mars, it is nine hundred and fifty-five minutes. For Venus, it is thus; and for Mercury, it is sixty-seven minutes. These [daily] motions, when combined, constitute the monthly motion; and over three months, this becomes the annual motion in days, deficient by one minute for these three [planets].
Thus, for Venus,
the values are five, four, and one— five being "arrows" (*iṣu*), four being "fire" (*adhi*), and one being "moon" (*candra*). In this way, the [period] of Venus becomes 546 days.
The eyes are twenty-two, the days fifteen, and the seasons six; this sequence was previously stated.
Thus, the sixty parts multiplied by eight, which constitute the monthly enjoyment of the *kālacakra*, should be understood as the *ghaṭikās* for the movement through the zodiacal signs.

Now, regarding the five planets beginning with Mars, because they enjoy three signs [in a year], their enjoyment of *ghaṭikās* is said to be equal to the number of days in three years, starting with the word "month" (*māsa*) and so forth: "In a month, the movement of Mars is ninety *ghaṭikās*; such is the worldly convention."
By its own nature, through the division of the mandala, the *ghaṭikās* obtained constitute a month; furthermore, a month consists of thirty and a half days.

Therefore, according to the measure of the Siddhānta, ninety *ghaṭikās*—derived from the motion of Jupiter and Saturn, and subtracted from the Sun among the three planets—is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

The number five hundred and one for the month-long consumption of Venus is not correct; because, according to the authority of the Siddhāntas, the solar longitude is subtracted from Venus to arrive at Venus [itself], therefore the month-long consumption of Venus is one hundred and thirty-five, and the aggregate of ghaṭīs is likewise for Mercury.

The mass of the fierce fire-consumer (the sun) is unified into a single lump; that becomes the mass of three hundred and sixty *ghaṭikās*. [Note: In manuscript *gha*, the portion beginning from "the principles" (*tattvāni*) up to "in sequence" (*krameṇa*) is absent;
this section is also absent in the Tibetan translation.
In manuscript *gha*, the portion beginning from "thus" (*iti*) up to "three" (*tisraḥ*) is absent.]
This portion does not exist even in the Tibetan translation;
in manuscript G, everything from "eleven" up to "in sequence" is absent,
and this portion does not exist in the Tibetan translation either.
In manuscript Gha, the passage beginning with "of Venus" and ending with "the Moon is one" is missing;
however, in the Tibetan translation, the passage beginning with "of Venus" and ending with "the seasons are six" is missing;
thus, there are ninety ghaṭīs for the three worlds.
In manuscript Gha, the portion from "yuktam" up to "śaśicaraṇavaśāt" in the verse is missing;
according to the Tibetan [translation], there are five [verses].

The monthly motion of these three is one hundred and eighty *ghaṭīs*—that is, the *ghaṭīs* of the days of the year divided by three—according to the statement of Siddhāntakaṭaṅkaṭa as spoken by Mañjuśrī: "In one month, the motion of Jupiter shall be the manifest *ghaṭīs* numbering thirty-four (*rudrapāda*), and the clear *yuga-ghaṭīs* are thirty *pāṇīpala*s; when these are unified, they are called 'days,' and even that tripled is a month and a half with its nights. This is the motion of the six planets, which is a daily debt of days in their respective motions."

"Devotion to the Guru shall be maintained for a month," and so forth—this verse from the *Siddhānta-vṛtti* was stated as a secondary meaning (kaṭākṣārtha) for the sake of removing worldly misconceptions. Regarding this, those [periods] of three fortnights are mentioned in the *Mūla-siddhānta* in connection with the motion of Ketu among the five planets; therefore, they are not to be added to the motions of Jupiter and Saturn. Now, the motion of Ketu is described based on the motion of Rāhu: "In this very month, the portion of the Lord of Wealth (Venus) that has not been traversed by the planets even in its slow motion (manda-karmaṇi) amounts to seventy-three and a half ghaṭikās."

The monthly motion of Rāhu is the position of the Sun and Moon minus half a nāḍī; the three ayanāḍīs of the Sun [are subtracted] on the day of the Moon’s love (the third lunar day), and five nāḍīs for the Moon.
Regarding the phrase "one month" and so forth:

here, in the previous calculation of the slow motion (*mandakārya*), there remains thirty-six and a half months; that very month which has not been traversed by the planets is multiplied by eight. From that, sixty parts are taken, and eight *ghaṭikās* are obtained. Among those, seven and a half *ghaṭikās* constitute Rāhu’s monthly consumption. Thus, within this very measure of a solar month, such is the monthly motion of Rāhu.

Regarding the phrase "the positions of the Sun and the Moon": the three qualities of the Sun—*sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—constitute three steps; the five qualities of the Moon—smell, taste, form, touch, and sound—constitute five steps. These eight steps constitute the seven and a half *ghaṭikās* of Rāhu, while the remaining half-*ghaṭī* is of the nature of being devoid of darkness (*nistama*). Subtracted by that, and further diminished by half a *nāḍī*, there are three *nāḍīs* belonging to Tisya (Loḍa), which consist of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. In the first fortnight of the Sun’s northern course (*ayana*) at the Capricorn transit (*makara-saṃkrānti*), these three *nāḍīs* represent the enjoyment of wealth (*dhana-bhoga*).
Likewise, in the first fortnight of Cancer, they represent the enjoyment of debt (*ṛṇa-paribhoga*).

Regarding the phrase "on the day of the moon and Rāhu" (*śaśimadanadine*): on the first day, in the first quarter, when fourteen parts remain in the *piṇḍasthāna* (the place of the aggregate), or when thirteen remain, there are five *nāḍīs* of the Moon, consisting of five-fold qualities. That half-*nāḍī* not consumed at the time of the seasonal day (*ṛtudina*) is the Moon diminished by a digit; it shall indeed be the excess of the Sun, calculated according to the Yuga-system. That is the day in a solar month. From the movement of Rāhu’s month, multiplied by twenty-four and divided by the monthly movement of a fortnight, the *nāḍīs* of Ketu are obtained at every daily interval from the monthly movement of Rāhu.

Beyond this point, no commentary on the *Sragdharā* section is found, nor is the reason for its omission recorded; as it is not available in the Sanskrit, so too it is not found in the Tibetan translation. Therefore, the commentary for this missing portion was composed by the great Tibetan master Khedrup Je in his own sub-commentary (*Dus 'khor Tik chen*). That may be consulted therein. [End of] the sixty-fold [analysis].

[In this] chapter, regarding the great instruction on the method of knowing the luminaries: when half a nāḍī has not been consumed—that is, when it has not been consumed by Rāhu—at the time of the seasonal day (ṛtudina), which consists of sixty-four days, that is the moon with diminished digits; the meaning is that the digits of the moon have perished.

That [intercalary day] would belong to the Sun; having become two *nāḍīs* for the Sun, it is multiplied by the yugas of each day. According to the rule "multiplied by the lunar days and divided by the Vedas" (*kā ta* etc.), that very day which falls in the middle of the month becomes the intercalary one.
In the solar month, which is the month of the *saṃkrānti*, there is one extra day; that alone should be understood as the middle limb (*madhyamāṅga*).

Regarding the phrase "from the monthly course of Rāhu multiplied by two": from the seasonal course of Rāhu, which is fifteen *ghaṭikās*, one should divide by the fortnightly course and then divide by four minus one-quarter (three and three-quarters). The resulting *nāḍīs* for Ketu are four at every daily time. Furthermore, having multiplied the monthly course of Rāhu by seven and a half *liptās*, it is indeed multiplied by the qualities (nine); thus Ketu moves with the Sun. One should subtract [the correction] when the Sun is ahead, and in its retrograde motion, when behind. In its direct motion, twenty-two and a half *liptās* arise from the Sun's course; such is the intended meaning of the *Karaṇa* according to its essential nature.

That which consists of three and a half multipliers—wherein the Sun’s daily consumption is four *nāḍīs* and twenty-six *pāṇīpala*s—one should subtract this from the Sun’s position when intending to perform the calculation (*karaṇa*). This solar position is established in the Siddhānta as four *ghaṭikās* and twenty *pāṇīpala*s, whereas [the calculation here] adds six *pāṇīpala*s. One should subtract [that amount] from that solar position; the remainder after subtraction becomes the *caraṇa* (foot/motion). Ketu moves together with the Sun: in its fast forward motion (*śīghracāra*), it moves through the *caraṇas* in regular order (*krama*); in its retrograde motion (*vakracāra*), it moves through the *caraṇas* in reverse order (*utkrama*). It moves step by step, moving from one *caraṇa* to the next.
In its movement, the solar orbit travels two *liptās* day by day, either in direct or retrograde order;
over thirty-six months, it travels [one degree] along with the *ghaṭikās*. Multiplied by the lunar days of the world (*lokatithi*), it is multiplied by three and fifteen, resulting in forty-five.

For one and a half months, there is a daily rising of two nāḍīs; indeed, for as long as it lasts—whether in direct motion (*śīghra*) or in retrograde (*vakra*), whether ahead or behind—it is seen rising in the mortal world.
But when it enters the *Śrī Kālacakra* again, it becomes invisible even within its annual course; once its portion of rising is known, its rising is known for infinite time.

For one and a half months, there is a daily rising of two *nāḍīs*. At the conclusion of three years, having abandoned the movement in *liptās*, for three fortnights, there is a daily movement of two *nāḍīs* in the fast motion (*śīghra*) when it is ahead, and likewise in the retrograde motion (*vakrā*) when it is behind; thus its rising lasts for one and a half months. However, for one month it is smokeless (*nidhūma*), and thereafter for the final fortnight it is smoky (*sadhūma*). Thus, the comet (*dhūmaketu*) becomes manifest to sentient beings for one month through its coming and going; with the abandonment of smoke, it appears like a star.

Furthermore, when he enters the three-year period within the Śrī Kālacakra, at the time of that year-period, he becomes invisible once his portion of arising (udayāṃśa) is known; thus, when his portion of Ketu's arising is known, even his arising is known for infinite time— so it is said.
From the end of Rāhu's portion,
at the beginning of the [next] sign-quarter (ga-pāda).
In the case of the intention to speak [of it],
[it is] *ga*.
In the Cakravāra [calendar],
according to the Tibetan tradition,
it is *ga*.
He performed both of those as well.

Now, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the mandalas of the planets are described—the days of the three years of Kālacakra multiplied by twenty-five, diminished by the days of the solstices (*ayana*), and increased by nine: "The days of the year multiplied by five, further struck by five arrows (25), and diminished by the days of the solstice (360), become the mandalas of the planets according to the power of their own motion: for Mars, it is sixty-seven thousand six hundred days; for Mercury, it is eighty-four thousand one hundred days; for Jupiter, it is thirty-four thousand three hundred days; and for Venus, it is twenty-one thousand six hundred days. (80)

"Varṣāhaḥ," and so forth. A "varṣāhaḥ" is one thousand eighty; that very number, multiplied by five—meaning struck or multiplied by five, as indicated by the word "iṣu"—becomes twenty-five times the value of the segment (khaṇḍa). Thus, it becomes twenty-five-fold.

The *ayanāha* (days of the solstice) are one hundred and eighty; [the total] is diminished by that. Due to the movement of the planets through the *ekāyana*, the days of the *ekāyana* become fewer. "Holes" (*randhra*) means nine; the orbs of days for the five planets, mixed with eight and multiplied by thirty-six, arise according to their respective movements. When combined into a single sum, this is two million six thousand eight hundred and twenty-nine. Then, for Mars (*bhauma*), "mountains, snakes, and six" (*śailāhiṣaṭka*) results in a total of six hundred and eighty-seven days.
In the north, for the Naga [Saturn], it is seven thousand eight hundred and ninety-seven (8,797).
For Jupiter (the Teacher of the Gods), it is four thousand three hundred and thirty-two (4,332).
For Venus (Bhārgava), it is two thousand two hundred and forty-seven (2,247).

The number of days for the solar mandala is one hundred and six (366). For the son of the Sun (Saturn), it is sixty-seven; for Mars, it is indeed fifty-one; for Mercury, it is multiplied by a hundred (100);

for Venus, it is diminished by four and eighty (84); for Jupiter, it is zero, sky, ten, and two (2010); and for Mercury, it is joined with zero, two, eight, and seventeen (17820), which constitutes a debt. (81)

O King, for Mars, [the degrees of motion] are nine and a half plus half; for Mercury, twelve; for Jupiter, six; and for Venus, the measure is one hundred and eighty. One should subtract all these from the total elapsed motion.

O Lord of Men, thereafter, through the movement of their respective birth-stars, purification occurs within their own sectors; for those in depression, purification occurs by virtue of their motion, while for those at their exaltation, it occurs within the span of the Sun.
Six times six [is] thirty-six; with the single vowel [a], it becomes one hundred thousand seven hundred and sixty-six, which is the number of days for the mandala of the Sun’s son (Saturn).
"The mountain, the two senses, and so forth for Mars," and so on, as previously stated, extends up to the two verses in the commentary.

Now, the collection of asterisms (*nakṣatra*) is stated for the sake of purifying the birth [horoscope] of the planets: "The monthly consumption, multiplied by six months, is also [to be calculated] in the months of the *Kālacakra* year; the quotient obtained by division shall be subtracted, and even for the Sun and Moon, there is no half-tick (*nāḍī*) that has not been consumed."
[The section on] the six groups of six. [The measurement is] one *śailāmbara* (107).

In the chapter on the Great Instruction on the Method for Knowing Luminosity: That which is greater than the fear of Ketu should be multiplied at every daily interval by the days of the Moon (30), and by the sixty-fold division, it becomes a *nāḍī* at every daily interval during the swift and retrograde risings. (83)

In the Siddhānta, it is established that purity [is attained] after six months for what was eaten during a month; however, this depends on the action [performed] according to the disposition of the being's intention (*sattvāśaya*). Furthermore, when Ketu rises, the station of its motion (*cārapada*) multiplied by twenty-one days results in a mass of one hundred and twelve and a half *liptās*. It should be understood that this very amount accrues daily from the rising of Ketu.
"The half-nāḍī obtained in the place of the stellar debt" is the statement of Mātṛmodaka for the purpose of maturing sentient beings.

Now, the strength of the planets in their motion (*cārabala*) is described: Mercury and Jupiter are powerful in fast motion (*śīghra*); Mars and Ketu are powerful in retrograde motion (*vakrā*); Saturn and Venus are powerful in slow motion (*manda*), according to the influence of their natural qualities; and the remaining [planets] are weak in other motions. In fast motion, they face the east; in retrograde motion, they turn their faces westward; in slow motion, they face south; and upon emerging from it, by the power of their own natural motion, they face north. (84)
"Sauma," and so forth.
Saumya is Mercury; Mantrī is Jupiter; when risen during its swift motion (*śīghracāra*), it becomes powerful and exerts influence in the first half [of the zodiac].
Bhauma (Mars) and Ketu—these two, Bhaumaketū—become powerful when they have traversed half the mandala during their retrograde motion (*vakre*) due to their movement in reverse order.

Mars, Saturn, and Venus are strong in the latter half [of their periods] according to the order of slowness; this is due either to the influence of their inherent qualities (*prakṛti-guṇa*) or the influence of their final quality. Furthermore, in the remaining three movements, Mars and the others are weak.

In swift motion, they face the east; all planets, during their swift course in the first half [of the orbit], face the east. Furthermore, having entered retrograde motion, they face the other direction—the west—and in slow motion, during the second half [of the orbit], they gradually become south-facing.
Due to the influence of their own natural motion, upon emergence, they face north in the second half [of the orbit] by way of reverse order.
This statement is for the purpose of determining the strength of the earth according to the *Svarodaya*.

The positions of the sun and moon are stated: the thirty days of a month multiplied by four [the oceans] equal eighty-four; this is the position of the Moon among the twelve zodiac signs, multiplied by four [the ages] and increased by four [the Vedas].

Within that, the decrease and increase occur respectively in reverse and direct order due to the motion of the solstices, across each half of the circle; O King, the entire calculation should be understood as being counted by eight times four [thirty-two]. (85)

The days of Mars multiplied by thirty-six (360) are those [days] of the ocean-deep (4). Those [days] of the moon multiplied by four are thirty (30). That which belongs to the moon is one hundred and twenty (120), which constitutes the *pada* [of the moon]. This must be stated in what is to be said later regarding the increase of the digits (*kalā*) over the period of seven days for the moon.

For the twelve signs (*rāśi*), when multiplied by four, the *pada* of the sun is eighty-four (84) over the period of six months; that very thing must be stated in what is to be said later. Here, this is the rule for these *padas* by way of summary alone.

In the midst of that, the decrease and increase, by virtue of the movement of the solstices, occur in reverse order (*utkrama*) through each half of the circle; the total count is eight times four, which is forty-eight counts, as should be understood when intending to explain the *karaṇa* system.
O Dhātuguṇa!
From whence [is this] yours?

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, the characteristics of Rāhu’s entry into the lunar disc are now described, beginning with the words "at the junction of the lunar phases" (*parvacchede*) and so forth: "At the junction of the lunar phases, Rāhu enters the lunar disc; the [solar] disc enters the [lunar] disc, and a total eclipse (*sarvagrāsa*) becomes pure by virtue of the moon, consisting of sixty nāḍīs.

When half is pure, there is a partial eclipse (*ardhagrāsa*) by virtue of the moon, lasting as many nāḍīs as there is a junction. The eclipse occurs at the time of day and night for the sun and moon, respectively, during the dark and light fortnights, in the east. (86)

At the end of a world-cycle (*lokadhātu-parvaccheda*), at the conclusion of the full moon, or at the conclusion of the new moon, Rāhu enters the orb of the moon; here, by the word "orb" (*maṇḍala*), sixty *ghaṭikās* are meant, which is the duration of the transit through one lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). That [transit] consists of twelve zodiac signs (*rāśi*) and should be understood as consisting of sixteen digits (*kalā*), according to the extent of the total eclipse; thus, the total eclipse becomes purified. If the lunar transit is completely cleared by the transit of Rāhu, then there is a total eclipse lasting for the full sixty *nāḍikās*.
When half the orbit is pure, there is a "half-bite" (ardhagrāsa); by the power of the moon's movement, the mandala consists of sixty nāḍīs and is composed of sixteen digits of the moon.
Thus, by the power of the moon's movement, as long as a nāḍī remains within Rāhu’s orbit, the conjunction of the planets should be known to last for up to a fourth part of one digit.
This [calculation] of Rāhu’s birth and so forth should be understood in detail according to the Siddhānta for the sake of external knowledge.
In this tantra, Mañjuśrī did not reveal [the details] due to the brevity of the cause;
here, only that which is suitable for internal application has been stated in summary.
Thus, the entire [system], including the planetary conflicts and so forth, is to be understood from the Siddhānta.

In this tantra, there is a dependence upon the Siddhāntas regarding the subject of astrology, such as planetary conjunctions and so forth; however, it is the Lord’s rule that there is no intention to discuss planetary conjunctions within the context of the inner self (*adhyātman*). It is not the case that when an external eclipse occurs, there is an internal grasping of *śukra* (semen); nor is it the rule that from an eclipse of the sun there is an internal grasping of *rajas* (blood). Therefore, it is the Lord’s rule that for the sake of thoroughly understanding the external world, Buddhists must know the Siddhāntas of Brahma, Sūrya, Yama, and Romaka.

Now, the entry of all the planets into the zero-sign at the end of the four ages is described, beginning with "of humans" and so forth: The hundred-year lifespan of humans, when multiplied by the annual motion of the planets, becomes a two-fold value; the portion obtained by dividing by ten (the directions) constitutes a debt which one should subtract from the sign at the top. Indeed, one hundred and twenty-six thousand six hundred and six is the number of years in half a *yuga*; furthermore, by means of two signs, the fixed number of years for the four [ages] arises. (87)

That which is one hundred years for humans is multiplied by the annual motion of the planets according to the Kālacakra system. Thus, the planets' motion over one hundred years occurs in one and a half days; in three days, two hundred years; in thirty days, two thousand years; and in thirty-sixty (360) days, twenty-four thousand years of motion occurs. When that [period] is multiplied by one hundred years and placed in two locations, it is divided by ten. The quotient obtained by the tenth part must be subtracted as a debt from the upper heap.

The remaining one hundred and sixty thousand (160,000) is indeed the measure of the *sragdharā* meter; however, the commentary on the final portion beginning with "the division (*cheda*) is the consumption (*grāsa*)" does not exist either in the Sanskrit or in the Tibetan translation. In manuscript *ga*, there is [mention of] the seal (*mudrā*) and so forth.
In manuscripts *ga* and *gha*, the term "six thousand" (*ṣaḍyutam*) is absent.
In the chapter on the Great Exposition of the Method for Knowing Luminosity (*Jyotirjñānavidhimahoddeśa*): The number of years, which is twenty-one lakhs and six thousand, constitutes the *yugas*.

From the end of half a *yuga*, there are five steps: four steps for the *Kṛta-yuga* and one step for the *Tretā-yuga*. Half a *yuga* consists of the spheres of ether, air, fire, water, and earth; in due order, this is the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*) of the Sustainer. Again, by means of two zodiac signs—that is, once more by the second sign consisting of five steps.

In that regard, there are two quarters for Tretā, two quarters for Dvāpara, and one quarter for Kali, consisting of earth, water, fire, air, and space respectively. Thus, the movement of the Lord’s vital breath (prāṇa) through the right channel consists of five mandalas in successive order.
In this way, by means of the two zodiac signs and the years of the mandalas in both channels, the number of years for the four ages is forty-three hundred and twenty thousand human years.
The two *bhatala* (160) [years] are due to the movement through the circles of the left and right channels (*nāḍī*).

Here, for each of the Yugas, the measure of the Kṛta-yuga is zero, zero, eighteen, and one hundred and seventy-four; in the Tretā, the well-known number of years is zero, zero, nine hundred and sixty.

In the Dvāpara age, the years are correctly [calculated as] zero, zero, sky (0), Vedas (4), tastes (6), and serpents (8); in the Kali age, the number of years shall be zero, space (0), sky (0), eyes (2), qualities (3), and oceans (4). || 88 ||
"Zero, zero, sky, snake, hand, sage, moon"—this is the measure of the Kṛta Yuga in years: seventeen hundred and twenty-eight thousand (1,728,000), due to the enjoyment of the four maṇḍalas.
"Sky, sky, zero, taste, ocean, maker of day"—the number of years for Tretā is well-known as twelve hundred and ninety-six thousand (1,296,000).
"Zero, zero, sky, Vedas, taste, arms"—in Dvāpara, there are correctly eighty-four thousand and six hundred thousand (864,000) years.
"Zero, sky, moon, and ocean" refers to the number of years in the Kali age as four hundred and thirty-two thousand;

thus, the Tretā age consists of three quarters, the Dvāpara of two, and the Kali of one quarter— consisting of three, two, and one mandalas respectively— with each mandala measured by the duration of a year in the Kali age.

By these years, at the end of the Yuga, the movement of the host of planets will come to rest in the void of the zodiac signs; likewise, the asterism beginning with Aśvinī, the Prabhava year, the month of Caitra, the day of the week, the yoga, the lunar day (tithi), and the karana will also be in that state. Furthermore, at that time, there will be a fierce battle between the gods and the dānavas upon the surface of the earth.

"At the end of these years, the movement of the host of planets stands in an empty zodiac sign. Regarding "at the end of these years," this refers to the aforementioned end of the *yuga*, the end of the four ages (*caturyugānta*);
the phrase "the host of planets" and so forth is easily understood.
When the [zodiacal sign] is empty at the end of Revatī,
the first lunar mansion, Aśvinī, and so forth, becomes the further transit of the planets; thus it becomes the Prabhava year, and likewise the month of Caitra and so forth occur accordingly.
At that time, the day was Sunday, the yoga was Viṣkambha, the lunar date was the first day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight, and the karaṇa was Vava; at that time,
nothing was written by the gods, but rather an exposition was commenced.

"Thus it has come down: 'It is certain that in the house of the Teacher, in the city of Vāgadāyā, which is the abode on the surface of the earth for the barbarians (mleccha) who give gifts, a fierce battle will take place. This occurs in the chapter of the *Vimalaprabhā* concerning the world-system (*lokadhātu*).

Then, as it will be the commencement of the Kṛta Yuga, when the lunar days and so forth are now situated entirely at zero in the planetary positions, the production of the constants (*dhruvaka*) is stated again: "Therefore, [the result] multiplied by the asterisms (twenty-seven) shall be divided by sixty *nāḍīs*; the motion [of the planets] occurs through the zodiacal circle, and the fixed [result] is obtained by division. When a full month has passed, there will certainly be a constant again in the units of days, *nāḍīs*, and signs; in the asterism, the solar position becomes the count of days, and one month is subtracted. Even now, in the great city of Baghdad in the land of Iraq,
this verse is not found in the printed editions of the *Kālacakra-tantra-rāja*, nor is it found in the Tibetan translation of its root text; however,
it certainly exists in the *Vimalaprabhā* and its Tibetan translation.
The venerable Tibetan master Kheṅ-sprul-rje accepts this verse as the root text;
therefore, it is also accepted here as the root text.

In his own commentary on the *Vimalaprabhā* titled *Vidyāsāgara* (*Rig pa’i rgya mtsho*), the venerable master Kheṅ-sprul-rje has revealed his own position that this ninety-first verse belongs to the *Mūlakālacakra-tantra* itself.

They have established this: although the Tibetan translator, the venerable Locavā Śoṅ-ton, did not provide a translation for this verse during the course of his translation of the *Mūlakālacakra-tantra*, and thus its translation was not presented in his own Tibetan version, nevertheless, it is clearly evident that his work was of a flawed nature; specifically, the Sanskrit manuscript he obtained for the purpose of translation was itself in such a state—lacking this verse and full of such omissions.

If this were omitted, the number of *kārikās* for the first chapter would be deficient; however, the venerable Kheṅdzubje himself, having observed this verse as part of the root text in Vibhūticandra’s own Sanskrit manuscript, commented upon it.
Having considered all of this, this verse is also accepted here as part of the root text.

In this regard, a certain statement by the venerable Khesa, Ḍuba, and Je is presented; namely: "It is very clear that these verses beginning with *de ni sgyu skar rnams kyis* are the root text (*mūla*). Furthermore, when examining the Indian manuscript of the Tantra in the personal collection of Vibhūticandra, they are present there, and in his manuscript of the commentary as well, there are clear indications that they are treated as the root text. Accordingly, they must certainly be accepted as the root text.

Since the Tibetan translation of the root verses by Di-med lacks the corresponding section, the fact that this [verse] does not appear within the root verses of the *Sron-hgyur* (the "Translated from the Original") version clearly indicates a fault resulting from a translation based on an incorrect manuscript.

This is because this verse exists in its original form within the handwritten manuscript of Vibhūticandra. Therefore, the two verses beginning with "tasmādṛkṣaiḥ" are clearly established as being part of the root verses (*mūlakārikā*), as this verse appears in its original form in the handwritten manuscript of Vibhūticandra.
Since this verse is accepted as a root verse (*mūlakārikā*) even in the manuscript of the *Ṭīkā*, it is certain that this verse is indeed a root verse. [End of] Chapter:

The Great Chapter on the Method for Knowing the Luminaries. Now, the constant values (*dhruvaka*) of the months are stated according to the years of the Kālacakra: The six groups, together with the measure of the sun, multiplied by the qualities (three), are the three years in the Sun; the first, known as "Svādi," consists of the digits of the moon multiplied by three (thirty) and a half-month in the Moon.

The channels beginning with *ha* have three measures; that which is tripled is the three nights of Rāhu. The [channels] beginning with the venerable *Śūnya* and *Anāhata* are also tripled; that is the three ascendants of Rāhu. || 91 ||

"The six groups together with the vowels" means that the six groups—ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, and sa—consisting of thirty consonants, become three hundred and sixty syllables when combined with the twelve vowels, due to the distinction between short and long vowels: a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, aṃ, and aḥ. By these [vowels], each individual letter beginning with *ka* becomes divided into twelve varieties; thus, the thirty consonants, divided by these twelve varieties, become three hundred and sixty.

Furthermore, those [vowels] beginning with *ka* are differentiated by the qualities of others (*paraguṇaiḥ*) through the *yaṇ*-substitutions; indeed, they are multiplied by the *guṇas*. The *guṇas* are: *a, e, ar, o, al, aṃ*; the *vṛddhis* are: *ā, ai, ār, au, āl, āḥ*; and the *yaṇ*-substitutions are: *ha-hā, ya-yā, ra-rā, va-vā, la-lā, haṃ-hā*.
Thus, there are three years, which in the solar reckoning amount to one thousand and eighty days; these consist of the letters beginning with *ka*.

The first fifteen short vowels are called "days" (*dinākhyāḥ*), representing the fifteen digits of the moon multiplied by three (*triguṇaśaśikalāḥ*). Together with the distinctions of short, long, and protracted (*hrasva-dīrgha-pluta*) vowels, this constitutes the period of one and a half fortnights (*sārddhamā tripakṣam*) in the lunar cycle.

Therein, the vowels of the three fortnights (*tripakṣasvara*)—namely *a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ; a, e, ar, al, ha, ya, va, ra, la; lā, vā, rā, yā, hā; āl, ū, ār, ai, ā; lū, ū, ṛ, ī, ā; āṃ, ī, ṝ, oṃ, āṃ, aiṃ, ā; au, ālaṃ, hāṃ, yāṃ, rāṃ, vāṃ, lāṃ*—become the channels (*nāḍī*) beginning with *hā*, numbering sixty according to the division of the twelve zodiac signs (*dvādaśalagna*). By the previously mentioned method, the short vowels [correspond] from midday until midnight; the long vowels [correspond] from midnight until midday, numbering thirty.

The five [deities] beginning with Śrī, Śūnyā, and Anāhatā, through the divisions of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and by way of the natures of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, are joined with the three junctions (*trilagna*) of Rāhu and the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*); this is the rule. O King, the elements numbering the sun and moon (twelve), having again abandoned one month and three fortnights, indeed become one and a half months as determined by the best of sages; the Kālacakra is thus divided.
The day of the week (*mākṣepaka-vāra*) consists of two units of sixty, each doubled by the number of kings (sixteen); below that, the wheel of days is divided and fixed by sixty deities.

If this verse were not a root verse (*mūlakārikā*), then the root verses would be incomplete; therefore, it is understood that the non-inclusion of this verse in the root text translated by the great scholar Śoṅ-ston Lo-tsā-ba is a deficiency, and that he performed his work of translation based upon an incomplete manuscript. In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is not stated in the book that the number of the elements of the world-system (*lokadhātu*) is [the same as] the sun and moon; furthermore, when divided by three years and three fortnights, they become one thousand one hundred and twenty-five. [This is because] "Indu" (moon) refers to a king, which signifies a half-month and three fortnights.
Having subtracted one and a half months, and then having subtracted another one and a half months, there remain one thousand eighty.

This is then divided by the seven excellent sages; the quotient obtained is the *laghu-kālacakra*, consisting of one hundred fifty-four units. Of the remainder from this division, two units remain within the mandala, representing wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*). That same [value] is the constant for the month (*māsadhruvaka*); having added thirty-two *ghaṭikā*s as a pair of aggregates, there is one lunar day (*tithi*) and five movement-steps (*cārapada*).

In the *Kālacakra*, within the one hundred and fifty-six [day-cycles], the day (*vāra*) is divided by sixty deities, meaning by sixty *ghaṭikās*. And thirty-two *nāḍīs* are for the deities who are eight times the number of sages (*munis*). Two *piṇḍakas* are to be added and subtracted; the first lunar station (*śaśipada*) is five, and here there are six. For the moon, three fortnights multiplied by three would be the days; this is well known in the solar calculation (*sūryabhoga*). And two [units] divided by sixty on the first day of the sun are the *nāḍīs* of Rudra together with their conjunctions (*sabhogas*). || 93 ||

With thirty-two *devatīs* (deities) for each *ghaṭikā*, the monthly constant (*māsadhruvaka*) is placed in the position of the *ghaṭikās*. The two *piṇḍas* (piles) become fifty-six by the *devatīs*; they are to be added and subtracted in the place of the *piṇḍas*, and thus there is one *devatī*. There are five *devatīs* which constitute five steps (*padāni*), and with one together with five, it becomes six.

Thus, the three fortnights of the Moon amount to forty-five days, and when tripled, it also consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; this is well known in the solar calculation (*sūryabhoga*).
And by dividing [the total] by two hundred and sixty, there are two nakṣatra-constants (*dhruvaka*) in one hundred and twenty *nāḍīs*.
On the first day of the Sun, when multiplied by four, eleven *nāḍīs*—that is, eleven *nāḍīs* plus four *ghaṭikās* and so forth—occur in the place of the *nāḍīs*; this is the rule everywhere.
This Śrī Kālacakra, together with the host of planets, is non-different from the external bodies; in the abode of the three worlds, it is the Sun in the form of Time.

[He is] the cause of withdrawal and expansion through the various divisions of wisdom and means, by means of equal and unequal families, swift and retrograde movements, and by the families of the supreme sages who are free from passion, as well as the gods such as Brahmā and Rudra. ||94||

This Śrī Kālacakra, together with the host of planets and so forth, according to the sequence stated [in the text], is non-different from the external and the body, being the cause of withdrawal and expansion. Within that abode, which consists of the three worlds—desire, form, and formlessness—it exists in the form of Time (*kāla*) and in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Regarding the "one thousand and ten days" of the sun, the noble Tibetan master Khedrup Je has established this very calculation of time in his own Tibetan commentary, following the practical application.

[In this] chapter, the "Great Summary on the Rules for the Method of the Instrument of the Arising of the Vowels" is an address to Mañjuśrī: "O Sūryaratha! [This was taught] through the divisions of wisdom and means related to the *Laghutantra*, by means of the divisions of day and night, the distinctions of the moon and sun, and so forth; and by means of even and uneven lineages. 'Even' refers to the long vowels and 'uneven' to the short vowels. It has not been understood by the passionless ones (*vītarāga*), nor by the supreme families of sages such as Brahmā, Rudra, and other gods, due to their movements being swift, retrograde, and so on."

Thus, by the previously mentioned method, this Bhagavān Kālacakra—who is established in the form of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), who is all-pervasive within all things pervaded, whether stationary or moving—was not known by these [beings] beginning with Brahmā. However, just as it was known by the Bhagavān Samyaksambuddha, the Omniscient One, in both worldly and supramundane forms of conventionality and ultimate reality (*vivṛti*), so too has it been revealed to Sucandra Vajrapāṇi; and by me, Sūryaratha, that very same Bhagavān Kālacakra has been briefly revealed, just as it was [revealed] by Mañjuśrī Yaśonarendra.

Thus ends the ninth great chapter on the method of the knowledge of astrology in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja*, consisting of twelve thousand verses, which follows the glorious *Mūlatantra*. 9.

(10) The Great Chapter on the Rules for the Instrument of the Arising of Vowels (*Svarodayayantra*). Now, the arising of vowels (*svarodaya*) is explained: The first five vowels, by virtue of the first lunar day (*tithi*), produce [their] rising at the end of the conjunction beginning with the "five joys" (*pañcananda*), O King, provided that Tuesday (*bhauma*) and the other days of the week do not occur there.
If, however, an unfavorable rising occurs on a Tuesday, and furthermore, it coincides with the conjunction of Kṛttikā, then for men there will be battle, disease, or death due to the first vowel.
"Ādi" and so forth:

those vowels of which "a" is the first are the five initial ones—*a, i, u, ṛ, lṛ*. This is because of the inclusion of the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated terms) as stated by Svayambhū in the *Śivasūtra*: "aiuṇ; ṛlṛk" (Śi0 Sū0 1–2), and from the recitation [of the subsequent rules]:
"e o (ṅ); [ai au]c" (Śi0 Sū0 3–4), the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*) are included. [This concludes] the ninth chapter, the Great Summary on the Method for Knowing Astrology, in the *Kāyā*.

The rule *iko yaṇ aci* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.77) is established because of the production of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* vowels such as *ai*, *au*, and *ṇ*; this is due to the specific exception provided by that rule, and also because of the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) found in the rule *ako 'ki dīrghaḥ* (Cāndra-vyākaraṇa 5.1.106; which can be more simply stated as *ako 'ki*—Siddhāntakaumudī—and corresponds to the sūtra *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* 6.1.101).

Those which are the five vowels at the beginning were prophesied by the Self-Arisen One (*svayambhū*). Being of identical form, they were written down by Mañjuśrī in his own prophecy according to their respective order, through the power of the primordial natures (*prakṛti*) such as space and so forth: *aiuṇ*, *ṛ*, and *ḷ*—having the natures of space, wind, fire, water, and earth respectively. Likewise, *a e ara o ala*, and *ha ya ra va la ṭa* were indicated by Mañjuśrī through the application of *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and *yaṇ* substitutions, by relying on the inherent nature of each respective primordial element.

"Those five vowels [are determined] by the power of the first lunar day (*tithi*). Thus, there are five initial lunar days: the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*), distinguished by the divisions of darkness. By virtue of those—that is, by the power of the first lunar day—there are the five yogas beginning with *Nanda* for the [five] vowels. For the five vowels, *Nanda* is the first lunar day, *Bhadrā* the second, *Jayā* the third, *Riktā* the fourth, and *Pūrṇā* the fifth. In this manner, it is likewise for the sixth and so forth, as well as the eleventh and so forth.

In this [system], regarding the conjunctions beginning with Nandā: if, at the end of the rising [of a lunar day], the weekday is not Mars and so forth—meaning, if on Nandā it is Mars, on Bhadrā it is Mercury, on Jayā it is Jupiter, on Riktā it is Venus, and on Pūrṇā it is Saturn—then when the weekday is not Mars and so forth in the case of Nandā and the others, that [conjunction] is "risen"; otherwise, there is an "unfortunate rising. O King, if there is an unfortunate rising on a Tuesday, and it occurs again on Nandā while being in conjunction with Kṛttikā, then if war or disease occurs on the lunar day Nandā, death will come to men—the meaning is "of the first vowel," i.e., of that man or woman whose name begins with the letter 'A' and so forth.

[In this chapter on the Great Chapter on the Rules for the Method of the Yantras of Svarodaya: On the second day of the bright fortnight, if there is a conjunction with Maghā on this day, the king dies; this is the first. If on the day of Jayā there is a conjunction with Āśleṣā and Jupiter occurs, he goes to death; this is the second. If on the Riktā lunar day there is Dhaniṣṭhā and Venus occurs, he goes to death; this is the third. If on the Pūrṇā lunar day there is Bharaṇī together with Saturn, the fifth one goes to death. || 96 ||

Thus, if the Maghā asterism occurs on a Saumya (Wednesday) during the Bhadrā tithi, then one whose name contains the second vowel *i* will die; likewise, if Aśleṣā occurs on a Bṛhaspati (Thursday) during the Jayā tithi, then one whose name contains the third vowel *ṛ* will die; similarly, if Dhaniṣṭhā occurs on a Śukra (Friday) during the Riktā tithi, then one whose name contains the fourth vowel *u* will die; and likewise, if Bharaṇī occurs on a Śani (Saturday) during the Pūrṇā tithi, then one whose name contains the fifth vowel *lṛ*—

Thus, even for those who are joyful, death occurs by the power of the asterisms and days of the week; in the case of the Sun, there is a conjunction with death for those born under the *Nandodayas*, and there will also be wounds and affliction for the sick. Under the Moon, the *Bhadrodayas* prevail, which certainly brings results in battle and likewise in illness. It is true that the *Pañcodayas* yield abundant fruit when free from the yoga of death; this should be understood regarding journeys to foreign lands and marriages. (97)

In the conflict of disease as well, there is likewise inauspicious or auspicious fruit; thus, on Sunday, for those born under the *Nanda* [lunar days], a wound occurs in battle, and for the sick, suffering arises. On Monday, this should be understood to apply to those born under the *Bhadra* [lunar days]. This is true for the five *udayas* (the vowels *ā*, etc.), which yield great fruit when they arise on their respective lunar days, provided they are free from the conjunctions of death (*mṛtyuyoga*). That very thing must be known by the practitioner of occasional rites (*naimittika*) regarding the inauspicious or auspicious fruit in disease and battle, as well as during journeys to foreign lands and at the time of marriage. Thus, within a fortnight, the constellations, weekdays, and the groups of vowels (*svaragaṇa*) and lunar days are distinguished by the divisions of the five elements.
The rising [of the signs] occurs here in a month, a half-year, or a year, and also in the sixty-year cycle beginning with Caitra;

the rising occurs here by means of the twelve limbs. That same division of fortnights constitutes the rising of the seventy-two [years] and so forth; in the division of months, it is the rising of the vowels.

Herein, the rising of *a* and the other vowels begins with Caitra and so forth: in each pair of months starting from Caitra there are sixty days, and within those, the vowels beginning with *a* arise sequentially in groups of twelve days each. From the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*) of Caitra until the first day of the bright fortnight of the second month, there are thus six cycles of the five vowels (*pañca-svara*) per season within a year.

Regarding the arising of the fortnights (*pakṣa*), there is a division of the fortnights every twelve days; in this manner, among the three hundred and sixty days of the year, the sequential arising of the seventy-two [vowels] beginning with *a* is to be understood.

This very [cycle] is the division of months beginning with Caitra and the first day of the bright fortnight; likewise, among the sixty years beginning with Prabhava, the five vowels arise in their respective order for each year. By six months, the movement of the limbs of the solstice occurs, and by twelve years, the completion of a cycle of the years takes place. Thus, the rising and setting of the five vowels occurs here repeatedly. In the first [year], the vowels are "children" (bāla) according to the power of their own lunar days; in the second, they are "youths" (prauḍha); in the third, they are "mature" (vṛddha) in sequence; and on the day of the fire-ocean (43rd year), in the fifth [cycle], they have set. || 99 ||

The rising occurs over six months with twenty-four revolutions; furthermore, according to the manner of the previous rule, there is the rising of the solstices (*ayana*), and the rising of the twelve years beginning with *Prabhava*. In this way, the rising of the years (*varṣa*)—consisting of the revolutions, *Prabhava*, and so forth—is to be understood. Thus, the rising of the five vowels occurs here, and they set again in the same manner. Regarding the division of the fortnights (*pakṣa*), the *Nandā* [tithis] last for twelve days, and likewise the *Bhadrā* and others. Regarding the division of the months, the *Nandā* lasts for seventy-two days, and likewise the *Bhadrā* and others. Regarding the division of the solstices (*ayana*), the *Nandā* lasts for one solstice, and likewise the *Bhadrā* and others.
In the division of the years, the twelve-year cycle proceeds through Nandā and the others in this manner.

At the beginning, the vowels are the "children" (*bālāḥ*); by virtue of their own lunar dates (*tithi*) and their qualities, and by virtue of the qualities of space, wind, fire, water, and earth—and by virtue of the qualities of sound, touch, taste, form, and smell—they correspond respectively.
Here, in *Nandā*, there is the arising of the vowel *a*; in *Bhadrā*, the vowel *i*; in *Jayā*, the vowel *ṛ*; in *Riktā*, the vowel *u*; and in *Pūrṇā*, the vowel *lṛ*.

Thus, on the second day from each respective day of their own arising, the venerable Kumāras are as follows: the letter *i* in Bhadrā, the letter *i* in Jayā, the letter *ṛ* in Riktā, the letter *u* in Pūrṇā, and the letter *lṛ* in Nandā. Regarding the "mature" (*prauḍha*) and "old" (*vṛddha*) [syllables], they occur respectively on the third day from their own day—namely, on the "fire" (third) day—the mature ones are as follows: the letter *a* in Jayā, the letter *i* in Riktā, the letter *ṛ* in Pūrṇā, the letter *u* in Nandā, and the letter *l* in Bhadrā.

This is the Great Chapter on the Rules for the Method of the Svarodaya Instrument: In the *riktā* tithi, the vowel *a* is "old" (*vṛddha*); in the *pūrṇā*, the vowel *i*; in the *nandā*, the vowel *ṛ*; in the *bhadrā*, the vowel *u*; and in the *jayā*, the vowel *ḷ*. Thus, they are set at rest (*astaṅgata*) in the fifth [tithi]. That is to say, in the *pūrṇā* the vowel *a* is set at rest; in the *nandā*, the vowel *i*; in the *bhadrā*, the vowel *ṛ*; in the *jayā*, the vowel *u*; and in the *riktā*, the vowel *ḷ*. In this way, the fivefold distinction of the arising (*udaya*) and so forth of the vowels is to be understood.

The first five vowels, when multiplied by the qualities (*guṇa*), become thirty in two ways; they are all to be joined with the letters of the consonant groups beginning with *ka*, according to the influence of the qualities of nature (*prakṛti*).

Here, the rising of the short vowels occurs during the bright fortnight through the division of the five elements, while that of the long vowels occurs during the dark fortnight, fixed by the yoga of emanation and withdrawal. 100.
The five original vowels, when multiplied by the qualities—namely, by the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas—become fifteen.

These are the thirty-fold *pūrṇā* vowels: *a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ, e, ai, o, au, aṃ, aḥ*; and *ha, ya, ra, va, la*, which are the threefold *nandā* and others in the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*). Likewise, in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), there are the *nandā* and others: *lā, vā, rā, yā, hā; ā, lā, au, ā, ra, ai, ā, ḷ, ū, ṛ, ī, ā*. Thus, for the thirty lunar days (*tithis*) of both fortnights, they are to be joined respectively among the consonant groups beginning with *ka* according to the influence of the qualities of nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*). All those vowels—short ones in the bright fortnight and long ones in the dark—are to be applied through the divisions of the five elements (*pañcatattva*).

In this context, regarding the consonants, those pronounced with a short vowel arise during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*); for long vowels, they arise during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). Thus, for a long consonant pronounced with a long vowel, its arising occurs in the dark fortnight.
Here, concerning the consonants, the solar transits (*sūryasaṃkrānti*) should be understood as the fortnights, due to the yoga of emanation and withdrawal (*sṛṣṭisaṃhāra*).

The twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the clear arrows (*sphuṭaśara*) in *ghaṭikās*, and the nine degrees (*navāṃśa*) of the solar ascendant (*sūryalagna*)—these possess three natures: stable (*sthira*), mobile (*cala*), and perfectly equal (*susama*), such as the ascendant of Aries (*meṣalagna*) and so forth.
Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn are the movable signs here; the others are fixed, and the remaining ones are dual-natured; they always rise during the periods of day and night. (101)

There are twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), which constitute the aggregate of the twenty-seven constellations. Among them, with two and a quarter lunar mansions each, there are twelve solar signs (*lagna*).

These are the "clear arrows" (*sphuṭa-śara*), consisting of five *ghaṭikās* each; these are the nine divisions (*navāṃśas*). Furthermore, these are of three natures: the vowels [corresponding to] Aries and so forth are movable (*cala*); Taurus and so forth are fixed (*sthira*); and Gemini and so forth, being dual-natured, are common (*sama*).

Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn are the four movable signs; Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius are the fixed signs; Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces are the dual-natured signs—thus they are. *Vimalaprabhā* [on the World System].

In this regard, at the time of inquiry, with the *caras* (movable signs), the task is swift; "the task" is thus always declared [to be so]. With the *sthiras* (fixed signs), it is stable for twelve [hours] day and night; with the *dvisvabhāvas* (dual-natured signs), it is middling.
Within that period of a day, there are thirty *muhūrttas*, and even sixty *nāḍikās*. Here, at the beginning, the rising of the twenty vowels occurs in every single *muhūrta*.

A ghaṭikā consists of thirty varga-syllables; through the division of short and long vowels, their rising and setting within the lunar day (tithi) and in the center of the moon have thus been declared. || 102 ||

In that [group], there are also thirty *muhūrtas*; in that collection of *lagnas*, even within the time of a day consisting of eight watches (*praharas*), there are thirty *muhūrtas*, and thus sixty *nāḍikās* (ghaṭīs) occur.
Here, at the beginning, in the first *muhūrta*, the rising of the twenty vowels indeed occurs in every *muhūrta*.

Regarding the phrase "in the lunar portion within the moon": having divided a single lunar day (*tithi*) into thirty *muhūrta* segments, one assigns the vowels to each *muhūrta* segment as follows: on the first lunar day (*pratipad*), the vowels beginning with *a*; on the second, those beginning with *i*; on the third, those beginning with *ṛ*; on the fourth, those beginning with *u*; on the fifth, those beginning with *ṝ*; on the sixth, those beginning with *lṛ*; on the seventh, those beginning with *e*; on the eighth, those beginning with *ai*; on the ninth, those beginning with *o*; on the tenth, those beginning with *au*; on the eleventh, those beginning with *ha*; on the twelfth, those beginning with *ya*; on the thirteenth, those beginning with *ra*; on the fourteenth, those beginning with *va*; and on the full moon (*pūrṇā*), those beginning with *la*. Thus, during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), the thirty vowels arise on each individual lunar day according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*). Thereafter, during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), on the first lunar day, the day of Nandā, the thirty vowels arise according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*). In that regard, on the first day, [the vowels] beginning with *la* (i.e., *lā*, etc.); on the second, those beginning with *va* (i.e., *vā*, etc.). In this manner, it applies to all the days.

The rising and setting [of the vowels] are indeed declared to occur within the moon during the lunar day (tithi) portion; therefore, the vowel that has risen on the first day of the bright fortnight (śukla-pratipad) and so forth has set on the first day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa-pratipad) and so forth. The sequence of the five vowels beginning with *a* is: space, wind, fire, water, and earth. Their respective presiding deities are Rāhu, Agni, Indu (the Moon), Kaṃsa (Brahmā), and Soma; and Venus, Jupiter, the weak one (Mercury), and Saturn.

In each of the previously mentioned single ascendants, the number of nāḍīs must be calculated according to the duration of the night or day; whichever vowel occurs therein becomes the planet, and it is by that [vowel] as the powerful one in the mandala that the calculation is to be performed. || 103 ||

Space, wind, fire, water, and earth are the families of the five primordial vowels (*ādi-pañcasvara*) according to the previously mentioned sequence; thus, for *ā* and the other vowels beginning with *ā*, their respective families are space and so forth.

The presiding deities are the planets, Rāhu and the rest, corresponding respectively to the short and long vowels: Rāhu and Kālāgni are the deities of the short and long *a*; Candra and Ravi are the deities of the short and long *i*; Budha and Bhauma are the deities of the short and long *ṛ*; Śukra and Guru are the deities of the short and long *u*; and Ketu and Mandu are the deities of the short and long *l*. [This applies also] to the *guṇa*-vowels beginning with *ā* (*guṇākārādīnām*).

(Regarding the vowels beginning with *vā* etc. [End of page 172] In this chapter on the Great Exposition of the Rules for the Method of the Svarodaya Instrument: here, according to the proper rule, the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*) are as follows.

Thus, in each of the twelve ascendants (*lagna*), one must calculate the *nāḍikā* therein by virtue of night and day; at the rising of the current ascendant, there are five months (or degrees). Among those, whichever vowel has occurred is the "planet" (*graha*); it is powerful, and by means of it the mandala is to be calculated. The sequence beginning with *śūnya* and beginning with *pṛthivī* is to be calculated according to the distinction between odd and even ascendants.

In this system, the arising of the short vowels occurs on the left, and that of the others on the right. On the left is the principle (tattva) beginning with space, along with the entire group of planets including Rāhu as their leader;

in the center is the principle beginning with earth. The rule for the group of planets is by means of the son of the Sun (Saturn) and the rest. Alternatively, externally, the time-artery (kālanāḍī), which is equal to the abode of the planets, should be calculated together with the vowels.

In the left [channel] there is the arising of the short vowels; here, in the left, during the odd *lagnas*, there is the arising of the consonants of the short vowels, while in the right, during the even *lagnas*, there is the arising of the others, the consonants pronounced as long. Thus, in the left, the principle of emptiness (*śūnya*) and so forth—the five mandalas alternating one by one, the movement of the host of planets beginning with Rāhu—meaning the entire group starting with Rāhu, Rāhu, the Moon, and the consonants beginning with *ka* pronounced by means of the vowels beginning with *ā*, arise in due order within the five mandalas at Capricorn (*makara*).

In this manner, within the jar (kumbha) and the five mandalas beginning with space (ākāśa), the consonants starting with *ṅa* pronounced with the short vowels are to be understood in reverse order (*viloma*).
Therein, *ṅa* arises in the first *ghaṭikā* in the space mandala; *gha* in the second; *ga* in the third; *kha* in the fourth; and *ka* in the fifth, in the earth mandala.
Likewise, *cā-chā-jā-jhā-trā* [arise] in Pisces (*mīna*); *ña-jha-ja-cha-ca* in Aries (*meṣa*); thus it is in the five mandalas.
Likewise, in the five mandalas of Taurus are *ṭā*, *ṭhā*, *ḍā*, *ḍhā*, and *ṇā*; in the five mandalas of Gemini are *ṇa*, *ḍha*, *ḍa*, *ṭha*, and *ṭa*.
Similarly, in Cancer are *pā*, *phā*, *bā*, *bhā*, and *mā*; in Leo are *ma*, *bha*, *ba*, *pha*, and *pa*, each in their five mandalas.
Likewise, in Virgo are *tā*, *thā*, *dā*, *dhā*, and *nā*; in Libra are *na*, *dha*, *da*, *tha*, and *ta*, each in their five mandalas.
Thus, in the [five] mandalas of Śaka (ha) in Scorpio, Ka (ha) in Sagittarius, and so on,
these are the consonants as presiding deities during the rising of the ghaṭikās.
Therein, the vowel uttered with a consonant becomes the phoneme-vowel (*varṇasvara*), while the vowel becomes the life-force-vowel (*jīvasvara*).

And that *jīva* (vitality) sound should be understood through its short and long distinctions within the lunar division (*candrāṃśa*), as well as through the divisions of the *muhūrta*, according to what was previously stated.

The emergence of the consonant (*vyañjana*) should be known through the divisions of the *ghaṭikās* of the ascendant (*lagna*). In this context, when the *jīva* (vitality) sound has set, death occurs; when the phoneme-sound (*varṇasvara*) has set, a wound occurs. For those who are ill, there is death or suffering. Nevertheless, in this case, there is no consonant in the first letter of the name; therein, the sound itself is the *jīva*. This is the doubt.
O sir, there is no [separate] vowel; rather, the other is the "vowel of the consonant" (*varṇasvara*).
In this way, within the self, the arising of the consonants is to be understood through the distinction of the flow in the mandalas of the left and right nostrils.

Or, "external time-channel" (*bāhya-kālanāḍī*) refers to the channel that has arisen at that specific moment; it is equal to the external planetary houses (*bāhyagrahabhavana*), which is the mandala of the planetary houses. It should be practiced with its vowels and consonants for the sake of thoroughly knowing the auspicious and inauspicious.

Now, the results of the auspicious and inauspicious from the inquiry are stated, beginning with the word "inquiry" (*praśna*): "In an inquiry, death prevails during the time of battle when the wind [element] has arisen in the 'void' (*kāla-śūnya*), or when the sun [has arisen]; there will also be defeat and even wounds when fire and Mars arise."

If Jupiter is in the *saṃdhi* water [sign], there will be no battle; if it is in the rising of earth or mandas, there is death. There will be suffering, wounds, and even happiness, as well as equanimity for the querent who is ill.

When a question is asked at the time of battle, death prevails if the [planets] Kāla, Śūnya, or Agni have arisen; and if one first utters the name of that person for the sake of the battle, and the right channel (dakṣiṇanāḍī) has arisen in the mandalas of Kāla, Agni, or Śūnya, then for that king or man, death occurs with certainty. Likewise, if Vāyu has arisen in the Vāyu-maṇḍala, there is defeat; if Bhauma or Vahni have arisen in their mandalas, there is even a wound; if Guru has arisen in the Toya-maṇḍala, there is a fracture; and if Mandocca has arisen in the Bhūmi-maṇḍala, there is no battle at all in the conflict—such is the rule regarding questions.

Thus, when a questioner asks whether for a sick person there will be death, affliction, a wound, happiness, or equilibrium in the empty mandala and so forth respectively, it occurs for the patients as follows: when Rāhu and the Sun rise in the Air (Vāyu) sign and the Moon is present, there is certain destruction of enemies in battle; however, there is defeat and even wounds in combat when the gentle planets and Fire (Agni) rise, and Venus is in Water (Jala). Likewise, in journeys and marriages, there is great fruit when Earth and Ketu rise on the left path (vāmamārga) along with the planets.

"In battle, there is the destruction of enemies": here, the phrase "destruction of enemies in battle" mentioned first is certain to occur when Rāhu rises in the void-maṇḍala (*śūnya-maṇḍala*) in the left nostril; the word *ca* ("and") is for the purpose of completing the meter. When Vāyu rises in the wind-maṇḍala (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), there is loss (*bhaga*). There is also a wound, O gentle one, when Saumya rises, in the case of a question concerning the extraction of an enemy (*satrōddhṛta-praśne*).
When Venus rises in the circle of water, there is gain of wealth;

even an enemy becomes submissive. When Mars (Bhūmikeṭu) rises, there is success in matters of battle. Likewise, in travel and marriage, there is great fruit when the planets are on the left-hand path. This is the rule for the rising of the *nāśika* at the time of a query, provided that the question is asked [when the planets are] thus situated.

The Great Chapter on the Rules for the Method of the Instrument of the Arising of Vowels (*Svarodayayantra*). Now, the inquiry regarding vowels is stated, beginning with "by the messenger" and so forth: The vowels indeed uttered by the messenger are multiplied by ten and mixed with the zodiacal circle (*rāśicakra*); they are further multiplied by five, added to the number of nearby people, and reduced by the remainder of division by seven.

If the moon [vowel] falls upon fire [3], arrow [5], or mountain [7]—that is, in an odd position—there is no success for men. If it falls upon eye [2], Veda [4], or taste [6]—that is, in an even position—there shall be success in the undertaking.

The vowels spoken by the messenger, when multiplied by ten— that is, multiplied by the [ten] mandalas of the left and right— and further mixed with twelve by means of the zodiacal wheel (*rāśicakra*), and again struck by the elements— that is, multiplied by five— when added to the "nearby person" (*nikaṭajana*)— meaning added to the person standing nearby, excluding the omen (*naimittika*)— the remainder after division by seven is the "remainder of the day's usage" (*vārabhogāvaśeṣa*). When the Moon stands upon one day, on the third day which is Fire, on the fifth day which is Arrow, or on the seventh day which is Aḍau (Drau), if such a remainder remains, there is no success for men.
Success in one's undertaking occurs when the Sun is on the first day, Mars on the second, Jupiter on the third, Saturn on the fifth, the Moon on the seventh, and Venus on the eleventh;

provided that Mercury and the remaining [planets] are situated in even lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and the Moon has entered an even sign (*rāśi*). This is the rule for inquiries regarding vowels (*svara-praśna-niyama*). Now, the specific distinctions for the year and so forth are stated, beginning with the word "year": The years, months, fortnights, days, nights, and times enter into the ascendant (*lagna*); the single ascendant, together with the host of planets, possesses the vowels and is divided according to the principles (*tattva*) by means of fivefold distinctions.

In reality, there exists one hundred and sixty breaths within the time-measure of a *nāḍī*. A *nāḍī* consists of sixty *liptās*, and its subdivisions are as follows: six breaths constitute a year; sixty such years constitute a [great] year (*saṃvatsara*); twelve [years] constitute a month; twenty-four [months] constitute a fortnight (*pakṣa*); day and night constitute a full day-and-night (*ahorātra*); and eight [day-and-nights] constitute a watch (*prahara*). These enter into the midst of the twelve zodiacal signs (*lagna*);
among them, for the sake of determining auspicious and inauspicious results, they enter into the midst of the ascendant and set within the ascendant.

For these [planets], there is no power other than that of the ascendant; thus, the single ascendant, together with the host of planets, becomes differentiated by its own sounds and divided into twenty-five principles (*tattvas*) according to the previously stated method.

One principle consists of six breaths (*śvāsa*), which, multiplied by more than a hundred—namely three hundred—exists within the time-measure (*kālanāḍī*) and the mandala-measure (*maṇḍalanāḍī*). The "parts of the sound" (*nādyaṃśāḥ*) are sixty seconds (*liptā*); the "subdivision" (*avayava*) refers to the seconds, and the "subdivision" here means a group of six breaths.

Now, the inauspicious and auspicious results within inhalation and exhalation are described: "The inauspicious and auspicious results within inhalation and exhalation are known by astrologers engaged in yoga, after they have purified the Sun and Moon in the temporal *nāḍīs* according to the elapsed days. [From the Vimalaprabhā, Lokadhātu-paṭala] ga. varttate; ga. gha. nādyaṃsāḥ. In the midst of exhalation (*niḥśvāsa*) and inhalation (*ucchvāsa*), the fruit of the inauspicious and auspicious is known by those practitioners of yoga who are skilled in astrology, having calculated it through the temporal channels (*kālanāḍī*) based on the number of days that have passed. The Sun and Moon are thus purified.

In this world, he who speaks of the fruit of the inauspicious and auspicious even when the present is known is like a blind man who, having grasped his object, enters a dense forest infested with elephants and lions. ||109||

Between exhalation (*niḥśvāsa*) and inhalation (*ucchvāsa*), there is respectively an inauspicious and a auspicious result. When the breath has gone out from the navel to the nostril at the time of questioning, an inauspicious result occurs; when it has entered from the outside into the navel and the nostril at the time of questioning, an auspicious result occurs. This alone is known through the application of yoga and not by others. Furthermore, by astrologers (*daivajña-jyotiṣibhiḥ*), it is known through the "time-pulse" (*kālanāḍī*) after calculating according to the elapsed days, having purified the sun and moon, and having purified the left and right mandala-pulses of the odd and even signs (*viṣama-samalagna*).

When the aforementioned present time is not known, he who speaks here in this world of the results of the inauspicious and auspicious—even if blind, having grasped his purpose, he enters the dense forest teeming with elephants and lions. This concludes the determination of the fruits of the auspicious and inauspicious. Now, the *lagna-yoga* is stated, beginning with "when not known": when the subtle yoga (*sūkṣmayoga*) is not known, the *lagna-yoga* endowed with planetary strength is bestowed. *Kālāgni* [is given] from the Sun and Mars in the seventh house from Saturn.
Death, disease, wounds, and indeed the total destruction of all wealth occur in that [lagna]; therefore, it must clearly be avoided according to my words, and another lagna should be assigned. 110.

When the previously mentioned subtle yoga of inhalation and exhalation is not known, and the subtle yoga is not understood, the planetary strength (*graha-bala*) is applied according to worldly convention through the junction of the ascendant (*lagna-yoga*). If Kālāgni is in the seventh house from the rising ascendant (*udaya-lagna*), then for one seeking auspicious results, death occurs. If the Sun is there, illness occurs; if Mars is there, a wound occurs; if Saturn (*śanaiścara*) is there, loss of wealth occurs.

Thus, since all these things occur when the planets are in the rising sign (*udayalagna*), the birth sign (*janmalagna*), or the seventh house, that [ascendant] must clearly be avoided by the counselor; according to the words of the *Samama*, another ascendant should be assigned. This is between the inhalation (*ga-śvāsa*) and the exhalation (*ga-niḥśvāsa*).

Furthermore, if all the lords of the ascendants are present in the twelfth houses accompanied by benefic planets, it results in auspiciousness.

If, moreover, the left channel (vāmanāḍī) occurs within one's own body, there will certainly be the accomplishment of all goals on the surface of the entire earth. Here, "pure days" (śuddhavāra) refers to: the Sun with the asterism Hasta; Jupiter with Puṣya; Mercury with Anurādhā; Saturn with Rohiṇī; the Moon with Śravaṇa; Mars with Aśvinī; and Venus with Revatī—these are the *siddhi-yogas*.

In this regard, the inauspicious [conjunctions] are as follows: the Sun with Anurādhā; the Moon with Kṛttikā; Mars with Śatabhiṣaj; Mercury with Aśvinī; Jupiter with Mṛgaśīrṣa; Venus with Rohiṇī; and Saturn with Hasta—these are the *mṛtyu-yogas* (death-conjunctions).
Excluding the burnt lunar days (*dagdhatithi*), all lunar days are pure with respect to all weekdays, provided one avoids those of special enjoyment (*viśiṣṭabhoga*).

Here, the burnt lunar days are as follows: the twelfth day is burnt by the Sun; the eleventh day is burnt by the Moon; the tenth day is burnt by Mars; the third day by Mercury; the sixth day by Jupiter; the second day by Venus; and the seventh day by Saturn.

These lunar days (tithis) are to be avoided for auspicious undertakings; however, for inauspicious undertakings, all cruel planets, lunar days, and so forth are to be accepted. In this regard, all astrological conjunctions (yogas) are recommended, with the exception of Vyatīpāta, Parigha, and Vaidhṛti;
likewise, for gentle undertakings, three ghaṭikās of the Viṣkambha yoga are to be avoided.
One should avoid [the birth] on Pañcaśūla; one should avoid it on the six [yogas], Gaṇḍa and Atigaṇḍa, and on the nine [yogas], Vyāghāta and Vajra—thus is the impurity of the *yoga*.

Likewise, purity of the day and lunar date according to worldly convention constitutes the purity of the weekday and so forth; however, in the ultimate sense, the auspicious or inauspicious fruit is produced for sentient beings as earned by their own prior karma—such is the rule of the Tathāgata.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is stated: "Having made the asterism three parts"—meaning these twenty-seven asterisms are divided into three parts by groups of nine, nine, and nine. Among those groups of nine, in each respective group of nine, the birth-asterism of the sick person or the warrior in battle occurs first at the beginning of the first group of nine; then, the asterism separated by one [intervening asterism] is the odd position (*viṣamapada*). If in that odd position there are malefic planets—the Sun, Mars, Saturn, Rāhu, or together with the Moon—at the ascendant (lagna),...

When [the planets] are so situated, then for the sick there is only death, or for a warrior in battle, victory is at hand; such is the rule regarding the strength of the stars (*tārābala*). Now, the *phaṇicakra* (serpent-diagram) is described, beginning with "Aśvinī": by means of the twenty-seven constellations starting from Aśvinī, the serpent is arranged across three channels (*trināḍī*) as far as the constellation Revatī. If the birth constellation of a sick person or a warrior falls upon the same channel as a "sinful moon"—meaning both a malefic planet and the moon—then for that person there is destruction, which is to say, death; such is the rule for the *trināḍī phaṇicakra*.

When the moon has moved through three *nāḍīs* separated by one [constellation] starting from Kṛttikā, and likewise from Ārdrā, and so on, whichever enters the battlefield first when the moon is situated within three *nāḍīs* [of a constellation] becomes the victor; whereas when the moon is situated outside the three [constellations], he who enters later becomes the victor—this is the third rule concerning the *phaṇicakra*.

The results of the *āyurdaśā* are now described, beginning with "six, fifteen," and so forth: Six, fifteen, eighteen, sixteen, twenty, nine, ten, twelve, and twenty-one years—these are the years that the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Saturn, and Venus consume respectively.

Within that [period], during the sub-period (*antardaśā*), furthermore, by means of the letters of the *aṣṭavarga*, the malefic planets cause misfortune, while those planets which are of gentle form bring supreme happiness.

In this regard, having constructed an eight-spoked wheel (*aṣṭāracakra*), one should then place the one hundred and eight years of the enjoyment of the planets starting from the Sun in order, beginning from the eastern direction.

On the eastern spoke, six; on the southeast (Āgneyī), fifteen, as it is said "the lunar day" (*tithi*); eight on the south (Yāmya); seventeen, as it is said "mountain-moon" (*adri-candra*), on the southwest (Nairṛtya); ten on the west (Vāruṇa); nineteen, as it is said "with nine" (*sanavadaśa*), on the northwest (Vāyavya); twelve, as it is said "the sun" (*arka*), on the north (Uttara); and twenty-one on the northeast (Īśāna).

The Sun (*Sūrya*) consumes six years; the Moon (*Candra*) consumes fifteen; Mars (*Aṅgāra*) consumes eight years; Mercury (*Budha*) consumes seventeen; Jupiter (*Guru-Bṛhaspati*) consumes nineteen; Rāhu, called "Bhujaga," consumes twelve years; and Venus (*Śita-Śukra*) [consumes] the asterism (*carkṣa*).
