Thus, for one hundred and eight years, the Sun and the other planets sever those [periods] in sequence according to their respective numbers.

Furthermore, regarding that "inner period" (*anantardaśā*), it is said here that during the gross period (*sthūladaśā*), the malefic planets—the Sun, Mars, Saturn, and Rāhu—cause unrest, while the benefic planets—the Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus—bring about peace.

Furthermore, here within a single period (*daśā*) lasting six years and so forth, there are again eight kinds of sub-periods (*antardaśā*); and within that sub-period, there are likewise [eight], according to the syllables of the *aṣṭavarga*. In this context, the class-syllables (*vargākṣara*) are twofold: some by way of worldly convention (*lokarūḍhi*), and others by way of the *Svayambhū* tradition.
Among these, by the worldly reading, the *avarga* consists of *a, i, u, e, o*; [by the *Svayambhū* reading] the rule is *aiuṇ*, *ṛlag*.

The *k*-group is *ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa*; likewise the *c*-group, the *ṭ*-group, the *t*-group, the *p*-group, *ya, ra, la, va*, and the *s*-group is *śa, ṣa, sa, ha*. According to the worldly recitation, there is the sequence *hayavaraṭ*, *laṇ*, *ña-m-a-ṅa-ṇa-na-m*, *jha-bha-ñ*, *gha-ḍha-dha-ṣ*, *ja-ba-ga-ḍa-da-ś*, *khaphachaṭhathaca*, *ṭatava* (*v*), *kapaya*, *śaṣasar*, and *[hal]*; this is the principle beginning with space (*ākāśa*). Herein, there is no purification of the letters of the groups by means of space and so forth, because of the recitation of the *Śaṃkaraprapañca*.
Furthermore, in this case, for the Sun, there is an eightfold enjoyment during the six-year major period (*sthūladaśā*) and the sub-periods (*antardaśā*) of *a*, *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, *ḷ*, and so forth.

Thus, in the fifteen-year period of the Moon, there is the sub-period (*antardaśā*) of *hayavara* (the letter *la*); in the eight-year period of Mars, there is also the sub-period of *ṅagha ga kha ka*; in the seventeen-year period of Mercury, there is also the sub-period of *ajha ja cha ca*; in the ten-year period of Saturn, there is also the sub-period of *ṇa ḍha ḍa ṭha ṭa*; in the nineteen-year period of Jupiter, there is also the sub-period of *ma bha ba pha pa*; in the twelve-year period of Saturn and Rāhu, there is also the sub-period of *X na dha da tha ta*; and in the twenty-one years of Venus, there is the sub-period of *ka śa ṣa sa ha*. Thus, there is an eightfold enjoyment (*bhoga*).

Thus, the eight groups, which have the nature of the sun, moon, space, wind, fire, water, earth, and the element of consciousness (*jñāna-dhātu*), consist respectively of five letters each: *e*, *o*, *ara*, *āra*, *ala*, *āla*, where the root nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is to be grasped. Among these letters of the eight groups, during the five-year periods, the Sun and the others are the enjoyers through the vowels of the *muhūrta* and the consonants of the mandalas; according to the fivefold division, this occurs within the eighth part of the sub-period (*antardaśā*) starting from the six-year period. Such is the rule for the wheel of the periods (*daśācakra*).
The individual planet is the enjoyer; in the first division, the lord of the life-period (*āyur-daśā*) is the ruler, and then the other seven follow in sequence—this is the rule for the life-periods.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is now explained: "In the month of Puṣya, when the sun has entered Capricorn and the sun is in the 'Jar' (*kumbha*) of the world-system, ignorance (*avidyā*) occurs; in Māgha, when the sun is in Pisces, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arise, O Lord of Men. In Phālguna, when the sun is in Aries; in Caitra, Vaiśākha, and Jyeṣṭha, consciousness (*vijñāna*); name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) when the sun is in Taurus and Gemini; the eye and so forth when the sun is in Cancer; and contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) when the sun is in Leo. (114)

O King, in Āṣāḍha and Śrāvaṇa, even for a woman, there arises craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*); in the month of Māgha (or Bhādrapada) and in Āśvina, becoming (*bhava*) occurs; in Kārtika and Vṛścika, birth (*jāti*) occurs; and likewise, when the sun is in Capricorn (*apastha*), death (*maraṇa*) occurs in Mārgaśīrṣa—in this sequence, O King, the twelve links [of dependent origination] arise through the distinction between the sun and the moon, by virtue of their dual movement.

In the month of Puṣya or Māgha, when the conjunction occurs and the sun has entered Capricorn, if death takes place on that [specific] day, O King, it results in ignorance (*avidyā*); if on the second day, it is birth (*jāti*); and likewise on the third.

Thus, all starting from existence (*bhava*) is multiplied by the sequence of progression up to twelve factors (*dvādaśāṅga*). Therefore, due to the movement in Capricorn, death may sometimes occur in the sixth month (*ṣaḍaṅga*), corresponding to the number three, four, and five.

The fortnights and lunar days are known by the day of the week according to the movement of the Sun; sometimes there is a correction (*saṃskāra*) of sixteen parts at the junction of the month of Māgha when the Sun has entered the water-jar (*kalaśa*).

Therein, that very correction is consciousness (*vijñāna*); it becomes name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) on the second day, and thus the limb of the two months occurs by the power of the Sun through the conjunction of creation and dissolution. || 117 ||

In this context, even the inauspicious portion of ignorance may become auspicious for all undertakings due to consecration and other rites; likewise, that which is inauspicious [becomes so] during an initiation, a procession, or a marriage.

Thus, by the divisions of the lunar fortnights according to the movement of the moon, there are twelve links in both the bright and dark fortnights, arising from the sequence of lunar days through the conjunctions of creation and destruction. || 118 ||

The Great Chapter on the Rules and Methods for the Instrument of the Arising of the Breath (Svarodayayantra): Regarding the passage beginning with "Puṣya," in the month of Puṣya, at the time of the exit of Puṣya and the entry into Māgha, ignorance (*avidyā*) is present here.

The twelve-spoked wheel is the zodiacal circle beginning with Capricorn (*makara*). Therein, on the first spoke, which is Capricorn, when the sun has passed [into that sign], it is the month of Māgha when the sun is in Aquarius; by the word "and" (*ca*), the consecration (*saṃskāra*) occurs right here at the end of Māgha, on the day of entering Phālguna. Likewise, at the end of Phālguna, on the day of Capricorn [ending] and Aquarius beginning in Caitra, there is discernment (*vijñāna*). Similarly, at the end of Caitra, on the day of Aries beginning in Vaiśākha, there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Thus, at the end of Vaiśākha, on the day of Taurus beginning in Jyeṣṭha, there are the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Likewise, at the end of Jyeṣṭha, on the day of the transition into Gemini beginning in Āṣāḍha, there is contact (*sparśa*).

Thus, at the end of Āṣāḍha, on the day of the transition (*saṃkrānti*) into Cancer beginning with Śrāvaṇa, there is *vedanā* (feeling); likewise, at the end of Śrāvaṇa, on the day of the transition into Leo beginning with Bhādrapada, there is *tṛṣṇā* (craving). Similarly, at the end of Bhādrapada, on the day of the transition into Virgo beginning with Aśvinī, there is *upādāna* (grasping); thus, at the end of Aśvinī, on the day of the transition into Libra beginning with Kārttika, there is *bhava* (becoming). Likewise, at the end of Kārttika, on the day of the transition into Scorpio beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, there is *jāti* (birth); and similarly, at the end of Mārgaśīrṣa, on the day of the transition into Sagittarius beginning with Puṣya, there is *jarāmaraṇa* (old age and death). These twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*) are to be known respectively within the twelve spokes.

The division of the three suns and the division of the moon are well-known everywhere; they occur by virtue of both motions, namely, by virtue of the solar transits (*saṃkrānti*) and by virtue of the lunar days (*tithi*) of the fortnight. Regarding the twelve links: when the conjunction occurs in the month of Puṣya or Māgha, with the sun having entered Capricorn, then on that day is *avidyā* (ignorance); from that day, on the second day, which is a Wednesday, is *jarāmaraṇa* (old age and death); on the third day is *jāti* (birth); on the fourth, *bhava* (existence); on the fifth, *upādāna* (clinging); on the sixth, *vedanā* (feeling); on the eighth, *sparśa* (contact); on the ninth, *ṣaḍāyatana* (the six sense bases); on the tenth, *nāmarūpa* (name and form); on the eleventh, *vijñāna* (consciousness); and on the twelfth, *saṃskāra* (formative predispositions).
Just as it was on the third day, so too is birth on the thirteenth; becoming (*bhava*) on the fourteenth; grasping (*upādāna*) on the fifteenth day;

and sometimes craving (*tṛṣṇā*) on the sixteenth day—these members [of dependent origination] vary according to the movement of the sun. In certain cases, within the system of transits (*saṃkrānti*), there is a sixteenth day due to the influence of the ascendant (*lagna*) being equal to Capricorn in the right channel (*dakṣiṇanāḍī*).

Thus, during the conjunction of Māgha and Phālguna, when the sun has entered Aquarius (Kumbha), on that lunar day (*vāra*) there is *saṃskāra*; on the second, *vijñāna*; on the third, *nāmarūpa*; on the fourth, *ṣaḍāyatana*; on the fifth, *sparśa*; on the sixth, *vedanā*; on the seventh, *tṛṣṇā*; on the eighth, *upādāna*; on the ninth, *bhava*; on the tenth, *jāti*; on the eleventh, *jarāmaraṇa*; and on the twelfth, *avidyā*. This occurs in the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*) by virtue of the zodiacal sign (*lagna*) whose domain is Aquarius, according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*).

In this regard, as in the third [month], so in the thirteenth there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), in the fifteenth there is contact (*sparśa*), and in some cases in the sixteenth there is sensation (*vedanā*);

thus the sequence of days of the week for the sun and moon is to be understood everywhere according to the distinction between even and odd [months], by means of the difference in the day of the week at the transition (*saṃkrānti*) in both fortnights.

In the *Vimalaprabhā* commentary on the *Lokadhātu*: here, the "uneven" (*viṣama*) portion—consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), sensation (*vedanā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and birth (*jāti*)—is auspicious for all peaceful rites. The "even" (*sama*) portion, beginning with formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth—which consists of formative forces (*saṃskāra*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), contact (*sparśa*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), becoming (*bhava*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—is inauspicious for peaceful rites; however, this even-uneven [division] is praised for cruel rites.

Thus, in the bright fortnight of the month of Puṣya, on the first day (*pratipad*), there is ignorance (*avidyā*); on the second and subsequent days, there is formative force (*saṃskāra*) according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). In the dark fortnight, on the first day there is ignorance, and on the second day there is old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). In this manner of dissolution (*upasaṃhāra*), the twelve links exist across the twelve lunar days. Just as the links beginning with ignorance occur in the month of Puṣya through the division of the bright and dark fortnights according to the sequence of emanation and dissolution, so too in the month of Māgha, the links beginning with formative force are to be understood through the division of the bright and dark fortnights according to the sequence of emanation and dissolution. Likewise, in the bright and dark fortnights of Phālguna and the following months, there are twelve links each, beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*).

In this very context, just as worldly convention is to be understood even by one devoid of specialized knowledge in astrology, so too is the law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); for that reason, it was not explained in detail. Now, the power of the *bhūmis* is stated: The Sun, Mars, Ketu, and Rāhu cause death to enemies when stationed on the right, the back, the left, or the front; likewise, the entire host of planets on the battlefield, as well as the Yoginīs, Viṣṭi, and the Rudras together with the Wind, grant happiness when on the right, the back, the left, or the front. When situated on both even and uneven [positions], these two powers bring about destruction in the form of death. || 119 ||
Regarding the passage beginning with "Sūrya" and so forth:

having understood here that the ground-force consists of the eight directions within the zodiacal circle (*rāśicakra*), one should observe the positions of the planets and lunar mansions (*nakṣatracakra*) upon the earth in the eight directions. Wherever the Sun, Mars, Ketu, and Saturn are situated—whether all together on the left, the right, or the back—they cause death to enemies when they stand facing them from the front or from the left.

On the left front, the entire host of gentle planets likewise causes the destruction of enemies on the battlefield; the rule is that the gentle group of planets—namely the Moon, Mercury, Venus, and Jupiter—standing to the right or behind the enemies causes their destruction. Likewise, in the manner to be described, the Karaṇas, Viṣṭis, and Rudras, together with the Winds, grant happiness when situated to the right or behind the enemies, but they become destroyers when standing on the left or in front.

When the planets are situated in equal and unequal positions, those that are half-malefic (ardhakūra) do not become malefic when on the right or behind; likewise, those that are half-benefic (ardhasaumya) do not become benefic when on the left or in front. At that time, they strike down two forces, and the rule is that there is death for both sides.

[End of] the Great Chapter on the Rules for the Method of the Svarodaya Instrument. Now, the power of the Yoginīs beginning with Brahmāṇī is described: Brāhmī, Raudrī, Kumārī, Khagapatigamanā (Gāruḍī), Śūkarī, Vajrahastā (Vaiṣṇavī), Cāmuṇḍā, and Lakṣmī arise on the eighth lunar day (vasu-tithi) starting from the first lunar day up to the ninth.

In Śakra (the east), Yakṣa (the northeast), Agnikoṇa (the southeast), Danu (the south), Yama (the southwest), Varuṇa (the west), Māruta (the northwest), and Īśabhūmi (the north), these [fortnights] rise; furthermore, they are divided into eighteen varieties according to the lunar days (tithis). ||120||

Regarding the passage beginning with "Brāhmī," etc.: here, whether in the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) or the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), on the first day (*pratipad*) Brāhmī is in the east (*śakra*); on the second day, Raudrī is in the southeast (*pākṣa*); on the third day, Kaumārī is in the southeast (*agnikoṇa*); on the fourth day, Vaiṣṇavī is in the southwest (*naiṛtya*); on the fifth day, Vārāhī is in the south (*yāmya*); on the sixth day, Aindrī is in the west (*vāruṇa*); on the seventh day, Cāmuṇḍā is in the northwest (*vāyavya*); and on the eighth day, Mahālakṣmī is in the northeast (*aiśānya*). Thus, on the eight lunar days (*vasutithi*), starting from the first day up to the ninth, [the goddesses are assigned].

Furthermore, on the ninth day, Brāhmī is in the east; on the tenth, Raudrī is in the northwest; on the eleventh, Kaumārī is in the southeast; on the twelfth, Vaiṣṇavī is in the southwest; on the thirteenth, Vārāhī is in the south; on the fourteenth, Aindrī is in the west; and on the fifteenth—the full moon and the new moon—at the half-tithi, Cāmuṇḍā is present, and at the [other] half-tithi, Mahālakṣmī is present. This is the rule. In this manner, they bring about their rising in these eight directions; these are the Yoginīs.

Furthermore, on the lunar days (*tithis*) beginning with the first quarter (*pratipad*), there are eight divisions in the first half and eight divisions in the second half; thus, it should be understood that they arise within those two sets of eight divisions during those lunar days. Among them, the first eighth-part of each respective lunar day is the "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) of the presiding deity of that lunar day. Subsequently, the seven [deities] have their enjoyments in the order previously described; this is the rule. The same should be understood for the second half of the lunar day as well. This is the regulation regarding the arising of the *Yoginīcakra*.

The rising of the *viṣṭis* occurs here in the bright fortnight in the directions of Indra, Yama, the ocean, and the corner [of Vāyu], and again in the dark fortnight in those of Agni, the Lord [Īśāna], the wind [Vāyu], and the corner [of Īśāna] respectively.

Rudra traverses the eastern and western halves according to the day; as the sun moves further and further north, it regularly proceeds from the western direction toward the fire-colored [southeast]; and as the sun moves further and further south, it proceeds toward the south.

Now the power of the *viṣṭi* is described: In the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), the rising of the *viṣṭis* occurs respectively on the fourth, eighth, eleventh, and full moon days in the directions of Indra (East), Yama (South), Varuṇa (West), and Soma (North).

In the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), the rising occurs respectively on the third, seventh, tenth, and fourteenth days in the directions of Agni (Southeast), Nairṛti (Southwest), Vāyu (Northwest), and Īśa (Northeast). This is the rule for the rising of the *viṣṭis*;
their function is as previously stated.

Now the power of Rudra is described: from the east (pūrvāt), from the eastern direction, Rudra proceeds as far as the west (vāruṇyām) in the latter half [of the year], by the force of the day, that is, by the force of the movement of the transits (saṃkrānti).

In the north, by way of counter-clockwise rotation (vāmāvartena), when the northern sun is situated in the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa)—that is, while Capricorn and the first half of Aquarius remain in the east—or again, in the west.
On the first lunar day (pratipad),
there is the enjoyment of meat.

In the twenty-fifth chapter of the *Vimalaprabhā*: when the Sun is in Pisces, it is in the northeast (Īśāna) at the end of Aquarius; in Aries, it is in the north (Uttara) at the end of Taurus; and in Gemini, it is in the northwest (Vāyavya) at the end of Taurus.

Then, when the sun is situated in the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*), from the western direction (*vāruṇya*) [the wind] goes to the south-east (*agnimanta*); Rudra moves to the south in Cancer; in Leo, he is in the west (*vāruṇya*); in the middle of Leo, in Virgo, he is in the southwest (*naiṛtya*); in Libra and the middle of Scorpio, he is in the south (*yāmya*); and in Sagittarius, he is in the southeast (*āgneyī*). This is the rule for the rising of Rudra. Thus, the monthly Rudra, the fortnightly Rudra, the daily Rudra, and the temporal Rudra—these six types are useless and have not been mentioned by him. Now, the strength of Rāhu for each half-watch (*ardhaprahārika*) is stated: from the eastern half-watch, he enters the northwest (*pavana*); likewise, he goes to the south.
In water, fire, yakṣas, while moving through the city of the Dānavas, in wind, or when the sun sets;
having abandoned the illustrious Mūlarāhu, even the Wind-god becomes victorious in hand-to-hand combat. In battle, Mūlarāhu devours the enemy force; there is no other equal to him. (122)

Here, during the seven watches [of the day], at sunrise, it enters the east from the eastern quarter; after half a watch, it enters the wind [quarter]; then, at the end of the subsequent half-watch, it goes to the south; again, at the end of the subsequent half-watch, it proceeds to the northeast (Īśa); then, at the end of the subsequent half-watch, it goes to the west (Varuṇa); then, at the end of the subsequent half-watch, to the southeast (Āgneyī); then, at the end of the subsequent half-watch, to the Yakṣa [quarter]; and then, at the end of the subsequent half-watch, it enters the southwest (Nairṛtī). This is the rule for the eight directions, from sunrise until sunset.

The same should be understood for the night. Having abandoned the illustrious Mūlarāhu, this victorious one prevails even in a hand-to-hand (aṅka) combat; in a battle between two warriors, however, Mūlarāhu devours the enemy force. There is no other Rāhu equal to him among the Rāhus of the months and so forth—this is the rule. Now, the strength of the warrior in a hand-to-hand combat is described: a warrior deficient in *mātrās* is slain by one who has more in a level or uneven encounter; victory in battle belongs to that one whose breath enters the heart of both [opponents].

One whose name begins with a vowel as stated by the messenger prevails as a victor; one whose name ends with a vowel is slain. When vowels and consonants are arranged in even or odd positions, the prediction is indeed fruitless.

A warrior whose name lacks the proper *mātrās* (vowel measures) is slain by one with a superior name—whether in open battle, hand-to-hand combat, a precarious encounter, a clash between two armies, or in even or uneven terrain—by means of a name possessing superior *mātrās* and syllables.

A short-voweled name is slain by one with long vowels; a long-voweled name is slain by one with protracted (*pluta*) vowels. However, this does not apply when there is a subsequent cause [such as a specific conjunction].
In a duel, victory belongs to that one of the two names which enters the heart during the breath.

He whose name exits with the breath externally dies. Another application: the one whose name is uttered first by the messenger prevails as the victor; he whose name is uttered last is slain—this is the rule.

By the "Noble Ones" (*āryaiḥ*) are meant the castes (*varṇa*), which are the noble ones: the banner, smoke, lion, dog, bull, donkey, elephant, and crow; as well as the dark, fair, red, and black complexions; and likewise the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra. In the chapter on vowels (*svarā-paṭala*), the rule for the procedure of the vowel-arising instrument (*svarodaya-yantṛ*) is as follows: the aggregate of consonants (*akṣara-piṇḍa*) is doubled, and the aggregate of vowels (*mātrā-piṇḍa*) is quadrupled; the remainder after division by seven is the result. By these vowels and others, through this extensive elaboration spoken by the Lord (*īśvara*), the prediction of results based on even and odd [counts] is indeed established. Why?

Because they lack the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), their speech—which, according to all worldly convention, produces delusion in the ignorant—is devoid of the experience of the fruits of one's own karma. Under the pretext of the power of planets and so forth, false compositions have been made by sages; likewise, those established in the dharma of the Lord have composed works on the "Rising of the Breath" (*svarodaya*). Thus, they deceive the world with the false claim that these were spoken by the Lord.
This elaboration should be explained in detail in the *Paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*; let it suffice here.

Now the power of Mūlarāhu is described, beginning with the word "Time" (*kāla*): If Time (*kāla*) is on the right and Rāhu (*tamī*) is on the left during the battle on the field of kings, then even the Lord of Gods, accompanied by Hari and Hara, is slain by men.

Therefore, one must know that the glorious Mūlarāhu is the conqueror of the three worlds among Vakra, Rudra, and the Asuras when situated upon the circle of the earth at the time of battle; otherwise, there is no destruction of the enemy. || 124 ||

Having placed the constellations on the ground according to the arrangement of the pair of sages (the *muni-yuga*) in the directions of Indra (East), Yakṣa (North-East), the Ocean (West), and Yama (South-West), that entire wheel should be understood as revolving by the power of the sun's course.

At whichever constellation the time [of birth] falls, and at whichever two [constellations] the shadow falls during the night, in a battle between those two, the enemy army will suddenly fall [into defeat], while victory shall belong to the one in the middle of the womb. 125.

When the planets are situated in the time of Rāhu, there occurs a battle with an equal fall of forces; however, for those who have emerged from the aspect-portion (dṛṣṭyaṃśa) due to the movement of the serpent [Rāhu], there is indeed a rout of the army. For those who have avoided the aspect-portion, victory prevails; and when both are in the "entry into the womb" (garbhavedha), it is known in the Kālacakra system that this occurs when Rāhu is in the position of Jupiter’s word (guru-vacana-gata).

Having placed the constellations here upon the ground, there are twenty-eight constellations. The constellation in which the sun resides is situated among the seven preceding constellations, with three constellations each to the left and right; thus, the seven [constellations] of the former age have been arranged here, just as the seven were in the east, so too in the north, west, and south—the wheel being rotated by the Lord (Īśvara).
[The term] *sarvva* [is used for] "everywhere."
This is incorrect.
According to the authorities on Dharma (who everywhere read "a" as "ā"),
this [reading] appears in the fifth chapter as *vihitāni* (not *vihatāni*).

All [seven]—this is not the case. Regarding the three verses numbered here, the sequence of the commentary has arrived as follows: first, the commentary on the verse concerning *tamas* (darkness) was begun; therein, after the explanation of the first line beginning with "prabhavati ca tamī," the explanation of two quarters of that *tamas* verse follows; then comes the explanation of the remaining portion of the *tamas* verse; immediately after that, the commentary on the *tamas* verse itself; and finally, at the end, the explanation of the last two quarters of the *tamas* verse.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, the arrangement of the constellations follows a clockwise rotation, while the arrangement of the stars follows a counter-clockwise rotation. Within a single day and night, each of the twenty-eight constellations has its own respective duration.

Here, by virtue of their movement, when the "tail-Rāhu" (*kāla-puccharāhu*) is present in a constellation, it prevails; and when the "mouth-Rāhu" (*mukharāhu*) is present, it prevails on the left. If this occurs on the battlefield of kings, then in that conflict, even the Lord of the Gods, accompanied by Hari and Hara, is slain by men through the mere casting of a glance.
In the battle between the two, Rāhu’s head and tail, the enemy army falls suddenly; thus, victory shall be within the womb.

In this regard, if the face is in the east and the tail in the west, then the gaze is in the south and the womb in the north; when the face is in the southeast, then the tail is in the northwest, the gaze in the southwest, and the womb in the northeast; when the face is in the south, then the tail is in the north, the gaze in the west, and the womb in the east; when the face is in the southwest, then the tail is in the northeast, the gaze in the northwest, and the womb in the southeast; when the face is in the west, then the tail is in the east, the gaze in the north, and the womb in the south; when the face is in the northwest, then the tail is in the southeast, the gaze in the northeast, and the womb in the southwest; when the face is in the north, then the tail is in the south, the gaze in the east, and the womb in the west; and when the face is in the northeast, then the tail is in the southwest, the gaze in the southeast, and the womb in the northwest.

Thus, for those situated in the mouth, the middle, or the tail of Rāhu during the period of Kāla, death occurs. An equal fall of the armies occurs for those who have emerged from the sector of the aspect (*dṛṣṭyaṃśa*).

Here, in the sector of the aspect, among the twelve lunar mansions that have come into view, three parts to the right and left—namely four *nakṣatras* on Rāhu’s side and four on Kāla’s side—constitute this. Indeed, due to the movement of the serpent, there is a rout of the army there.

Among the twelve lunar mansions situated within the aspectual portion (*dṛṣṭyaṃśa*) that are free from the womb, one-third is the entry into the womb; four mansions are on the right and four are on the left.
Here, those situated in the aspectual portion have entered the womb-segment and are facing [the planet]; with them, there is battle.
Thus, the illustrious Root Rāhu is known in the Kālacakra according to the words of the Guru.
"The word of the Guru is the word of the Buddha.

For that reason, the illustrious Mūla-Rāhu is the conqueror of the three worlds and is *vakra* (crooked). The planets are the Rudras, and the *āsurī* is the sixty Yoginīs; he is the conqueror of them, being *vakra* among the Rudras and Āsurīs. He is to be known as situated on the terrestrial mandala at the time of battle, for otherwise there is no destruction of the enemy. Such is the rule: Rāhu is to be known according to the sequence thus described.

Having abandoned the Yoginīs, Viṣṇu (or Viṣṭi), Rudra, along with the planetary seizures, as well as the rising of the sun—all these are to be seized by the kṣatriyas alone, who are victorious over the three worlds;

he by whom Indra and Sūrya, who cause fear to the thirty gods, are swallowed—those of fierce form and resembling collyrium—who wanders day and night across the earth from east to west, south, and north. || 127 ||

In this matter, having abandoned all forces such as the yoginīs and others, the Kṣatriyas must seize this single planet Rāhu—by whom the moon and sun are eclipsed, who is terrifying to the gods, who possesses a fierce form with the luster of collyrium, and who revolves across the earth from east to west within a day and night, moving through the southern, northern, and other divisions of the eight directions; it is this very one that must be seized, according to the rule that at the time of battle, the individual [planetary] enjoyment occurs during the leftward period (*savyakāla*).
By humans, the fetus (*garbha*) is slain [everywhere the term *rbha* is used].
Omitted; not in the manuscript;
the limb of vision.
Entry;
gone; wheel.

Saṃgrāmabala; [Chapter] on Power (bale). The Great Compendium on the Rules for the Application of the Machine of the Arising of the Vital Breath (Svarodayayantra): Now, the machines are described for the purpose of destroying the fortresses of wicked enemies, beginning with the word "saṃgrāme" (in battle): "In battle, the enemy, having been broken, may sometimes suddenly enter the middle of the fortress. Having constructed machines outside, by means of incessant falls of stones, fire, and arrows, and by means of machines that sever with swords and the like, as well as cage-like structures on the surface of the earth and 'horn-breakers' (śṛṅgabhedas), one should pulverize that fortress and subdue that wicked one within a few days. (128)

If, at some point, one whose enemies have been broken in battle suddenly enters the middle of a fortress, then, having placed mechanical engines outside, one should protect one's own residence with those open engines by means of incessant showers of stones, fire, and arrows, as well as cutting machines such as swords; then, having pulverized that fort with diamond-cages and horn-breakers situated upon the ground, that wicked one is to be subdued within a few days—this is the rule.

Regarding the characteristics of the stone-engine (pāṣāṇayantra) for the ramparts and fortresses here, it is said, beginning with "four," and so forth: Four pillars, measuring sixteen cubits [in height], with eight sections pierced at even and uneven intervals, are joined at their base by cross-beams (*argalā*) of four, two, and four cubits respectively, along with a rear support (*pṛṣṭhakā*).

The measurement of the engine at its base is ten cubits; at the top portion, it is half of that. The shaft (*yaṣṭi*) is reduced by those two [sections], and the sockets (*kaṇaya*) at the summit consist of ten parts.

There are four pillars, each measuring sixteen cubits in height—namely, two of eight cubits each—and they are square in shape. For the superior machine, their width is sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*); for the middling one, the pillars are fourteen cubits high with a width of fourteen finger-breadths; and for the inferior one, the pillars are twelve cubits high with a width of twelve finger-breadths. These are perforated at eight locations by means of even and uneven steps: the "even" refers to the front and back edges, while the "uneven" refers to the left and right edges. At those eight positions they are pierced, and the hole is one-third of the width.

And these [gates] are pierced by four bolts on the east, four on the south, four on the north, and one on the rear lower part; thus there are five apertures in the two rear pillars and eight in the two front pillars. The measurement of the machine is ten cubits at its base and five cubits in height; the staff is two cubits less than the pillars, and the measurement of the socket-ring is six cubits, shaped like a cow's tail on the left and right sides of the ring.

The circumference is two and a half cubits, regulated according to the sage’s [proportions], with a single hole of two finger-breadths; indeed, the staff enters one cubit, fixed by a pin at the socket. At the back, it is bound with fifty cords; on the head is a circlet, and on the crown of the head is a measuring circle. At the end of the staff, a ring with a finger enters; the circumference is one span. || 130 ||

Regarding the statement "the non-stationary [wind] is diminished by two," the *Vimalaprabhā* states: In the center of the world-system, the circle is two and a half cubits; from both sides it is twenty finger-breadths [wide]. At the front of the two jars, it is thirty finger-breadths. In the middle of the central circle, there is a hole fourteen finger-breadths in length and seven finger-breadths in width. Into that hole for the rod (*kaṇaya*), having set aside one cubit, one makes thirteen cubits in the shape of a cow's tail; the rod enters into that hole and is secured by being pinned with an iron nail on its back side.

At the top of the staff, at a distance of one cubit and one-third, there are two holes. In those two holes, there are two rings, sixty finger-breadths in circumference and six finger-breadths in width, made of circular iron rods; fifty ropes are tied to each [ring] on the head and the ring. At the end of the staff, there is a loop twelve finger-breadths in circumference, which enters the tip of the staff by one finger-breadth. Together with the staff, it is pinned with two pegs and a tongue; a finger is to be known at the tip of the tongue, and the tongue is six finger-breadths long. Measured by the size of the loop, the tongue is inserted within the space between the loop and the staff.
With a staff three cubits long and a sling-rope of one and a half cubits, a stone is fixed in its center and whirled forcefully with thorny sticks;
once released, it flies swiftly through the air and suddenly falls upon watchtowers, gateways, and the like, pulverizing them entirely as it strikes the ground like a thunderbolt. || 131 ||
In this case, with a staff [measured] by the finger [unit], the throwing distance is three cubits and the rope is one and a half [cubits]; here is the hide.

The sling (*kṣepaṇa*) is twenty-four finger-breadths in width, twelve finger-breadths at the middle, and shaped like a cow’s tail on both the left and right sides; on both sides there are two cords made of thread, measuring two and a half cubits and so forth. A stone enters into the middle of that sling, being bound by strong thorny ropes. Once released, it flies swiftly through the air; having gone, it suddenly falls upon a watchtower, a wall, or a rampart. Having reduced everything to powder, the stone goes to the ground just like the falling of a thunderbolt.
On his finger is a half-moon; on the surface of the earth is the Brahma-line; on both sides of the two [lines] are eight points of liberation; from the closing of both palms comes release.

At the point of liberation, there is indeed the touching of the ground by those standing within the mechanism with even or uneven steps, and the falling of stones at will according to the threefold movement for the purpose of destroying the fortress. || 132 ||
The half-finger [width] of that machine is shaped like a crescent moon; on the surface of the earth, the Brahma-line lies beneath the finger, becoming equal to the [span of the] hand.

On both sides of it, there are eight points of release for the stone, each separated by one span (*vitasti*); from the closing of the fist, their release occurs from both palms. [End of] Chapter [on] the Great Summary of the Rules for the Method of the Svarodaya Machine. 145.

At the time of liberation, the stone touches the ground; it enters with equal steps using the right feet when entering the interior of the machine, or with uneven steps using the left feet—due to the threefold movement of the stone falling according to one's own will, and due to the movement of the left, right, or middle paths, for the purpose of destroying the fort. This is the rule for breaking land forts: if an elephant suddenly falls by his blows, what small creature can remain? If he should strike down the entire enemy force stationed outside, what need is there for those staying in the towers of the citadel?

What rivalry can there be with him, that archer dwelling upon the surface of the earth, in a siege-war? What enemy would enter that fortress which is like the very mouth of Yama, where the blows of mechanical engines fall? (133)
The verse beginning with "aibhaṃ yasya prahāraiḥ" is easy to understand.

Now, the characteristics of the water-mechanism (*jalayantra*) for the purpose of capturing a fortress protected by water are stated: There should be six pillars (*stambha*) on each side, acting as arms; the interior chamber (*garbha*) between the pair of hands (the two sides) should be equal to both wings, measuring twelve cubits (*arka-hasta*), neither more nor less. Every single compartment (*koṣṭha*) must be covered with leather bags filled with fruits, beeswax, and cloth. One should construct a single mantra using the six seasons, the eight defects, and three times the twelve [fingers]. (134)
"Six," and so forth.

Here, for the purpose of the water-mechanism (*jalayantra*), [the structure] is made of wood sixteen finger-breadths thick and fourteen cubits in width; for the elephant-mechanism (*hastiyantra*), twenty-four finger-breadths; for the horse-mechanism (*aśvayantra*), twenty finger-breadths; and for the human-mechanism (*narayantra*), sixteen finger-breadths. With six pillars situated at intervals of twelve cubits, it is equal to both sides, neither more nor less. Within each chamber (*garbha*) there is one [pillar], twelve cubits [in height]. In the lower and upper chambers, with a space of two cubits between them, or a space of four cubits, there are six pillars such that each chamber consists of two chambers; this is the rule.
Every individual compartment should be covered with wooden planks (*phalaka*).

Having fashioned arms on both sides here, one should fashion them on one side of each plank; on the other side, having protected the upper and lower edges of the planks, one should insert one finger’s breadth between the planks in the middle and secure it, so that there is no ingress of water—this should be done everywhere: below, above, front, back, left, and right.

The interior cavity (*garbha*) of elephants is three cubits in height, that of horses two and a half cubits, and that of men two cubits. These should be sealed at the joints of each individual plank with leather and waxed cloth (*sikthavastra*), using leather and waxed cloth melted together, so that the water of the waves does not enter. Inside the cavity, it should be made two cubits high at the position of the neck to allow for entry into the interior.
By means of these cavities—distinguished as inferior, middling, and superior—various types of machines are produced.

The womb-machine (*garbhayantra*) is formed by six seasons, or by eight defects, or by eighteen; or by thirty-six, which are three times the number of suns (*dinakara*), or by twice that, or by twice that again, up to a thousand wombs for the purpose of crossing the great ocean. In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the world-system (*lokadhātu*): two by two are placed within the intervals of the wombs; even if it falters, it is secured on all sides by the arms. On the back, there are six sections (*kāṇḍa*) of support, equal on both sides of the arms, and the machine-drivers are positioned in front.

There, his own army, mounted upon a vessel secured by pillars like wells and set in motion by fluttering sails driven by the wind, proceeds across the ocean for the purpose of destroying the enemy's fortress situated on the water.

Here, on the exterior, within each of the four-armed [sections], in the two pairs of front and back arms, and on the left and right sides of the body—among these six, specifically within these four arms—the pillars are fixed into the arm-holes that have emerged from the openings of the arms; these pillars, which are one-third the width of the arms, are joined by a wooden plank three cubits long with holes at both ends, so as to interlock all the inner chambers with one another at the four corners of the chambers.

One should attach the *kītivāla* (hair-tassels) in the remaining places of illumination. Either sealed at the top or extending from front to back all around—excluding the locations for the flow of the *kītivāla*—there are six *kāṇḍadhārā* (shaft-streams) on the back of the entire machine; thus they range from twelve, twenty, up to a hundred, with both arms equal and the tips aligned. The carriers of those *kāṇḍadhārā* shafts number up to a thousand, according to the dimensions of the machine.

Alternatively, having ascertained that they are defenseless, one may move that water-machine by means of wind-cloths (vātapata) attached to well-poles, which flutter in the moving wind; having ascended it, one proceeds with one's own army into the ocean for the purpose of destroying a watery fort or for seizing another island—this is the principle for subduing the wicked, and such is the description of the water-machine.

Now, the wind-machine for the purpose of discharging fire and oil to destroy mountain fortresses is described: On a single platform, with a moving cloth-fan driven by wind and secured to a staff with a flag, it moves even when obstructed by people on its sides or back; yet, by means of a rope, it travels over the heads of men. When raised by the wind, it indeed goes through the sky to the summit of the mountain fortress; from there, the discharged fire and oil burn the enemy force and the entire fortress on all sides.
"Single," and so forth.

Here, upon a square wooden board or pedestal measuring four cubits, there is a central pillar three cubits high, twelve finger-breadths in circumference, and circular in shape. At the left, right, rear, and front corners, there are iron pegs with rings; one should secure the top of the pillar to these rings with ropes.
Both sections of the mechanism, from top to bottom, should be covered with a firm cloth.

In this corner, there are five banners, each two cubits in width; at the lower left and right corners, there is a framework with three ropes extending for two cubits. Among them, one is equal in length to the height of the mountain fort when combined; by means of that rope, when people pull it from behind, the machine, being lifted up by the wind as the rope moves over the head, travels through the sky for the purpose of destroying the mountain fort.

Into that machine, upon its head, one should insert a single man together with fire and oil; by means of that man, the fire-oil released from that wind-machine burns the enemy force on all sides, including every fortification—this is the certain rule for the destruction of mountain forts. [In this] chapter, the great section on the rules and procedures for the *svarodaya* (astrological) machines: a wheel is set in motion at the base, and another wheel is placed at the front of the axle-pin; furthermore, it is constructed all around the edge of the mandala at intervals of two finger-breadths.
The wheel is two and a half cubits [in diameter], and there is another handle above it; at the tip of the handle, a sharp sword rotates with lightness when the base of the machine is turned.
(137) The *katūrī* machine is to be understood through direct observation; it has also been clearly described in verse.

Indeed, by means of a rope-machine, the enemy's messenger travels through the sky from his own location step by step; having measured the rope as it moves toward the difficult-to-reach fortress, one should likewise perform the measurement on the ground. When the peaks of the enemies have been pierced, one should burn their peak and set fire to the entire circle at the base of the enemy's dwelling.
In this way, the "horn-splitting" [mechanism] and the wind-machine have also been clearly revealed by means of this verse; there is no further intention for a commentary here.

Furthermore, a great temple constructed at the top portion of the wheels, circular in shape and made of iron and wood, though closed on all sides with these fruits or buffalo hides, when set in motion by humans, travels level upon the earth as far as the pit; then, having filled that pit, it suddenly enters through the gate-tower into the wall of the fortress.

// 139 // Likewise, in the *Vajrapañjara* as well, there is no intention [to describe it]. Now, the iron-arrow machine (*nārācayantra*) for piercing elephants with sugar-cane arrows in battle is described: having fixed the bow, even with its string, immovably upon two pegs on the base, two iron pegs are placed at the back, and on the well-fashioned notch, there are half-moons of the size of a finger-breadth.
By the power of the finger-guard, the abundant and level arrows— sharp iron shafts released at the time of battle— penetrate and pass through even the bodies of elephants armored with leather.

Having fashioned a lion six *aṅgulas* long with a steel arrow, one should fix iron rods, six *aṅgulas* each and square in cross-section, at its bottom, top, right, and left sides; these rods should have their holes sealed with iron pins. Having secured the bow, complete with its string, so that it remains immovable by means of two joints at the middle, one should then insert two square iron pins on the back side, to the right and left respectively, into the holes of the iron rods, with the two tips of the pins entering the two ends of the bolt. Within the middle of the bolt, there should be six, five, four, three, or two small balls (*aṅgulikā*).
Below, a single iron rod (*lauhaikadaṇḍikā*) measuring the size of the little finger in width and three finger-breadths in length should be inserted into the ring of the lower peg (*kīlakaṭaka*).

Above, one should fix the strings (*guṇa*) at the tips of the fingers. There, at each joint of the fingertips, there are steel arrows (*nārāca*) with strings; thus, when released by the sharp external steel arrows equal in number to the many strings, they proceed at the time of battle, piercing through the bodies of elephants armored with sugar-cane. This is the rule for the steel-arrow machine (*nārācayantra*).

Now, the *pātālakhaḍgayantra* for the protection of the royal palace is described: "Two pillars"—two pillars are firmly fixed in the ground and wrapped with ropes; between the two ropes, the hilt of the sword is placed, having been wound many times along with a spring. In their midst, the sword-hilt remains fixed, yet it can be moved or locked by means of a rotating seal; thus the excellent sword is concealed and immobilized at its tip.

In this regard, there are two square pillars, twelve *aṅgulas* in measure, four *hastas* in width; two *hastas* are embedded in the ground within the pit, and two *hastas* rise above the middle of the pit. There, having left one and a half *hastas* above the level of the pit, one should insert iron bolts (*argalā*) into the holes of the lower left and right pillars. Having left six *aṅgulas* from the top, one should wrap them with ropes for the sake of securing the ring so that it does not move. Between those two ropes, the fist of the sword (*asi-muṣṭi*) is inserted into the middle of the ring.

First, a ring is formed by many coils; within the middle of that ring, the hilt of the sword enters. It is fixed on the side of the master (ācārya). Likewise, it is coiled in reverse order between two pillars in front. It is secured at the tip of the sword by means of the seal located at the sword's point. At the tip of the sword-point seal, it is secured with a cord. At the tip of the sword-hilt, there is a socket (kaṇaya) measuring six finger-breadths (aṅgula). Above that, there is a line of holes, and on the blade (phalaka) there is an exit for the moving sword. One small, uncut crescent moon should be placed in the middle portion above.

He whose foot suddenly falls upon the moon-crested [liṅga] shall have it severed by a sword; at the end of the gate in the king’s palace, there is a striking machine. Then, one should avoid the emergence of the sword above with wooden planks, so that for one who moves it, it becomes lightened by iron.

"Candramā" is the secret terminology for "madhya" (the middle). Here, a shield should be placed above the ring at the tip of the sword-hilt; on that shield, whoever’s foot falls [upon it] is cut—that is his nature as "asi" (sword); this is the rule for the sword-machine (*khaḍgayantra*), meaning the characteristics of the sword-machine.

Thus, various machines [are used] for the destruction of the fortress gates (at the end of the gates), during times of battle, and always in the palace of the king, excepting the main gate and the path; the machine itself is the striker—this is the rule for the *pātāla-khaḍga* (underworld-sword) machine.

Now, the characteristics of the war-chariot (*syandana*) for the battle of the Kṣatriyas are described: The base of the axle-pedestal (*mūlapīṭha*) is twelve [units] high; the measurement of the wheel is nine parts, with pillars and bolts at the corners. The uneven and even chariots are measured from the pedestal by one and a half units. On the iron ground, the terrain for the warriors is either uneven or level according to the horses or elephants. From that, on the ground marked by the half-measure, mirrors, garlands, banners, and so forth are fashioned above. (143) [This concludes] the great chapter on the rules for the method of the machine of the *Svarodaya* in the section on the cause of iron.
"Beyond the senses," and so forth.

Here, for the sake of the chariot, the axle must first be made firm. The measurement of the horses and the chariot wheel is two and a half cubits; the axle is four finger-breadths thick (with some adding a certain increment), and by that same measurement it is square and circular. Above the axle is the pedestal (*pīṭha*); in the cardinal directions and the center, the measurement of the wheel is nine parts, consisting of nine compartments. That very pedestal is formed by twelve arms—the twelve rays of the sun—with a width of six finger-breadths, six facing east-west and six facing south-north.

The axle (*akṣa*) is fourteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in width; having divided it into three parts and leaving aside the middle part, one should bore two holes in each of the two [upper] positions. Having inserted the axle-pin (*cakrāra*) into those two holes, one should fasten it with the axle. When the iron pivot (*lauhakaraṇaya*) is fixed immovably in the circular rim of the base-hole, the wheel rotates together with the axle. Then, at the four corners of that pedestal (*pīṭha*), there are four pillars, equal in width to the arms of the pedestal and twice as long.

And those [chariots] are pierced by crossbars on the four sides, and pierced from below and above. A "level chariot" (*samaratha*) is moved by level horses; an "uneven chariot" (*viṣamaratha*) is moved by uneven horses—two, four, or six being level horses, and three, five, or seven being uneven horses. Regarding the measurement from the pedestal (*pīṭha*): the upper portion is the combat area (*yodhabhūmi*). Having set aside one part of the pillars' height as the measure of the pedestal, the combat area is in the middle part; it is half the measure of the pedestal above the pedestal. It may have an even or uneven surface for the horses—or rather, for the elephants—and in width it is eight finger-breadths, in length it is double the pedestal, and it is fastened with bolts together with the crossbars. Then, from the lower and upper parts of the pedestal, it becomes half [the size] by means of the marks.
Surrounded by four finger-widths, on that ground are fashioned mirrors, garlands, banners, and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), chowries, canopies, bells, and the like are included. These are the marks of the battlefield.
Between the two grounds, there is illumination in the four directions for the purpose of battle.

One and a half, two, three, and one and a half parts are for the moon, the sun, and the fire [respectively], pertaining to the base, the pedestal, and the bolt. The circular [mandala] is equal to one and a half parts; the lotus, the chariot, and the earth are equal to the divisions of nine.

The measurement of the wheel with its base is one and a half cubits, and it is twofold according to the horse and elephant [types]. The lotus type was ordained by the Son of the Gods [Brahmā], and the Nandi type is for men. || 144 ||

Thus, there are two and a half divisions each. Specifically, there is one division of the base pedestal (*mūlapīṭha*) in the fighting-ground (*yodhabhūmi*), and a half-division in the light-space (*prakāśa*); these two divisions are marked by the moon and the sun. Above the base pedestal, for the pillars and cross-bars (*stambhārgala*) which are four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) [in height], there is one division in the place of the lintel (*dhurāsthāna*). From that, there are two divisions of four finger-breadths for the pillars in the fighting-place. Above those, there are three divisions of four finger-breadths, and above that is the ground for the marks (*cihnabhūmi*) of the banners and so forth.

The circular bases (*pīṭha*) are formed by one and a half parts, as previously described; on the ground-circle of one and a half parts, there arises the lotus of the *kamalaratha*. Regarding the phrase "by the divisions of *nandi*," in the division of the *nandiratha*, the ground becomes square.

Thus, according to the stated sequence, the measurement of the wheel together with its base for the *turagaratha* (horse-chariot) is one and a half cubits. The measurement of the *gajaratha* (elephant-chariot) is double the measurement of the *turagaratha*; such is the rule for the wheel, the base, the bolt, the insignia, and so forth. Here, for the gods, the lotus-type chariot is circular.

"Constructed by the son of Surasūti": the canopy of Arjuna was of the *nandījāti* type and square; for other men, the chariot of Kṣatriyas is also prescribed to be square. Here, the great chariot is of three kinds: half-square, equal, and divine; the sun’s chariot has one wheel, while the uneven-horsed chariot is the destroyer of the Asuras.

In battle, the great chariot may be either uneven or even; for Kṣatriyas, when broken, it faces forward in an uneven-even encounter, whereas in a level battle, it would be broken from behind in an even manner. || 145 ||
In this context, the great chariot (*mahāsyandana*) is threefold: half-chariot (*ardharatha*) and full chariot (*samaratha*).

Here, with four axles (*akṣa*) and eight wheels (*cakra*), one becomes an irreversible (*avaivartin*) great chariot-warrior (*mahāratha*) in battle; whereas with two axles, four wheels, above and below, one becomes a half-chariot-warrior.
Therefore, "eight" refers to the wheels; "ocean" (*ambhodhi*) refers to the four axles; thus, "threefold" refers to the four-wheeled [chariot], as well as the two [axles] and the axles themselves.
"Equal to half the speed of a chariot" means it is equal;

"the divine one has a single wheel like the sun's chariot" means that the divine chariot exists with a single wheel, and likewise, it is "uneven" in the case of the sun, and so forth, which is easy to understand.
With one axle and two wheels, a chariot becomes balanced when the front and back of the yoke are broken [into equal parts]; this is the rule for the characteristics of land-based vehicles.

Now, the characteristics of the celestial palaces (*vimāna*) of the gods and the moving palanquins (*yātrācala-gṛha*) of kings are described: In the celestial palace of the immortals, the height from the top of the pillar-base to the upper part is divided into sixty-five-four-three (138) parts, and it is symmetrical and perforated according to the requirements of the city.

Likewise, on earth, for kings, during regional processions and festivals, the great revolving palanquin (*mahābhrāmarī*) functions with a space of half a cubit between the hands, extending in all directions. (146)
Therefore, from that [chapter], the Great Chapter on the Rules for the Method of the Svarodaya Machine begins with "six," and so forth.

Here, there are four pillars, twenty *hasta* in length and twenty *aṅgula* in width; these have four corners pierced through, which are equal: one corner-piercing is at the six-*hasta* division, the second at the five-*hasta* division; therein, the third occurs at the four-*hasta* division, [the fourth at the three-*hasta* division]; having excluded one *hasta* each from the bottom and top, the corner-piercing faces inward.

In the *mūlabhāsa* [type], thirteen cubits are on the ground; in the *mūlabhāsa* [type] above that, half a portion is on the ground, making seven and a half cubits. This occurs according to each individual city on the city-ground; in the *gaṇavimāna*, there is a floor four stories high above the ground.

Thus, on the ground of kings, according to the three types of cities, in the case of festivals and processions, there is a *bhrāmarī* (rotating gallery) everywhere formed by panels above an external bolt protruding from a hole outside the pillar in the first city; this *bhrāmarī* is three cubits [in height]. In the second city, it is one and a half cubits. This is the conclusion regarding the characteristics of the houses for the departure of divine chariots in all directions.

Now, for the sake of the spring festival (*vasantotsava*), the characteristics of the circular swing (*cakradolā*) are described: on the top of the pillar of the wheel, there are swings in all directions according to the three types of cities; from the two [sides] and eight [spokes], there are supports with four arms reaching toward the intermediate directions; thus, on the three levels, as it revolves above and below, the seats of the women held by the arms are positioned internally and externally, moving in the eight directions, located below and above.

"Above the wheels," and so forth. Here, as before, there are eight wheels and a root pedestal (*mūlapīṭha*). Above that, by means of elephant-chariot pillars, there are four pillars. Like a celestial palace (*vimāna*), there are swings (*dolā*) consisting of three types of cities. Above four sets of four crossbeams (*gala*), there are two, eight, and eight; thus, twenty-two [in total]. In the first city, in the four directions, there are sixteen swings; in the second, eight; and in the third, four.

In the first city, there are swings supported by ten arms positioned on the east and west, both right and left, situated above the *argalā* (crossbar). In the second [city], there are six [arms] representing the seasons (*ṛtu*), and in the third, four. Thus, the arms of the swings are the supports (*ādhārāḥ*) upon the three floors. Each pair of arms is inserted into the holes of each of the two rings (*kaṇaya*). Within each ring, there are four seats for women. These are arranged internally and externally, positioned below and above, and moved by the eight directions. This is the rule for the characteristics of the wheel-swing (*cakradolā*).

Now, the characteristics of the water-wheel for the purpose of irrigating gardens and the like are described, beginning with the word "ūrdhva" (upwards): The instrument, shaped like a tube, has a curved measurement from top to bottom. At the tip of the pipe, there is the mouth of a jar (*kumbha*) which is also perforated; when [the water] reaches the measure of the hole in the tube, it draws up the water. Even if the water released from the jar's opening is spilled, it flows level across the ground wherever it is led, whether into a garden or a grove.
“The fourth [is] in the division of three cubits (caturthī trihasta-vibhāge). According to the Tibetan [version], it is ‘four times four’ twice—bāī bāī ga. in the celestial palace (vimāṇe).”

"O! 'Half' refers to the following: In the upper, lower, left, and right directions, there is a mechanism (*yantra*) shaped like a hollow tube (*nālā*). In the center, there is a central part with a hole, four cubits in length, which serves as the primary mechanism (*mūlayantra*). At the tip of its tube, a jar-mouth (*kumbhamukha*) is attached, and its neck enters the tip of the tube. Below, at the jar, there is a hole the size of the tube's aperture. Another tube must be made to enter the middle of the water from the rear tip of the mechanism's tube. Then, one should seal either the hole in the jar where the water exits or the hole in the front tube. Thereafter, one should cause water to enter through the hole in the primary mechanism until the mechanism is filled with water."

Then, by means of a drop in the middle of the water (or a hole in the jar, or a hole in the tube), the jar is simultaneously drawn up from the water; that very water goes to a garden or a grove, and is carried to wherever it travels upon level ground—this is the rule for the characteristics of the water-lifting machine (*jalaśeṣakayantra*).

Now, the instruction on the Sūryaratha-observance of Mañjuśrī is spoken regarding the wicked—namely, for the sake of subduing the wicked and for the victory of the righteous upon the surface of the excellent earth. All that was previously taught by the Guru of the Three Worlds to Sucandra in the *Ādibuddha*, a portion of which has been clearly explained here today by me in this context; therefore, for the sake of protection in your own place, perform all of this. O Sūrya, do not [neglect it] out of hatred or greed.

In this regard, for the sake of subduing the wicked, that which was previously taught by the Teacher of the Three Worlds, Śākyasiṃha, to Sucandra—the emanation-body of Vajrapāṇi—concerning the characteristics of all the *svarodaya* instruments, from within that [teaching], specifically in the midst of that chapter on the *svarodaya* instruments, a certain portion has been clearly taught here in this land called Sambhala. O Sūryaratha, I, Mañjuśrī Yaśonarendra, have taught this today for the purpose of its protection in your own domain. Just as there is this rule for Sūryaratha—"Do not let all this be taken by those with hatred or greed"—so too is there this rule of the Blessed One regarding the other thorough understandings of the Kālacakra.

Thus ends the tenth great chapter on the rules for the procedure of the instruments of the arising of vowels (*svarodayayantra-vidhi-niyama*) in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja* in twelve thousand [verses], which follows the glorious *Mūlatantra*.

The eradication of the Mleccha-dharma and the establishment of the Buddha-dharma is indeed the beginning; now, since the eradication of the Mleccha-dharma and the establishment of the Buddha-dharma by the Great Cakravartin is easily understood, it was not stated [by him]. Thus ends the first chapter, named "The World System," in the Commentary. In the midst of the ocean of wine and milk, situated upon the earth-circle of the Sage, the Karma-bhūmi extends for a hundred thousand yojanas; there the lord of men wanders through the solar regions in succession. This is the rule for the method of the Svarodaya instrument, the Mahoddeśa.

* Beyond this point, there is no commentary; only the root text (*mūla*) exists in manuscript *ka*. Therefore, only the root text is presented here. ** From this point onward, instead of the "page number reference" for the Tibetan translation of the root text located in the margin, the manuscript page number reference from manuscript *ka* is provided within brackets.

In this chapter, the eradication of the Mleccha religion and the establishment of the Buddha-dharma is the primary subject. This single section consists of twenty-five thousand *yojanas*, together with the eight petals (*vasudala*). In its center is Kailāsa, surrounded on all sides by the excellent Snowy Mountain (*Himagiri*). || 150 ||
On the ground, there is the region of Kailāśa together with the Himagiri mountain; its three parts are surrounded on all sides by outer petals adorned with the lands of the sun’s domains.

In the left half is the place called Sambhala, the abode of the best of sages, inhabited by ten million villages; indeed, a domain consists of ten million villages, and a maṇḍala is composed of one hundred thousand villages. || 151 ||

Divided by the categories of one, two, three, and four, and further distinguished by the divisions of the five worlds and so forth—such as the universal monarch (*cakrī*), the lord of men (*narendra*), the seeker (*anveṣaṇīya*) by the wise, the wheel-bearer (*cakrī*), the half-wheel-bearer (*ardhī*), the fragmentary ruler (*khaṇḍī*), the regional king (*viṣayanarapati*), and the one with the seal in hand (*mudrahasta*) who is other than those—the division of external time indeed occurs just as it does for the Lord of the World. 152.

In this world, there are seven oceans, mountains, and days; likewise, the Sāttvika incarnations from divine wombs are eight: the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, along with Nṛsiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma, and Kṛṣṇa, who bring fear to the race of Danu. At the end of thirty-two Viṣṭaras, the enemy of Danu, the wielder of the discus, appears as the Bhūta-yoni (the source of beings) with a lifespan of one hundred years.

Ādra, Anogha, Varāhī, and five others in the lineage of Danu and Bhujaga who are of the nature of darkness (tāmasa); that eighth one is Mleccha Śvetavastrī, the destroyer of Madhumatī, and he is Andhaka.

The manifestation of the seventh is clearly in the region of Makha, in Vāgādā and other cities, where the world of the Asura-faction dwells—powerful, merciless, and possessing the form of a Mleccha. || 154 ||

O King, where camels, horses, and cattle are slaughtered, and there is food for men consisting of blood and raw meat, or some cooked pure meat, beef, juice extracted from meat, ghee mixed with pungent spices, rice mixed with vegetables cooked over a fire, and fresh fruit; and where the drink consists of the eggs of birds—that is the realm of the Asuras. (155)

The Bindu, Śakti, Añjaneya, Garuḍa, the celestial river, Nārada, Kāmadhenu, Durgā, and among the learned, Vidyā, Akṣara, Paramakalā, and the divine languages—through these forms of movement, the all-pervading Jñānakāya of the Jina descends; it proclaims everything—the Vedas, logic, and other scriptures—pertaining to the past, the present, and the future. (156)

O King, glorious one, after a few days you shall go to your own place in the famous city named Sambhala, surrounded by mountains, measuring four hundred and fifty *yojanas* on all sides, having installed Sureśa as the preeminent lord; for seven [generations] there will be kings in the illustrious Śākya lineage, and the eighth will be the illustrious Yaśas. (157)
This very Śrī Mañjuvajra, saluted by the best of gods, as Kalkī of the Vajra lineage, having bestowed the Vajra-consecration, shall reduce all the families of sages to a single *kalka* (impurity).

Mounted upon the Perfect Vehicle (*samyagyāna*), the bringer of fear to the clan of Danus, bearing the glorious fame and the spear in hand, he shall manifest the Great Kālacakra for the sake of the liberation of sentient beings. || 158 ||
In the midst of that, at the end of the age, there will appear in the lineage of Kalkī a lord of gods, honored by the best of deities, the fierce Kalkī;

he will be of peaceful form and a bestower of happiness upon the virtuous. Likewise, as the destroyer of the Mleccha tribes, he will be a wheel-bearer mounted on a mountain-horse, with a spear in his hand, possessing the splendor of the sun, and a slayer of all enemies.

In the midst of the Kalkī lineage, when four ages multiplied by eight (32) have passed along with sons and grandsons, at that time, indeed, the practice of the Mleccha religion shall prevail in the region of Makha;

and as long as the wicked Mleccha king remains, and for as long as the fierce Kalkī—who is honored even by the best of the gods—remains, during that time a terrible battle between those two shall take place upon the surface of the earth.

He who, with his fourfold armies, shall slay the Mlecchas in battle across the entire surface of the earth; who, at the end of the age on Mount Kailāsa in the city fashioned by the gods, shall offer as attendants Rudra, Skanda, the Lord of the Gaṇas, and Hari; and who, together with Kalki, shall provide mountain-like horses, lordly elephants, golden chariots, kings, and warriors with weapons in hand—[to him] [Kalki shall give]. (161)

Accompanied by an army consisting of mountains, horses with the speed of the wind, elephants multiplied by their qualities (*guṇa*), ten million chariots of various colors, a hundred thousand known as *Veda* (four), a hundred thousand slow-moving rutting elephants, six hundred thousand chariots, sixty *akṣauhiṇīs*, ninety-six clans, and kings with bound crests, Kalkī— joined by Hari and Hara— will bring about the destruction of the Mlecchas.

The uprooting of the Mleccha religion and the establishment of the Buddha-dharma shall indeed be the first task; the host of Mlecchas must be slain by the noble and fierce warriors, by the lords of elephants among men, by the mountain-like steeds of Sindh, and by kings against both even and uneven terrain.

Aśvatthāman, the son of Mahācandra, and Hanūmān shall strike with sharp weapons; and Rudra, as the fierce Kalkī whose mind is intent on the welfare of all, shall slay the lord of the Mleccha chiefs along with all the Danupati kings.

Having slain the mlecchas in battle, Kalkī—the sole leader of all armies—accompanied by Hari and Hara, shall go to Mount Kailāsa; and when the Discus-wielder is established in that city built by the gods, at that time the entire body of waters on earth will be filled with dharma, desire, and wealth, and the trees will bear grain and forest-produce, bending low under their steady fruit.

When the host of Mlecchas, along with their retinues, has been exterminated at the end of the Manu-era, Kalkī will attain perfection in the city built by the gods upon the lofty summit of Mount Kailāsa.

Brahmā and Sureśa shall become the sons of the Guru of the Thirty-three Gods during the Yuga-dharma; Brahmā shall rule over the single western region, while Sureśa shall become the sovereign of the eastern land.
Having completely eradicated the barbarian dharma from the three worlds, O Teacher of the World, Siddha shall rule for eight hundred years and establish the Brāhmaṇas in their place of happiness.

Furthermore, O Lord of Men, within that very [realm] there will be a division of castes; among those sons, some will become lords of Asuras, others kings, and others sages, while the rest will be commoners.

For the sake of destroying the Mlecchas, the Lord of the Gods (Indra) proceeds accompanied by twelve Indras; and in every region, the Discus-bearer (Viṣṇu) proceeds after having struck down the Mleccha-dharma.

His two sons, Brahmā and Sureśa (Indra), follow behind the Preceptor of the Thirty-three (Bṛhaspati) in the same manner. Behind them, in the lineage of Brahmā and others, there arise many various divisions upon the surface of the manifold earth.

In the age of Brahmā and others, this period of eighteen hundred human years is for men; half of that belongs to Kāśyapa on the surface of the excellent earth, and likewise half of that belongs to Nṛsiṃha.
Similarly, at the time of every day, the lifespan of a person, beginning from Vāmana up to Kalki, amounts to a number of one hundred years.

10.156 Thus, in all the regions (*khaṇḍas*) as well, the duration of the age (*yugasamaya*) is as follows: the Mleccha dharma prevails for one hundred and eighty years; thereafter, the Mleccha dharma is destroyed.
From that point, the Buddha-dharma prevails for twenty thousand years minus one hundred. By this power of the *śakti*, the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages proceed upon the earth. || 169 ||

The origin of the world-system, the simultaneous movement of the planets, the appearance of the Wielder of the Discus, the destruction of the Dharma by the barbarians, and the granting of the path by Kalki to the state of supreme bliss—all this has been told by me to you, Sucandra, exactly as it is. Furthermore, for the sake of the welfare of all people and for the purpose of liberation, what more do you ask me concerning the three times? (170)
Thus ends the first chapter, on the arrangement of the world-system, in the glorious Mahākālacakra extracted from the glorious Ādibuddha. || 1 ||
2. The Second Chapter, titled "The Inner Self" (Adhyātmanāma): (1) The Great Summary on the Arising of Body, Speech, and Mind, and the Determination of the Four Noble Truths. Homage to Śākyamuni!

He who, though liberated from the bonds of existence, performs this "conception" (*garbhādhāna*) for the sake of maturing great men and for the path of living beings; he whose virtuous garland of various *jātaka* tales is seen for the benefit of sentient beings.
Having first bowed to the Protector, the Buddha of great supernatural power,
and having prostrated to Vajrasattva, the glorious Śākyasiṃha, the Tathāgata, this commentary on the "Inner Chapter" is being written by Puṇḍarīka.
Impelled by Mañjuśrī and prophesied by the Sugata, I, the glorious Lokanātha, whose very soul is compassion for the world, [have spoken].

Here, in the glorious great jewel pavilion at the end of the eastern gate of the mandala house of the illustrious *Mahākālacakra*, the Blessed Lord Mañjuśrī—the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) known as King Yaśas—having been requested by Sūryaratha, spoke with his first verse to the Blessed Śākyamuni regarding the request of Sucandra for the teaching of the Inner Chapter (*adhyātmapaṭala*), which is the supreme awakening: "O Father of the Victors, the measure of the universe was not known by me as it was taught by you; furthermore, I desire to hear how the entirety of the three worlds could exist within the center of the body."

Having heard the words of Sucandra, the Sugata, bestowing a cry of "Excellent!", spoke out of supreme compassion for the sake of the liberation of sentient beings, his entire body manifesting with confidence.

In this chapter on the internal (adhyātma), I shall expand upon the summary of the narrative concerning the requester and the teacher, as taught in the *Laghutantra* by Mañjuśrī, the compiler, beginning with the words "not known" (*na jñātam*). Here, within the body, the measurement of the universe (*viśvamāna*) is not known. "O Father of the Victors" (*jinajanaka*) refers to Vajrasattva Śākyamuni; the "Father of the Victors" is the progenitor of the undefiled aggregates (*skandha*), and this is his address: "O Father of the Victors! You have taught the measurement of the universe externally, but that is not known within the body. Therefore, I desire to hear once more how and in what manner the entirety of the three worlds might exist within the body.

Therefore, having heard this request consisting of Sucandra’s words, the Sugata, granting his approval (*sādhukāra*) to Sucandra, speaks with excellence out of supreme compassion for the sake of the liberation of sentient beings. By the word "and" (*ca*), he establishes that the entire *tantra* is within the body;
thus, he speaks of all other *tantras* as being within the body for the purpose of teaching the second chapter. This is the summary of the requester and the teacher.
— 2. Homage to the glorious Kālacakra (namaḥ śrīkālacakrāya).
Existence (bhava).
The designation "ka" and "kha" is due to the letter "kha."

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, he states the verse concerning the teaching [86a], beginning with "Earth," and so forth: "Earth, water, fire, and wind; the thunderbolt, the rainbow of the gods, and the winds; the wheel of the zodiac signs, the moon and sun, Rāhu, Meru, the serpents, humans, and gods; the retrograde movements of the signs along with the stars; the transits, months, fortnights, days, nights, and lunar dates—all this within the body is to be known by the yogi through the divisions of the voids (*śūnya*) according to their respective colors and the threefold movement of the paths.
[Regarding] *adhyātma* (the internal): here, within the body, the entire aggregate beginning with earth is to be known by their respective phonemes (*varṇa*).

That is to say, earth is to be known by the dental phonemes, water by the labials, fire by the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*), and wind by the palatals. Thus, earth, water, fire, and wind correspond to the retroflexes;
furthermore, lightning corresponds to the thunderbolt (*kuliśa*).
The celestial bow (the rainbow) is by the *da* sounds; the ten winds are by the *tālu* (palatal) sounds;

the wheel of the zodiac is by all the letters beginning with *a* and *ka*; the moon is by the *bindu* (anusvāra); the sun is by the *visarga*; Rāhu is by the vowelless consonant; Meru is by the letter of one's name; the abode of the serpents is by the syllable *oṃ*; the abode of humans, the mortal world (*martyaloka*), is by the letter *ā*; and the abode of the gods, heaven (*svarga*), is by the letter *hū*.

The planets, Maṅgala and the rest, are crooked [due to their retrograde motion] by means of the previously mentioned right and left seed-syllables; the transits (*saṃkrānti*) are likewise through the divisions of the twelve groups; the months are also thus; the fortnights are through the divisions of half the six groups; and the days, nights, and lunar dates (*tithi*) are through the previously mentioned [syllables] beginning with *ka* together with the vowels. All this within the body is to be known by the yogin.

The threefold movement of the yogin through the divisions of the voids according to the previously stated sequence is also the threefold movement of the threefold Vajrasattva—whose nature consists of the desire, form, and formless realms—because he abides as the Self of all through great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
