And that [is to be known] "by the divisions of emptiness," meaning by the divisions of the four drops of *bodhicitta*; thus ends the rule for the summary of the collection of the universe within the body. Now, he speaks the third verse beginning with "In the body," which summarizes the causal complex for the arising of the human body: "In this body, the entire multitude of constituents (*dhātu*) arises indeed from the consumption of food and drink of six tastes; and the six tastes [arise] from the elements (*bhūta*); and the multitude of elements is manifestly and invariably [present] in the element of space (*khadhātu*)."

In the void, knowledge becomes blended, of equal taste (*samarasa*), imperishable, and eternal; thus, that which is established in such peace should be known as pervading the threefold existence within one's own body. Here, in this body, there is the collection of elements (*dhātuvṛnda*)—namely, hair, skin, blood, flesh, bone, marrow, and so forth; indeed, this entire collection of elements arises from food and drink of the six tastes. The six tastes are: salty, sweet, pungent, bitter, astringent, and sour; by the power of these foods and drinks, the collection of elements comes into being.
"From the elements, the six tastes": from earth, water, fire, wind, and space, as well as taste, the six tastes arise;
"the collection of elements in the space-element": the collection of earth, water, fire, wind, and taste exists within the space-element, which is the previously mentioned nature of atoms.

"In the void, knowledge is mixed": here, by way of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader, that consciousness of all sentient beings which exists within one's own body according to conventional truth—that very consciousness becomes, through the power of meditation, mixed with the void in the reflection of emptiness, such that the apprehending mind and the appearance of the apprehended mind become of one flavor, imperishable and eternal.

Regarding this, the rule for the collection of causes and effects for the arising of the body—beginning with conception and so forth—is stated by the verse beginning with "The seed," etc., in the section on the Yogin within this chapter on the internal (adhyātma): "The earth holds the seed situated in the lotus; thereafter, water makes it sprout; fire produces consciousness; wind devours the essence of fluids and brings about its growth. This concise explanation of the present verse is to be explained in detail in the forthcoming chapter on Knowledge (*jñānapaṭala*), concerning the attainment of the knowledge of the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara-jñāna-siddhi*). Thus, he speaks of the causal complex for the production of the body, starting with conception. The earth holds the seed situated in the lotus; thereafter, water makes it sprout; fire produces consciousness; wind devours the essence of fluids and brings about its growth.
O Lord of Men, they grant space for growth and, through time, accomplishment; thus the divine ones assume various states at the time of birth and during the period of infancy.
Here, that which is emitted from the union of the two organs—the semen and blood—is called the seed within the secret lotus.

The earth holds that seed; the meaning is that it is the earth-element within the secret lotus. "Situated in the lotus" means situated in the secret lotus. Therefore, from this secret lotus, water causes it to sprout, and subsequently, fire brings about its awakening. When this seed has been made to sprout by water, fire brings about its awakening—that is, it consumes the essence of essences. It consumes the six flavors (ṣaḍrasa) which consist of the various tastes eaten and drunk by the mother. Thus, fire consumes the essence of essences.
O Lord of Men— this is an address— the wind causes this seed to grow, and from that growth, space provides the void as an opening.
Success occurs in this manner over time;

thus, by this sequence, the success of the fish and so forth—the production of the embryo—comes about. They bring about the "divine" states; that is, they produce the ten divine states beginning with smoke (dhūma).

The ten stages beginning with the embryo, childhood, and so forth, as well as the time of birth and infancy, constitute the temporal sequence of the rules for conception; this describes the function of the seed's own constituent elements. Regarding the seed and so forth: Water brings about the growth of this seed, providing clear heaviness and density; Fire effects its maturation; the excellent tenfold Wind further grants space for its growth; and Space, through various manifold states over time, expands it. Thus, the powers of body, speech, and mind—emanation itself—cause it to expand.

Here, that which is the earth-element of the seed—the semen and blood—having consumed the six flavors residing in the secret lotus, clearly effects a state of heavy density; water likewise effects fluidity for the sake of the body's production; fire effects the digestion of the consumed flavors; the preeminent tenfold wind, beginning with *prāṇa*, effects their growth for this seed’s body; and space indeed provides the room for that growth. Thus, from time, creation proceeds according to the previously described method.

"Constantly sounding through various and manifold states"—this refers to the statement regarding the function of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and elements (*dhātu*), wherein the powers (*śakti*) of body, speech, and mind—smoke and the others—are emanated as the attributes (*dharmin*) of body, speech, and mind.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, the ten states of the internal mind-holding Viṣṇu are described starting with the words "In the secret [lotus]" (*guhya*): when the seed of enlightenment (*bodhibīja*), even though fallen into the midst of the blood in the secret lotus, becomes endowed with life, it becomes the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, the Dwarf, Rāma, and Rāma.

Kṛṣṇa becomes the Buddha, the Lord of Men; and there are these ten stages: three in the womb, one at the time of birth, two in childhood, another in boyhood, one more in youth, one great stage in full maturity, likewise one in old age, one peaceful stage, and the final one is death for those born from a womb.

In the Matsya [Kalpa], he remains in the form of a fish for several days; in the Kūrma [Kalpa], he is in the state of a tortoise; in the Vārāha [Kalpa], he has a solar abode; and in the Nārasiṃha [Kalpa], there is his birth. ||7||

In this case, when the seed of enlightenment—that is, the semen—falls into the center of the red [fluid] within the secret lotus, being endowed with life and accompanied by the *ālayavijñāna*, and having fallen into the secret lotus, it then possesses the characteristics of the ten stages.
Among those, within the womb, there are three stages: those of the fish, the tortoise, and Rāhu;
likewise, at the time of birth, there is one stage, that of Narasiṃha.

Even in childhood there are two stages: from the eruption of the teeth until the falling out of the teeth is the stage of Vāmana; from the falling out of the teeth until the sixteenth year is the first *vipulā* stage, the stage of Paraśurāma during youth; likewise, the other *vipulā* is the stage of Kṛṣṇa from the sixteenth year until the appearance of grey hair; the stage of Buddha is from the appearance of grey hair until the day of death; and on the day of death, because all elements have become unified within the body, the stage of Kalki occurs.
Even in old age, there is a single state of peace, and for those born from a womb, death is the final state; such is the rule of the ten stages.

Regarding the internal, O Vajradhara of the Mind, the activity of Viṣṇu’s ten stages is described by the words beginning with "Matsya" (the Fish): here, in the state of the Fish, the Bodhicitta-Vajra becomes the form of a fish for Viṣṇu for a certain number of days, up until the day of the *ṛtu* (seasonal period);
then, in the state of the Tortoise (*kūrma*), the state of a tortoise occurs, and by the word "and" (*ca*), this continues until the next day of the *ṛtu*.
In the state of Vārāhī, the abode of the sun—the source of the twelve sense-bases—arises from the Viṣṇu of the *bodhicitta*; this lasts until the third seasonal day.

Likewise, until the day of birth after seven months, birth occurs in the state of Nārasiṃha through the tearing open of the womb by the two hands. In the state of Vāmanī, the state of childhood arises until the emergence of the twenty teeth; then, in Rāmyā, they fall out again. Even though it is clear, she herself would employ deception in her activity.

In the Buddha [age] he performs peace; in the Kalki [age] he undertakes vows and observances and even goes to death. In Śukra, the marrow, bones, and channels arise; indeed, in Rajas, the skin, blood, and flesh. ||8||

In the [chapter on] the arising of body, speech, and mind, the great instruction on the determination of the four noble truths: The red seed germinates within the womb, having attained the essence of nectar; after one month, ten extremely subtle channels arise from the friendly sprout of the seed.

At the navel, there are another eight times eight [channels], which, moving upward toward the hands, feet, and mouth, slightly manifest the hands, feet, and mouth here when the second month is complete. 9.
In the state of Vāmana, the previously mentioned state of childhood occurs; in the state of Rāma, thirty-two teeth emerge; and in the state of Paraśurāma, they fall out.
He, that very Viṣṇu of the *bodhicitta*, would manifest deceit even when it is clear; he would employ illusion (*māyā*) in the state of action, and brings peace in the Buddha-state.
Even the vow and the discipline of sentient beings proceed toward death in the Kalki state.
When the state of Kalki arises, one undergoes death according to the previously mentioned procedure; this is the "ten incarnations" (daśāvatāra).

Regarding the Purāṇas composed here by wicked Brahmin sages, such as those concerning the Fish incarnation and others, they are intended to deceive the ignorant and serve as causes for attaining hell—this must be explained in detail in the forthcoming *Paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*.

The transformations of the semen and the menstrual blood residing in the mother’s womb, from conception until birth, are described by the words beginning with "semen" (*śukra*). In this body, six sheaths (*kośa*) arise for the newborn: from semen, marrow arises; bones arise; and sinews and ligaments arise. From the menstrual blood, skin and blood arise; and flesh arises from one [type of] blood, due to the sprouting of the seed of blood.

In this womb, for the duration of one month, the seed-blood sprouts while contained within the essence of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). After that, regarding the sprout of the seed: from the first month onward, ten kinds of channels (*nāḍī*) arise in the center of the heart as the supports for the vital winds (*prāṇa*) and so forth, which have become the sprout of the *bodhicitta*.
These are extremely subtle, with a measure equal to a hair.
At the navel, in the region of the navel, there are sixty-four channels—eight times eight—that carry the [vital energies] like staffs.

Although extremely subtle and unmentioned, there are twelve channels that serve as the support for the sixty-four [channels] by virtue of the transits of the twelve zodiac signs; likewise, all those aforementioned extremely subtle navel-channels, moving upward for the purpose of performing the actions of the hands, feet, and mouth, proceed from there toward the locations of the hands, feet, and mouth due to the power of their movement.

When the second month is complete, there is the emergence of the face, hands, and feet; here, after some time has passed from the previous fish-stage, five swellings appear at the locations of the face, hands, and feet during the tortoise-stage.

The two hands, two feet, and the neck become fully formed with a symmetrical head at the completion of the third month. In the fourth month, subtle channels (nāḍikā) form in the hands, feet, face, and the region of the neck. According to the Tibetan translation, the sequence is: "In the *paraśurāmya* [period], they emerge for thirty-two days and two royal [periods]; in the *rāmya*, they fall away."
The head, feet, and hands (*mukhacaraṇakara*);

in the *Vimalaprabhā*, based on the internal flesh, the bones, the marrow, and the crest [of the hair] arise in the fifth month, and in the sixth month, the flesh, blood, sensation, pleasure, and pain come into being. (10)

The tortoise state (*kūrmāvasthā*) occurs when the hands, feet, and neck have formed with a symmetrical head; furthermore, other subtle channels (*sūkṣmanāḍyaḥ*) appear in the hands, feet, face, and the region of the throat—namely, the extremely subtle *sahaja-sambhoga* channels at the six joints of the hands and feet and at the mouth and throat—once the fourth month has been completed.

In the fifth month, in the Vārāhī bhāva, relying upon the flesh and bones, there are three hundred and sixty bones and an equal number of joints, according to the rule "the sacrificial fire [is] with the essence. And in the sixth month—by the force of the word "and" (ca)—in the Vārāhī bhāva, flesh and blood come into being; sensation arises, and one experiences pleasure and pain. Through the power of higher knowledge (*abhijñā*), one recollects former lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*); by means of one's own mind, one practices detachment, censures the suffering of existence, and praises the path of the Buddha.

The eyebrows, the hair of the head, and the body hairs also arise in the best of sages; the remaining channels (nāḍikās) indeed appear after one month. Day by day, the count of the eyes [increases] by zero-zero (i.e., they remain as two).

The vital points (marmas), the bones, the marrow, the tongue, urine, and feces come into being. And in the eighth month, known as the "Orifice" (randhra), there is terrible suffering for the one oppressed by the birth canal at the time of delivery.
Then there are the hair, the pores, and the eyes and so forth.
Moreover, in the state of Vārāhī, when the seventh month of the best of sages is complete, the sense bases (*āyatana*) become fully formed.
Here, from the time of the month of conception onwards, at every daily interval, there are two hundred channels (*nāḍikā*), numbering as many as the "void-void eyes" (two hundred).

Then there are three hundred and sixty vital points (*marmāṇi*) and bones; within them is the marrow. The tongue arises as the *rasanā*, for the production of the gustatory faculty, while the eyes and other [senses] previously mentioned become solid. Then, at the time of the production of the tongue, urine and excrement arise here in the eighth month.

In the state known as Vārāhī, which is the ninth house, when the ninth month is complete—sometimes in the tenth, eleventh, or twelfth month—at the conclusion of the Vārāhī state, there occurs terrible suffering at the time of birth for the one born from the womb who is oppressed by the birth canal in the state of Nārasiṃha; such is the rule regarding the emergence of the fetus.

Regarding the Four Noble Truths, he speaks of the truth of suffering for those in cyclic existence, beginning with "in the womb" and so forth: "In the womb, there is the suffering of being in the womb; at the time of birth, and even in infancy, there is suffering; in childhood and youth, there is the great suffering of afflictions struck by the loss of wealth and power; in old age, there is the suffering of death; and once again, one takes up suffering from the six realms of existence, which is terrifying from the very beginning. This entire world is afflicted and deluded by illusion. (12)

In this world, for transmigrating beings, first of all, while remaining in the womb, there is suffering comparable to being boiled in a cauldron (*kumbhīpāka*); at the time of birth, it is like being crushed by a mallet or a mechanical press; even in infancy, it is like a pig consuming excrement; in childhood and youth, there is the suffering of separation from women, and the suffering of being deprived of wealth and prosperity due to its absence;
in old age, there is the suffering of decay and death; and again, at the end of death, there is the fear-inducing Raurava and other hells within the six realms of existence.
From the very beginning, fierce suffering arises in the realms of hungry ghosts and animals due to the power of evil and the abandonment of the ten wholesome actions.
Thus, through suffering, one grasps further suffering; this entire world, deluded by illusion (*māyā*), undergoes the arising of body, speech, and mind within the whole of existence.

In this *saṃsāra*, deluded by illusion—which consists of the notions of "I" and "mine"—one experiences suffering in the states of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. This is the great summary of the determination of the Four Noble Truths regarding the arising of body, speech, and mind.

He speaks of the Truth of the Path, beginning with "In cyclic existence" and so forth: "In cyclic existence, human birth may perhaps occur; at some point, an inclination toward the Dharma might arise. From that, through the power of merit, devotion to the Buddha arises and one enters the Primordial Vehicle (*Ādiyāna*). From that, a complete intelligence regarding the glorious Vajrayāna may occasionally exist, and within that, the cultivation of meditation. Within that, the desired state of Buddhahood exists in the station of supreme bliss—alas, entry [therein] is exceedingly difficult! (13)

In this saṃsāra consisting of the six realms of existence, human birth may occur somewhere; thereafter, at some point, humans may develop an inclination toward the Dharma, such as the teachings on giving and so forth found among non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthikas).
From that, by the power of merit, an attachment to the Buddha may occasionally arise, as well as an attachment to [the practice of] giving and so forth.
Furthermore, by the power of merit, one may enter the Initial Vehicle—that of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Therefore, "engagement in the glorious Vajrayāna" [is as follows]: *Vajra* is that which is indivisible, indestructible, and great.
That very vehicle is the Mantra system and the Pāramitā system, consisting of result and cause; when these have become unified into one, engagement in that is "engagement in the Vajrayāna."

Then, in some cases, one whose mind is entirely focused remains in a certain meditation—one consisting of non-referential compassion supported by referential emptiness—by the power of merit and wisdom; yet, in that meditation, Buddhahood is desired [only] thus. Alas, entry into the state of supreme bliss is exceedingly difficult and far, far more remote for worldly beings who long for the pleasures of cyclic existence!

He speaks of the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*) with the verse beginning "In the womb," and so forth: "In the womb is the perfectly pure body (*saṃśuddhakāya*); at the time of birth is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); and during the stage of the teeth [appearing] is the Enjoyment-body (*sambhogakāya*), O King.

From that, the Emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) arises for men, fixed until the limit of death. Thus, it exists in four ways, both internally in the womb and externally, through the division of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*). (14)

In this regard, first, according to worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*), the purified body and so forth are seen within the body of one born from a womb; subsequently, that very [body] of the Blessed Buddha, consisting of the perfectly purified body and so forth, is to be understood by yogins through the Dharma.
Here, as long as he remains in the mother’s womb, the embodied being possesses a body that is completely pure and endowed with the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijña*);
thereafter, beginning from the time of birth until the emergence of the teeth, it becomes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
From the emergence of the teeth until the falling out of the teeth, that is the *saṃbhogakāya* of the Victor, the Bodhicitta-vajra;
"O King" is an address.

From that falling out of the teeth, consciousness, the moon, and the sun, having entered the lotus in the womb, become the *śuddhakāya*. That which arises from the elements (*dhātu*) and aggregates (*skandha*) is the tenfold *dharmakāya* of the Victor.

Therefore, the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) arises by the power of qualities when hearing, sound, and so forth are produced; therefore, when hair and so forth are produced, the time of birth here is the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya). || 15 ||

In this womb, first of all, consciousness (*vijñāna*)—which is the *ālayavijñāna*—being present, together with bliss and gnosis (*jñāna*), as well as the moon and sun, which are the semen and blood, these three, situated within the lotus—that is, within the mother’s lotus—become unified for the sake of the formation of the embryo. That pure body (*śuddhakāya*) within the womb is called the Blessed One (*bhagavat*). From the state of the singular bliss of the *ālayavijñāna* of the mother and father, there arises the tenfold emergence of the elements and aggregates; that is the *dharmakāya* of the Victor (*jina*), the Vajra of Bodhicitta.

Therefore, when the internal sense faculties such as the ear and so forth, and their objects such as sound and so forth, have arisen, the *saṃbhogakāya* comes into being by the power of the [three] qualities (*guṇa*) and the power of the days.
Consequently, from the initial emergence of hair and so forth,
the production of body hair, feces, and urine, the time of birth, and the arising from the womb within the womb are called the *nirmāṇakāya*.

15–16. That which arises at birth, produced by the breath (*śvāsa*), is devoid of qualities and is the *śuddhakāya* (pure body); therefore, that which arises when the teeth emerge—even though speech is not yet distinct—is likewise the *dharmakāya*.
From the falling out of the teeth, O King, the *saṃbhogakāya* of the Jina is produced; and until the limit of death, the external *nirmāṇakāya* of the Lord of Jinas exists.

Then, when the four bodies arise externally, that which is the first emergence of the breath occurring in the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) is the *saṃśuddhakāya* (completely pure body) with respect to the sphere of *vāgvajra* (the vajra of speech), being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). That very [body] remains the *śuddhakāya* (pure body) through the flow of the central channel for as long as it lasts—that is, until the group of fifty-six and a quarter breaths.

Thereafter, by the power of the movement of the vital winds (*prāṇa*), the emergence of teeth occurs; that which is indistinct speech is the characteristic of *saṃjñā* (perception), and that is the *dharmakāya* with respect to the sphere of *vāgvajra*.
Therefore, for the twice-born, the falling of the teeth occurs at dawn; until the age of eight years, the Saṃbhogakāya exists due to clear speech.
Once the teeth have fallen, until the end of life, the Nirmāṇakāya exists externally.
Here, within the womb, there is a fourfold division of the body according to the differentiation of the bodies.

Externally, through the division of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇasaṃcāra*), there is a fourfold division of the body; internally and externally as well, there is the accompaniment of body and breath.

Here, the division of the body pertains to the semen (*śukra*), and the division of speech pertains to the blood (*rakta*). Thus, by way of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader, there is a fourfold division of the body through the division of the mind (*citta*); likewise, there is a fourfold division of the body through the division of knowledge (*jñāna*) characterized by the states of waking and so forth, and by way of the fourfold nature beginning with bliss (*ānanda*). This is the rule for the arising of the Sahaja-kāya and the others within the body and externally.

He describes the arising of body, speech, mind, and gnosis with the verse beginning with "In the womb," etc.: "In the womb, first there is here the glorious Body-Vajra; at birth, it produces the nature of Speech; at the emergence of teeth, Mind; and again, upon falling [from the teeth] and their regrowth, Gnosis-Vajra.

Gnosis mixed with consciousness, together with sun and moon—all this, beginning with Gnosis-Vajra, having taken root in the womb, gradually arises powerfully through the sequence of Body-Vajra and the rest. (17)

In this [chapter], the Great Summary on the Determination of the Four Noble Truths regarding the Arising of Body, Speech, and Mind: Here, within the mother’s womb, gnosis (*jñāna*) is coemergent bliss (*sahajānanda*), the *ālayavijñāna* mixed with consciousness (*vijñāna*). Accompanied by the sun and moon, and joined with the female and male reproductive elements (*rajas* and *śukra*), all [factors] beginning with Gnosis-Vajra and beginning with coemergent bliss come into being.
Once established in the womb, it gradually arises powerfully through the Body-Vajra and the rest.
In this regard, first, the glorious Body-Vajra (*śrīkāyavajra*) exists in the womb until the time of birth; the meaning is that it is the completion of the limbs of the body.
Then, upon giving birth, the vajra of speech arises; from that comes the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) and the emergence of the vital breath;
and from that, when the thirty-two teeth have appeared, there occurs the grasping of the designation of the mind (citta).
The word *vai* means "certainly" or "definitively.

Furthermore, from the falling out of the primary teeth until the emergence of the thirty-two teeth, the state characterized by the descent of seminal essence (*śukra*)—which is the characteristic of the *jñānavajra* and the characteristic of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*)—should be understood to last for twelve years in women and sixteen years in men; this is the explanation of the perfection of body, speech, mind, and gnosis.

He explains the relationship between the support and the supported with the verse beginning with "pṛthvī": Fire has the earth as its womb; yet it does not [possess] the earth and wind. Water has the womb of both wind and earth, for it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

O King, water is the support of the earth, and fire is the support of water. Wind is the support of fire, and space (*śūnya*) arises as the support of wind; thus indeed, that which is the support becomes the supported. (18)
[91] Here, fire (*hutāśa*) is the embryo (*garbha*) of earth, yet it does not belong to that family (*tatkulī*), because it lacks the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of the qualities of earth.

Earth and wind do not belong to the same family as that which resides in the womb of space (*ākāśagarbha*), in the midst of emptiness, because they lack the qualities of space. Likewise, water becomes the embryo of both wind and earth; that very [water] remains within the womb of wind in accordance with its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Wherever the wind moves, there it goes along with it.
That which is situated within the earth is seen as its inherent nature, appearing in a liquid form when the earth is being excavated;
furthermore, in this case, space is the support for all [elements] such as earth, while earth and the other elements are the supported.
Here, the support and the supported exist in their respective order.
Regarding the earth: just as the water-mandala is the support for the earthly sphere (bhūmimaṇḍala) externally, so too within the body, the fire-mandala (jvalana) is the support for the water;
and "anila" refers to the wind-mandala, which is the support for that water-mandala.
Just as wind is the support for the purifying circle of fire, and the void—space—is the support for the circle of wind, so too the void is the support for all elements, beginning with earth.

Regarding the support and the supported within the aggregate, he says "the aggregate," and so forth: the elemental [body] is indeed the support for the aggregates; in the excellent body, the channels are the support for the collection of elements; the vital breath is the support for the channels; and the tenfold consciousness is the support for the vital breath.

That mind possesses a dual nature by virtue of its qualities; it is both with-nature and without-nature. And the one who is the supporter and the support of these two—the unstruck (anāhata), all-pervading Lord who is bowed to by the three worlds—[is that very mind]. || 19 ||

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the internal [treatise]: here, in this body, the support for the five aggregates (*skandhas*) is indeed the elemental [body], the collection of elements such as earth and so forth.
For what reason? Because here, due to the absence of the primary nature (*prakṛti*) of earth and so forth, there is no causal condition (*pratyaya*) such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest;
and in the absence of the conditions of ignorance, formative forces (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth, there is an absence of the aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and the rest.

Since form consists of the four elements and the Great Being (mahāpuruṣapuṅgala) consists of the six constituents (dhātu), the physical body is indeed the support for the aggregates. Within this excellent body, there are seventy-two thousand channels (nāḍī) as the support for the collection of elements; and the vital breath (prāṇavāyu) is the support for those channels as well. Due to its being the cause of conditioned formations (saṃskāra), that breath is of ten kinds, which will be explained and described below.

Volition (*cetanā*) is the support for the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*). That volition becomes that very mind (*citta*) which possesses a dual nature: by the power of the qualities (*guṇa*), specifically through the power of *sattva* and *rajas*, it has a nature characterized by the states of waking and dreaming; and by the power of the quality of *tamas*, it becomes devoid of nature, characterized by deep sleep and lacking the sense faculties.
Furthermore, the master and support of these two—the one with nature and the one without nature—is the sustainer of the states of pleasure and pain for transmigrating beings.

And he who is devoid of pleasure and pain, honored by the three worlds, becomes the unstruck (*anāhata*), all-pervading, the end-maker of pleasure and pain, and the ultimate ground. Thus arises fragrance in the earth; likewise, taste in fire, the element of form in water, touch in wind, and sound in the space of peace (the *śānta*); and the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) in the sky.
Indeed, the progenitor of the Victors perceives emptiness as sound, the wind as the element of phenomena, fire as fragrance, water as form and taste, and the earth as touch alone. (20)

He explains the relationship of producer and produced among the elements (*dhātu*) with the words beginning "smell" (*gandha*), etc.: here, whether externally or internally, the production of smell occurs primarily in the element of earth (*dharaṇī*); furthermore, the word "also" (*api*) indicates possibility, meaning that the production of taste (*rasa*) and so forth occurs secondarily. In the fire-element (*śikhin*), which is the element of fire, the production of the sixfold taste occurs due to the cause of the fire's maturation; for that reason, from the element of form (*rūpadhātu*) in water...

In this world, the sprouting and so forth of rice and other plants arise primarily from water, which possesses various colors and various shapes; secondarily, however, there is also the production of sap and other elements.
Likewise, in the wind and the wind-element, the production of touch occurs; in the peaceful element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*), the production of sound occurs.
In the ether (*ambare*), within the fivefold essence-element (*rasadhātu*), the production of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*)—that is, the element of bodhicitta—occurs during the state of bliss.

Now the relationship between the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka) is explained: here, the accomplishment of the effect occurs through union with another family (parakula), because there is a contradiction in action within oneself through union with one's own family (svakula).
Therefore, union with another family is the cause for the arising of the body;
thus, the auditory faculty, which arises from the family of emptiness (śūnyakula), perceives sound, which arises from the element of consciousness (jñānadhātu).

"Indeed, [the verse] 'The progenitor of the Jinas' is certain; it describes how the mental faculty (*manaindriya*), which has arisen from the element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*), perceives the object-field (*viṣaya*) that has arisen from the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), namely 'wind. Because of the inseparability of the produced and the producer, the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*), which has become wind, perceives the object-field of odor (*gandha*), which has become the earth-element (*bhūmidhātu*). This is the verse beginning with "fire," which has been written as an addition.

Chapter 1: The Great Summary on the Determination of the Four Noble Truths Concerning the Arising of Body, Speech, and Mind. [The eye faculty] arises from the fire element and grasps the object of form produced from the water element; the tongue faculty arises from the water element and grasps the object of taste produced from the fire element; the earth element gives rise to the body faculty and grasps it; and the object of touch arises from the wind element. This is the rule regarding the characteristics of the subject and object, the grasper and the grasped, among the sense objects and their faculties.

He states the establishment of the aggregates (skandhas), such as form and so forth, within each element according to worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*), beginning with the words "established" (*siddham*) and so on: Form is established in the earth element, and in the water element that is the abode of the three worlds; the perception (*saṃjñā*) is established in fire, and sensation (*vedanā*) arises in the wind; the mental formations (*saṃskāra*) are established in the wind, and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is established here in this body when mixed with gnosis (*jñāna*) in the space-vajra; and all [factors] such as the elements and aggregates arise through the union with passion (*rajas*), the bodhicitta, and so forth. (21)

Here, the identity of the elements and the aggregates is stated as established: here on earth, form (*rūpa*) is established primarily, while perception (*saṃjñā*) and the others are established secondarily.
This applies within the domain of the three realms, which is the abode of the three worlds, but it does not apply to the phenomenon of nirvāṇa;
by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), perception is established in water.

In this system, Saṃjñā is the Moon of the nature of sound and phenomena; Śukra is of the nature of water. Because it is of the nature of water, Saṃjñā is established [as such], and "water" is the certainty. And in the case of Vahni (Fire), Vedanā is present; here, Sūrya is of the nature of fire and is Rajas. Kālī is the Rajas of Sūrya, and Vedanā has the nature of Kālī;
therefore, Vedanā is primarily established in Vahni, while the others arise secondarily.

In the wind element, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is established; thus, here the wind is that which moves body, speech, and mind, and is the producer of formations. Therefore, the formation whose nature is wind is established.

Likewise, consciousness (*vijñāna*), mixed with gnosis (*jñāna*) and accompanied by gnosis, is established respectively in the space of the vajra together with space—that is, in the sky—as consciousness characterized by auditory consciousness and so forth.
In the *kuliśa* (vajra), which is the element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*), gnosis is accomplished at the end of the emission of the bodhicitta, consisting of the moment of bliss;
here, the letter *kā* refers to the Great Being (*mahāpuruṣapuṅgala*) who consists of the six elements.
Why [is he so called]? He says: "all," meaning the elements, aggregates (*skandha*), and so forth.

Due to the union with *bodhicitta* and so forth, all that exists here in the body—the elements (*dhātu*), aggregates (*skandha*), and so on—becomes "dust" (*rajas*) through its conjunction with the states of the moments of bliss of the *ālayavijñāna* and the seminal essence (*śukra*).

He explains the nature of the apprehenders, such as the ear and so forth, by virtue of their grasping objects such as sound; thus he says "the ear," and so on: "The ear, O Lord of Men, has the nature of the Vajra; the mind has the nature of space; the nose has the nature of earth; and likewise, the tongue has the nature of fire."

The eye has the nature of water within the abode of the three worlds, and the body has the nature of air; thus, everything including the ears and other senses comes into being through the power of the qualities (guṇas) by means of the union of knowledge (jñāna) and consciousness (vijñāna). || 22 ||

In this context, regarding the nature of the body, the ear is characterized by emptiness as the subject; through its grasping of the object of sound, it has the nature of a vajra and the nature of sound.

Here, the subject-factor (*grāhaka-dharma*) is said to be a division of the body, while the object-factor (*grāhya-dharma*) is a division of existence (*bhāva*). Therefore, O King—this is the address—the nature of the produced and the producer is to be understood by means of the nature of the object.
The mind (*citta*) and the intellect (*manas*) have the nature of space and the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, because they grasp the objects of the *dharmadhātu*.

The nose has the nature of earth and the nature of odor; and because it grasps odor, the tongue likewise has the nature of fire, just as previously [stated] in the *Vimalaprabhā* regarding the birth of fire, it has the nature of taste because it grasps taste.

The eye has the nature of water, because it perceives forms produced by water within the abode of the three worlds; and since the body is not in *nirvāṇa* but possesses its own nature, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is produced by wind, because it perceives the object of touch.

In the sequence thus stated, everything beginning with the ear comes into being through the power of the qualities (*guṇa*); that is, by the power of sound, the *dharmadhātu*, smell, taste, form, and touch, there arise the ear, mind, nose, tongue, eye, and body—these six sense-faculties (*indriyadhātu*) are to be understood through their connection with primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*). By virtue of these six elements, he speaks of the six mental fluctuations such as stinginess and so forth, beginning with "stinginess": "Stinginess arises in the element of primordial wisdom; in Varatanu (the earth element) and in space, the diamond-mind of hatred [arises]; indeed, the mind of envy is manifested in air; likewise, the mind of passion [arises] in fire."

In water, the glorious Vajra-mind [arose] by the power of its natural quality; on earth, the Moha-vajra-mind arose; and in air, fire, water, and earth, all the others—speech, hands, feet, and anus—came into being. || 23 ||

In this body, the mind’s envy [is located] in the element of knowledge (*jñānadhātu*); here the locative case is used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe saptamī*), meaning that by virtue of the element of knowledge, there is a mind of envy in sentient beings.
In the sky, there is the "vajra of hatred" (*dveṣavajra*)—that is, by virtue of the space element (*ākāśadhātu*), there is a mind of hatred in sentient beings.

Likewise, by virtue of the wind element, there is a mind of jealousy (*īrṣyācitta*); by virtue of the fire element, there is a mind of passion (*rāgacitta*). This very point was made manifest by the Sage.

In the same way, pride arises in the mind by the power of the water element; delusion arises by the power of the earth element. Nature (*prakṛti*) consists of the qualities and intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of the elements such as gnosis (*jñāna*); by the power of those intrinsic natures, stinginess and other afflictions arise in the minds of transmigrating beings.
Regarding the action faculties (*karmendriya*) according to the elements, he says "speech," and so forth:

here, the speech faculty arises from the wind element, the hand faculty from the fire element, the foot faculty from the water element, and the anus faculty from the earth element. Since it was not explicitly mentioned, the secret faculty [arises] from the space element.
At the end of sixteen years, the divine faculty arises within the element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*); this is the regulation of the six organs of action.

From the six elements, the winds beginning with *apāna* are described by the verse beginning with "In *apāna*" and so forth: "In the element of gnosis, *apāna* is threefold; *prāṇa* is in the void (*śūnya*); *samāna* is in the center of the wind; furthermore, *udāna* is in fire; *vyāna* is indeed in water; *nāga*, *kūrma*, the wind *kṛkara*, *devadatta*, and *dhanañjaya*—these four arise respectively in wind, fire, water, and earth. (24)

In this body, the apāna wind arises from the element of gnosis (jñānadhātu); here too, the locative case is used in the sense of the ablative, and it is threefold due to its extraction of feces, urine, and semen. And the prāṇa wind arises in the void (śūnya), from the element of space (ākāśadhātu); by the word "and" (ca), that too is threefold according to its flow through the left, right, and middle channels.
Between the winds, the samāna wind arises from the nature of the wind element itself.
Furthermore, in the fire element (*agni-dhātu*) of Śikhin, there is udāna; in water, the water element (*udaka-dhātu*), there is vyāna;
and on earth—that is, in the earth element (*bhū-dhātu*)—there is nāga.
Intrinsic nature (svabhāva) truly arises (saṃbhavanti).

[Chapter on the Arising of Body, Speech, and Mind: The Great Summary on the Determination of the Four Noble Truths. Now, immediately following this, there are four winds beginning with Kūrma: from the wind element comes Kūrma; from the fire element, Kṛkara; from the water element, Devadatta; from the earth element, Dhanañjaya; up to the end of sixteen years, from the space element comes Ānandavāyu; and from the gnosis element comes Sahajānandavāyu.

By the power of the elements (*dhātu*), the joints of the hands and other parts of the body are called "wheels" (*cakra*) and so forth, beginning with the "uṣṇīṣa": The *uṣṇīṣa* of gods and humans arises from the element of space (*śūnyadhātu*); the secret place [the genitals] from the element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*); the heart-lotus from the element of wind (*vāyudhātu*); and the throat-wheel (*kaṇṭhacakra*) from the manifest fire (*śikhin*).

The lotus between the eyebrows, having eight petals (the Vasus) and sixteen petals (the Vasus), and the navel-wheel (*nābhicakra*) arise from water and earth respectively. There are six joints in the hands and feet; they correspond to earth, water, fire, and wind, numbering three each. (25)
In this context, from the element of space (ākāśa), there arises either a turban-lotus or a wheel;
the number of petals shall be stated later.
For gods and humans, it arises from the element of gnosis (jñāna-dhātu) as the secret, meaning the secret lotus.
The heart-lotus arises from the wind element;
the throat-chakra clearly blazes forth from the fire element; "hi" indicates certainty; and the lotus between the eyebrows arises from the water element.
The *vasu-vasu* [eight-eights] sixty-four-petaled navel-cakra (*padma*) exists in the earth element;
the singular number is used for the plural "six joints.
In the left foot of the hands and feet, there are three [joints] arising from the division of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas within the earth element.
The word *mahī* is a synonym for *bhū* (earth) with a short vowel;

there are three [cakras] in the right foot due to the division of the three qualities (*guṇas*) of the water element; there are three in the left hand due to the division of the three qualities of fire; and there are three in the right hand due to the division of the three qualities of wind—thus, the number three applies to the Maruts. These twelve cakras are to be explained in what follows; this is the rule for the eighteen cakras.

Now, he describes the arising of the fingers according to the elements with the verse beginning "Earth," etc.: In the five elements beginning with Earth, by the power of the threefold qualities (*guṇa*), there arose on the feet and hands ten fingers each, starting from the thumb and so forth, consisting of all the joints multiplied by three; these are to be understood as ending with the nails. Furthermore, in the division of the principles (*tattva*), whatever else exists on the beautiful body ending with the body hair, that likewise arises in the element. (26)

In this context, the fingers and toes of both the left and right hands, beginning with the thumb and ending with the little finger, consist of three joints each by virtue of the nature of the five elements and the three qualities (*guṇa*).
Thus, by the power of the earth element (*pṛthvīdhātu*), there is the thumb; by the lineage of the three qualities of the earth element, there are the three joints of the thumb.

Likewise, the index finger is of the nature of the water element (*toyadhātu*); similarly, the middle finger is of the nature of the fire element (*tejodhātu*); likewise, the ring finger is of the nature of the air element (*vāyudhātu*); and the little finger is of the nature of the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
Just as it is with the left hand, so it is with the right; thus it should be understood for the two feet.
Therefore, in both hands and both feet, the thirty joints—ten multiplied by three—along with the nails, are to be taken in their entirety.
The ten teeth are described as follows: here, if first two upper teeth appear for a child, then the right one has the nature of earth (*bhūmi*) and the left one has the nature of water (*toya*);
if they appear below [the upper row], then the right one has the nature of fire (*vahni*). [This is] clear (*sphuṭa*), O Lotus (*padma*).
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is stated: "The left [side] has the nature of wind (*vam*).

Likewise, again, the upper part has the nature of fire and wind; the lower part has the nature of earth and water; again, the lower part has the nature of wind and fire; and again, the upper part has the nature of earth and water.
Thus, by way of the four elements in both direct and reverse order, from top to bottom, the thirty-two teeth are to be understood."
When there are curved teeth, then it is the space element (*ākāśadhātu*);
thus, the body hairs and head hair are to be known through the differentiation of the elements.

Whatever else exists on the beautiful body up to the ends of the body hair, all that is to be understood as consisting of the five elements; such are the transformations of the elements, comprising three and a half million varieties according to the distinctions of their functions.
The transformation of the elements occurs through the power of the semen and the menstrual flow; "the truth of origination is by means of the body" was thus spoken by the Blessed One.

This concludes the first great chapter, the Determination of the Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path of Suffering regarding the Arising of Body, Speech, and Mind, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja* following the *Śrīmūla-tantra*. || 1 ||

(2) The Great Summary on the Truth of Origination and so forth: Now, the collection of the support and the supported is described with the words beginning "In the secret," and so on: "In the secret place, the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*), and the navel, the innate body of the Victor is of the nature of being without intrinsic nature; in the heart wheel, O King, it becomes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); in the enjoyment wheel of the Victor, it becomes the Emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) by virtue of the [bodily] drops (*bindu*) and through the sequence of the presiding deities.
In the heart wheel, the throat wheel, and the head, there are the lotuses purified as the Dharma, Enjoyment, and Pure [bodies]. (27)

In this body, there are six wheels (*cakras*) which serve as the supports, and four bodies (*kāyas*) which are the supported. Among these, within the three secret lotuses (*guhyakamala*), the *sahajakāya*—due to the distinction between having intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāva*) and lacking intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)—is the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) of the pure body (*viśuddhakāya*); it is devoid of intrinsic nature, its nature is non-conceptualization, and it is like a reflection (*pratisenopama*).
In the heart lotus is the *dharmakāya*, and in the throat lotus is the *saṃbhogakāya*, which is the presiding deity according to the division of the bodies.
"In the *bindu*" refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* as the presiding deity in the head-lotus, the *śuddhacakra*;

by way of the division of bodies, the *nirmāṇakāya* is the presiding deity in the navel, the *nirmāṇacakra*. This is the rule regarding the division of bodies. "By virtue of qualities" refers to the qualities of the wheels (*cakras*): the qualities of space and gnosis belong to the supports of the *sahajakāya*; the quality of wind belongs to the support of the *dharmakāya*; the quality of fire belongs to the support of the *saṃbhogakāya*; and the quality of water belongs to the support of the *nirmāṇakāya*. Thus is the relationship between the support and the supported.
According to the stated sequence, there is a lotus at the heart-cakra, the throat-cakra, and the head, known as the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Śuddha [cakras].

Likewise, in the navel, throat, secret place, head, and heart, and similarly in the center of the uṣṇīṣa, there exist for the Mother and the Father, respectively, the threefold Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind.

These are the six families: the wheel, the jewel, the space-lotus, the water-born [lotus], and the excellent sword, joined with the vajra. These [families] correspond to the three channels above and below, which proceed along the three paths through the divisions of moon, sun, and fire.
ga. *tattadevañca* from the root [text] of Dhātubho; dBen Pas (*viveka*); ka. kha. *mūla*.

In the chapter on the Great Summary of the Truth of Origination and so forth, the six families (*ṣaṭkula*) are taught according to the divisions of the support of the body, beginning with the words "in the navel" (*nābhau*) and so on: here, in this body, by virtue of the six elements, there are six families in the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*) respectively—three are the families of the mother, and three are the families of the husband, the father.

In the navel, at the earth wheel, there is the Wheel family (*cakrakula*); in the throat, at the fire wheel, there is the Lotus-Jewel family (*padmaratnakula*); in the secret place, at the gnosis lotus, there is the Sword family (*katikākula*). These correspond respectively to the body, speech, and mind of the mother.
Thus, on the head, in the water-lotus, there is the Lotus family; in the heart, in the wind-lotus, there is the Sword family;
likewise, in the center of the uṣṇīṣa, in the space-element lotus, there is the Vajra family.
Furthermore, the body, speech, and mind of the Lord are respectively the families of the female and male sexual fluids (rajas and śukra).
Of the transformations produced from the elements such as earth and so forth, in their respective order.

He explains those very things through the division of the channels of the winds, beginning with the words "those very" and so forth. Here, due to the division of the three channels of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, there arise the characteristics known as the "three channels": the feces channel, belonging to the *Cakra*-family, is in the *apāna*; the sun channel, belonging to the *Ratna*-family, is in the *prāṇa*; and the semen channel, belonging to the *Kartika*-family, is in the *apāna*. Thus, these are the three families (*tri-kula*) of the Mother, which are body, speech, and mind. Likewise, the moon channel, belonging to the *Kamala*-family, is in the *prāṇa*; the urine channel, belonging to the *Khaḍga*-family, is in the *apāna*; and in the center, in the *prāṇa*, the Rāhu channel, belonging to the *Vajra*-family, is present. These are the body, speech, and mind of the Father. This is the rule of the six families (*ṣaṭ-kula*).

The colors of the elements for the entry into the nature within the body are described by the words "in the body" and so forth: "The entry into the nature in the body is like space, of equal taste; and the body within the nature is to be known by those joined in yoga through the divisions of the colors of the elements and so on, according to the power of the qualities of the primary constituents (*prakṛti*):

yellow, black, and red are the colors [of earth, air, and fire]; white is [the color] in water; and blue and green occur in the space of gnosis (*jñāna*) and space (*ākāśa*), according to the specific divisions of the body and its nature. (29)
In this body, there occurs a mutual distinction between the grasping and the grasped among the elements (*dhātu*).

Therein, whichever element is the grasper becomes designated as "body" (*kāya*) by virtue of the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*); whichever is the grasped becomes designated as "entity" (*bhāva*) by virtue of that same totality.
Therefore, there is a mutual identity and a state of equal flavor (*samarasatva*) between the grasped and the grasper; thus, the entry of the entity into the body occurs.

Within the state of being (*bhāva*), the body is like space, possessing an equal flavor; it should be understood by those engaged in yoga through the distinctions of the elements, colors, and so forth, according to the power of their *prakṛtis*.

Here, the *prakṛtis* are the elements such as earth and the rest, which belong to the four [factors]: the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and so forth, and the objects of smell and so forth. Here, by way of the divisions of the body: the body-faculty, the object of smell, and the anus-faculty are yellow in color due to the nature of the earth-body and the influence of the state of being (*bhāva*); they are black in color due to the nature of wind (*vāyu*).

Likewise, the olfactory faculty, touch, the vocal faculty, and the excretion of feces are of the nature of wind and are black in color due to the differentiation of the body; earth is yellow due to the differentiation of its state. The visual faculty, taste, the manual faculty, and movement are of the nature of fire and become red in color by virtue of the body; they are white, being of the nature of water, by virtue of their state.

Likewise, the tongue faculty, color-form (*varṇarūpa*), the foot faculty, grasping, and the water-natured [elements] become white in color through the differentiation of the body; by virtue of the state of the fire-nature, they become red in color.
Thus, one should understand the colors according to whether they belong to the earth, wind, fire, or water: in the earth-nature, the wind-nature, the fire-nature, or the water-nature.

Similarly, the ear faculty, the object of the heat-element (*gharmadhātu*), the bhaga-faculty, and the emission of semen—these are space-natured and are green in color through the differentiation of the body; while those of the earth-nature are yellow.
O Kha Dog Gi, regarding form (*varṇarūpa*):

according to the division of the nature of internal gnosis (*adhyātmajñānaprakṛtibhāva*), the eyes, the mental faculty (*manendriya*), sound, the divine faculty, and the emission of urine—these, being of the nature of the gnosis element (*jñānadhātu*), are blue by way of the division of time (*kālabheda*). Being of the nature of space (*ākāśaprakṛti*), they are green by way of the division of existence (*bhāvabheda*).

Therefore, in the space of gnosis (*jñānākāśa*), there arises blue and green through the various distinctions of bodily states; such is the rule for the colors of the natural bodily states. Regarding the embrace of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*) and the elements such as bone and flesh, he says "wisdom" and so forth: Wisdom and means are bone and flesh, along with water and blood; fire is urine, and wind is feces. In the excellent body, the void is semen, and the illustrious *rajas* is mind itself. From the ear arise sound and the others, according to the family of their respective Conquerors, as well as speech, form, and so forth. Thus, the goddesses together with the Buddhas—the objects and the subjects—are to be understood within the mandala. (30)

In this body, wisdom (*prajñā*) is the bone element (*asthidhātu*) and method (*upāya*) is the flesh element (*māṃsadhātu*). Their mutual conjunction is like that of earth and the formative factor (*saṃskāra*). According to the teaching that "that which is the state of solidity is the earth element," wisdom and method are thus bone and flesh. Likewise, wisdom and method together with the water element—namely, saliva and blood—are the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*); similarly, fire is heat and urine is perception (*saṃjñā*); these two arise from wisdom and method.
Now, is it not the case that the semen-element is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), and why then is it called urine?

Here, in this body, that which is perception arises from the flow of urine in a newborn infant; that knowledge of great bliss (*mahāsukha-jñāna*) occurs until the limit of sixteen years due to the nature of the emission of semen. Therefore, because of the distinction that urine is the property of perception and semen is the property of knowledge, urine is the aggregate of perception.

Thus, wind is the element of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*), and the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is emptiness; the dust-element (*rajodhātu*) is the semen, which is the consciousness-element (*vijñānadhātu*).
Thus, in the excellent body, wisdom and means exist as the glorious dust, the object of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is indeed the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

In this way, from the ear, sound and the others are distinct: sound is wisdom (*prajñā*) and the ear is the means (*upāya*); smell is wisdom and the nose is the means; form is wisdom and the tongue is the means; touch is wisdom and the body is the means; the *dharmadhātu* is wisdom and the mind (*manas*) is the means; the discharge of feces is wisdom and the anus is the means; movement is wisdom and the feet are the means; grasping is wisdom and the hands are the means; speech is wisdom and the organ of speech is the means; the act of urination is wisdom and the female organ (*bhaga*) is the means; or else, the male organ (*liṅga*) and the emission of semen are wisdom and the *śaṅkhinī* organ is the means.
According to the power of their own respective Buddha-families, the deities—earth and the others—are of the nature of speech and so forth, as well as the organs of action and so forth;

thus, in the order described, these goddesses, earth and the rest, together with the Buddhas Vairocana and the others, are to be explained in the mandala to be described as the objects and subjects. This is the rule for the mutual embrace of wisdom and method (*prajñopāya*). Now, the function of the moon, sun, semen (*śuka*), and ovum (*rajas*) is stated, beginning with the words "the channel" (*nāḍī*):
Having established six thousand channels within the womb, multiplied by the sun [twelve], when a year is complete, the moon abandons its increase and the sun brings about its increase,
O Body;
these are wisdom and method.
The portion "ka pustake nāsti" is not present in manuscript *;
"sarvabuddhā" is not present in manuscript *; [the portion] "kha pustake nāsti" is not present in manuscript *; and "ga. sarvabuddhā" is not present in manuscript *kha.
In twelve years, the Sun abandons the increase of the elements within its own body; it produces the cutting of the channels (nāḍī) day by day, according to the sequence of the number of pairs. [31]
In this body, from the first month of gestation onwards, two hundred channels (nāḍīs) arise each day;

within a month, by means of thirty days, the number reaches six thousand. By the end of twelve months, through three hundred and sixty days, the number of channels reaches seventy-two thousand, as six thousand multiplied by the sun (twelve) and doubled [for both sides] occurs within the womb.

By the word "and" (*cakārāt*), even externally, up until the end of twelve months, there is the *garbhādhāna* [of the elements] for him; having excluded one month, when the year is complete, the Moon (*śaśadhara*) abandons its increase. By the word "and," it is by thirteen months that the Sun (*arka*) effects the increase. Then, once the measurement of the number of the lunar and seminal channels (*nāḍī*) and the elements (*dhātu*) has been determined, the Moon causes the increase of the elements and the menstrual flow (*rajas*) for twelve years.
By the word "and," the semen (*śukra*) also effects the increase of the elements.
In twelve years, the sun abandons the increase of the bodily constituents within its own body; for women, this lasts until the onset of menstruation (*rajaḥ*), which is the increase of the sun.
For men, it lasts until the age of sixteen, until the production of semen (*śukra*); the word "and" (*ca*) is used here as a conjunction.

In this way, the cutting of the channels (*nāḍī*) also occurs daily when giving birth, following the sequence of even numbers; this shall be explained in detail as it is about to be stated. This is the rule for the increase of the channels and the elements (*dhātu*).

Now the principles (tattvas) beginning with space are described, starting with the words "the venerable elements" and so forth: "The venerable elements, the ten sense organs, the five organs of action, and the five subtle elements (tanmātras) are declared; along with the mind possessing qualities, as well as intellect, ego, and the divine [principles]—these are the principles within the body, the abode of the three worlds. This is the experience of the All-pervading Lord, who consists of the five aggregates, who has entered the threefold state of existence, and whose nature is acquired through his own karma. (32)

In this body of the child, there are the five elements, the five sense organs, and the five [elements] beginning with space, such as the ear and so forth; thus, these ten are together in one place. Likewise, the five organs of action and the five subtle elements (tanmātras)—namely, the subtle element of sound and so forth—are said to be present.
Furthermore, the mind is endowed with qualities; that is, the mind is accompanied by the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas.

Thus, intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and the divine primordial nature (prakṛti)—these are the twenty-four principles; this is the experience within the body, which is the abode of the three worlds, as well as externally. Of what kind of Lord is this?

The experience of the *puruṣa*, who possesses the nature of a grasper, consists of the twenty-fourfold *prakṛti*—which, according to worldly convention, comprises the five aggregates, exists within the three realms of existence, and is acquired through one's own karma. Now, the characteristics of earth and the other elements within the body are described, beginning with "earth": Earth is solidity; water is fluidity; fire is heat; wind is lightness; space is the cavity or void; the skin is firm bone; Mount Meru is the best among mountains; and here, rain is nectar.

In the Vimalaprabhā, the vajra and sound are wind; excrement and the ghaṭikās are the pair of inhalation and exhalation; by pairs [of these], there is one transition (saṃkrānti) consisting of eighteen hundred [breaths]; and by the luminaries, there are the divisions of the apertures. ||33||
In this body, earth is solidity, water is fluidity, fire is heat,
and wind is lightness, by which it performs contraction and expansion.

The cavity is the void; the firm bone is the spinal column, extending from the waist to the shoulders, which is Meru, the best of immovable mountains. The rain that is external is here in the body the nectar (*amṛta*), the flow of *stukā* from the tongue and the *lambikā*.
The thunderbolt (*vajra*) is the sound in the heart; the roar is that of the intestines.
The wind,
which externally consists of sixty *pāṇīpala*s in one *ghaṭikā*, is in the body a pair of inhalations and exhalations— a pair of outgoing and incoming breaths— known as the *prāṇa* wind; thus,
a single *saṃkrānti* occurs through eighteen hundred of these pairs, that is, two times nine hundred.

Externally, there is a transition every three months and three days; internally, there are five channels that carry the five maṇḍalas, and in astrology, the planets beginning with the Sun constitute the ten divisions of the apertures (randhra).

Here, the anal aperture is the Moon, the urinary aperture is the Sun, the seminal aperture is Kālāgni, the oral aperture is Rāhu, the right eye aperture is Maṅgala, the left eye aperture is Budha, the right nostril aperture is Bṛhaspati, the left nostril aperture is Śukra, the right ear aperture is Manda (Saturn), and the left ear aperture is Ketu.

Furthermore, the differentiation of the six sense organs for these [planets] beginning with Maṅgala will be explained in the fifth chapter as it is about to be stated; such is the rule regarding Earth and the other elements.

Now, the constellations and so forth are described by the verse beginning with "nakṣatram": The constellations are the rows of teeth; the daily ghaṭikās arise from the divisions of the joints. The channels (nāḍīs) are the rivers, the machines, and the clouds; the lunar digits are the elements of dual nature.

The body hair, lice, semen, and the host of worms constitute the fourfold source of beings (bhūtayoni). The joints of the big toe begin with Nanda; the lotus is the head, and the power (śakti) is the secret lotus.

Together with Abhijit, there are twenty-eight constellations (*nakṣatras*) according to the division of the wheel of seven spokes; four are the staff-constellations (*daṇḍanakṣatra*), and four are the spoke-constellations at the four corners—thus there are thirty-two.

Due to the distinction of the forward and reverse movement of the teeth, fourteen constellations are situated in the upper wheel and fourteen in the lower wheel. Because of the division of the two half-wheels, the rows of teeth are formed above and below; thus, the row of teeth is the constellation.

In this context, the divisions of the junctions (*sandhibheda*) consist of the days and *ghaṭikās*; thus, every day there are sixty *ghaṭikās*, and by means of the days of the years, these become the number of breaths (*śvāsa*).
Those *ghaṭikās* amount to three hundred and sixty days, and those likewise become three hundred and sixty junctions; such is the junction (*sandhi*).

Regarding the statement "the channels are the rivers": in this world-system, externally there are seventy-two thousand rivers that flow to the ocean; internally, there are seventy-two thousand channels that carry the vital essence (*rasa*).
The term *antrameghāḥ*—where *antra* is an indeclinable word—means that the intestines (*antrāṇi*) are clouds, because they flow with essence and possess the characteristic of roaring.

The elements of the other lunar digits possess a twofold nature; here, "digit" (kalā) is twofold: one is by way of the transformation of the elements such as hair and so forth, and the other is by way of the quality of the emission of semen (*śukra*). Furthermore, among these two, those which exist through the transformation of the elements such as hair and so forth are also twofold, according to their further division.

In the chapter on the Great Summary of the Truth of Origination and so forth, titled "The Portion of the Moon," it is stated here that the subtle hair and the coarse hair correspond to the first and second lunar days (*tithi*); likewise, the skin corresponds to the third and fourth; the blood to the fifth and sixth; similarly, the flesh to the seventh and eighth; likewise, the channels (*nāḍī*) to the ninth and tenth; similarly, the bones to the eleventh and twelfth; likewise, the marrow to the thirteenth and fourteenth; and similarly, the semen corresponds to the fifteenth and sixteenth portions (*kalā*). This is the rule regarding the elements (*dhātu*) having a dual nature.

Now, the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) is described by the passage beginning with "hair" (*loma*), etc.: here in this world-system, the source of beings is fourfold. Here, the earth-source is external stationary beings (*sthāvara*), while internally it is hair; the wind-source is externally egg-born beings (*aṇḍaja*), while internally it is lice; the water-source is externally worms and the like born from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*), while in the body as well there are worms and the like; the external womb-born (*jarāyuja*) are produced from semen, while internally it is semen itself; and since it was not mentioned externally, the space-element consists of spontaneously born beings (*upapāduka*) in the form of fluids, while internally they are subtle living beings in the form of eggs. Thus, the source of beings is fourfold.
Regarding the phrase "Nandā and so forth, on the thumb-joint": here, the five lunar days beginning with the first (pratipad) are called Nandā and so forth.

Due to the distinction between the bright and dark fortnights, these lunar days—Nandā and the rest—correspond to the joints of the fingers of the left hand, consisting of three joints each, starting from the little finger and the thumb, according to the division of the elements beginning with space (*ākāśa*).

The joints of the fingers of the right hand are fifteen, according to the divisions of earth and the other elements, and according to the divisions of the joints of the thumb and the other fingers; likewise, the joints of the toes of the feet are to be known by the divisions of the lunar days (tithis) of the second month. Thus, for each season, there are six revolutions in a year consisting of six seasons; this is the rule for the joints of the thumb beginning with Nanda. Furthermore, the lotus [of the heart] is the head, and not reaching the navel is the Śakti; thus it becomes the Sahaja-body according to the previously mentioned method—this is the rule for the Śakti.

Now, heaven and the other realms are described, beginning with "The Egg of Brahmā" (brahmāṇḍam): "The Egg of Brahmā is the world of heaven; the hands and feet are the worlds of mortals and the netherworlds (pātāla). The oceans, continents, and mountains are the elements—liquid, soft, and hard—which possess the three natures.
The salt ocean is their urine; O King, the ring of fire is their blood and skin; and all the Siddhas are their hair, established through manifold divisions within the abode of the three worlds. (35)
In this body, from the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) down to the throat center (*kaṇṭhacakra*), the heavenly world (*svargaloka*) exists;
the two hands are the mortal world (*martyaloka*);
and the two feet are the netherworld (*pātālaloka*).
The oceans, the islands,
and the seven mountains are, respectively,
the seven liquid elements in the body, which are the seven seas.

Among those, the salt ocean is urine; the wine ocean is sweat; the water ocean is phlegm (*stuka*); the milk ocean is the milk of women and the phlegm-constituent (*śleṣmadhātu*) of men; the curd ocean is the brain matter of the head; the ghee ocean is fat; and the honey ocean is semen—thus it is stated in the *Vimalaprabhā*. Likewise, as for the continents: Jambūdvīpa has twelve spokes; in the twelve sections of the hands and feet, the flesh is Raudra, the liver is Kālaja, the Krauñca is the kidneys (*bukka*), Kuśa is the fat (*meda*), Sitābha is urine, and Candra is the channels (*nāḍī*)—these are the soft constituents (*mṛdudhātavaḥ*).

The "mountains" (*śailāḥ*) are the vajra-mountains; the toes and fingernails are the Snowy Mountain (*Śītādri*); the bones of the forearms are the Droṇa mountain; the bones of the upper arms are the Maṇikara mountain; the bones of the feet are the Niṣadha mountain; the bones of the shanks are the Mandara mountain; and the bones of the thighs are the Nīlābha mountain—these are the seven mountains of the solid elements.
The eighth is Meru; this is the rule for the skeletal frame of the body from the waist up to the shoulders.
The elements possess the three natures of fluid, soft, and hard; "the circle of fire and wind" means the circle of fire is red, and "the circles of wind are skins," O King— this is the address.
The hairs are all perfected; they are perfected through many divisions within the abode of the three worlds.

Here, in this external world-system, they are perfected in three ways: those who move in the sky (*khecarāḥ*), those who move on the earth (*bhūcarāḥ*), and those who dwell in the netherworld (*pātālavāsinaḥ*).
Among them, the sky-goers are the hairs of the head; the earth-goers are those produced in the armpits; and the netherworld-dwellers are those produced in the female organ and the male organ.
Because they have not been specifically mentioned, the rule regarding heaven and so forth is that they possess three and a half crores of characteristics.

Now, the triad of fires is described starting with the word "heart": "In the lotuses of the heart, throat, and navel, the thunderbolt (Indra), the sun (Agni), and the fire-arrow (Yama) shine forth in sequence; [these are located] in a bow-shaped, circular, and four-cornered sacrificial pit for daily oblations.

Above them is the Supreme Fire, whose pure hands are radiant, whose form is knowledge, and at the end of whose darkness neither the sun, nor lightning, nor the Lord of the East (Indra), nor the moon, nor the planets, nor the stars and so forth are found. (36)
In this body, there is a triad of fires: the Dakṣiṇāgni, Gārhapatya, and Āhavanīya.

Correspondingly, in the heart-lotus shaped like a bow, the Paviragni (lightning-fire) resides; in the circular throat-lotus, the Sūryāgni (sun-fire), which is the Gārhapatya; and in the square pit of the navel, the Kravyādāgni (flesh-eating fire), which is the Āhavanīya. These manifest in succession, and there is a rule regarding the daily oblation in the ocean-cornered pit.
Above them is the supreme fire, which has pure, flashing rays and is the embodiment of gnosis (*jñānamūrti*); it is unbroken at the end of darkness within the secret lotus and the forehead lotus.

In that place where neither the sun, nor lightning, nor the moon, nor the planets, nor the stars and so forth exist, there is first the "flesh-eating" fire (*kravyādāgni*), then the fourth, the true fire which is the embodiment of gnosis; such is the rule regarding the three fires.

[99a] Now, the days of the week (*vāra*), the *ghaṭikās*, and so forth are explained starting with the words "the days": The days of the week are on the petals of the heart-lotus; the *ghaṭikās* are manifest on the navel-lotus; and the sixty [units] are indeed the place of the day at the center of the earth. O King, the *manu* is also in the wheel of enjoyment (*sambhogacakra*), and the lunar mansion (*ṛkṣa*) is likewise there. Furthermore, the yogi should know that the *ghaṭikās* are in the navel-lotus; the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*) are the *pāṇīpalas* throughout the entire manifest body, at the joints of the hands, feet, and so forth. Here, externally, there are seven days of the week.

The eighth *kulikā* is the *bhukti* (consumption) within your body; there are eight [planets] in the eight petals of the heart-lotus: the Sun on the eastern petal, the Moon in the southeast, Mars in the south, Mercury in the southwest, Jupiter in the west, Venus in the northwest, Saturn in the north, and Ketu in the northeast during the consumption of the *kulikā*; Rāhu is in the other half of the consumption. These are the manifest *ghaṭikās*, and there are sixty in the navel-lotus as well.
There are four petals that carry the empty *ghaṭikās*; the remaining sixty petals are those that carry the sixty *maṇḍalas*, and thus there are sixty *ghaṭikās* for each day of the week.

Among the sixteen petals at the center of the brows, two petals carry the void (*śūnya*), while on the fourteen petals are the fourteen words of the Moon, beginning with "bhūta-abhūteṣu" and so forth.

There, on the first petal is *bhūtā*, which is a word consisting of five *ghaṭikās*; likewise on the second and third is *vedā*, which consists of four *ghaṭikās*; on the fourth petal is *śikhini*, which consists of three *nāḍīs*; and on the fifth is the word (*padam*).
The word *kara* is a term consisting of two *ghaṭikās* located on the sixth petal;
the word *śaśin* is a term consisting of one *ghaṭikā* on the seventh, which is the seventh petal.

Thus, in reverse order, there is a term of one *ghaṭikā* on the eighth, one of two *ghaṭikās* on the ninth, one of three *ghaṭikās* on the tenth, one of four *ghaṭikās* on the eleventh, and one of five *ghaṭikās* on the twelfth. It should be understood that it is the same for the thirteenth and fourteenth as well.
"O King," is the address; "the lunar steps (candrapadāni) are as many as the number of men"—
in the enjoyment wheel (sambhogacakra), that is, the throat wheel with thirty-two petals, four petals are empty.

On the other twenty-eight petals, there are the twenty-eight lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) together with Abhijit; these are arranged counter-clockwise on the seven prior spokes: in the middle [spoke], ending with Revatī;

in the second, Aśvinī; in the third, Bharaṇī; in the fourth, Kṛttikā; and from there, the staff-mansion (*daṇḍanakṣatra*) is on the seventh spoke. These are known as the channels (*nāḍīs*) of the seven-petaled [lotus].

Then, on the seven northern spokes, moving counter-clockwise: Rohiṇī is on the first spoke, Mṛgaśiras on the second, Ārdrā on the third, Punarvasu on the fourth, Puṣya on the fifth, Aśleṣā on the sixth, and Maghā on the seventh. In this same manner, the others are to be understood as well. Furthermore, it should be known that there are sixty *ghaṭikās* within the central nave of the constellations.

The *nāḍīs* are sixty *pāṇīpala*s; there are three hundred and thirty-six of these in every joint of the limbs, such as the hands and feet, as will be explained in detail later. This is the rule for the days of the week and so forth. Now, the movement of the power of the vital breath (*prāṇa-śakti*) through the wheels (*cakras*) starting from the navel is described with the words beginning "at the navel" (*nābhītyādi*): "At the lotus of the navel, which has twelve petals like the sun, the supreme digit (*parakalā*) revolves, migrating in succession. This transition occurs in two hundred and eighteen breaths (*prāṇa-yugma*), O King, at the junction of the Kali age."
