That lagna in which the sun remains and revolves day and night is to be known; one should understand the measure of the lagna, as well as the wealth, the debt, the equinox, the solstice, and the clockwise measurement.

(38) Just as here in the external world the sun revolves through the twelve zodiac signs by means of the different transits (*saṃkrānti*) throughout the year, so too within the self the vital energy (*prāṇaśakti*) revolves through the twelve signs every day by means of the different transits.
The supreme power, the vital energy, revolves in the lotus of the navel upon the solar petals; moving in succession, it passes through the petals of the twelve zodiac signs.
"Transit occurs by pairs of breaths, [numbering] two hundred and ninety.
Here, externally, one transit of the sun occurs in eighteen hundred *daṇḍas*; likewise, there is no "half" (*dala*) among the *bhṛta* and *abhṛta* [days], O [Bhagavan].
Regarding the elements and non-elements (*bhūtābhūteṣu*),
there is one *ghaṭikā* of the word.
O, thirty-six hundred! (3,600)
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is stated that with eighteen hundred breaths, the vital energy (*prāṇaśakti*) undergoes a transition (*saṃkrānti*) into one petal;
and that occurs here at the Cancer (*karkaṭa*) ascendant, O King, for externally, Cancer is the birth sign (*janmarāśi*) of the Sun.

In this way, among all birth stories (*jātaka*), the zodiac sign in which one’s birth occurs should be understood as being designated "Cancer" (*karkaṭa*), according to the principle that "the sign of birth is the locus of life. Thus, there is the address "O King" (*narendra*) when the Cancer ascendant (*lagna*) is present.
That [sign] should be understood by means of the division of the seven sticks (*saptasalākā*) as being where the sun, situated externally, revolves day and night from the time of its rising.

It should be understood that just as the duration of the sun’s transit (*saṃkrānti*) outside is to be known through days—whether deficient or excessive—so too within the self it is to be known through breaths (*śvāsa*), whether deficient or excessive. Thus, by means of the division of the sun’s hours (*daṇḍa*), there is a regulation of breath in the body: for the vital wind (*prāṇa*), there is a debt or wealth, and an equinox (*viṣuva*); from Cancer onwards, by virtue of the sun’s quarters (*pāda*), there is debt, while from Capricorn onwards, there is wealth.

According to the procedure stated in the *Jyotiṣa*, the day of the equinox (*viṣuva*) or the day of the transit (*saṃkrānti*) consists of fifty-six and a quarter *daṇḍas* externally; internally, it consists of breaths according to the distinction of each zodiacal sign (*lagna*) transit. Thus, there is the revolution of the twelve transits.

Now, the flow of the five mandalas within each lotus petal is described, beginning with the words "one by one" (*ekaika*), etc.: In each lotus petal, Earth flows in the west and Water in the north; Fire flows in the right (south) and the east, and Space flows in the middle of the petal.

The transition (*saṃkrānti*) flows through five divisions, and the equinox (*viṣuva*) consists of sixty minus one breaths (*niḥśvāsa*). Thus, the divisions of the transitions occur at every moment of the day according to the divisions of the zodiac signs (*lagna*).
In this external world, during each single transition of the sun, there is the enjoyment of the five mandalas.

The enjoyment of the five mandalas occurs in thirty days; the enjoyment of one mandala occurs in six days, which is three hundred and sixty *daṇḍas*. Likewise, internally, the enjoyment of the five mandalas occurs in eighteen hundred breaths, and the enjoyment of one mandala occurs in three hundred and sixty breaths; such is the rule.
In this regard, on each individual petal of transition there are five locations—the west, north, south, east, and the center.

Therein, on each lotus petal, the earth mandala flows in the west; on the north petal of the leaf, the water mandala flows; the fire mandala flows in the south; furthermore, the wind mandala flows in the east;
and in the middle of the petal, the space mandala flows.
In each [transition], the vital power (*prāṇa-śakti*) consists of three hundred and sixty exhalations; thus, each transition occurs in five divisions.

In these maṇḍalas, within the midst of three hundred and sixty breaths, the equinox (viṣuva) flows, taking eleven and one-quarter breaths at each junction of the rising of the ascendant; it flows for sixty minus breaths, which is to say, it flows for thirty and three-quarters breaths. Now, the presiding deities of the five maṇḍalas are described, beginning with "Śūnya": the five principles beginning with space flow fixedly in the north; on the right [side] are earth and the others;
Rāhu and Agni; the Moon and the Sun; the Buddha and the Son of Earth (Mars); the Minister of the Daityas (Venus) and Jupiter.

“Fire, Earth, and so forth—these are the ten lords in the mandalas. O King, the Moon is the lord for six months in the north, and the Sun is the lord in the south. [End of] Chapter [XV]: The Great Summary on the Arising of Truth and so forth.

Here, externally, in the odd signs such as Aries and the rest, there is the enjoyment of the mandalas of space and so forth by the Sun; in the even signs such as Taurus and the rest, there is the enjoyment of the mandalas of earth and so forth.
Likewise, internally, the five principles beginning with space flow in a fixed manner through the left nostril: space, wind, fire, water, and the mandala of earth.
"Earth and so forth" means that the mandalas of earth, water, fire, air, and space flow through the right nostril.

Among these ten mandalas in the left (the non-right) and the right, respectively, during the time of their flow: in the left, the mandala of space has Rāhu as its presiding deity; in the right, Kālāgni; in the left, the mandala of air, Candra; in the right, Sūrya; in the left, the mandala of fire, Budha; and in the right, Maṅgala.
In the water mandala on the left is Venus, and on the right is Jupiter;
in the earth mandala on the left is Ketu, and on the right is Saturn.
Thus, there are ten lords over the mandalas beginning with space who are the possessors of the fields.

In this manner, for six months the Moon is the lord [of the breath] in the zodiac signs of Aries, Gemini, Leo, Libra, Sagittarius, and Aquarius, while the Moon— the lord of the semen-element (śukradhātu)— resides in the left channel (vāmanāḍī) in the north;
in the south, during the signs of Taurus, Cancer, Virgo, Scorpio, Capricorn, and Pisces,
the Sun is the lord of the blood-element (rajodhātu).
"O Lord of Men" is the address; this is the rule for the sovereign of the mandala.

Now, the winds beginning with *prāṇa* are described by the words "of that," and so forth: "In the region of the heart above that, situated upon an eight-petaled lotus, is the wheel of channels (*nāḍicakra*), where the host of winds beginning with *prāṇa* resides—the Sun, Moon, and Fire in the left, right, and middle respectively.

In the left, the white lunar channel indeed flows; in the right, the red solar channel; and in the middle, the one in the form of the fire of time (*kālāgni*) flows during the equinox (*viṣuva*), at sixty breaths less. (41)

Here, within the navel-cakra, there is a four-petaled [lotus] in the center; surrounding it is an eight-petaled one; surrounding that, a twelve-petaled one; and surrounding that, a sixty-four-petaled one.
By the word "petal" (dala), the channels (nāḍīs) characterized by the movement of breath are meant.

Above that navel-cakra, at a distance of twelve and a half finger-breadths upward, situated in the region of the heart, is the wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra), which has eight spokes and consists of eight channels.
Within those [petals], the group of winds beginning with *prāṇa* resides in the eight-petaled lotus.
"Fire" refers to Rāhu.

On the left, the lunar channel (*candranāḍī*) flows as the moon, white in color; on the right, the solar channel flows, red in color. In the center of the eight petals, the channel in the form of the fire of time (*kālāgni*), the channel of Rāhu, flows. At the equinox (*viṣuva*), at the junction of the rising of the ascendant, there are fifty-six breaths plus one-quarter (*sapāda*).
In this eight-petalled heart-lotus, the channels of the transits at each three-hour period (prahara) are to be known.
These are the carriers of the five maṇḍalas within the nostrils.
The movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) from channel to channel occurs through one hundred and twenty-seven inhalations and exhalations, which corresponds to seven and a half daṇḍas.

Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna, nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya—these ten kinds of winds are situated within the wheel of the channels (nāḍī-cakra) according to their various functions; they extend from the heart-lotus, which begins with the letter *i*, up to the śaṅkhinī, encompassing the entire navel-wheel.
kha. maṇḍaḥ; bho. pa (Śani); ka. dharmiṇo.
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the internal [system]: there, the *prāṇa* flows upward;
the *apāna* flows downward from the navel;
and the *samāna*, whose presiding deity is in the eastern petal, flows in the *rohiṇī* channel.
Udāna is in the southeast petal in the hastijihvā channel;
vyāna is in the southern petal in the piṅgalā channel;
nāga is in the southwest petal in the pūṣā channel.
Kūrma is in the western petal in the Jayā channel;
Kṛkara is in the northwestern petal in the Alambuṣā channel; Devadatta is in the northern petal in the Iḍā channel.
In the eastern petal, Dhanañjaya resides in the sky;

in the Suṣumnā is Prāṇa. In the Śaṅkhinī, which corresponds to the number of directions (ten), Bodhicitta flows; its presiding deity is Apāna. Thus, in this wheel of channels, the ten kinds of winds are situated according to their various functions.

The pervasion of all these, beginning with *prāṇa*, occurs throughout the seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍīsahasra*), yet the birthplaces of the eight [winds] are in eight locations. From the *śaṅkhinī* down to the heart-lotus of one’s own body, including the navel-cakra, constitutes the entire birthplace of the *samāna* and the others; such is the rule regarding the cakras. Now, the functions of *prāṇa* and the others are described, beginning with the word "prāṇa": *Prāṇa* performs the function of *prāṇa* while situated on the paths of the sun and moon, [consuming] all food and drink. *Apāna* leads [it] downward; *samāna* leads everything into a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) within the body.

The udāna wind vibrates within the body; the vyāna wind, by the power of its natural qualities, produces singing and dancing with the mouth, hands, and feet, and likewise causes disease as well as the bending of the limbs.
In this body, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), moving along the paths of the sun and the moon, produces vitality (*bala*);
the path of the sun is *piṅgalā* or *rasanā*,
while the path of the moon is *iḍā* or *lalanā*.
Regarding the phrase "gone along its path": the particle *tu* is for the sake of emphasis.
According to the tradition (*āgama*), all food and drink—that which has been consumed as solid nourishment or drunk as water and so forth—is led downward entirely by the *apāna* wind.
The wind called *samāna* leads everything to a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*), meaning it makes the seven constituents (*dhātu*) of equal flavor throughout the body.
The wind called *udāna* vibrates within the body; by means of the mouth, hands, and feet, it performs song and dance.
In this body, that very *udāna* produces singing and so forth with the mouth, such as laughter and conversation, performs dance with the hands and feet, and [performs] walking and so on.

Vyāna produces disease according to the power of its inherent qualities; thus, by the power of its watery nature, it causes a breaking of the limbs just as it causes disease. Nāga produces belching; Kūrma-vāyu, contracting the hands and feet, produces yawning; Kṛkara-pavana produces anger and total agitation; Devadatta produces yawning; and Dhanañjaya, O King, is the sole wind that does not abandon the body when it has reached the five elements. In this way, all the winds do not abandon the qualities inherent in their respective natures.
The *nāga* wind indeed causes belching; the *kūrma* wind, contracting the limbs and feet, causes them to become rigid; the *kṛkara* wind produces all forms of anger and agitation;
the *devadatta* wind causes yawning;
and when the body has reached the state of the five elements (*pañcatva*), the *ghanañjaya* wind does not abandon it.
"O Lord of Men" is the address.
"The wind alone is the winner of wealth" (dhanañjaya).

According to the sequence thus stated, all the winds—prāṇa and the others—do not abandon the qualities inherent in their respective natures; that is, they do not abandon the qualities of the natures such as space (ākāśa) and so forth. This is the rule regarding the functions of prāṇa and the other vital airs.
[In this] chapter: The Great Summary on the Truth of Origination and so forth.

Now, the designations of the channels (*nāḍī*) are stated by means of the terminology of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*), beginning with "Piṅgā" and so forth: "Piṅgā, Sūkṣmā, and Iḍā—the first [group]—are situated in the three paths; then Rohiṇī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, and the sixth, Jayā; Agā as well, and Vasu in the ninth, Alambuṣā, and Śrīkuhā.

O King, the tenth is Śaṅkhinī, which flows at the end of bliss; the essence of awakening (*bodhicitta*). This is the glorious wheel of channels (*nāḍicakra*), which exists in many forms through numerous varieties of junctions. (45)
The tenth *śaṅkhinī*, which is the *saṃkhyā-śaṅkhinī*, is that *śaṅkhinī* through which the bodhicitta flows at the end of bliss.
This is the glorious wheel of channels (*nāḍicakra*), which becomes manifold through numerous divisions of joints.
Here, in this body, the divisions of joints number three hundred and sixty; by means of those divisions of joints, there come to be three hundred and sixty divisions of the wheels of channels.
The rule regarding the network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) is that the non-differences between the nature of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are likewise to be understood in this way.
In Indra, Agni, Yama, Daitya (Nirṛti), Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yakṣa, Rudra, and in the center—in these locations, Śakti revolves day and night, assuming their respective forms.

Above that, in the throat-center (*kaṇṭhacakra*), the wheel of the constellations (*ṛkṣacakra*) is situated together with the host of planets; in the Brahma-egg, at the illustrious forehead, it flows as a white drop surrounded by vowels.

Now, the presiding deities of that very wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) are described, beginning with the word "Indra": here, on the petal of Indra, the power of breath (*prāṇaśakti*) assumes the nature of Indra for the duration of one watch (*prahara*);

on the petal of Agni, the nature of Agni; on the petal of Yama, the nature of Yama; on the petal of Nairṛti, the nature of Nairṛti; on the petal of Varuṇa, the nature of Varuṇa; on the petal of Vāyu, the nature of Vāyu; on the petal of Dhanada, the nature of Dhanada; and on the petal of Īśa, the nature of Rudra.
Thus, the vital energy (*prāṇaśakti*) revolves within these eight petals, assuming their respective natures; this is the rule regarding the natures of Indra and the other deities.

Now, the throat-cakra is described: here, at a distance of twelve and a half finger-breadths above the heart-lotus, in the throat-cakra, resides the wheel of the planets (*graha*) together with the wheel of the asterisms (*cakṣa*).
There are four staff-asterisms (*daṇḍanakṣatra*) and twenty-eight principal asterisms (*pradhānanakṣatra*).
By these [factors], there are thirty-two petals.

Having excluded the fourteen dandas of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the twenty-eight petals in a single day and night is determined by dividing sixty *dandas* and taking the quotient; this is the circulation within each individual petal.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa*, on the illustrious forehead, there is a white drop surrounded by vowels, which is flowing.

Above that throat-lotus, at a distance of twelve and a half finger-breadths, in the forehead-lotus which has sixteen petals, the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) occurs over fourteen petals—having omitted two petals—during one day and night.
From sixty *daṇḍas*, the omission of each individual petal occurs according to the quotient obtained by dividing by fourteen.
(From the *Vimalaprabhā*)
The internal emission of the drops (*bindu*) should be understood as occurring within the *kaṇikā* (pericarp), which is called the lunar station (*candrapada*).
Furthermore, in the navel wheel there are sixty-four channels (*nāḍī*) known by names such as Bhīmā and others; in the heart, eight [channels] known by names such as Iḍā and others;
and in the throat, [sixteen channels] known by the names of Aśvinī and others, as well as the names of the four twilights (*sandhyā*).
In the channel of the forehead, by means of the designations beginning with the first lunar day (*pratipad*);
and in the crown (*uṣṇīṣa*), by means of the four designations of the principles (*tattva*) according to the division of the four twilights (*saṃdhyā*).
Thus, one should understand that the eight-petaled wheel is contained within these petals of the lotuses of the throat and the forehead.
Thus, at the navel, heart, throat, and forehead, there is an eight-spoked wheel whose nature consists of earth, water, fire, and air;
at the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa), there is a four-petalled [lotus] whose nature is emptiness;
and at the navel, there is a four-petalled [lotus] whose nature is gnosis.
In the secret [cakra] there are thirty-two petals;
on the sixteen outer petals are the channels of the vowels;
on the ten inner petals are the channels of the aggregates and elements.
Then, in the inner petals, there are six void-nāḍīs;

thus, the total number of channels in the six cakras is one hundred and fifty-six. This should be stated regarding the six cakras that will be described hereafter. Such is the rule for the six cakras. At the base, earth and water flow in the left [nostril]; fire flows in the right; wind at the head; and space flows in the middle. Between the two nostrils, the equinox (viṣuva) flows according to the sequence of the nasal apertures.

These [channels] pierce through, and the power (*śakti*) proceeds to the supreme state, the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*), the end of the digits (*kalānta*). All [the channels], beginning with the fields (*kṣetra*) and others, are located in the hollow of the hands and feet, ending at the thumbs. Now, the flow of the five mandalas within the two nostrils is described by the verse beginning with "mūle" and so forth: here, in the left and right nostrils, the earth mandala flows at the base, in the lower part; water flows in the left [nostril], and in both the left and right nostrils [the other elements follow]. This is because of the indicator that Meru stands to the north of all [the directions] relative to the central line between the two nostrils.
The fire-maṇḍala flows in the right [nostril], and the right [maṇḍala] is the outer portion of both the left and right nostrils;
thus, the wind-maṇḍala flows at the top [of the head]. Between both nostril-pits—in the middle of the two voids, amidst the earth, water, fire, and wind-maṇḍalas—the space-maṇḍala flows.
When there is movement associated with the left conjunction, the flow of the maṇḍala is in the left; when there is movement associated with the right conjunction, it is in the right.
Furthermore, the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti) flows simultaneously through both nostrils as the equinox (viṣuva), which is the mandala of knowledge.

Thus, piercing these—the mandalas of the navel, heart, throat, forehead, crown (uṣṇīṣa), and nostrils—it proceeds by means of the divisions of the staff (daṇḍa), zodiac signs (rāśi), planets (graha), asterisms (nakṣatra), lunar days (tithi), and the mandalas of the twilights (sandhyā).

This energy, the vital power, goes to the supreme state, the supportless end of the twelve (dvādaśānta), which is the limit of twelve finger-breadths (dvādaśāṅgulānta), the end of the digits (kalānta), which is the limit of the sixteen digits (ṣoḍaśakalānta).
In this context, the wind of the earth-mandala flows from the nostril for twelve finger-breadths and then returns;
the wind of the water-mandala flows for thirteen finger-breadths and then returns;
the wind of the fire-mandala flows for fourteen finger-breadths and then returns.
The wind of the wind-maṇḍala travels fifteen finger-breadths and then returns;
the wind of the emptiness-maṇḍala travels sixteen finger-breadths and then returns;

the wind of the gnosis-maṇḍala, having entered the center at the ends of the earth-maṇḍala, flows for twelve finger-breadths in both nostrils, and having entered the middle at the end of space, it flows for sixteen finger-breadths.
In this context, when [the breath] increases externally, then it becomes short internally;

when it becomes short externally by sixteen [units] through the power of the *vāyu-nāḍī*, then it increases by four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) at the navel—this is the rule for the flow of the vital energy (*prāṇaśakti*).

Now, the fields (*kṣetra*) and so forth are described, beginning with the word "field": here in the body, there are two fields at the two joints of the arms; two secondary fields (*upakṣetra*) at the two joints of the thighs; and two *chandoha*s at the two upper arms—thus it is not [otherwise].

At the end of the maṇḍala, this is the great chapter on the origin of the family of channels (*nāḍīkula*) within the *Kālacakra-kulatant*ra concerning the battle between the Cakravartin and the Mlecchas at the two joints of the [arms]. The *upacchandoha* is at the two knee joints; the two *melāpaka*s are at the two wrist joints; the *upamelāpaka* is at the two ankle joints; the two *śmaśāna*s are at the palms of the hands; the two *upaśmaśāna*s are at the soles of the feet; the four great *śmaśāna*s are at the fingers of the hands; and the four *upaśmaśāna*s are at the fingers of the feet—such is the rule for the sacred sites (*kṣetra*) and so forth.

Thus ends the second major section, beginning with the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*), in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja*, which follows the *Śrīmūlatantra*.

**The Major Section on the Battle between the Cakravartin and the Mlecchas, the Kālacakra Kulatantra, and the Origin of the Family of Channels.** Now, the battle between the Cakravartin and the Mlecchas within one’s own body is described, beginning with the words "The Cakrin": The Cakrin is in the vajra [of the body]; the lords of the best of gods (the sense-faculties) are the twelve links [of dependent origination] obstructed; right knowledge is indeed Kalkī; and the elephants, horses, chariots, and servants are the noble Pramāṇas.
Each one possesses the name Rudra; Hanumān is the disciple of living beings, and the evil Mlecchendra is that which produces even the unwholesome and, being of wicked mind, bestows suffering.
Here, in this human body, he who was described as the external *cakrin* in the first chapter is the *vajrī* within the body, meaning the *cittavajra*.
Those twelve lords of the best of gods, beginning with Īśvara and the others, are the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*) that have been restrained.

He who is Kalkī is indeed perfect knowledge within his own body; for that reason, those external elephants, horses, chariots, servants, and the four noble immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are within the body. He who is Rudra externally is designated as the knowledge of individuality (*pratyekajñāna*) within the body; he who is Hanumān externally is the knowledge of the disciples (*śrāvakajñāna*) within his own body. Thus, within his own body, he becomes the Great Cakravartin together with his retinue, and Kalkī likewise.
Furthermore, he who is the wicked Mleccha king externally is the sinful mind within the body.

He whose mind is set on the external is the giver of suffering; thus, within the body, there is the path of unwholesomeness (akuśalamārga) known as Aśvatthāman, and ignorance (avidyā) is the entire host of Danu’s forces. In the battle against them, the fourfold destruction is the end of the fear of worldly existence (bhava), and glorious victory is the path to liberation (mokṣamārga).

On Mount Kailāsa, there is the gift of Dharma which removes the fear of existence, and the earth is filled with wealth. He who stands behind and before the teacher of gods and men has Brahmā and the Lord of Asuras as his sons.

Mañjuśrī, the Lord of the World, the conqueror of the three realms, is Śrīraja, the *bodhicitta*. On his back are the lineages of Brahmā and others; on the various great earths are the many pure Buddhas. O! Outside, in the great charnel ground (*dur khrod chen po*), there is indeed the illusory form (*māyārūpa*); in the external land of Makha, there is a battle with the Mlecchas, yet it is not a [physical] battle. He who is Aśvatthāman outside is the activity of ignorance (*avidyā*) within the body. That which is the army of Danu outside—consisting of elephants, horses, and infantry—is the fourfold faction of Māra within the body.

His withdrawal in battle is the destruction of the fear of worldly existence within one's own body; that which is the victory of the external Great Chakrin Kalki over the Mlecchas is the attainment of the path to liberation within one's own body;
and that which is the bestowal of Dharma by the Great Chakrin on Mount Kailāśa externally is the removal of the fear of worldly existence within one's own body.
That earth which is filled with external substances is, within the body, the pure collection of elements (*dhātu*).

Those two sons of the Wheel-Bearer (*cakrin*) who existed externally as Brahmā and Īśvara became, respectively, the teacher of Dharma in the single region behind [the center] and the Lord of the World (*lokanātha*), together with Mañjuśrī, the conqueror of the three worlds, in the foremost region in front, seeking the destruction of the Mleccha religion. That is the passion (*rajas*) and the bodhicitta that bestows bliss; it is the mind of aspiration (*praṇidhānacitta*) and the mind of setting out (*prasthānacitta*).

Those various lineages beginning with Brahmā that exist in the back [of the body] are, within one's own body, the many pure Buddhas whose nature consists of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense-bases (āyatana). Thus, there certainly occurs a battle between the Mlecchas and the Indras within the bodies of embodied beings; for the external realm of sacrifice is indeed an illusory form, yet it is not a battle with Mlecchas. The detailed explanation of this is to be told in the fifth chapter, "The Attainment of the Knowledge of Supreme Unchanging Syllable" (paramākṣarajñānasiddhi), which will be spoken of hereafter.

Now, the middle [cycle] of three fortnights and the division of the three years—the divisions of the *tantras* such as the *Samāja* and others belonging to the *Tri-kula* and so forth—are described by the verse beginning with "In the year of time" (*kālābde*). In the year of time numbered by fire (three), multiplied by the total number of days in a year, there are the six families from the numerical value of the solstice (*ayanāṅka*). From the division of thirty-six months, and from the flavors (six) multiplied by the flavors (six), the families of the Yoginīs are obtained by the division of the days of the week; these are the manifest and fixed deities in the Wheel of Time (*Kālacakra*). O King, the designation occurs through the deities and goddesses during the cutting of the fortnights.

In this case, within the year of time—the intermediate year consisting of the number of fires (three)—when multiplied by the number of years (three) and divided by the total number of days in a year (three hundred and sixty), the result is a total of one thousand and eighty days.
That very triad of years constitutes the three families (*trikula*) of body, speech, and mind, which, according to the division of the years, have the nature of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
Then, from that total number of days, when divided by the number of days in a solstice (one hundred and eighty), the quotient represents the six families (*ṣaṭkula*).
Furthermore, by dividing that total number of days according to months, thirty-six *kula*s are obtained through the division by thirty;
since "six times six" means multiplied by six, these are the thirty-six *kula*s of the Yoginīs.
Thus, they are the *kula*s of both the Yoginīs and the Means (*upāya*).

From that total of one thousand and eighty days, by means of division by the [week]day, the manifest and fixed deities of the Kālacakra maṇḍala are obtained as one hundred and fifty-four; the remainder is the pair consisting of Wisdom and Means. Thus, there are one hundred and fifty-six [deities] in the Kālacakra. The remainder of seven parts is the presiding deity of the station of Kulikā, the wheel of gods and goddesses characterized by Kulikā. Furthermore, from that, the previous day is understood.

O! Regarding the Great Chapter on the Origin of the Families of Channels from the *Kālacakra-kulatantra*, the Wheel-Turning King of the Central Channel, which is the battle against the Mlecchas: from the one thousand eighty [verses], at the time of the cutting of the wings, there is a designation by means of the deities and goddesses obtained through a division of fifteen.

Together with the couple who are the lords of Kālacakra, there are seventy-two characteristics of deities and goddesses; this is the rule for the Yoginītantras according to the divisions of three years.
According to worldly convention, the three families, the six families, and the thirty-six families constitute the Yoginītantras; such is the rule for the Yoginītantras.

The *Māyājāla* consists of thirty days; it is of three types: [the first] correctly by forty-nine [days], the second by forty-four [days], and the third by forty-three [days]. The *Śrīsamāja* has seasonal divisions [of sixty days] by fifty-five [days]; that which is called *Tattva* is by fifty-six minus six [fifty days];
and another is distinguished by half-divisions of those two. Furthermore, when mixed, it is of two types: by thirty-nine [days] and by forty-nine [days] with the *tattvas*.

Now, the *Kriyā*, *Yoga*, and *Yogatantras* are described according to the division of eighteen types, beginning with the words "here" (*iha*), etc.: here, the middle three fortnights are forty-five days; these, multiplied by twelve, are...

The limbs of the day (*dināṅga*) number five hundred and forty, due to the division of twelve *lagnas* each day. From those five hundred and forty limbs of the day, the *Māyājāla*, though threefold, is subtracted: the first consists of forty-nine pairs of deities (*randhravedaiḥ*), the second consists of forty-five pairs of deities (*bhūtārṇavaiḥ*), and the other consists of forty-three pairs of deities (*śikhijalanidhibhiḥ*).

Therefore, when the components of the day are subtracted from the three signs, there are one hundred and thirty-seven; when doubled, the number of deities and goddesses becomes two hundred and seventy-four. This is the rule of the *Māyājāla*; its detailed exposition shall be stated in the fifth chapter. This is the rule of the *Māyājālakriyāyogatantra*.
Now, the sixfold division of the *Samāja* is described: "From that remainder of the subtracted components of the day, there is the seasonal division of the *Śrīsamāja*."

The term "known as reality" (*tattvākhyam*) refers to that which consists of twenty-five; therefore, from those days and limbs (*dināṅga*), by subtracting twenty-five, there arise pairs of deities. Furthermore, twenty-five minus six is nineteen; thus, by subtracting nineteen deities, there arises another division, namely a division divided by the halves of those two [groups] consisting of twenty-five and nineteen.
Twenty-five, half [of that] is twelve and a half; nineteen, half [of that] is nine and a half; from this, half enters into twelve and a half.
Therein, one assembly consists of nine members, while another consists of thirteen;
furthermore, there is yet another mixed assembly which becomes twofold.
"Tridaśa" means thirteen;

"navadiśā" means nineteen. With these thirty-two pairs of deities, there is the first assembly (*samāja*). Together with the nine apertures (*randhra*) and the twenty-five principles (*tattva*), there is a second assembly consisting of thirty-four pairs of deities.
Thus, the *Samāja* is divided into six classes.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding these six *tantrarājas*, the number [of deities] is doubled by means of the one hundred and thirty-two pairs of male and female deities, resulting in a total of two hundred and sixty-four male and female deities.

Thus, in the nine *tantrarājas*, including the *Samāja* and *Māyājāla*, there are five hundred and forty male and female deities, together with the pair of presiding lords, which corresponds to the number of days and limbs.

In these tantras, just as there is a distinction in the womb according to the different ways the aggregates, elements, sense bases, moon, and sun are accomplished, so too it must be explained in the fifth chapter according to the distinction of seats; such is the rule of the Yoga Tantra.

In this context, for one born in the womb, there is a ninefold *samāja* through the perfection of the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*); likewise, a thirteenfold [assembly] through the perfection of the aggregates, elements, and the wheels of the innate (*sahaja*), enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*), and emanation (*nirmāṇa*); likewise, a nineteenfold [assembly] through the perfection of the aggregates, elements, wheels, and objects; likewise, a twenty-fivefold [assembly] through the perfection of the aggregates, elements, wheels, objects, and the six [faculties] such as the eyes;
and likewise, a thirty-two-fold [assembly] through the perfection of the aggregates, elements, wheels, objects, faculties, action-faculties, and the secret, crown, and lotus [centers].

Likewise, by way of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), the six wheels (*cakra*), objects (*viṣaya*), sense organs (*indriya*), action organs (*karmendriya*), and divine organs (*divyendriya*), as well as bliss (*ānanda*), the *Samāja* consists of thirty-four [components].
This rule of the *Samāja*—that for children there is a sixfold arising from conception until the age of sixteen—is to be explained in detail in the fifth chapter.

Thus, in the *Māyājāla*, the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*) consist of nine, the eight elements beginning with hair (*loma*), the twelve sense-bases (*āyatana*), together with the four wheels (*cakra*), and together with the elements of wind, bile, phlegm, and their combination (*sannipāta*), as well as the six action-faculties (*karmendriya*). This constitutes the *Māyājāla* consisting of forty-three [components].

Including the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) and the secret lotus (*guhyakamala*), it consists of forty-five; and including passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), and pride (*māna*), it consists of forty-nine. This is the rule for the *Māyājāla*, which is to be explained in detail in the fifth chapter; this is the rule for the arising of the *Yoginīyogatantra*.
Now, the outer and inner seal (*mudrā*) is explained: here, in all cases, the effect is to be sealed by the cause, and the cause is to be sealed by the effect.

Because it possesses the nature of *rajas* (passion), the sun is the cause, which is wisdom (*prajñā*); because it possesses the nature of *śukra* (semen), the moon is the effect, which is means (*upāya*).
Relatively speaking, because it possesses the nature of *śukra*, the moon is the cause, which is wisdom; because it possesses the nature of *rajas*, the sun is the means, which is the effect.
Thus, in all cases, wisdom (*prajñā*) is the cause of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and skillful means (*upāya*) is compassion (*karuṇā*).

Regarding the lunar portion, those six days which are indeed obtained by dividing the total number of days by the number of weekdays constitute the six mudrās of the Vajrin. The remaining number of days are the mudrās of body, speech, and mind.

In the *Yoginīyogatantra*, they are clearly established as fixed within the three junctions of the body of wisdom (*prajñākāya*): the powers (*śakti*), the wrathful ones (*krodha*), and the ten and five Buddhas and goddesses arise in sequence. (53)

In this context, from those forty-five days that constitute the lunar portion, six days are obtained by dividing by the [lunar] weekday factor; these six days become the six seals (*mudrā*) of the Vajrin: the wheel, the earring, the necklace, the bracelet, the girdle, and the ashes and sacred thread. The remaining days of the *Kālacakra* are three in number—body, speech, and mind—which are the seals within the internal Vajrin. Thus, nine seals are to be understood as existing both externally and internally.

In the *Prajñākāya* and *Prajñātantra*, and in the *Upāyakāya* and *Upāyatantra*, the three attachments— consisting of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and characterized by body, speech, and mind— are revealed as the rule for the *mudrās* in the *Yoginīyogatantra*. [This passage] does not exist in manuscript *kha* of the fifty[-chapter version].

[Chapter on the Characteristics of Body and Speech] The Great Chapter on the Arising of the Family of Channels in the *Kālacakra-kula-tantra* concerning the Battle between the Cakravartin and the Mlecchas. Now, the number of the male and female deities of Kālacakra is stated, beginning with the word "powers" (*śakti*) and so forth: "In this [system], the host of deities whose nature is the universe of the channels of the six wheels arises as powers and wrathful ones in groups of ten. This means there are ten powers, which are the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), and ten wrathful ones, such as Uṣṇīṣa and the others; thus, there is a group of ten for each.
The "pentad of the Buddha-deities" refers to the five Buddhas beginning with Akṣobhya and the five goddesses beginning with Vajradhātvīśvarī; thus, there is a pentad for each.

Furthermore, O King, the group of deities consists of the six [senses] beginning with form and the six [objects] beginning with the eyes; the sixty-two [deities] include the eight Yoginīs and the eight Caṇḍa-Nāgas. All this in the world is doubled, making one hundred and four in the glorious Kālacakra.
Half of that—sixty—is the number of daily ghaṭikās that emerge within a month in the solar portion of the three realms.

"The sixfold group of form and so forth, and eye and so forth" refers to the six such as Rūpavajrā and the six such as Kṣitigarbha; thus, each [set] is a group of six. Furthermore, "the host of deities in groups of two-six" refers to the twelve beginning with Indra. "The eight Yoginīs, Nāgas, and Caṇḍas" refers to the eight beginning with Cāmuṇḍā, the eight beginning with Ananta, and the eight beginning with Śvānāsyā. All this assembly of deities is to be described individually by their distinct names in the *Sādhanāpaṭala*.

Regarding the term "bhuvana" (world), both externally and internally, all this is again doubled by way of the division of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). This *Śrī Kālacakra* consists of one hundred and four [deities], and its half consists of fifty-two deities.

Thus, through the further unification of the divisions of sun and moon, the *Kālacakra* should be understood as consisting of one hundred and fifty-six deities; such is the rule concerning the host of deities residing in the pericarp of the lotus.

Now the goddesses of the lotus petals, beginning with Carcikā, are described: from the wheel of breaths, by dividing the solar portion into thirty-two parts, two *ghaṭikās* are obtained for each day; over the thirty days of a month, these become sixty *nāḍīs*, which take the form of Kulikā.

All those Yoginīs, multiplied by two and mixed with the [number of] worlds (three), are doubled in the solar portion; thus, the entire multitude of Yoginīs, when condensed in the mantra, become the threefold solar days along with their designations. In the case of the Moon, there is a division of fortnights, while in the Sun, there is a complete division of Vargas. ||55||
And those Yoginīs, when mixed with the ascendants (lagna) and mixed with the four junctions (sandhyā) and Kulikā of the ascendant, become sixty-four;
these, doubled by the division of wisdom (prajñā) and means (upāya), become one hundred and twenty-eight in number.
Furthermore, within the solar portion, the day is divided into three hundred and sixty days, which constitute the host of deities characterized by the lunar dates (tithi) beginning with Caitra.

That same [group], when doubled by adding the twelve [goddesses] beginning with Lāsyā, becomes a host of deities numbering seven hundred and twenty; thus they are "all condensed together. These goddesses, together with their namesakes—the seventy-two deities—and along with the six mudrās, amount to one thousand and eighty, which is three times the number of solar days (360) or the days of three years. Therefore, the intention [of the *Yoginītantra*] is that these deities and goddesses should be understood as being of the nature of the aggregate of days of three years.

Thus, there is a division of solar years in the Moon; there is a total division of fortnights in the *Māyājāla* and *Samāja* tantras by means of the assembly of five hundred and forty-nine deities in nine ways—this is the section [on] the *Vimalaprabhā*. Thus, therein in the *Ādibuddha*, the deities and goddesses of the self-hand and the lords of men consist of wisdom and method; indeed, there is an equal division of night and day at midnight and at midday.

He by whom [this] is known within his own body through the divisions of day and night, months, and transits of the sun—he is the glorious Mañjuvajra, the destroyer of the fear of cyclic existence, a Buddha in this very life. (56)

Thus, through the union of the hosts of deities of the sun and moon, he becomes Ādibuddha; when he has manifested therein, his own rays are the lords of men, numbering sixteen hundred and twenty. Of those deities and goddesses, wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*) are "night" and "day" respectively: wisdom is the portion of night, and means is the portion of day; their equal division is midday.

At midnight, from midnight until midday, the division of the night consists of thirteen and a half constellations, or eight hundred and ten *daṇḍas*, or *ghaṭikās*. Likewise is the division of the day.
Thus, in the glorious *Nakṣatramaṇḍala* of the *Ādibuddha*, the host of deities is said by the Blessed One to consist of the number of constellations and *nāḍīs*.

Just as there is an external enjoyment of the constellations and *ghaṭikās* by all the planets, so too within oneself, in body, speech, mind, and gnosis, there is [the enjoyment] of the phenomena of the six sense faculties.

He by whom it is known within his own body, through the sequence thus described, that the *Ādibuddha* consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*)—known within one's own body through the divisions of day and night, the junctions (*sandhyā*), the watches (*prahara*), and so forth, as well as the twelve divisions of the months and transits (*saṃkrānti*)—that glorious yogin becomes Mañjuvajra, the destroyer of the fear of existence; he is a Buddha in this very life. This is the rule for the arising of the deities of the *Laghutantra* and the *Mūlatantra*.

From that [total], by a thirtyfold division, the deities are fixed as three times [that number] in the Kālacakra: two in the uṣṇīṣa, eight in the heart, sixteen (the number of teeth) in the head, sixty-four (eight times eight) in the throat and the navel, and twice sixteen (twice the number of kings) are well-known in the middle of the secret place. || 57 ||
Here, from the *Paramādibuddha* consisting of sixteen hundred and twenty [verses], fifty-four deities are obtained by dividing by thirty.
These are again multiplied threefold by body, speech, and mind, resulting in one hundred and sixty-two.

Among these, the number of mandala-deities (*māṇḍaleya*) is one hundred and fifty-four; this includes the pair of the Lord of the Mandala (*maṇḍaleśa*) as wisdom and method, along with the six external mudrās.

The *Kālacakra* has emerged from the *Paramādibuddha* by way of a tenfold division according to the distinction of the channels beginning with *iḍā* and ending with *śaṅkhinī*; this is the outer *neyārtha* (interpretable meaning), according to the rule of the *Laghukālacakra*.

Here, in this body, there are three channels of the three families (*trikula*) which sustain the drops (*bindu*) of body, speech, and mind, located at the navel, the secret place, and the jewel (*maṇi*). Likewise, there are six channels of the six families (*ṣaṭkula*), namely *lalanā*, *rasanā*, and *avadhūtī*, which carry feces, urine, and semen.

Likewise, there are thirty-six family channels (*kulanāḍī*): the six channels of the six wheels beginning with the *uṣṇīṣa*; two that perceive sound, two that perceive touch, two that perceive taste, two that perceive form, and two that perceive smell—these ten channels;
the twelve channels of the transits (*saṃkrānti*) in the secondary mandalas within the center of the navel wheel; and the eight channels of the watches (*prahara*).

Thus, all thirty-six *kulanāyikās* (leaders of the families) come into being: six having the form of the tastes (*rasa*), six having the form of the elements (*dhātu*), six having the form of the sense-faculties (*indriya*), six having the form of the objects of the senses (*viṣaya*), six having the form of the organs of action (*karmendriya*), and six having the form of the objects of the organs of action. Thus, there are thirty-six *kulanāḍīs* that set in motion the six [aggregates]: six setting in motion feeling (*vedanā*), six setting in motion perception (*saṃjñā*), six setting in motion mental formations (*saṃskāra*), six setting in motion consciousness (*vijñāna*), and six setting in motion gnosis (*jñāna*). It should be understood that by way of the relationship between the support and the supported (*ādhārādheya-sambandha*), these become seventy-two.
Thus it is said: "The channels of Kālacakra are double at the uṣṇīṣa," meaning they take the form of four petals; these four are active during the four junctions (*saṃdhyā*).

At the heart, there are eight channels, beginning with Rohiṇī, which serve as the support for the *samāna* and other winds, flowing through the eight days of the week according to the division of the watches (*prahara*) each day.
Here, the wind to be supported [as the breath] flows downward and upward through two *nāḍīs*.

Thus, there are sixteen "kings" (*nṛpati*) in the head which initiate the lunar days (*tithi*), and the number of teeth in the throat; that is, in the throat-cakra, there are twenty-eight constellations (*nakṣatra*), and thirty-two which initiate the four *daṇḍa*-constellations.

At the navel, in the navel-lotus, outside the *rāśi-nāḍīs*, are the *ghaṭī-nāḍīs*: sixty-four channels (*nāḍīs*) multiplied by eight; they carry the sixty mandalas, they carry the four voids, and they set in motion the sixty-four *daṇḍas*—thus "twice the kings" (thirty-two). In the center of the secret place, the channels of the secret lotus set in motion the thirty-two constituents (*dhātu*), beginning with semen.

The six channels that obstruct the chakras, which seize the ten sense objects and are of the nature of the *sannipāta* (combined humors), are doubled again and again; further multiplied, they become the portions of phlegm, bile, and wind.

These indeed are the "death-channels," yet by the power of the Guru’s injunction, they bestow longevity and health. In the six chakras, these very wind-channels remove the fear of death for yogis—of this there is no doubt.

Among these, six channels are the obstructors of the six wheels (*cakras*); ten are the carriers of the objects of the senses, and they are of the nature of the *sannipāta* (combined humors). These are doubled again as portions of phlegm (*śleṣman*), making twenty; further doubled as portions of bile (*pitta*), they become forty; and again doubled as portions of wind (*anila*), they become eighty. Thus, one hundred and fifty-six channels situated within the six wheels are to be understood as the channels of the Kālacakra.
Indeed, these are the channels of death, yet by the power of the Guru’s instructions, they bestow longevity and health.

The channels of time (*kālanāḍī*) within the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*), which remove the fear of death when cultivated through the guru’s instruction, have been described; that these are for yogins is no wonder. In the crown (*uṣṇīṣa*) there are four [channels]; in the forehead (*lalāṭa*), forty-eight, which are the disturbances of the phlegm element (*śleṣmadhātu*); in the throat (*kaṇṭha*), thirty-two, which are the disturbances of the bile element (*pittadhātu*); in the heart-lotus (*hṛdabja*), forty-eight, which are the disturbances of the bile element; at the navel (*nābhi*) and the secret place (*guhya*), sixty-four, as well as sixteen, which are the disturbances of the wind element (*vāyudhātu*). At the secret place, another group of six is clearly established as the obstructions caused by the combined humors (*sannipāta*). (59)

On the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) there are four channels; on the forehead (*lalāṭa*), "four times the oceans" means sixteen channels—these twenty channels cause the provocation of the phlegm constituent (*śleṣmadhātu*).

At the throat, "the teeth" refers to thirty-two channels; at the heart-lotus, "four times the eyes" refers to eight channels—these forty channels cause the provocation of the bile constituent (*pittadhātu*). And at the navel and the secret place (*guhya*), respectively, "sixty-four" refers to sixty-four channels.
The king [of channels] is also in the secret lotus; externally, in the surrounding circle, there are sixteen channels—these eighty channels are the outbursts of the wind element.

In the secret [lotus], there are ten other channels beginning with the "other" (anya) direction, and six others in the middle surrounding circle, and [six] in the womb-surrounding circle, respectively.
The *sannipātas* (conjunctions) and the provocations of *sannipāta* are the cessations (*nirodhas*); they are by nature the cessation of the six wheels.

Thus, the one hundred and fifty-six channels of the *Kālacakra* abide as the nature of male and female deities; when cultivated together with the channels of the six families, they bestow death upon the ignorant, but bestow happiness upon yogins. The *Kālacakra* consists of one hundred and sixty-two channels, which are the essence of the channels of the six wheels.

Furthermore, among those one hundred and sixty-two channels (*nāḍī*), each individual channel becomes tenfold by way of the movement of the ten winds and the nature of the ten aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*).
Thus, all of them multiplied by ten become sixteen hundred and twenty in number—namely, those that flow as the *ghaṭikā* of the twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).
In this way, O Glorious One, in the Paramādibuddha of the Mandala of the Lunar Mansions, there are this many deities through the union of wisdom and method (*prajñopāya*).

Therefore, from this extensive mandala of constellations, according to worldly convention, the goddesses who carry the elements such as phlegm and so forth—extracted by Mañjuśrī for the sake of accomplishing mundane siddhis or for the accomplishment of physical perfection—are the leaders of the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakranāyikā*). This is the rule regarding the intermingling of the channels (*nāḍī*) of Kālacakra: these six channels, which obstruct the wheels and proceed along the three paths through the divisions of moon, sun, and fire, must be protected within the body; otherwise, by the power of the Guru’s injunction, they bestow death upon living beings.

If the entry of the vital breaths into the six [channels] occurs for men, then indeed death is destroyed; for when [the breath] has not entered the subtle [channel], the domain of immortality is severed by the yogis.

In this body, those six channels (*nāḍīs*) which are said to obstruct the wheels (*cakras*), which proceed along three paths—namely, the paths of the moon, sun, and Rāhu, corresponding to the left, right, and middle paths—and which proceed upward and downward through the paths of feces, urine, and semen according to the division of the moon, sun, and fire—these must be guarded by the yogi within the body. Why? Because of the constraint of the Guru.

The "constraint of the Guru" is the yoga of six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*); by means of that, these channels—which bring death to living beings when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) enters them for six months—must be protected from death.

If the entry of the vital breath (prāṇa) occurs at all times within these six [channels] for human beings, then death is indeed destroyed. Among these six, the subtle Avadhūtī is the middle one; when the vital breath does not enter that subtle [channel], the domain of death is severed by yogis, and it is not the case that the domain of death is not severed.

In the *Dvādaśasāhasrikā*, within the *Mahoddeśa* on the Origin of the Family of Channels (*Nāḍīkulotpatti*) from the *Kulatantra* of the Wheel-Turning King and the Mlecchas of the Kālacakra, [Chapter] 4: The *Mahoddeśa* on the Signs of Death through Untimely Death (*Ariṣṭamaraṇalakṣaṇanāḍīccheda*). Now, the signs of untimely death for embodied beings are described, beginning with the word "prāṇa": "If the vital breath (*prāṇa*) flows through a single channel day and night, life lasts for a full year. If it flows uninterruptedly through one side [of the channels] for a fortnight, life lasts for men for one and a half years; this is the third [sign]. (3)

[Chapter on] the Great Instruction on the Signs of Death by Unnatural Causes and the Severing of the Channels: O King, if [the breath] flows for one uninterrupted month, life lasts exactly three months; thus, O Kālacakra, the yogi knows death as the movement of the moon within his own body. 61.

In this body, there is the navel-cakra, a twelve-spoked wheel of the zodiac (*rāśicakra*). It consists of alternating odd signs beginning with Aries and even signs beginning with Taurus. Consequently, the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇasañcāra*) occurs in the left nostril during the six odd signs beginning with Aries.
In the ascendants equal to Taurus and the others, the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) occurs in the right nostril;
there are twelve transits (saṃkrāntis) every day, occurring every five *daṇḍas*.
Thus, in a full day and night of sixty *daṇḍas*, there are twelve transits: six in the left nostril, six in the right nostril, and twelve entries in the central channel (*madhyamā*).

The equilibrium of the elements (*dhātu*) exists in those bodies free from disease, whereas for those overcome by disease, there is a disorder of the *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman* elements. From this disorder arises a disorder of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). If it flows for a day and night through the left channel (*nāḍī*), then the lifespan is a full hundred years; if it flows through the middle [channel] for half a fortnight, then the lifespan of men becomes characterized by a full hundred years, and if it flows [through the right], then the lifespan is slightly less than that, after which one goes to death.
If [the breath] flows uninterruptedly and continuously through the left channel for one month, then the lifespan becomes three months;
thus, the yogi perceives the death-sign of the moon's movement within his own body according to the *Kālacakra*.

Here, regarding the matter of fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*), the *Kālacakra* is the twelve-spoked wheel of the zodiac signs; having drawn that very wheel upon the ground, one should place the "fatal day" on the first petal and the thirty-six months of the life-span.

Then, for one month it does not flow; there is an increase of "fatal" (*ariṣṭa*) days. At the end of the second month, upon entering the third month, it flows for two days in the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*) on that very same petal. Then, for the third month it does not flow; at the end of the fourth month, upon entering the fifth month, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) flows in the left channel for three days. From the fifth month, it does not flow in the sixth month. Thus, in six months, there are three fatal days; in the middle [of the period], there are three days; and at the end, the right and left channels possess the characteristics of the fatal signs.
*Ariṣṭa* is untimely death; *riṣṭa* is death within the limit of a hundred years. Thus, from the thirty-six months plus the days of *ariṣṭa*, six months of life have passed.
Thereafter, there is no movement of the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) on that leaf [of the life-span].
A day and night passes by means of eleven transits, consisting of twenty-one thousand six hundred inhalations and exhalations;
here, there is no deficiency in the cycle of breaths even when the leaf of the zodiacal sign is abandoned.
Thereafter, it flows through the second leaf for four days, five days, and six days, respectively, during the seventh, eighth, and ninth months.
Then, another three months of the thirty-month lifespan have passed.
Thereafter, having taken twenty-seven months, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) moves through the third leaf and abandons two leaves.
It completes one day and night through ten transits (*saṃkrānti*), as the vital breath migrates through ten leaves.
From the twenty-seven months, in each month again the left channel flows for seven days, eight days, or nine days.
Consequently, another three months are subtracted from the twenty-seven months.
In this manner, according to the previously mentioned method, one discards the third zodiacal sign-chart.
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) performs its transition through nine petals;
likewise, it flows through the left channel for ten days, eleven days, or twelve days,
and thereafter it abandons the fourth petal.
Then, after twenty-four months, three months less remain of one's life.

Likewise, [there are periods of] thirteen days, fourteen days, and fifteen days; [this occurs] on the leaf (*patra*). *Bho.* and *Kha.* read "flows" (*vahati*); *Ka.*, *Kha.*, and *Ga.* read "in the machine" (*yantra*); *Bho.* reads "on the leaf" (*hDab ma La*).
ka. kha. savyā0;
not found in manuscript ga.
In the Tibetan translation: rTsar (in the channel).

The word "tataḥ" (then) is not present. In the *Vimalaprabhā*: Then he abandons the fifth petal; he effects a transition (*saṃkrānti*) into the seven petals. Out of twenty-one months, three months become deficient; likewise, he flows for sixteen days, seventeen days, and eighteen days respectively each month. Then he abandons the sixth petal; he effects a transition into the six petals. Out of eighteen months, three months become deficient of his life-span.
In this manner, it flows for nineteen days, twenty days, and twenty-one days.
Then it abandons the leaf of the seventh mansion, and the vital breath (prāṇa) transitions through the leaves of the five mansions within a single day and night.
Consequently, after fifteen months, one's life is reduced by three months.

When it flows continuously for twenty-two days, twenty-three days, and twenty-four days, then it abandons the eighth petal and performs four transits; three months are subtracted from the twelve months of life.

When it flows for twenty-five days, twenty-six days, and twenty-seven days, then it abandons the ninth petal and performs transits across three petals; three months are subtracted from the nine months of life.

Likewise, when it flows for twenty-eight days, twenty-nine days, or thirty days, then it abandons the tenth petal; it effects a transition between two petals, and three months are subtracted from the six-month lifespan.

Similarly, when it flows for thirty-one days, thirty-two days, or thirty-three days, then it abandons the eleventh petal; it effects a transition upon a single petal, and ninety days are subtracted from the three-month lifespan.
Then, after flowing for three days on the first petal, it flows for two days on the twelfth petal.

Thereafter, it abandons the twelfth petal and flows for one day in the pericarp (*karṇikā*) until the cessation of the breaths of the vital wheel (*prāṇacakra*) occurs. Then, those men who are non-yogins meet their death through the *ariṣṭa* (fatal omen) in the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*). This is the rule regarding the lunar *ariṣṭa* in the left channel.
Due to the differentiation of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, the number of days of misfortune (*ariṣṭadina*) increases by one each month.

Herein is the arrangement of the zodiac wheel (*rāśicakra*): having made the zodiac wheel two-layered, one places the days of misfortune in the first layer and the remaining months of life in the second layer.
Here, on the first spoke of the wheel, there are three days of misfortune and thirty months; on the second layer, there are six days of misfortune and twenty-seven remaining months of life.

Thus, in the third spoke, there are nine days of misfortune (ariṣṭa) and twenty-four months; likewise, in the fourth, twelve days and twenty-one months; in the fifth, fifteen days and eighteen months; in the sixth, eighteen days and fifteen months; in the seventh, twenty-one days and twelve months; in the eighth, twenty-four days and nine months; in the ninth, twenty-seven days and six months; in the tenth, thirty days and three months; and in the eleventh spoke of the wheel, there are thirty-three days of misfortune. At the end, there is a loss of three months.

Then, for three days prior to ascending [to the next stage], it flows through the first petal of the wheel for two days in the right channel (*dakṣiṇanāḍī*) in order to exhaust the constituents (*dhātu*) of the right channel; for one day it flows in the central channel (*madhyamā*), the *avadhūtī*, in order to exhaust the wheel of breaths.
Thereafter occurs the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇotkrānti*). This is the rule regarding the lunar fatal sign (*candrāriṣṭa*) in the left channel.

Now, the solar *ariṣṭa* (fatal sign) in the right channel is described with the verse beginning "From five," and so forth: "From five, the movement of twenty-five days ascends by an increase of five; from that, by an increase of one [per day], it reaches thirty-three, up to exactly [that point].
[The variants] "kha. viṃśatieka0" and "ka. kha. pustakayornāsti" do not exist in the manuscripts *ka* and *kha*.

In the *Pauṣṇa* (Revatī) lunar mansion, all the months—namely three, two, six, three, four, and one—are the remaining days of life; these are fifteen, ten, thirty, twenty-four, and two respectively. || 62 ||

In this body, the Moon, having taken up the qualities of the Sun—sattva, rajas, and tamas—manifests the days of death (ariṣṭa); the Sun, having taken up the qualities of the Moon—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—manifests the days of death.

[The movement proceeds] by five and then five more until reaching the fifth house (pañcarāśi); then two houses by increments of one. Then, starting from the base, it ascends for thirty-three days: it leaves the eighth house in fifteen days, leaves the ninth house in ten days, the tenth house in five days, and the eleventh house in three days.
In this manner, the vital breath ascends through the right channel for thirty-three days.

Then, within the twelve zodiac signs, it remains for two days in the left channel for the purpose of depleting the constituents of the left channel, and for one day in the central channel for the purpose of depleting the wheel of breaths; thereafter, death occurs.
For example, from the fifth limit-day until the twenty-fifth day, the movement of the day ascends by increments of five.
Fifteen, fifteen, twenty, and twenty-five births in five zodiacal signs.

Therefore, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) ascends by one [sign] at a time through twenty-six and twenty-seven days in each of the tenth, eighth, ninth, and tenth zodiac signs (*rāśi*). Thence, in the eleventh sign, there is a month plus three days; this constitutes a full year (*samā*) of remaining fatal days (*ariṣṭa-dina*) within the wheel of zodiac signs, starting from the birth sign among the twelve signs. For the "three-eyed moon" (the three-year period), in the birth sign there are three years of remaining fatal days; in the second sign, two years; in the third, one year; thus these are the years of life with remaining fatal days. Then, regarding the phrase "six, three, four, and moons": in the fourth sign, there are six months; in the fifth, three months; in the sixth, two months; in the seventh, there is one month of life with remaining fatal days. From that point, the seventh place from the birth position is the *pauṣṇa* (the sign of the Moon, Cancer), which for those born from a womb is the month of conception (*ādhāna-māsa*), namely Capricorn (*makara*). From that, the seventh is the month of the birth of the breath (*prāṇa-janma-māsa*), Cancer, due to the abandonment of the increase of the lunar channels (*candra-nāḍī-vṛddhi*). At the end of the twelve signs, it becomes Capricorn again; thus, the thirteenth month from conception is Cancer, which is the birthplace of the breath, not of the Sun. From there it rises; therefore, when Capricorn rises at birth, the rising of the seventh sign is called the "setting of the Sun," which is the *pauṣṇa* time. From that time, the breath becomes irreversible; it cannot be stabilized in the body by gods, asuras, or humans. The night portion is the time of the moon's rising; thus, the "rising of the moon" means the entry of death into the semen-element (*śukra-dhātu*), while the "rising of death" does not mean the semen-element itself, but rather the entry of the fatal wind (*ariṣṭa-vāyu*). From that *pauṣṇa* time, the breath ascends through thirty-three days in the right channel (*dakṣiṇa-nāḍī*) for the purpose of depleting the semen; then two days in the left channel (*vāma-nāḍī*), and one day in the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*). These are the remaining days: fifteen (tithi), ten (dig), five (iṣu), three (guṇa), and two (dvi); one day remains of life. This is the rule for the single explanation of the solar fatal sign (*sūryāriṣṭa*). Now, the second explanation is stated beginning with "from its own place" (*svasthānāt*): "From its own place, it abandons the wheel of zodiac signs by the loss of the remaining digits (*kalā*) through equal years, months, and days—by the 'three-eyed moon' (three years), by 'six, three, four, and moons' (six months, etc.), and by the *pauṣṇa* [time]. The loss is equal to the fifteens (15), the directions (10), and the qualities (3). When [the breath] has entered the pericarp (*kaṇikā*), death occurs at the end of the 'piercing by three' (3) days through the conjunction of the fatal sign of the Sun. (Verse 63) **Note:** The term *trinayanaśaśinaḥ* refers to the three-year period; *ṣaṭtriyugmendavaḥ* refers to the six-month period and so on. The *pauṣṇa* time marks the transition where the breath begins its descent toward death. The "piercing by three" (*tribhidina*) refers to the final three days of the process. The "fatal sign of the Sun" (*dinakarāriṣṭa*) signifies the culmination of the solar cycle of death. The "pericarp" (*kaṇikā*) refers to the central point of the subtle body where the breath finally dissolves. Death occurs when the breath reaches this point after the specified number of days. The "loss of the remaining digits" corresponds to the depletion of the vital essence (*śukra*) and the progressive shortening of the lifespan. The numbers 15, 10, and 3 represent the sequence of the final days of life. The "equal years, months, and days" refer to the specific durations assigned to each stage of the breath's movement through the zodiacal signs. The *pauṣṭha* (or *pauṣṇa*) time is the critical juncture where the breath ceases its outward movement and begins its terminal descent. The "piercing by three" days marks the final phase before the breath's departure from the body. The "conjunction of the fatal sign of the Sun" indicates the alignment of the solar cycle with the fatal winds, resulting in the cessation of life. The "pericarp" is the locus of the heart-center where the breath's dissolution is finalized. The entire process describes the exhaustion of the vital energies and the inevitable onset of death following the completion of the prescribed astrological and physiological cycles. The "loss of the remaining digits" is the mathematical representation of the gradual depletion of the life-force. The "equal years, months, and days" provide the temporal framework for the breath's movement. The *pauṣṇa* time is the threshold between life and death. The "piercing by three" days is the final countdown. The "conjunction of the fatal sign of the Sun" is the moment of death. In this body, within the navel lotus, there is the wheel of the zodiac (*rāśicakra*) consisting of twelve channels (*nāḍī*). Therein is the place of birth, the first channel of the zodiac; for the child born from the womb, whatever the ascendant (*lagna*) may be, that very sign—Taurus and so forth—is of the nature of the *samanā* channel. From that own place, the twelve-spoked wheel of signs, which is the wheel of channels consisting of sixty mandalas, is abandoned by the supreme digit (*parakalā*), the power of breath (*prāṇaśakti*). By means of the "remainders of loss" (*hāniśeṣa*), which are equal [to the days of ascent]: the loss consists of five, ten, fifteen, twenty-five, and twenty-six, and twenty-seven days. The remainders of loss are three years, two years, one year, six months, three months, two months, and one month. By these remainders of loss, starting from the first petal up to the seventh petal of the channel, the sequence proceeds by years and months. With three eyes and moons (three years), it abandons three channels; with six, three, two, and one (six months, three months, two months, one month), it abandons the seventh channel. And by days equal to the loss, starting from the time of the asterism Puṣya (*pauṣṇa*), until the limit of the Puṣya-time, [the process begins] from birth.

The seventh position from the starting point is the time of the sun's setting, which is the period of *rajas*. From that *pauṣṇa* [position], during days of equal ascent and lifespan, the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*) abandons the zodiacal channels (*rāśi-nāḍī*). A lunar day (*tithi*) is fifteen days; ten directions (*dik*) are ten days; an arrow (*iṣu*) is five days; and a quality (*guṇa*) is three days. By these thirty-three days, it abandons through the solar flow the eighth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh zodiacal channels, which carry the five mandalas.
Through the flow of the right channel for twelve days, or through the left channel for two days, and through the middle channel for one day, [the breath] has thus entered the pericarp;

in this way, after thirty-six days from the onset of the heat, death occurs for men due to the conjunction with the portents of the Sun. Thus, in the second [chapter], it says: "In the east, he abandons the world of the five arrows and the three fires."

The number of days for three solar years is [1095]; from that, the ascending [period] is 243, then 1302, then 1913; in the third [cycle], it is 578, and another 88 in the seventh, and from that, the ascending [period] again; all this, beginning with the lunar days (tithis), constitutes the total number of days, extending as far as the pericarp (kaṇikā). || 64 ||

Now, the abandonment of days from one petal to the next over three years is described starting with the words "first" (*pūrva*) and so forth. Here, in the wheel of zodiac signs (*rāśicakra*), the nāḍī of the birth-ascendant (*janmalagna*) is called "first. Within that birth-ascendant petal, from the total of one thousand eighty days, the vital energy (*prāṇaśakti*) abandons a group of thirty-three and thirty-five days—that is, thirty-five days—over the course of three years.
Then, having rendered that petal empty and taken the remaining group of days, the vital energy enters the second petal.
From that total number of days, one subtracts three hundred and forty-five days—consisting of ten days for ascending from the eastern petal along with the subsequent petals—to reach the second petal;
then, taking the remainder, one enters the third petal, where the second [count] becomes zero.
Again, from that very point, one subtracts one hundred and seventy days—along with fifteen days of ascent—from the third petal.

Taking the remainder, it enters the fourth; the third becomes empty. Then, together with twenty days beginning from the ascent, it abandons a total of eighty-two days—namely, two and eighty—and taking the remainder from the fourth petal, it enters the fifth; the fourth becomes empty.
Again, together with twenty-five days of ascent, it abandons fifty-seven days at the fifth petal;

having taken up the remainder, it enters the sixth, and the fifth becomes empty. Again, together with twenty-six days of ascent, it abandons twenty-eight days at the sixth petal and then enters the seventh petal, and the sixth becomes empty.
Then, on the seventh [petal], it abandons twenty-seven days of the group and,
taking the remaining thirty-six days of the group, enters the eighth petal; thus the seventh becomes empty,
and from there it abandons fifteen days on the eighth.
Having taken the remaining twenty-one days, one enters the ninth; the eighth becomes empty.
Then, from the ninth, one discards ten days;
having taken the remaining eleven days, one enters the tenth, and the ninth becomes empty.
Then, in the tenth [month], having abandoned five days and taken the remaining six days, one enters the eleventh; the tenth becomes empty,
and therein one abandons three days.
Taking the remaining three days, he enters the twelfth; the eleventh becomes empty, and there he abandons two days.
Taking the remaining one day, he enters the pericarp (kaṇikā); the twelfth petal of the zodiacal channels (nāḍī-rāśi-patra) becomes empty.

Thus, by means of one thousand and eighty intermediate days of the sun, the vital power (*prāṇaśakti*) abandons the twelve-spoked wheel of the zodiacs; thereafter, it flows through the pericarp for one day, and then, having abandoned the wheel of breaths, consciousness (*vijñāna*), together with the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*), undergoes a transition elsewhere to the six destinations. This is the rule regarding the fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*) of the sun.

Here, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is as in the previous *nyāsa*, according to the distinction of years and the distinction of the abandonment of days. In the first enclosure (*puṭa*), there is the placement of the days of misfortune (*ariṣṭa*); in the second enclosure, the placement of the remaining days of life; and in the second wheel, the placement of the abandonment of days. On the preceding petals, there is the sequential placement of zeros. This is the rule for solar misfortune (*sūryāriṣṭa*) for those born at an even ascendant in the right channel (*dakṣiṇanāḍī*), and for lunar misfortune (*candrāriṣṭa*) for those born at an odd ascendant with short lifespans. Thus ends the rule on solar misfortune.

Now, the refutation of the "medium-term fatal signs" (*madhyamāriṣṭa*) regarding the sun according to the sequence of years—which was taught by ignorant outsiders (*tīrthika*) and which causes delusion among beings concerning the limit of a hundred-year lifespan—is stated here: In this regard, it is indeed said by the outsiders (*tīrthika*): "If there is a flow of five *nāḍīs* in the right channel, the lifespan is one hundred years; with a flow of six *nāḍīs*, the lifespan is ninety years; with a flow of seven *nāḍīs*, the lifespan is eighty years; with a flow of eight *nāḍīs*, the lifespan is fifty years; with a flow of nine *nāḍīs*, the lifespan is thirty-three years; with a flow of ten *nāḍīs*, the lifespan is twenty-six years; with a flow of fifteen *nāḍīs*, the lifespan is fourteen years; with a flow of thirty *nāḍīs*, the lifespan is twelve years; with a flow for one day and night (*ahorātra*), the lifespan is ten years; with a flow for two days, the lifespan is eight years; with a flow for three days, the lifespan is six years; with a flow for four days, the lifespan is five years; and from that, with a flow for five days, the lifespan is three years. Such is the rule of the *nāḍīs* and breaths of the outsiders regarding the southern path.
That very [assertion] does not hold when examined through reasoning according to the words of the Omniscient One;
for here, in the absence of death omens (*ariṣṭa*) among men, the vital breath flows for five *daṇḍas* in the left and right channels during even and odd *lagnas* respectively.

For a person with a lifespan of one hundred years, the increase of breath occurs for seven years on the left and right sides according to the division of the solar transits (*ayana*); thereafter, for sixty years, there is an increase of *pāṇīpala*s according to the division of the increase of the transits; thereafter, for thirty years, there is an increase of *nāḍīs* according to the division of three-month periods; and thereafter, for three years and three fortnights, there is an increase according to the division of days—this is the principle of the increase of time.

According to this principle, for one who suffers an untimely death—such as the death of an infant within three years, five years, twelve years, twenty years, or more from birth—the sequence of the flow of six or seven *nāḍīs* beyond the five *nāḍīs* is useless, because the limit is set by the death occurring three years after birth.

In this regard, if the death of the newborn occurs after a month has passed, then starting from the day of birth, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and life-force (*āyuḥ*) ascend the lunar days (*tithi*), directions (*digi*), and qualities (*guṇa*), etc., from the time of the constellation Puṣya.

Thus, at the end of two months, three months, four months, six months, one year, two years, or three years from conception, death occurs by reversing the ascent of thirty-three days down to an ascent of five days in the right channel through the destruction of the five qualities, sound and so forth; and in the left channel, it occurs through the destruction of the three qualities, sattva and so forth, over the course of one day.
