furthermore, when the body has been swallowed by various states, it emits again those infinite [deities] transformed during the daytime at the time of withdrawal—this is the meaning of "it abandons.

For the sake of creation, that is, for the sake of producing others anew, it emits them through the sequential abandonment of the elements beginning with earth, in order within the supports of the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown; such is the rule for the agent of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).

Now, the performance of actions and so forth is described according to worldly convention by means of the verse beginning with "sound and so forth": "The sixfold group of sound and so forth constitutes the action; the sixfold group of sense organs is indeed the instrument; the years, months, fortnights, days, nights, lunar days, the moon, and the sun are the agent.

There may be another here who is the agent of their withdrawal, but he is not the agent of creation. The one who pervades space, the Space-Vajra-holder, is devoid of objects, without qualities, and without intrinsic nature. (83)

When this body has been produced, there arises the sixfold object-group consisting of sound, touch, form, taste, smell, and the dharmadhātu; the sixfold instrument-group of the sense-faculties consisting of ear, body, eye, tongue, nose, and mind;

the twelve months and years according to the division of the zodiac signs and the division of the lunar digits; the twenty-four fortnights; day and night (ahorātra); the fifteen lunar days (tithis); and both the moon and the sun—all these constitute the instruments.
The agent is characterized by the *ālayavijñāna*, the moment of the emission of semen, and is known as *sahajānanda* according to worldly convention.

If there were another agent here who were the performer of the destruction of these [factors]—the moment of death and so forth—as their agent, instrument, and object, then the creator of emanation would not be the agent.

Therefore, the Sahajakāya (Innate Body)—which is all-pervasive like space, possesses the space-vajra, is devoid of objects, free from qualities (*niḥguṇa*), devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), partless, associated with the *sarga* (emanation), and pervasive—is the one;
thus, there is no creator characterized by *nirvāṇa* who performs emanation and destruction. This is the rule regarding the cessation of the agent.

Now, the origination and so forth are described beginning with the word "smell": Smell, color, taste, and touch—earth, water, fire, and air—these eight indeed possess form; they are the objects of the aggregate, unified and principal in their totality.

This entire triple world undergoes emanation and dissolution through the power of Time. O Lord of Men, sound is indeed the void and formless, as are the sphere of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and the mind.

In this saṃsāra, arising occurs from a collection, not from a single element. Here, "collection" refers to smell, color, taste, and touch; and earth, water, fire, and air—these eight are the material elements (*rūpin*). Taken together, they constitute a single primary subject in their entirety.
Among these eight material elements, one quality becomes primary while the remaining ones become secondary; this has been stated previously.
Sound, the void, formlessness, and the mind-element—these four, O Lord of Men, are non-material.
Here, by the word "void," the semen-element is meant.
This entire triple world undergoes emanation and dissolution through the power of time, which means through the power of the moment of death.
Thus is the rule regarding origination.
[This is] not in manuscript *ga*.
In manuscript *ga*, it is "all-pervading."

Now, the bondage of saṃsāra is described with the words "The Self binds itself," and so forth: "The Self binds itself by means of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) through the qualities residing in *prakṛti*, just like a silkworm [binds itself] with its cocoon. Yet, by means of the mind itself, the Self releases itself once again from the state of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpa*). Therefore, O King, who is the agent that performs pleasure and pain arising from one's own actions and the qualities of *prakṛti*? Who acts? One devoid of *prakṛti* is liberated; it is the ignorant world that is deluded. (85)

In this body, the self (*ātman*) is the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), which consists merely of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the ego-conception (*ahaṅkāra*); and that self binds itself through conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) by means of the qualities residing in primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Primordial nature is the collection of aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; the qualities residing therein are the objects such as odors, characterized by arising and ceasing, and characterized by the conceptual constructions of existence and non-existence belonging to the mind of cyclic existence. By those conceptual constructions—the qualities residing in primordial nature—it binds itself, just as a silkworm binds itself with threads produced from its own body.

Furthermore, by means of the mind itself, one releases the self from conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*). Thus, that self, freed from the conceptualizations belonging to the qualities of *prakṛti*, becomes free from conceptualization; therefore, with a non-conceptualizing mind, it releases itself from the suffering of saṃsāra. Therefore, O King, one's own action—consisting of pleasure and pain arising from the qualities of *prakṛti*—is what acts. Who is the agent? What does it do? Being devoid of *prakṛti* and devoid of the eighteen elements, it does nothing. Thus, the ignorant world is deluded by the false imagination of a self as an agent; such is the rule regarding the bondage of karma.

Now, the eightfold primordial nature (prakṛti), beginning with earth, is described by the words "earth" and so forth: earth, water, fire, wind, space, mind, intellect, and ego-consciousness. It is threefold—gross, subtle, and supreme—according to the states of the three qualities (guṇas).

Through the divisions of phonemes, points (bindus), and so on, the primordial nature is attained as the gross within the gross senses; it is subtle within the subtle mind; and in the case of knowledge, it is the embodiment of knowledge—a primordial nature that is unevolved, yet has become the living soul (jīva), though not [itself] an element. || 86 ||

In this body, there is first an eightfold *prakṛti*, consisting of earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṅkāra*). Of these, for the transmigrating consciousness, there is again a threefold division: gross (*sthūla*), subtle (*sūkṣma*), and supreme (*parā*). These are "gone to the qualities" (*guṇagatā*), meaning they reside within the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. The "gross" (*sthūla*) is that which, through the divisions of phonemes, points, and so forth, resides in the gross and subtle senses and possesses the characteristics of the waking state (*jāgrat*); it is called "gross" because it grasps the objects of the waking state. This pertains to the gross consciousness (*sthūlacitta*), which is the grasper of inert latent impressions (*jaḍavāsanā*).

The subtle state of mind has as its substrate the dream state, because objects are perceived through the mental faculties (*manomayendriya*) as being like an illusion; thus, it is subtle. The supreme state has as its substrate the deep sleep state, characterized by the cessation of all the senses; it is supreme because of the relinquishing of all objective phenomena. Regarding this, they say, "He does not see," characterized by such passages as "having become one. Thus, *prakṛti* possesses the threefold nature of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep according to the divisions of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Alternatively, it is characterized as gross and so forth; the subtle is characterized by the twilight (*sandhyā*), and the supreme is characterized by the great night (*mahāniśā*).

By the word "and" (*ca*), there is a fourth nature, the embodiment of gnosis (*jñānamūrti*). Because that [nature] is the cause for the arising and cessation of sentient beings, belonging to the state of the fourth mind—the mind of gnosis—at the time of the emission of the semen, it is therefore the "embodiment of gnosis. Furthermore, that nature is unchanging, the essence of the living being, the essence of the great vital breath, and the very nature of the *dharmadhātu*;
thus, it is "not an element," meaning it does not consist of the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, or semen.
In this way, there is a fourfold rule of the nature according to the divisions of the cyclic mind, such as the waking state and so forth.

[In the chapter on the non-arising and non-ceasing of sentient beings, this is the Great Exposition on the Kṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa-Kālacakra. Now, the designations and phenomena of the fourth state (*turyā*) and so forth are explained, beginning with the word "first" (*ādyā*): The first are the five voids; nature (*prakṛti*) is the unmodified (*avikṛti*). [Then there are] the glorious *kalā*, *bindu*, and *nāda*; time (*kāla*), mind (*citta*), and intellect (*buddhi*); likewise, nature (*prakṛti*) and the other vowels beginning with wind (*māruta*); the gross syllables of the consonant groups (*varga*); the ten multiplied by three (thirty), and the sixteen others which are the modifications (*vikāra*). In the midst of these, Vajra is neither nature nor modification; he is all-pervasive and devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). ||87||

In this saṃsāra, the designation of the object and the subject of cognition serves to establish their meaning, and that designation exists by way of the relationship between the signified and the signifier.

Herein, the first five voids of the nature of consciousness (*jñānaprakṛti*) are as follows: beginning with the Unstruck (*anāhata*), there is the void of the letter *a* in the center; the void of the letter *i* in the east; the void of the letter *ṛ* in the south; the void of the letter *u* in the north; and the void of the letter *l̥* in the west. These are the first five voids. Nature (*prakṛti*) is the unevolved;
it consists of the venerable *kalā*, *bindu*, *nāda*, time (*kāla*), mind (*citta*), and intellect (*buddhi*).

*Kalā* is the sun; *bindu* is the moon; *nāda* is Rāhu; *kāla* is the fire of time (*kālāgni*); and *citta* is the intellect (*buddhi*). Thus, *prakṛti* also possesses the nature of the state of deep sleep. The other vowels are the winds and so forth—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) referring to ether and the rest—namely: *a, i, ṛ, u, ḷ, a, e, ar, o, al, ha, ya, ra, va, la*.
Thus, "long" (dīrghā) is the nature of dream;
the gross syllables of the classes (*varga*), numbering three hundred and sixty together with the twelve *mātrās*, are the nature of the waking state;
and the other sixteen are the gross modifications (*vikāra*).

By taking fifteen vowels for each individual syllable together with a consonant, there are sixteen transformations (*vikāra*). Thus, everywhere, the five elements, the five sense faculties, and the five objects are the transformations; these, together with the mind (*manas*), make sixteen. Among these [sixteen], beginning with earth, *vastu* (the reality) is neither the primal nature (*prakṛti*) nor a transformation (*vikṛti*); it is all-pervasive and devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Since it is free from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of cyclic existence and possesses the nature of consciousness (*cittadharmin*), that mind exists which is "mind that is no-mind."
There exists no other mind of nirvāṇa apart from the mind of saṃsāra; this is the rule regarding the fourfold nature as spoken by the Blessed One under the designation of "Vajrī.

Now, the experience of the fruits of their own karma by sentient beings is described by the words beginning with "In saṃsāra": "In saṃsāra, pleasure and pain exist as they pertain to the qualities of nature (*prakṛti*), and they are born of that karma; this karma of humans may be of three kinds: gross, subtle, and tranquil."

"I am the agent, but Vikarman is another Paśupati who is the agent"—this is action; "I am not the agent, nor is the other, for he is known to be devoid of material nature (prakṛti)"—that is not action. || 88 ||

In this saṃsāra, whatever happiness, suffering, or a mixture of happiness and suffering a sentient being experiences—whether it pertains to the qualities of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) or to the previously mentioned qualities—it is self-made;
that is to say, it is born from karma and produced by one's own actions, and thus is "born of karma" (*karmaja*), meaning it is experienced as the result of what one has done.
This very [experience] is here threefold—gross, subtle, and supreme—according to the power of body, speech, and mind.
Action is threefold: *vikarman* (mis-action), *karman* (action), and *akarman* (inaction).
Among these, that in which the thought "I am the doer" arises is designated as *vikarman*. Another [teacher] says: "Paśupati, Anya, Ga, Ai, R̥, U, La..."
Or, as stated in the *Vimalaprabhā*: "Is there a creator? That mind which arises is designated as 'action' (*karman*).

I am not the creator, nor is another; I am devoid of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and devoid of the collection of aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth. That mind which arises is designated as 'non-action' (*akarma*)."
Thus, it is known that that which is devoid of a self, another, or an agent is not a karma performed by an agent, nor does it have an agent as its cause;

rather, the arising of karma occurs through the power of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Just as rice is produced from a rice seed, so too is the production of the fruit of a virtuous deed from a virtuous deed; and just as *kodrava* grain is produced from a *kodrava* seed, so too is the production of an unwholesome fruit from an unwholesome deed.
This is the determination of the fruit of karma, which will be explained in the passage beginning with "not from itself, nor from another."

Now, it is stated that action is fruitful even without an agent, beginning with the words "tasmāt" (therefore): "Therefore, there is no agent here who burns or takes away the happiness and suffering of living beings in saṃsāra; rather, it is past karma—performed in three ways—that arises as the yielder of fruit. This notion that 'he burns' or 'he takes away,' [or] that he is the creator of creation and destruction, belongs to the intellect of the deluded. They do not perceive the opening within the body, wherein immeasurable merit is being carried away by their own senses. (89)

In this saṃsāra, no creator bestows or takes away the happiness and suffering of living beings; for one's own previously committed karma alone prevails as the yielder of fruit—whatever has been performed in its threefold manner. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no creator who gives or takes.
This notion that "he gives and he takes, being the agent of creation and destruction" is the intellect of the deluded.
Why?

Because they do not perceive the openings in their own bodies while immeasurable merit is being carried away by their own eyes—that is, by their own sense organs—which are engaged with external objects and, from the perspective of the inner self, are devoid of the bliss of non-influx (anāśrava). This is the rule regarding the experience of the fruits of one's own karma.

Now, the state of mutual conjunction of the agent of desire and the others is described by the verse beginning with "desire" (icchā): Desire is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) within one's own mind; the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) is that of the world, being the third; it effects the entry of the light of existence (*bhāvāloka*) and the perception of objects (*arthopalabdhi*) in the process of making [all things] of equal flavor (*samarasakaraṇa*).

The fourth is the abandonment [of duality], which is bowed to by the three worlds, non-dual (*advaya*), and indeed, among those [powers] in sequence, O Lord of Men, the Vajrin swallows nothing at all, nor does he ever release anything. (90)

In this world, that power of the mind's own desire (*svamanasīcchāśakti*) which brings illumination to objects means that it causes the activity of the mind; it performs the action of entering into objects. The power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) effects the attainment of the object by bringing about the state of aesthetic flavor (*samarasa*) with the object; "attainment of the object" means the ascertainment of the object, which is to say, the ascertainment of knowledge. Furthermore, the fourth [power], which is bowed to by the three worlds and is non-dual (*advayā*), sequentially effects the abandonment of previous knowledge—that is, its relinquishment. Thus, these are the four powers of the mind; among these four, none devours anything.

Entering the light, achieving the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*), the attainment of the object, or the relinquishing of cognition— whosoever whose self is a pure mind does not abandon these, that is the discipline of will (*icchā-niyama*) which destroys the fruit of destruction.

It burns; it bestows; it seizes [the objects] of the mental plane. This is the Great Chapter on the Rules of Kālacakra Concerning the Characteristics of Moments. Now, the giver of suffering and happiness is described, beginning with the words "The self," etc.: "O King, the self is not the agent there, nor is it the giver of suffering and happiness. O Lord of Men, neither bondage nor liberation exists apart from the power of the mind."
Just as space enters into the middle of a jar yet the water being carried does not [enter], so too the Space-Vajra, pervading the sky and devoid of sense objects, is likewise within the body. 91.

In this saṃsāra, O King, the self (*ātman*) is not the agent; it has no power there as the bestower of suffering and happiness. There is no one at all within the abode of the three worlds who is the bestower of suffering and happiness, with the exception of the power of consciousness (*cittaśakti*). Here, the powers of consciousness are characterized by the four states: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (*turyā*). Among these, the bestower is the fourth state, which possesses the nature of arising and ceasing. Apart from that power of consciousness, there is no other self, agent, or bestower of happiness and suffering.
There is no other bondage or liberation for sentient beings apart from the emission of semen; this means that apart from the mind of saṃsāra.

Furthermore, the mind of nirvāṇa—which transcends saṃsāra and abides within all bodies—is neither bound nor liberated by anything. Just as space enters into the midst of a jar yet is not carried away when the water is being taken out, so too is the mind that pervades the sky, known as the Space-Vajra, purified by the liberations such as emptiness.

"Khavajrī" means that which is devoid of objects and free from qualities (*nirguṇa*); this signifies being free from the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the constituents of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, as well as being free from the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (*turyā*).

"Niḥsvabhāva" (devoid of intrinsic nature) refers to that within the center of the body; likewise, "śveto bhāva" means white existence, while "uccheda" means non-existence. He in whom these two do not exist is "Vajrī," meaning the pure mind (*viśuddhacitta*). This is the rule concerning the minds of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

Now, the doctrine of karma is stated with the words beginning "thus" (*evam*), etc.: "Thus, he is one who asserts the existence of karma; he is the Blessed One, the sole Teacher, not a creator, the omniscient Primordial Buddha (*Ādibuddha*) bowed to by the three worlds, the Kālacakrin, not [the mundane] Cakrin.

I bow to that Kālacakra, the progenitor of the best of Jinas, at the root of whose lotus-feet Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra have sought refuge—he who is devoid of qualities and free from conceptual construction. (92)

By this sequential process as described, one who asserts the existence of karma becomes a proponent of non-existence regarding the agent, and thus a proponent of selflessness; that Blessed One is the pure essence of mind.
He is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor even of the nature of neither; he is the sole teacher in the three realms, not a creator.

He is the omniscient Primordial Buddha, possessing omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of the aspects of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*); he is honored by the three worlds, the Lord of Kālacakra, whose nature consists of all phenomena in their every aspect and the bliss of the unconditioned (*anāśrava*).
Viṣṇu is not the Wheel-bearer (Cakrī).
Why?

Because Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra have all sought refuge at the base of his lotus feet; I bow to him as the Kālacakra. Thus, I am Mañjuśrī, the progenitor of the supreme Victors, devoid of qualities and free from conceptual construction, possessing the characteristics previously described—this is the rule for the proponent of emptiness.

Now, he describes birth at the end of death according to the state of being (*bhāva*), beginning with the words "In a peaceful state," and so forth: "In a peaceful state, O Lord of Men, immortality occurs; in a *tāmasa* state, one becomes a denizen of hell; in a *rājasa* state, an animal; and in a mixed state, on this excellent earth, one attains human status.

On this earth, the state of a living being (*bhūta*) is of three kinds—*sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*—or else they are mutually mixed. Whatever state a creature remembers with the mind at the time of death, there its rebirth occurs. (93)
[The Inner]—In this world, due to the power of their own karma, sentient beings possess various qualities and states; from those states, he speaks of their arising.

Here, at the time of death, by the power of virtuous karma, a peaceful state consisting of the qualities of a sentient being occurs. When that state has arisen, at the end of death, immortality is attained. "O Lord of Men" is an address to Sucandra.
Through the power of inauspiciousness, a fierce state consisting of the quality of darkness (*tamas*) arises; in that state of darkness, one attains the condition of a hell-being.
Through the power of middling inauspiciousness, a passionate state (*rājasa*) arises; when that passionate state exists, one attains the condition of an animal at the end of life.
Furthermore, human birth on this excellent earth is mixed; human existence occurs when [karma] is a combination of both auspicious and inauspicious.
The earthly realm (*bhūtalama*) is of three kinds: characterized by *rajas*, *tamas*, or *sattva*, each mutually mixed with the others.
Here, when *sattva* predominates, the *pretas* are superior; when *rajas* predominates, they are middling; and when *tamas* predominates, they are inferior.

As for the *asuras*, they are indeed included within the category of gods. Likewise, among humans, those in whom *sattva* predominates are happy; those in whom *rajas* predominates are miserable; and those in whom *tamas* predominates are constantly miserable. This applies everywhere, even in places such as heaven.

The ripening of the infinite fruits of karma for sentient beings occurs through the power of their own individual karma; therefore, whatever state a being remembers at the time of death, rebirth occurs there for that creature—this is the rule for the arising of existence.

Now, the divisions of gods and so forth are described, beginning with "the state of a god": the state of a god has eight divisions in the abode of the excellent deities; the state of a human is likewise one; animals are indeed of four types; and in the realm of hell, the state of a hell-being is likewise one.

Bound by the snares of karma, a living being wanders through these states, following the flow of worldly existence; unless liberated, it does not attain liberation—the state of supreme bliss—even after many hundreds of thousands of births.

In this abode of the supreme gods, heaven, divinity arises through eight modes: by means of the cultivation of the totality of earth, the totality of water, the totality of fire, the totality of wind, the totality of space, the totality of the moon, the totality of the sun, and the totality of Rāhu—through the power of merit such as generosity and the abandonment of the ten unwholesome actions, divinity arises in these eight modes. Human existence is likewise one, yet consists of six types.
Animals are of four kinds, categorized according to the ocean [of births].
That which consists of the six elements is likewise the state of being a hell-being; within the destiny of hell, it arises from the latencies of the six elements and is like a dream.
The state of being an asura is included within that of the gods, and the state of being a preta is included within that of the hell-beings, due to the experience of suffering.

In these fourteen locations—within the eight, four, and one-fold births—the sentient being, whose nature is the *ālayavijñāna*, wanders through the six realms of existence (*rasagati*) bound by the noose of karma. Not released from the noose of karma, he does not attain liberation, the state of supreme bliss, even after many hundreds of thousands of births; such is the rule for the distinctions among gods and other beings, according to the disposition of sentient beings.

Now, the cause of bondage is stated by means of the verse beginning with "by the aggregates" (skandhaiḥ): Bound by the aggregates, elements, and sense-faculties; by the five organs of action along with the subtle elements (tanmātras), the defects of karma, the qualities (guṇas), and the mind; and by intellect, ego, and the rest—bound indeed by these, the living soul (jīva) wanders repeatedly in the course of the fluids (rasagati) in a subtle state. When existence is abandoned, it goes to the imperishable supreme state where one who is born does not exist again. (95)
In this saṃsāra of the six realms of existence, the living being (jīva), whose nature consists of the consciousness of the abode of vital breaths (prāṇālayavijñāna), wanders bound. By what means?

Bound by the six elements that constitute the trunk [of the body], by the sense organs, by the fears of the threefold existence, by the six objects and their subtle essences (*tanmātra*), by the five organs of action, by the defects of action—both auspicious and inauspicious—together with the qualities, the mind, and the intellect, ego, and the rest (the word "and the rest" including the vital energy *prāṇa*, the power, and primordial nature *mūlaprakṛti*); indeed, the individual soul (*jīva*) bound by these wanders in the movement of the vital sap in a subtle state. Furthermore, through the bliss of non-falling away, there is bondage in both subtle and gross forms, characterized by the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (*turya*).

And when this state is abandoned, one proceeds to the imperishable supreme state, having reached which one is no longer born again as a transmigrating being; such is the rule regarding the ignorance of the latent impressions of saṃsāra.

Now, its opposite, *vidyā* (knowledge), is described by the verse beginning with "The Veda with its limbs" (*sāṅgo vedaḥ*) and so forth: "The Veda with its limbs, together with the *Smṛtis*, the *Mata-s*, the *Tarka* (logic), and the *Siddhānta-yukta-śāstra*—and whatever other treatise has been composed in this world by poets such as Vyāsa, Vaiśvānara, and others—is not *vidyā*. In this world, *vidyā* is declared by the sages to be the science of the self (*adhyātmavidyā*), which is the Imperishable (*akṣara*). Within it, O Lord of Men, the entire three worlds exist, and within it they dissolve once again. (96)

In this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), within the worldly conventions of life, that which is knowledge regarding the subject of ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*) is [actually] ignorance (*avidyā*).

First, "Veda" refers to the Veda together with its six limbs (*aṅga*); the limbs being Sūtra, Geya, Vyākaraṇa, Chandas, Nirukti, and Jyotiṣa—the meaning is "together with these. Furthermore, it is accompanied by the *Smṛtis*; the *Smṛtis* are those of Manu and others—it is conjoined with them.

The qualification "endowed with" refers to logic (*tarka*), the treatises on worldly objects and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-śāstra*), the established doctrines (*siddhānta*), and the dharmas consisting of conceptual meditations (*vikalpa-bhāvanā*) such as the *maṇḍala-cakra* and other means for achieving mundane accomplishments (*laukika-siddhi*). Likewise, there is another scripture composed in the world by poets such as Vyāsa, Vaiśvānara, and others. Here, "Vyāsa’s poetry" refers to the *Mahābhārata*; "Vaiśvānara’s poetry" refers to the dharma of meditation (*bhāvanā-dharma*); by the word "and others," Vālmīki’s poetry, the *Rāmāyaṇa*, Mārkaṇḍeya’s poetry, the Purāṇic dharmas, and so forth are included. [The implication is that] knowledge is not produced by these poets.

Then, he asks: "What is knowledge (*vidyā*)? He says: Knowledge is non-conceptual inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*), emptiness endowed with all aspects; furthermore, the syllable (*akṣara*) is also knowledge, which is without objective support (*anālambinī*) and has the nature of bliss free from all substrates (*anāśrayasukhātmikā*).
Knowledge consists of cause and fruit, being a single fusion of cause and fruit, like the light of a fire that is a single fusion with its burning power.
This has been proclaimed here in this world by the sages of the past and present who abide in the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).

He states what its nature is: "In which the entire three worlds [dissolve]. Because from that moment of bliss the entire three worlds come into being at the time of origination, and they dissolve back into it again at the time of death—in that very moment the aggregate of phenomena dissolves. That very moment, which is the moment of imperishable bliss (*akṣarasukha*), is called the "imperishable" (*akṣara*).
From this, the Buddhas arise for the sake of turning the wheel of Dharma; in this, O King, is indeed the Great Parinirvāṇa. This is the rule concerning Vidyā.

Now, the power of the practice of former yoga is described, beginning with the words "the lord of yogis": "The lord of yogis who has not attained yoga may, at some point, meet death with a distracted mind; however, endowed with glory, he is born in the human world into a lineage of eminent sages, joined with yoga. By means of that previous practice, he again attains the vast yoga of knowledge; once knowledge is obtained, he proceeds to the imperishable supreme state where one is no longer subject to birth. (97)

If here in this mortal world a yogin, while practicing the yoga of knowledge (*vidyā-yoga*), should meet death without having attained yoga—perhaps due to a distracted mind—the illustrious one is reborn in the human world within a preeminent lineage of sages, that is, within the family of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Yoga is the pure reality, the pure mind, which is the indivisibility of emptiness and compassion; one who is joined with that is "yoga-endowed" (*yogayukta*), yet not one who has perfected yoga. Furthermore, by means of that previous practice, he attains it, for he has obtained the vast yoga of gnosis (*jñāna-yoga*). The sense is that it is not partial, but rather possesses all aspects (*sarvākāra*).

When knowledge is fully attained, one proceeds to the "indestructible supreme state" (*akṣaya-parama-pada*). The analysis of the compound is as follows: that whose destruction does not exist is the "indestructible supreme state. To explain what that is like, he says: it is that wherein one who is subject to rebirth no longer comes into existence; that is the state of all Buddhas, the supreme state.

Now, the time for the arising of knowledge among the Buddhists, the Asuras, and the Mlecchas is stated, beginning with the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*): "At the time of the sun's day for the Jinas when knowledge arises; at midnight and the end of night for the Asuras; and at midday for the Vasus (gods).

When perfect knowledge or its fragmentation occurs, their speech becomes respectively Sanskrit and Prakrit, and their action—whether peaceful or fierce—is likewise either spiritual (*pauruṣa*) or material (*prākṛta*) within the abode of the three worlds. (98)
In this regard, there are indeed three types of practice of yoga: the Buddhist (*bauddha*), the demonic (*āsura*), and the elemental (*bhauta*).

Among these, Buddhist yoga consists of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*); the demonic consists of the nature of conceptual construction (*kalpanā-dharma*); and the elemental is of two kinds: eternalistic in form and nihilistic in form.
Thus, there exists a yogi of these three types, because he is one who delights in the practice of that respective yoga.

Among them, the arising of knowledge for Buddhist yogins occurs during the day; for Asura yogins, it occurs during the night; and for Bhūta yogins, the arising of knowledge occurs at a time devoid of the four junctions (saṃdhyā). This is the division of time regarding the arising of knowledge for the Jinas: at the time of the sun’s day, at midnight, at the end of the night, and at midday. For the Asuras, it is at the time of the moon’s night;
and for the Bhūtas, since no specific time is mentioned, it is at a time devoid of the junctions, following the departure of Indra.

At this time, at midnight or during the morning twilight (*pūrvasandhyā*), there occurs the empowerment of the knowledge of speech for the Buddhists; for the Asuras, it occurs at midday twilight or at sunset twilight. For the Bhūtas, there is the empowerment of eternal knowledge (*śāśvata-jñāna*) during the fourth watch of the day, and the empowerment of nihilistic knowledge (*uccheda-jñāna*) during the night portion—these respectively for the Buddhists and the Asuras. Correct knowledge arises for the Buddhists, while for the Asuras, there is a distorted [knowledge] which is opposed to that Dharma.

How is it known that right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is like daylight, seeing all things, while divided knowledge (*vibhaṅgajñāna*) is like the light of night, seeing only some aspects of the birth and death of sentient beings? To this, he says: "By means of the teaching of the Dharma. Here, within right knowledge, both refined (*saṃskṛta*) and vernacular (*prākṛta*) speech arise.

For those who have produced right knowledge, their speech is refined and consists of all sounds; for the teachers who have produced divided knowledge, their speech is vernacular, being in a single regional dialect among various languages.

The knowledge of the Buddhists, which teaches peaceful activities, consists of compassion for all sentient beings; the knowledge of the Asuras, which teaches fierce activities, is for the purpose of eating the flesh of those who harm animals.

[In this chapter] is the Great Summary on the Rules of Kālacakra regarding the Characteristics of Moments: in the abode of the three worlds, the knowledge of the Buddhists teaches human activity; on earth, the knowledge of the Asuras teaches ordinary activity;
and it teaches the mixed activity of spirits upon the earth—such is the rule for the teaching of knowledge.

Now, the time for the enjoyment of the Buddhists and Asuras is stated, beginning with "from midday": From midday until midnight, during the times of day and night, is the period of enjoyment for those two. Their food is beef, a meal of many kinds of flavors; their drink is the semen of the *maṇḍala*;

their clothing is red and white, like the movement of the sun and moon; their dwelling is in heaven and the underworld; their dharma is non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and violence according to the power of the preceptor’s rules; and their seat is the Vajra-demon (*vajradaitya*). ||99||
In this context, from midday until midnight is the period of day;
from midnight until midday is the period of night.

Within those periods of day and night, the time for eating is the latter half of each respective period. This is the rule that applies to ascetics (*tapasvins*) of both the Buddhists and the Mlecchas, but not to householders.
Furthermore, regarding the food and drink of the Buddhists and the Asuras, they are respectively as follows:
the food of the Buddhists is more distinguished, while that of the Mlecchas is accompanied by beef;
their drinks are respectively sweet, providing many kinds of flavors for the Buddhists, and the drinking of semen from the eggs of cocks and other such creatures for the Mlecchas.
Regarding the clothing, according to their respective order: the Buddhists wear red garments, while the ascetic Mlecchas wear white; for householders, there is no fixed rule.

Likewise, at the end of life, their abodes are according to their respective order, like the movements of the sun and the moon: the movement of the sun is upward, and the movement of the moon is downward. Corresponding to their movements, the residence in heaven is like the movement of the sun for the Buddhists, and the residence in the netherworld (pātāla) is like the movement of the moon for the Asuras. As the Blessed One said in the *Sekoddeśa* of the Root Tantra: "At death, the lunar nectar of all embodied beings goes downward."
Above are the Sun, the Dust, and Rāhu; consciousness is characterized by its ontological state.
Likewise, the dharma is according to their respective numbers:

the dharma of the Buddhists is non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), while that of the Mlecchas is violence. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that for living beings, during the time of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and at the time of praising one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) under the influence of strict observances, the postures are respectively prescribed: the *vajrāsana* is recommended for the Buddhists, and the *daityāsana* is recommended for the Mlecchas. By the word "and," another posture is indicated as being common [to both]; therefore, there is neither a specific injunction nor a prohibition regarding it.

Here, regarding the Daityas on the surface of the earth: from the extension of the left knee, the right foot is above the left knee; the extension of the right knee is above the left foot; and by the word "ca" (and), the right foot is below [the left]; the right foot is above, and by the word "ca," even on the sole of the foot, it is stated that the hips rest upon the back—this should be explained as in the *vajrāsana* and other postures to be described later. This is the rule for the ritual actions (*kriyā*) of the Buddhist Asuras. For the Bhūtas, mixed action prevails; their speech is mixed Paiśācika, and their dharma consists of both non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and indeed violence (*hiṃsā*), along with faults such as the killing of living beings due to strict observances toward their gurus.

O Lord of Men, there occurs engagement for the sake of sacrifice and the like, or sometimes cessation; food and drink are mixed, and due to the movement of the sun and moon, the path is mixed in the other [world]. (100)

Furthermore, regarding the mixed ritual of the elements (*bhūta*) previously mentioned, it was not clearly explained here in this verse. It is as follows: the mixed ritual of the elements (*bhūtānāṃ miśrakarma*) prevails, as does speech that is mixed with *paiśāca* (demoniac). Dharma is non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), whereas violence (*hiṃsā*) indeed arises from the fault of killing living beings due to heavy restrictions.

Engagement for the sake of yoga—by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), meaning for the sake of cattle and the like, or for the sake of battle—is engagement in violence. For the sake of results, there is cessation, which is engagement in non-violence (*ahiṃsā*).
O Lord of Men, there may sometimes be a cessation [of activity].

From the movement of the Sun and Moon, food and drink are mixed; the path is mixed in the other case. Thus, in the mixed path, the entire [process] of the elements (bhūtas) is to be known. This is the rule for the activity of the elements. Now, desiring to explain the path, he says "Light," and so forth: Light is the course of the Sun; the bright fortnight and the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa) constitute half a year. The Moon is light and the night; this is the dark solstice (dakṣiṇāyana) on the path of smoke (dhūmamārga).
O Lord of Men, the radiance of the gods shines in heaven; that of the asuras resides in the bodies of the nāga-world; and in the mortal world, it becomes mixed for pretas, animals, and humans. (101)

In this context, there are indeed three paths: the path of light (*jyotirmārga*), the path of smoke (*dhūmamārga*), and the mixed path (*vimiśramārga*). Among these, "light" refers to the sun; it is the bright fortnight, the northern course (*ayana*), characterized by the increase of the day, and constitutes half a year externally, while internally it consists of the six zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn (*makara*). This is designated as "rising and setting."

The path of smoke (dhūmamārga) is light, the moon, and night; this is the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana). In the southern path of smoke, beginning with Cancer, there is the six-month southern solstice; where there is an increase in the duration of night, that is the southern course. From sunset until sunrise, such is the rule. Here, the path of light (arciḥ) is for the gods to travel to heaven, while the dark course—the path of smoke—is for the asuras to go to the world of the nāgas.

The rule of the path is thus revealed: the mixed nature of day and night leads to birth as a human, a preta, or an animal upon entering the world of mortals; this occurs by virtue of the inherent qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* produced by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of previous births. Now, the grasping of these impressions by sentient beings is described through the passage beginning with "Whichever among those... [referring to] those devoted to the practices of Śrāvakas, Buddhists, Asuras, or Bhūtas: "O Lord of Men, whichever group one has entered and delights in its vows and observances, being bound by the fetters of karma, one comes to exist within that very group according to one's own nature, through the influence of that specific class."

O King, as long as there is the existence of the mind under the influence of the threefold states of being, so long will there be the experience of pleasure and pain; thus, one wanders here in the terrible cycle of saṃsāra—among gods, mortals, and below.

In this saṃsāra, by the power of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of karma, one becomes devoted to the activities of gods, asuras, or spirits; whichever [group] one has entered among them, being intent on vows and observances, one is bound by the fetters of karma. One is bound by the ritual actions (*kriyā*) of that particular dharma; within that [group], one exists according to one's own respective nature. "O Lord of Men" is an address; "by the influence of that family"—meaning the family of gods, asuras, or spirits—refers to the grasping of that state of being.

By that [process], one is born into the families of gods, asuras, or bhūtas, through the ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*) characterized by the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, according to the previously mentioned method; thus, up to the point where it is said: "The state of the mind is threefold by virtue of the three types of existence. This is the *Mahoddeśa* on the rules of the Kālacakra regarding the characteristics of moments.

In this context, for the mind within saṃsāra, due to the power of the threefold existence—that is, by the power of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the realms of desire, form, and formlessness—there is saṃsāric sensation consisting of pleasure and pain. To that extent, O King, there is the wandering of the mind, characterized by suffering, through the celestial and human worlds; and downward, there is the wandering of the *ālayavijñāna* through the six destinies, such as the gods, humans, and hells. This is the rule regarding the grasping of latencies.
Therefore, one who has transcended the threefold latencies stands at the far shore of saṃsāra, established in the state where all that was to be done has been accomplished.

The Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Gnosis Body (*jñānakāya*), whose lotus-feet are worshipped by gods, asuras, nāgas, and others, is *Kālacakra*; this is the rule for the removal of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).

Now, just as the production of consonants and vowels occurred in the womb, so too the characteristics of death are described by the words beginning with "the letters starting with *ka*": "The letters starting with *ka*, along with their vowel measures, multiplied by the qualities (*guṇa*), and the thirty consonants together with the vowels of the three fortnights—death ascends through these by the power of the threefold course."

The movements of the five planets, the positions of the Sun and Moon, and the stations of Rāhu and Ketu, as well as the thirty-two years and fortnights multiplied by three, are distinguished by the Moon, the Sun, and Fire. (103)
Here, at the time of conception, the female element consists of the thirty consonants and the male element consists of the thirty vowels;
their union is presided over by the *ālayavijñāna*.

In this production of the embryo, regarding the first fortnight, the thirty consonants beginning with *ka* are presided over by short vowels, while in the other fortnight they are presided over by long vowels; thus, these two groups of consonants become manifest at death.

Thus, there is the entry of the semen (*śukra*) into the space element (*ākāśadhātu*); during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) of the menses (*rajas*), and during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), there is the entry into the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*).
In this way, whether the menses are manifest or unmanifest, there is the entry of the earth and space elements into the seminal element.

Thus, in the first fortnight of the second month, the consonants presided over by the vowel *i* [enter], while in the menses there is the entry into the wind element (*vāyudhātu*); in the latter fortnight, the consonants presided over by the vowel *ū* [enter], and there is the entry into the water element (*udakadhātu*).

In the first fortnight of the third month, there is the entry into the fire element presided over by the vowel *ṛ*; in the second fortnight, there is the entry into the fire element presided over by the vowel *ṝ*.

In the first fortnight of the fourth month, there is the entry into the water element presided over by the vowel *u*; in the second fortnight, there is the entry into the air element presided over by the vowel *ī*.

In the first fortnight of the fifth month, those presided over by the vowel *ḷ* are for the entry into the earth element; in the second fortnight, those presided over by the long vowel *ā* are for the entry into the space element.

Thus, through the distinction between emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), there is the entry of space and so forth, and earth and so forth, into one another within the semen and the menstrual blood.
For the sake of presiding over the sense organs and the organs of action, the qualities, the *vṛddhi* vowels, and the *ādi* vowels—the short and long vowels—effect their entry into the consonants.

In the first half of the sixth month: *a*; in the second half of the first half: *ha*; in the first half of the second half: *āla*; in the second half of the second half: *lā*. For the seventh [month], likewise: *e*, *ya*, *o*, *vā*. For the eighth: *ara*, *ra*, *ār*, *rā*. For the ninth: *o*, *vā*, *ai*, *yā*. For the tenth: *ala*, *ra*, *la*, *ā*, *hā*, *lā*. Thus, through the thirty consonants over ten months, there is the completion of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), and so forth; this occurs from after the month of conception onwards. It is the union of semen and blood, the radiation of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases according to the sequence of emanation and withdrawal.
Thus, in the eleventh month, [the channels] are presided over by the *bindu*, and in the twelfth month, they become presided over by the *visarga*.

Therefore, this is the determination of the production of the lunar element (*candradhātu*), the semen element (*śukradhātu*), the channels, the marrow, and the bones. The sun (*arka*) increases the *rajas* of the Prajñā for twelve years, and that of the Upāya for sixteen years; thereafter, *ala al ā*.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, the maturation of the element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*) is the maturation of the *rajas* of wisdom (*prajñā*), and the maturation of the semen (*śukra*) is that of method (*upāya*). Thereafter, for another twelve years of wisdom and another sixteen years of method, there is the maturation of the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*).
From this limit, the sattva portion becomes middling.

For wisdom (*prajñā*), the maturation of the water element (*toyadhātu-pāka*) lasts eighteen years less one day; for means (*upāya*), as before, the maturation of the water element lasts sixteen years, twenty-two days, and one month and a half.
As before, there is likewise the maturation of the fire element (*agnipāka*) for wisdom, and for means as well, it is the same.

Thus occurs the maturation of the wind element (*vāyudhātu-pāka*) and the maturation of the space element (*ākāśadhātu-pāka*). The maturation of all the elements through the divisions of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* occurs at ninety-six years and ten and a half months.

Then, by means of the measure of the middle channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*)—which is the measure of a year, a fortnight, or a day, and the measure of thirty consonants—the time (*kāla*) emerges through a total of one thousand one hundred and fifty-five days.

This consists of the previously mentioned groups of letters beginning with *ka*, together with their vowels, multiplied by the qualities (*guṇa*), amounting to one thousand eighty days; as well as the vowels of the three fortnights (*tripakṣa-svara*)—short, long, and protracted—and the forty-five consonants.
These emerge according to the threefold movement, namely, by way of the left, right, and middle channels; these [letters] are death (*mṛtyu*).

Thus, one ascends those very steps—the previously mentioned eleven hundred and thirty-four steps of the five planets beginning with Maṅgala—consisting of the movements of the Sun and Moon; the eleven-step portion for Rāhu and Ketu consisting of seven and a half [steps]; and the rising step of Ketu consisting of two *ghaṭikās* per day.
These steps, measured in *ghaṭikās*, number three years, three fortnights, and thirty consonant-days; it is upon these that death ascends.

Thus, there are thirty-two fortnights multiplied by the qualities (guṇas), divided by the moon, sun, and fire, and divided by the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—that is, ninety-six fortnights. In another way, there are ten and a half months and fortnights in ninety-six years. For all three years, the fortnights are subtracted from the moon; the qualities are two fortnights of the fire of time (*kālavahni*). In a hundred-year lifespan, the remaining fortnights follow both even and odd courses. The days and nights are numbered as eight, two, and three; all the groups (*vargas*) are deprived of their lords. Due to the movement of the sun and moon, death occurs through the vowels and consonants according to their respective paths. || 104 ||

Among the fortnights of the hundred-year period consisting of the left and right channels, there are seventy-two fortnights for three years; furthermore, for the Moon (the breath), there are three fortnights of qualities, and for Time-Fire (Kālāgni), two fortnights. Thus, seventy-seven fortnights are subtracted from the total heap of fortnights in a hundred-year period, which numbers twenty-four hundred; the remaining fortnights for the Sun and the Moon in the right and left [channels] number two thousand three hundred and twenty-three, according to the count of "world-eyes" (lokākṣi) and "fire-eyes" (agnyakṣi).

Thus, death devours all the time-units of day and night devoid of their lords—thirty-six thousand such units within a hundred years; or rather, death devours the groups of consonants (*vyañjana*) and vowels (*mātrā*) of the sun and moon, along with the months, days, and so forth, according to the movement [of the breath] on the left and right channels. Starting from the *ariṣṭa* (signs of death), death devours them during the intermediate period. Specifically, death devours those thirty-two and a half channel-measures of the wheel, excluding the lunar measures and the measures of the weekdays, by means of the divisions of day and night consisting of wisdom and method. Death devours these as well.

Thus, one should recite the groups [of consonants] with their respective measures, together with the collection of vowels; likewise, the consonants themselves [should be recited] according to the number of days, whether in the deficient, the middling, or the desired [period], when there is the death of the Moon or the Sun, and when the consonant is the presiding deity.

[In this] chapter, the Great Summary on the Regulation of the Kālacakra of Momentary Characteristics: Thus, the wheel-nāḍīs are indeed one and a half; the number of the wheel and one and a half [revolutions] corresponds to the eighteen zodiac signs. Multiplied by one hundred and twenty-five, they become ghaṭikās numbering two thousand four hundred and thirty. The lunar steps (śaśipada), through the divisions of sequential and non-sequential, are four hundred and so forth among the elements and non-elements; those devoid of them, or the lunar steps devoid of them, are the seven nāḍīs of the days. Devoid of those, the total number is three thousand two hundred and twenty-three. Death perceives these through the various divisions of wisdom and means, by the distinctions of dissolution and emanation, during the time of night.

Thus, the groups [of consonants] with their respective measures, together with the collection of vowels, and likewise the consonants themselves, are repeated [in sequence]. In the case of a "low" (hīna) death through the moon's misfortune (*ariṣṭa*), or a "middling" (madhyama) death through the sun's misfortune, it is said that the deity presiding over the consonant (*adhidaiva*) is involved. Thus, in the case of a low death through the moon's misfortune, a middling death through the sun's misfortune, or a middling death through the deity presiding over the consonant, the previously stated rule applies: when the thirty-two [vowels] have passed in conjunction with the moon and sun, this is the cutting of the channels (*nāḍikā*). Furthermore, after thirty-six nights, one abandons the aggregates, elements, sense-faculties, and so forth, along with the vajra.
Having abandoned the lunar and solar channels, the vital breath enters the Śaṅkhinī for one day, until there is a cessation of the elements of earth, water, fire, air, and space. 106.

Then, for thirty-three days—counted as thirty-two [days] plus one—the moon and sun move together; that is, while moving to the left, they proceed through the channels (*nāḍī*) by way of the right. This is the common [sign] of the lunar and solar *ariṣṭa*. Furthermore, at the time of death, after another three hundred three-nights (*trirātra*), on the thirty-third day, they abandon the defiled aggregates, elements, sense-faculties, and so forth, along with body, speech, and mind.

Then, having abandoned the channel of the moon and sun, he enters the female tongue, the Śaṅkhinī-avadhūtī, until the severance of the various vital winds of the elements of earth, water, fire, air, and space.

Here, on the day of death in the central channel, having entered [the central channel] and being overcome by the wind of time, one abandons the earth element of fivefold nature at the navel; thereafter, the interruption of the earth element occurs. At the heart, one abandons the water element of fourfold nature; the interruption of the water element occurs. At the throat, one abandons the fire element of threefold nature; thereafter, the interruption of the fire element occurs. At the forehead, one abandons the wind element of twofold nature; thereafter, the interruption of the wind element occurs. At the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa), one abandons the space element of singlefold nature; thereafter, the interruption of the space element occurs.

The abandonment of the elements of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) occurs as follows: above and below the navel, one abandons the *apāna* which has the nature of the seminal drop (*bindu*); from that, the exhaustion of the waking state occurs. At the secret place, one abandons the speech-bindu which has the nature of the seminal drop; from that, the cutting off of the dreaming state occurs. At the jewel (*maṇi*), one abandons the mind-bindu which has the nature of the seminal drop; from that, the cutting off of the deep sleep state occurs. Likewise, above [the head], one abandons the vital breaths which are drops of the passion-element (*rajas*); from that, indeed, the severance of body, speech, and mind occurs.

At the time of transition, one abandons the sixth element, the element of gnosis (jñānadhātu); one abandons the semen below throughout all the limbs and abandons the menses above, whereby the severance of the fourth state occurs. Such is the rule for the time of death for those born from a womb.

Thus ends the fifth great chapter, "The Rule of Kālacakra Concerning the Characteristics of Moments that Serve as the Causes for Arising and Cessation in Worldly Convention," in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakratantrarāja* following the *Śrīmūlatantra*. 5.
ka. kha. The sequence as stated is not found in manuscript kha. ka. kha. [The vehicle] consisting of dharma.

First, for the sake of accomplishment, the mantra-practitioner must protect the body of the complete Victor; for in the absence of the body, there is no accomplishment, nor is supreme bliss attained in this life.

Therefore, for the sake of the body, one should daily practice the yoga of the channels (*nāḍīyoga*). When the body is perfected, other accomplishments in the abode of the three worlds come under one's command. (107)

In this very cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), the *prāṇa* and *apāna* of sentient beings exit the body by way of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-krama*) and enter it by way of the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-krama*). Just so, the Blessed One stated in the *Mūlatantra*, in the *Sekoddeśa*: “In the lotus of the navel, the heart, the throat, the forehead, and the crown of the head—earth, water, fire, wind, and space—flow out by way of withdrawal;
entering, she enters the earth by way of emanation.”
Likewise, the apāna power, carrying body, speech, and mind, flows out from and enters into the lotus of the navel and the secret place; it is of the nature of both withdrawal and emanation.

For this reason, at the outset, the body of all the Victors—the body consisting of the five aggregates and so forth—must be protected by the practitioner for the sake of accomplishment (*siddhi*). In the absence of the body, there is no accomplishment, nor is the supreme bliss, the untainted bliss, attained in this life. Therefore, for the sake of the body—and "for the sake of the body" means for the sake of the *bodhicitta*—one should daily practice the yoga of the channels (*nāḍī*) for the purpose of protecting it. Through the union of *lalanā* and *rasanā*, one should practice the yoga of the channels in the *madhyamā*; one should contemplate the *prāṇa* wind [therein], and the *apāna* [wind] in the *śaṅkhinī*, which is the yoga of the channels of feces and urine.
At the time of day and night, in the twelfth ascendant, one should meditate here upon the *nāḍī-yoga*.

By means of this meditation, the perfection of the body is attained; when the body is perfected, other worldly perfections come under its service. This is the rule for the accomplishment of worldly perfections.

Now, the path for accomplishing supramundane siddhis is described, beginning with the word "empty" (*śūnya*): "In the empty [state], one should meditate on the path of smoke and so forth, up to the limit of the universe, within the wheels of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) by means of the Guru’s instructions. Thereafter, one makes the prāṇa and apāna winds firm;
then, like a planet [seizing] the moon, the yogi effects the arrest of the bodhicitta. Therefore, whatever is desired is attained here in this very life within a few days. (108)
Here, in the void, by means of the path beginning with smoke and so forth, according to the constraint of the guru and the sequence to be described,

one should meditate on the "universal moon"— the universe in all its forms— up to that limit as being the mind within the channel-wheels (*nāḍīcakra*). From that point, the yogi makes even the *prāṇa* and the *apāna* wind stable in the navel-wheel.
Afterwards, O Indu, who is this that says "cessation," like Rāhu, the planet? O friend,
this [is it].
"Kha" means "subsequently" (*paścāt*); "nirodham" means "the definitive cessation of the moon" (*paścād-indu-nirodham*).
In this chapter, [the section on] the Great Instruction on Alchemy and the Science of Child-Rearing: The yogin effects the union of the *bodhicitta*.

Yoga is the mutual conjunction of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*; he who possesses that is a yogin. He brings about the cessation, the pacification, and the immutable state—beginning with the outflow (*niṣyanda*)—of the moment of emission of the *bodhicitta*. Therefore, whatever is desired, such as the outflow, the maturation (*vipāka*), the human effort (*puruṣakāra*), and the purity (*vaimalya*), or even that which is inexpressible, is attained within a few days in this very life.

"A few days" refers to the three years and three fortnights of the *Kālacakra* system; by these, the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā is attained through these aggregates purified by the liberations such as emptiness—this is the rule for the path of accomplishing Mahāmudrā. Now, the deception of untimely death is described with the words beginning "Mārttaṇḍa": "The cessation of the Sun and Moon, their entry into the central Fire during the movement of the even and uneven [channels], and the union of both Prāṇa and Apāna on the first day—this is the deception of the time of death."

Having filled [the body] with the vital breath (prāṇa), the yogi should meditate upon the Buddhas and their Consorts within the six cakras—extending from the hands and feet to the joints of the fingers and the tips of the nails—with their lotus-like hands in the gesture of granting fearlessness. || 109 ||

In this context, when a yogi perceives the signs of untimely death (*akālamaraṇa*), then there is the cessation of the Sun and Moon, which is the cessation of the right and left channels (*nāḍī*) during their even and uneven movements—that is, during the processes of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) and emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). One must effect the entry into the central fire, namely Rāhu and Kālāgni, within the middle channel.
When the flow of both prāṇa and apāna has entered the middle channel for one day, that constitutes the "deception" of untimely death for yogis.

Having filled [the body] with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) that flows through the five mandalas, together with the yoga of the central channel (*madhyamā*), and having filled the hands, feet, fingers, joints, and nails with the breath, the yogi should meditate upon the Buddha-deities with their lotus-hands in the gesture of fearlessness within the six chakras, beginning with the *uṣṇīṣa*, according to the sequence to be described; this is the rule for deceiving untimely death. Now, the pacification of wind-diseases and so forth is stated, beginning with "by the downward breath" (*apāna*): "In the case of all wind-diseases in the excellent body, the contraction of the downward breath (*apāna*) is desired; in the case of phlegm (*kapha*), there should be breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*); and furthermore, in the case of the fault of bile (*pitta*), there should be the releasing of both."

The complete cessation of the upward and downward breaths brings happiness during the onset of fever; the prāṇa-vāyu above the navel removes all ailments, while the other [apāna] at the root of the navel does the same.

In this body, the eighty previously mentioned channels cause the disorder of wind (vāta); for the purpose of balancing their constituent elements (dhātu), the contraction of the downward breath (apāna) is desired and brings happiness to practitioners of mantra when all diseases of wind, such as colic and the like, afflict the fair-bodied woman.
Likewise, in the forehead and the crown of the head, there are twenty channels that cause the disorder of phlegm (śleṣman);
for the purpose of balancing their constituent elements, breath control (prāṇāyāma) is desired.

"In the case of phlegm" means that when a disease of phlegm has arisen, the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) must be performed by the yogin; furthermore, "the release of those two" occurs in the case of a bile disorder (*pitta-doṣa*). When a bile disorder has arisen, having released those two—the *prāṇa* and *apāna*—to the exterior, one should take in the external air with a hissing sound (*śītkāra*) according to the method to be described, place the tongue upon the uvula (*lambikā*), and perform the drinking of nectar (*amṛta-pāna*) through the *stūka* and other [channels].
In all bile disorders, [this method] does not exist [otherwise].
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the internal channels: there are forty channels in the throat and the heart that cause the disorder of bile (*pitta*).

To bring equilibrium to their constituent elements (*dhātu*), this yoga must be performed; thus, the complete cessation of the upward and downward flows brings happiness in cases of the combined disorder (*sannipāta*) and fever.

In this secret [teaching], there are ten channels that cause the gathering [of the humors]; for the purpose of bringing equilibrium to those elements, the restraint of the upward-moving *prāṇa* and downward-moving *apāna* breaths is desired. Why is this desired in the case of fever? Because the *prāṇa* wind flows above the navel, it removes all diseases; therefore, the *apāna* flows at the root of the navel, and another [wind] below the navel removes all diseases—such is the rule for the pacification of diseases caused by *vāta* and the other [humors].

Now, teaching the remedy for the pacification of abdominal diseases, he says with the words beginning "contracting" (*ākuñcya*): By contracting the downward-moving wind (*apānavāyu*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) situated in the three paths upward, until the fire becomes powerful and pervading the entire body, it destroys even the diseases of the liver (*jagrī*), the spleen (*plīhā*), and hemorrhoids located in the abdomen through a month’s practice; as well as upward-breathing (*ūrdhvaśvāsa*), cough (*kāsa*), the three types of poison, eye diseases, and so forth.

In this case, when waking and other states occur within the stomach, then one should contract the apāna wind that has gone down the three paths—that is, the paths of feces, urine, and semen—and likewise contract the prāṇa itself which has gone up the paths of the moon, sun, and fire. Through their friction, the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*) becomes powerful and pervades the entire body.

This Agnigrī destroys diseases such as *yakṛt* (enlarged liver), *plīhā* (enlarged spleen), hemorrhoids, and abdominal dropsy (*jalodara*) through its application for one month; it also cures upward breath (*ūrdhva-śvāsa*), cough, and all three types of poison—stationary (*sthāvara*), mobile (*jaṅgama*), and artificial (*kṛtrima*)—as well as eye diseases, headaches, and so forth. This is the rule for the pacification of abdominal diseases. By forcefully pressing the breast from the left and right armpits while restraining the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the left channel (*nāḍī*) no longer flows from the left, and the right armpit [channel] likewise [ceases].

A yogi engaged in yoga removes even within half a month the ill-omened signs that bring death; and by placing his feet in the vajra posture with palms held like lotuses, he effects the destruction of back pain.

Now, the method for binding the channels (*nāḍībandha*) in order to deceive death is described, beginning with the words "from the armpit" (*kakṣāt*) and so forth: Here, when a yogin is unable to cause the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to enter the central channel (*madhyamā*) for a full day and night, he then causes the movement of the breath to shift from the left to the right in the event of a left-side omen of death (*ariṣṭa*), and causes it to shift from the right to the left in the event of a right-side omen. For half a month or up to one full month—by virtue of this stated reason—he forcefully presses even the breast on the left or right side from the armpit due to the obstruction of the breath.

When the right breast is pressed, the left channel does not flow; when the left armpit is pressed, the right channel does not flow. Thus, even by [this method], one who is engaged in yoga removes the omen of death that grants death within half a month. "Yoga" is the unification of inhalation (*pūraka*) and exhalation (*recaka*), which is retention (*kumbhaka*); one who is joined with that is "engaged in yoga" (*yogayukta*). "Removes" means he takes away; this is the rule for deceiving untimely death, provided it is not done excessively upward—there is no [result] above that. O Lord!
Above the navel (*nābhyūrdhva*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which has been raised up must be drawn back;

this is the great instruction on elixirs and so forth, as well as the science of pediatrics, in the [relevant] chapter. Now, the method for destroying back pain is described: "The two feet are situated in the *vajrāsana*. Regarding the *vajrāsana*: the left foot is placed upon the right thigh, and the right foot is placed upon the left thigh. Those two feet, with the arms crossed behind the back in the *vajrabandha* posture—held by the left hand is the right foot, and by the right hand is the left foot—those two feet, held by the hands like lotuses, effect the destruction of back pain.

O Uddhava, by restraining the breath, one removes all phlegmatic diseases from the body, including those affecting the feet and head; and within a few days, the flow of urine destroys dysuria through the restraint of breath.

At dawn, having rubbed the rows of teeth with the two ring fingers while the mouth is devoid of water, it becomes an ointment for the eyes that removes eye diseases, or alternatively, splashing them with water serves the same purpose.

By restraining the breath, one removes phlegm-related diseases from the entire body, including the feet, head, and lower torso; thus, through the practice of *prasrāva*, it destroys all difficulties (*kṛcchra*) within a few days by means of mantra. At dawn, when the mouth is free of water and not yet rinsed, one should rub the rows of teeth with the two ring fingers; this rubbing serves as collyrium for the eyes and becomes a remover of eye ailments.

Beating [the eyes] at dawn or applying water relieves pain in the eyes; thus, one who has slept with their face turned upward destroys indigestion and colic by holding a handful of *dhūtūra* flowers to the navel. When boils (*gaṇḍa*) arise, sweating them with salt and ghee destroys their growth.

An application of *arka* milk may sometimes [cure] tooth-worms; however, when there is pain, the smoke of *vyāghrī* seeds held here through a tube and the like destroys worms and other such parasites.
When one is asleep, the navel is raised by the left hand; that which is thus held is "Dhṛtakarakamalā," and it destroys indigestion and colic when accompanied by *prāṇāyāma*.

Regarding the emergence of swellings (*gaṇḍa*): at the time of the appearance of swellings, pustules, and the like, applying salt with ghee and binding it with a cloth provides fomentation, which indeed destroys their growth.
Furthermore, the application of milk is the rule for the prevention of the emergence of swellings and the like.
Sometimes the tooth-root (*dantakoṭa*) becomes painful; then, by holding the smoke of *vyāghrī* seeds through a tube or similar means, the destruction of the tooth-root occurs.

"Vyāghrī" refers to *kaṇṭakārī*; this is the general rule for the pacification of diseases. It removes [the pain]. Now, the remedy for the pacification of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) is stated, beginning with the word "half-year": "In half a year, it removes white leprosy from the beautiful bodies of practitioners; what else could it be? Even the wisdom of one's own mind, though always faltering, [is purified] through the constant restraint of the vital winds."

When seventy years of old age have passed and the hair has turned grey, at the completion of two years, the accomplishment of the *mudrā* occurs; beyond that, it happens within a few days through attachment to the *mārgacitta*. This is the Great Yoga (*mahāyoga*), accomplished by means of the previously mentioned signs such as smoke, through the restraint (*yāma*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Having caused the *bodhicitta* to flow out through union with the *mudrā*, that very *bodhicitta*, having flowed out through the yoga of the *mudrā*, becomes blissful due to the cessation of the origin of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*. Within half a year, it removes white leprosy from the excellent bodies of the practitioners; what else could it not do?

If it does not remove leprosy, then the yogi should practice with a sixteen-year-old consort (*mudrā*). Within six months, his *bodhicitta*—having slipped during the churning of the womb (*yonimanthana*)—is held firm by means of the yoga of breath-retention (*kumbhakayoga*), and it removes the disease of leprosy; there is no doubt in this regarding the word of the Tathāgata.
Not only does it remove leprosy, but even the seventy-year-old aging accompanied by graying hair is removed when the *bodhicitta* slips upon union with the consort at the completion of two years.

By this very yoga, for the yogi, within a few days—specifically after the three years and three fortnights of the Kālacakra—the perfection of the Mudrā occurs, following the destruction of old age; this is due to the application of the path-consciousness. This is the rule for the pacification of leprosy. The sound which exists in the region of the heart of excellent men is heard through the openings of the ears; from there above, it indeed enters the *muṣṭī* (the fist/center), having been made into a single element and abandoned as equal flavor (*samarasa*).

O Lord, whatever sound exists in the world of living beings, whether produced by strength or otherwise, that the yogi hears from afar; this distant hearing, O All-pervading One, is indeed to be cultivated through meditative realization.

Having assumed the cross-legged posture (paryaṅkabandha) with an open face, one should touch the teeth against one another; the external wind, drawn in and equal to the essence of nectar, enters the navel-cakra.
When restrained within the excellent body, it removes heat, hunger, and thirst, as well as poison. A white drop, surrounded by a circle of bliss on the forehead, releases nectar.

When the external wind is drawn in with force by the *prāṇa* through both nostrils and the mouth of the fire, and the *apāna* wind is struck [against it] like lightning-fire at the navel through yoga at the proper time, it attains a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) in the midst of the moon, sun, and fire; it removes hunger, thirst, and the need for food in the excellent body and bestows immortality.

The Great Chapter on Alchemy and the Science of Child-rearing: Having observed one’s own shadow standing in the sunlight with a fixed gaze while facing away from the sun, and then looking toward the sky, one sees a smoke-colored person of equal flavor (*samarasa*) through the yoga of six months of practice; this reveals the hidden treasure. Likewise, having entered the shadow of a tree upon the ground, the garland of drops (*bindumālā*) is meditated upon within the expanse of the sky.

That power which proceeds from the center of the navel to the supreme station, the end of the twelve [fingers], the end of the digits (kalā)— if it is firmly restrained at the navel, or if it rises in the form of a staff, or indeed moves with a soft and graceful gait from one wheel to another within the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) until it forcibly touches the aperture of the crown (*uṣṇīṣa-randhra*), it is then fixed like a needle. 120.

At that time, by means of supreme force, one should impel the downward breath (*āpāna*) upward; having pierced the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*), it proceeds to the city [of the Buddha] when the pair of winds is restrained.

Thus, through the awakening of the vajra, O fair-bodied one, he attains the state of a sky-walker (*khecara*); furthermore, this Mother of the Universe becomes for yogins the very nature of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*).

Now the rule for breath control (prāṇāyāma) is stated: One should perform breath control in the heart and likewise in the head until heat arises; for beyond that, one enters into a swoon. If uncontrolled or performed with force, it pierces the crown (uṣṇīṣa) and departs to another body, abandoning the aggregates and elements. Lost through attachment to the mudrās, it does not bestow the fruit of bliss upon men in this very life.

In this body, the practitioner of mantra should perform the *kumbhaka* breath-retention; [he should do so] in the heart and likewise in the head. As long as there is pain from the fire, the heart burns and pain occurs in the head; the rule is that one should not perform it beyond that point. If he does perform it further than that, O fair-limbed lady, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) enters into a state of fainting within the navel-lotus.

For one who is unrestrained may indeed pass away by force, having broken through the *uṣṇīṣa* and abandoned the aggregates (*skandhas*) and elements (*dhātus*); therefore, breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) that has lost its union with the *mudrā* does not grant the fruit of happiness to men in this very life. This is the rule for breath control.

The *mudrās* have been described for the sake of meditative cultivation during the times of day and night, neither for the sake of destroying passion nor for the sake of satiating the *vāgvajra*; indeed, it is said that for practitioners, [the practice] does not cause intoxication. Thus it is taught.

Every meal is for the sake of comfort at the appropriate time each day; it is not prescribed as a cause of indigestion. According to the *Śrīcaryāsiddhi*, one should not consume even a single grain at night for the purpose of "nailing down" the mind.
