A commentary on this verse is not found in the Sanskrit manuscripts, yet it is found in the Tibetan translation; while investigating the reason for this, the venerable Ācārya Khedrup Je stated that in authentic Indian Sanskrit manuscripts of the commentary, only the following is found: "Now, the rules regarding the mudrās, tastes, food, and conduct of yogins are being explained—this is easy to understand. Even that portion was not seen by me in the Sanskrit manuscripts. Here, the personal opinion of the venerable Khedrup Je must be recorded.

He said: Now, the medicine for the *avadhūta* yogi is described in this chapter on the great instructions concerning alchemy (*rasāyana*) and so forth, as well as pediatrics. Slightly warm *Akṣobhya* (urine) pacifies mouth diseases and toothache; at dawn, nasal drops of *Akṣobhya* remove pain in the head, and likewise, nasal drops [of it] in the ear remove eye disease. Warm or cold urine, and nasal drops of *Akṣobhya* combined with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), provide relief when one is afflicted by spirits or bitten [by a venomous creature].

In this regard, when a disease of the mouth occurs for a yogin, if he makes a small amount of Akṣobhya lukewarm and holds it in his mouth, it brings relief from the pain of the mouth as well as toothache— the word "ca" (and) implying also the pain of dental caries. When there is a disease in the head, then at dawn, if Akṣobhya is used as a nasal drop (*nasya*), it removes the pain in the head.
"Likewise, for yogins, there is the *toyanasya* (urine-sniffing).

When ear disease occurs, warm urine is prepared and introduced into the ear; when eye disease occurs, cold [urine] is prepared and introduced into the eye. In this sequence, it removes the pain of both. "Warm and cold urine" refers to its application for one afflicted by spirits (*bhūtārta*), meaning one seized by ghosts, *pretas*, and so forth; the *akṣobhya-nasya* combined with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*) bestows happiness even when bitten, that is, it bestows happiness even when bitten by a snake. This is the rule for the pacification of mouth diseases and the like.
O King, feces, urine, semen, and blood, when consumed along with *tālasa*, bestow longevity; the nasal application of *puṣpa* with meditation removes grey hair and wrinkles born of passion;
and the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*), when eaten mixed with the vomit of a fly, removes all diseases; likewise, female menses mixed with semen, when consumed for a year, destroys disease.

Now, the *pañcāmṛtayoga* for the purpose of increasing longevity is explained with the words beginning "viḍ" and so forth. Here, according to the statement "as it is externally, so it is in the body," there are five substances externally; by unifying these five substances within the internal self (*adhyātman*), there is the *pañcāmṛtayoga*. Consequently, it is accepted even by the Tibetan master Śrī Paṅlo and others that the consumption of the *pañcāmṛta* shall grant longevity to yogins. This portion of the commentary found in the Tibetan translation does not exist in the original Sanskrit, but rather this section was interpolated into the Tibetan translation by some Tibetan scholar.

Regarding this matter, the words of the venerable Khedubje that ought to be cited are as follows: "In all the authentic Sanskrit manuscripts of this [text], it says: 'Now, by means of the so-called mudrās and so forth, the rules for the yogins' mudrās, food, drink, and movement are taught; this is easy to understand. Although there are no such words in the commentary, most scholars such as Paṇchen Lo and Chöjé Bu maintain that what appears here was inserted by some unlearned Tibetan."
Some say that the mark on the forehead extends for eight finger-widths.
(From the *Vimalaprabhā-ṭīkā-ṭippaṇī*,
The Collected [Works]).

Volume 3. New Delhi, Ga, page b). In the *Vimalaprabhā*: "Regarding the external and internal, by the word *viṭ* (feces), Vairocana is *vali*; by the power of *vali*, *gandhaka* is called *viṭ*. Internally it is simply feces. These two are in equal parts.
Urine externally is King Viṣṇu, the essence of *bhiṅgarāja*; internally it is simply urine. Blood externally is *abhraka*; internally it is female menses. 'Equal parts' refers to these."
Externally, mercury is the semen; internally, it is the semen itself. These two are in equal parts.
Thus, externally, human flesh is the *triphalā*; internally, it is the marrow. These two are also in equal parts.

In this manner, there is one part of feces (*viḍ*), three-quarters of a part of flesh, half a part of blood, and one-quarter of a part of semen. Having combined these, one should saturate them with urine seven times.

Having dried it repeatedly in the sun, then consuming one *karṣa* daily with ghee and honey for a period of six months results in longevity; this is the rule for the *pañcāmṛta*, provided there is avoidance of leafy vegetables, sour things, oil, and salt.

Now, the practice of nasal drops (*puṣpanasya*) is described starting with the words "together with meditation" (*sadhyānam*): here, "meditation" (*dhyāna*) refers to the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the central channel (*madhyamā*); thus, "together with meditation" means accompanied by that meditation.

"Flower" refers to female menses (*strīrajas*). Externally, "keśarājikā" is *bhṛṅgarāja*; its juice, when used as a nasal drop (*nasya*) along with meditation (*dhyāna*), equal to female menses, removes grey hair, wrinkles born of passion, and the signs of old age within six months—this is the rule for the nasal treatment (*nasya*). Now, the "five lamps" (*pañcapradīpa*) is described: the meat of cow, horse, elephant, donkey, and man, mixed with the vomit of flies and honey, when consumed, becomes the "five lamps" which removes all diseases. Furthermore, together with the vomit of flies and *mādhavī* (wine), it removes all diseases—this is the rule.

The previously mentioned female flower (*strīpuṣpa*), mixed with semen and taken internally or externally, removes old age when consumed for a year; this concludes the aforementioned rule regarding diet. Now, the pacification of wind (*vāta*) and the other humors is described: Alkaline water (*kṣāramambu*) is a destroyer of wind (*vātaghna*); that which is sweet is the enemy of bile (*pittaśatru*); astringent (*kaṣāya*) destroys phlegm (*śleṣmaghna*). Likewise, all bitter substances, whether medicinal herbs or their juices, as well as pungent ones, destroy phlegm. Goat’s milk mixed with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*) is the enemy of phlegm; buffalo’s milk is the enemy of bile; warm cow’s milk is a destroyer of wind; and cow’s ghee (*sarpis*) alone removes the three types of disease. (126)

Alkaline water is a subduer of wind (*vātaghna*); sweet substances are enemies of bile (*pittaśatru*); astringent substances subdue phlegm (*śleṣmaghna*); and everything bitter, when combined with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), does the same—whether it be a medicinal herb or its juice, whether eaten or drunk. Goat’s milk subdues phlegm when combined with the three pungents; buffalo’s milk is an enemy of bile; cow’s milk with sugar is a subduer of wind; and warm milk with rock salt (*saindhava*) removes the three types of disease respectively; thus, [cow’s milk] combined with rock salt and so forth is a subduer of wind, bile, and phlegm.
Cow's ghee alone is the pacifier of the three types of diseases for those free from fever; this is the rule. (Regarding *nasya*: camel's milk.)

O Rnam mchog ma (*Rnamohiho ma*). [Note: This portion is not found in manuscript *ka*, but is taken from manuscript *kha* and others. Chapter on the Great Exposition of Alchemy and the Science of Pediatrics.

Now, for the purpose of pacifying diseases of the mouth and so forth, the decoctions, oils, and other remedies are described, beginning with the word "jāti": Warm water from a decoction of *jātī* flowers pacifies diseases of the mouth and likewise toothache. An oil cooked with bladderwort (*vastu*) water and the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*) and salts destroys ear disease.
Clarified butter boiled with milk and *ahirakti* always destroys diseases of the nose; likewise, *karkoṭī*, *lāṅgalan-drī*, and *sahakharā*, when applied as a paste, remove *gaṇḍamālā*.

Here, water eight times the quantity of all the ingredients, or water eight times the quantity of *jātī* leaves, reduced to one-fourth, and then mixed with some warm water from a decoction of *jātī*, serves as a cure for diseases of the mouth.

For toothache, one should prepare sesame oil with equal parts of *vastu* water and goat urine; when cooked until only the oil remains, it should be mixed with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*) and salts in a quarter-part proportion. When administered into the ear after the cooking process is complete, it destroys ear diseases. Likewise, for nasal diseases, one should take clarified cow’s ghee and eight times its amount of milk; at the conclusion of the decoction, snake-gourd (*ahi*), *nāgakeśara*, and red saffron are added in a quarter-part proportion. An errhine (*nasya*) applied with this ghee destroys nasal diseases.

*Karkoṭī*, *vandhyakarkoṭī*, *lāṅgalī*, *indrī*, and *indravāruṇī*—these bitter herbs, when applied as a paste along with *gardabhā* and *gaṇḍamālā*, remove [the disease]. This is the rule in brief; it should be understood in detail from the medical treatises (*vaidyaśāstra*).

Now, the pacification of *vajrakaṇṭhaka* is described, beginning with "one should make the hands... and so forth: one should make the hands hang down while the feet are in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), and restrain the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) until no falling upon the ground occurs for the body, and there is the release of the fever.

Again and again, in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one should destroy those thorns that cause the fear of death; for the Mother of the Universe (*Viśvamātā*), resembling a stainless moon, is meditated upon within the heart-lotus above the moon.
When, in this world, there occurs an affliction from evil diseases, first there arises fever, pain in the joints of the hands and feet, and the head aches;
having recognized these symptoms, one should take recourse in meditative absorption.

In this regard, the procedure is as follows: having entered a windowless room, the one afflicted by fever should let both arms hang down to the level of the thighs and place his feet evenly together like lotuses. He should perform *kumbhaka* (retention) by restraining the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), until the falling of the body upon the ground occurs due to the fever. If there is no falling, he should repeatedly perform *prāṇāyāma*; this is the rule. This should be practiced as long as the fever has not subsided; once the fever is released, he should not continue—this is the rule.
Again and again, one established in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) shall indeed destroy the thorns that cause the fear of death.

Within the heart-lotus, the Mother of the Universe (*Viśvamātā*), stainless and resembling the moon, is to be meditated upon; by means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), she has two arms and one face, holds a lotus and the gesture of granting boons (*varada-hasta*), is seated upon a *vajra-padmāsana* on a lunar disc—this is the rule. Thus is the pacification of sins and diseases.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, the medicine for the purpose of pacifying sinful diseases is now stated: Having ground [the substances], the Sun and the Moon with cold water destroy the thorns of men afflicted by fever. When rubbed together with Akṣobhya, it removes terrifying [symptoms]; at the end of the fever, one should perform protection on the head, throat, heart, navel, secret place, and so forth, using the skull and the mantra preceded by *Oṃ*, consisting of the names of Water, Fire, and Wind preceded by *Vajra*. // 129 //

In this case, when the signs of a "sinful disease" (*pāparoga*) appear—such as fever and pain in the joints of the hands and feet—one should grind *masūrī* beans with cold water and give them to those afflicted by fever; this destroys the thorns [of the disease]. Likewise, at the end of the fever, on the third day when the thorns are about to arise, one should take the skull of a person who died of a sinful disease; if such a skull is unavailable, one may use whatever is obtained. Having rubbed it and mixed it with *Akṣobhya*, a man should drink it from a human skull, and a woman from a female skull.
If it is not obtained, one drinks whatever is available; this removes the terrifying thorns [of disease]. Regarding the phrase "a skull obtained as it may be at the end of a fever," this is the rule.
Here, there is a mantra for the consecration of lentils (*masūrī*) and so forth, and that mantra is preceded by the syllable *oṃ*; thus, the mantra begins with *oṃ*.

The *oṃkāra* of water (*jala*), fire (*śikhin*), and wind (*marut*) is first: "water" refers to the second letter of the *pa*-group, the water element, which is *pha*; "fire" refers to *ra* below; and above is *e*. The unity of these—water, fire, and wind—is *phreṃ*; the anusvāra is space (*ākāśa*) because it is all-pervasive.

The name of the thorns begins with *vajra*. One should perform protection (*rakṣā*) by means of that very [name], just as one does for lentils (*masūrī*) and so forth when consecrated seven times. In the same way, one should perform protection upon the head, throat, heart, navel, and secret place; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) is included. The rule is that one should perform protection at these six locations during the three junctions of the day.
Here is the mantra: *oṃ phreṃ viśvamātaḥ vajrakaṇṭakān nāśaya nāśaya mama śāntiṃ kuru kuru svāhā*; for the sake of protecting others: *devadattasya śāntiṃ kuru kuru svāhā*. This is the rule.
This is the Blessed One’s injunction: this [mantra] of the Blessed Mother, the Universal Mother, should be remembered in all calamities for the protection of oneself and others.

Having empowered *masūrīkā* seven times with this mantra, it should be ground with cold water and given to drink. For one afflicted by fever, a skull should be ground with Akṣobhya and given. For one possessed by a spirit, Akṣobhya together with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*) should be ground and given. This is the rule for the pacification of evil diseases.

Now, the rule for quelling the heat of the sun’s rays is set forth with the words beginning "equal" (*tulya*) and so on: One should boil an equal amount of *dhātrī* and grain, as well as another portion of powdered *tintiḍī* leaves, in water purified by the moon and sun until it is reduced to one-quarter.

This decoction, mixed with sugar, should be drunk again on the following day; if this is consumed for three nights during the summer, it removes the burning sensation from the sun’s rays and even that which has entered the seven bodily constituents (*dhātu*), which would otherwise lead to death. (130)

In this context, when there is the heat of the sun’s rays on a journey during the summer, then "equal *dhātrī*" refers to the powder of *āmalakī* fruit; "*dhānya*" refers to *kustumburu* (coriander), and "equal" means equal to that; likewise, the powder of *tintirī* (tamarind) leaves and the powder of *bandhulī* leaves are equal [to one another]. Having thus made all these in equal parts, one should boil them in water "frequented by the moon and sun," meaning touched by the rays of the moon and sun, specifically in water free from impurities such as moss; one should boil the three substances until one-quarter remains—that is, until the decoction is reduced to one-fourth its original volume—having added water eight times the weight of the substances.

In this case, there is no measurement by the *tulā* (balance); rather, the rule is that in all instances regarding decoctions (*kvātha*), the measurement is by *āḍhaka*. Having taken one-fourth of that decoction mixed with sugar-candy, it is drunk again on the following day. In this manner, for three nights at the time of dawn during the summer, it removes the burning heat of the sun's rays; and as for the phrase "if it has entered the seven constituents" (*saptadhātu-gata*), this refers to its having entered the hair, skin, and so forth—the word "and" (*ca*) implies that it also removes other [afflictions], such is the rule.

Now another elixir is described, beginning with "heme'rka" and so forth: One should cause mercury to be processed with copper, iron, magnetite, mica, or human flesh by means of a fly (*makṣika*) using even half a seed-measure (*bīja*). Once the mercury is free from impurities, one should cause it to be processed with six *palas* [of the aforementioned substances] and then break it into pills. Having indeed dried it with a fierce fire, one should take the supernatant liquid (*agramastu*) here; it should be boiled again in a vessel of *kalki* along with the auspicious paste until it has reached half its original measure. || 131 ||

In this body, whoever seeks an external elixir (*bāhyarasāyana*) should perform this intermediate elixir (*madhyarasāyana*) in the absence of the perfected elixir (*siddharasa*). Its procedure is stated as follows: Regarding "in gold" (*hemni*), this refers to purified gold; "arkam" refers to copper; "kānta" is magnetite iron; "paṭalaja" is mixed iron; and "ayasaṃ tīkṣṇam" is steel. Of each of these, having prepared equal parts, one part—equal to the gold—of *mākṣika* (pyrite) powder should be blown with a bellows into an open crucible (*mūṣā*) by means of a strong blast until the gold remains; that itself is the seed (*bīja*). With half of that seed—that is, with two *palas* of gold—one should cause six *palas* of paste to be made by performing seven purifications (*pātana*) upon four *palas* of mercury from which impurities have been removed.

Then, having removed the butter from the *gotraka* (curd), one should cause it to be split by a sharp flame—that is, by a fierce fire—and having strained it through a cloth after it has been split, the clear whey (*mastu*) should be taken; discarding the sediment, that very whey should be boiled again with gold-dust in a magnet-stone vessel until it reaches half its original measure. Having removed it, eight *pala* of impure sugar should then be added as before. Indeed, this food should be consumed at all times, free from disease, for as long as one lives.

Within six months, one attains a divine body; even one overcome by wrinkles and grey hair attains immortality through this. Therefore, that very substance should be consumed at every daily occasion, provided it is free from flour. 132.

Then, having extracted eight *pala* of pure sugar-candy, one should add to it black pepper powder— one sixty-fourth part of the sugar-candy— varying from nine down to seven parts according to the digestion of the food by those who are not kings and so forth; this very preparation is to be eaten at all times,
free from illness, and for as long as six months, whereby one attains a divine body and, being freed from wrinkles and grey hair, reaches immortality.

In this drinking [rite], the chewing of betel is prescribed; setting aside the paste of the betel, that very food—namely, whey—is to be eaten at all times according to that rule, with [the leaf] ground with gold. 2.

Afterwards, [one should practice] at all times without her;
this is the rule for the elixir (rasāyana).
Now, for the sake of enjoying food and other such things, he speaks of that which is superior to gold, beginning with "pūrvoktam" (the previously mentioned), etc.:
"The previously mentioned king of seeds (bījarāja), even when equal [in weight], having been digested (jārita) in mercury, [is used] in the amount of half a mātrā. (11–13)

Having ground mercury with alkaline and sour substances along with various kinds of salts until it attains a state of unity, one should likewise grind cinnabar and realgar with bile, acids, and sulphur compounds in quantities equal to the mercury. By applying that paste, a silver leaf attains the state of gold even in a short time through the addition of an excess [of the agent]. 133.

In this context, the previously mentioned king of seeds (*bījarāja*), though equal in measure, is also processed (*jārita*) with half a portion of mercury; having been ground with alkaline and sour substances and many various *viḍa* salts to be described later until it attains oneness,
it is then [treated] with bile and acids such as sulfur (*gandhaka*) and so forth, and likewise with vermilion (*darada*).

10. Regarding "stone" (*śilā*): here, for the purpose of transmuting mercury (*rasakrāmaṇa*), one should grind three substances equal in quantity to the mercury together with the mercury, using bile and acids—either cow-bile, fish-bile, or fruit-acids such as *bījapūraka* and others, whichever are available—as well as sulfur (*gandhaka*), cinnabar (*darada*), stone (*śilā*), 20.
orpiment (*tālaka*), *śaśaka*, *kākṣī*, *kāśīṣa*, blue vitriol (*tutthaka*), and *hemagirikam*. Of these, [the following] of the sulfur and other substances... 21.
Two juices, one great juice (mahārasa), and three substances equal to the juice:
by smearing these upon it, a silver leaf placed beneath a furnace for three days becomes gold when cooked by the furnace fire, along with half as much gold.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth rule from the Hemādri [section], chapter twenty-three.
Now, the preparation of the *puṣpa* is described, beginning with the words "sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*) and so forth— 27.

The sharp [mercury] born from the sky (space), however, is produced from alkaline salt and barley-ash; it should be increased gradually by double each time in the sun (ark) until the remainder of the sun is burnt through the process of making them of equal flavor. Again, purified by means of alkali, it becomes soft when sprinkled with cow-dung and other substances. 28–30.
When offered to Tārā, even a third part that has been stolen becomes filled and attains the state of pure flowers. || 134 ||

Cardamom (*elā*), camphor (*karpūra*), jasmine (*mālā*), nutmeg (*vala*), myrobalan (*ghanaphalinī*), *vāyasa*, and rock salt (*adrija*); 50.

This wheel consists of eight spokes, a hub, and a rim; it is cool, a field of battle, with leaves, petals, water, and creepers as its other garments.

In the fifth [month], *sihlakacūrṇa* (resin powder); in the fifth [period], *ghana* (musta) and *mustaka*; in the sixth, *phalinī*, *priyaṅgu*, and flower; in the seventh, *vāyasam* and black *agaru*;

In the sequence thus described, the quantities of cardamom and the other ingredients are arranged in order within five sets of five compartments. By these five substances located within the city of the *kakṣapuṭa* (the aromatic casket), fragrance is produced. "City" refers to the compartment; by means of pure substances whose parts are called "days" (fifteen), that is, fifteen parts—namely, one, two, three, four, and five combined—this is the rule for the proportions of substances in the *gandhakakṣapuṭa*.
Cardamom and the others, along with the cardamom vine, are to be cast into the leaf-vessel city in due order.

97. For the purpose of incense, one should prepare an incense consisting of lac, sarja resin, milk, and white *pura* (gum). 98. One should make it with pieces of camphor, combined with the juices of flowers, portions of fire [resin], and *nakha*.
99. Having ground that with fragrant water, one should produce an incense-wick (*dhūpavarti*) free from honey.

Now, the *kakṣapuṭa* for incense is described beginning with the word "jātī" and so forth. Here, among the substances previously cast into the *kakṣapuṭa*, one should remove five substances beginning with *jātī*; in their place, five others should be given in due order. Among these: first, *jātī* means the nutmeg (*jātīphala*); second, *elā*; third, *latā*, which is musk (*kastūrikā*); fourth, *dala*, which is the leaf of *tamāla*; and fifth, *kalaśa*, which is *kakkola*. These are to be cast into the respective compartments (*koṣṭha*) in sequence: lac (*lākṣā*) into the nutmeg compartment, resin (*sarjarasa*) into the cardamom compartment, "milk" (*duḥkha*, meaning *śrīvāsa*) into the musk compartment, "resin" (*pura*, meaning *guggulu*) into the leaf compartment, and "white" (*sita*, meaning *kunduruka*) into the *kakkola* compartment.
Thus, regarding the preparation of incense, the rule is that one should prepare the incense with five substances in the previously mentioned proportions.

Where there is sugar-candy (*khaṇḍa*) along with camphor pieces, honey should be added; together with the sugar-candy, the "claws" (*nakha*), and the portions of fire (*vahnibhāga*), there are thus eighteen parts, which constitute the six-ingredient incense (*ṣaḍaṅga-dhūpa*). When combined with camphor, sugar-candy, honey, and musk, it becomes the ten-ingredient incense (*daśāṅga*); such is the rule for the substances in the *dhūpakakṣapuṭa*.

Now the incense-reed (*dhūpavarti*) is described, beginning with the words "that [incense] ground," and so forth. Here, one should grind the ingredients mentioned in the *Kakṣapuṭa* on incense—excluding *madhūka*—with scented water mixed with a little sugar-candy. With that, one should fashion an incense-reed in the shape of an iron arrow (*nārāca*). This is the rule for fumigating garments and the like for the sake of the images of the True Dharma (*saddharma*). In the navel and other parts, one should cast [the powder] into lion’s urine within the city of the moon and sky (the *śaśigaganapura*); this is for the application of bathing. Furthermore, there are the knots (*granthi*), tiger [skin], *hareṇu*, and likewise the powdered conch-shell bark, in three parts.

Grain, *mūrvā*, *śatāhvā*, and *damanaka*—these likewise [are used] for sweetening; and when the previously mentioned [massage] has not ceased, water-born [lotus] and *granthiparṇa* are used in the oil.

Now, the *snānakakṣapuṭa* is described starting with the words "in the navel, etc. Here, among the substances cast into the previous *kakṣapuṭa*, having extracted four (five) substances beginning with the navel, other [substances] are to be placed in their respective squares within the *snānakakṣapuṭa* according to their number. Among those, one should place *granthiparṇa* in the square of the navel; [Ga. has] seventeen [and Bho.
has] Na (five).

In the chapter on the Great Instruction on Alchemy and the Science of Child-rearing (*rasāyanādibālatantramahoddeśa*): lion’s urine is for the *koṣṭha* [receptacle]; tiger’s claw for the *śaśipura*; *hareṇu* for the *gaganapura*, as well as *kacoraka* which is called "the slain";
likewise, for the purpose of incense, "conch" refers to *nakha* (onycha), of which one-third part is used; similarly, three parts of bark are to be given.
In the application for bathing, among the bathing substances, thus in eighteen parts, the bath is performed with six substances.

Regarding the rule for substances in the *snānakakṣapuṭa*, the *udvartanakakṣapuṭa* is now described: here, as in the *snānakakṣapuṭa*, three parts out of the five substances should be given; these are: *dhānya* (coriander), *mūrvī* (maruvaka), *śatāhvā* (śatapuṣpā), *dama* (damanaka), and *madhura*. These three parts of the five [substances] constitute the eighteen-part *udvartana*.
The rule for the substances used in *udvartana* (massage with unguents) has been established;

now, for the purpose of preparing cooked oil (*pakataila*), the procedure for the "oil-pouch" (*tailakakṣapuṭa*) is described, beginning with the words "here, previously mentioned," and so forth. Here, when the group of substances for the previously mentioned "fragrant pouch" (*gandhakakṣapuṭa*) has not been exhausted, one should add "aquatic" (*jalaja*)—meaning *nakha* (onychophore)—and "thin like the aquatic" (*tanur iva jalaja*)—meaning *tvak* (cinnamon bark)—as well as *granthiparṇa*. Having added three parts of these two, one should cook the oil together with the five substances of the fragrant pouch, making seven substances in total, using eighteen parts according to the sequence to be described; this becomes "various-fragrance oil.
This is the rule for the substances of the oil-pouch.

In this way, one should prepare various well-composed mixtures of perfumes, incense, and so forth, through three hundred different varieties, using substances that are pure, processed by fruit-pouch cooking (*phalapuṭapāka*), scented, and pierced—such as powders, pills (*granthi*), and likewise thin pastes for drinking, scenting, and mouth-freshening; as well as *tvagvola*, *granthiśaṅkha*, and those cooked in fruit-pouches or leaf-pouches, and those beginning with *haṃsa*. || 139 ||

Regarding "in the powder" (*cūrṇe*), "in the context of the powder" (*cūrṇaviṣaye*), and "and likewise in the knot" (*granthi ca tadvat*): *granthiparṇaka* is to be added among the five substances as in the case of *nakha*.

There, it is to be given in a thin form for the perfuming of drinks (*pānavāsa*), and for the perfuming of the mouth (*mukhavāsa*) there is the fourfold substance consisting of *tvak*, *vola*, *granthi*, and *śaṅkha*; three parts of this [fourfold] substance are to be used in the ripening of fruits (*phalapāka*), in the leaf-cup cooking (*dalapuṭapāka*), in the *haṃsapāka*, and at the beginning of the swing-cooking (*dolāpāka*) which will be described later.

Having spoken thus, one who desires fragrance should prepare, according to the aforementioned sequence, thirty well-composed varieties of applications of perfume and incense—namely, thirty distinct combinations of perfumes, incenses, and so forth, including baths, ointments, and the like. With what kind of substances? With pure substances, those ripened in fruit-caskets, perfumed, and pierced; such is the rule for the collection of materials. Now, the preparation of incense is described: "In the beginning, an eighth part," and so on. In the beginning, there is a decoction (kaṣāya) [of herbs] in proportion to the petals; twice that amount is the potent incense (ugradhūpa); thereafter, there should be an amount of jaggery (guḍa) equal to the measure of the other substances. This increases through application during the summer season.

One should burn a paste consisting of one-quarter part of conch-shell incense, along with Madhuka and sugar equal in measure to the substance; likewise, a ball the size of a conch-shell made of light Malaya sandalwood mixed with moon-fragrance (Karpūra).
ka. kha. *siṃhasūtra*; ka. kha. *hṛtam iti*; bho. *Ha Ta* (*hata*);
ka. kha. *tvagvargayoḥ*.
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the application of fragrances (*gandhayoga*), there are three types of petals—inferior, middling, and superior.
Among these, the inferior are: *mustaka*, *śailēya*, *uśīraka*, *pālaka*, *kapittha*, *vilva*, *murā*, and *māṃsī*; these are the inferior petals.

According to the proportion of these petals, first, a decoction mixed with jaggery and powdered *harītakī* becomes the incense (*dhūpa*). With that, one should first fumigate the petals for one day using one-eighth part [of the powder]; then, having performed the "flower-soaking" (*puṣpavāsa*) for two days, on the third day one should mix in the medium-sized petals. Then, doubling that is the "intense incense" (*ugradhūpa*);
thus, the intense incense for the preceding and following [parts] is double that amount.

Lākṣā, sarjarasa, śrīvasa, rāla, guggulu, and kunduruka—these five primary substances, when mixed with jaggery, constitute a potent incense (*ugradhūpa*). Of these, double the amount of *kaṣāya* (resin) should be added, and one-fourth part of *dala* (leaf).

Here, the "middle leaf" refers to the category of flowers; *candana* and *aguru* belong to the category of fruits; *nakha* belongs to the category of bark; and [the others] belong to the category of exudations (*niryāsa*).

In this manner, one should fumigate for two days with the *ugradhūpa*. After an interval of two days, one should perform the "flower-soaking" (*puṣpavāsa*). Thereafter, one should burn the measured quantity of the substance along with jaggery (*guḍa*) together with the incense during the summer. Then it increases due to the summer conditions: in the rainy season, double the amount of substance should be given; in the winter, triple the amount should be given. When the jaggery has been burnt, one should burn conch-shell powder (*śaṅkha*)—that is, *nakha*—to the extent of one-quarter part together with the jaggery for two days according to the previous procedure. Then, one should burn *madhuka*, white sugar (*sitā*), and *sārākarā* in quantities equal to the [other] substances, together with the *piṇḍadhūpa*.
One should burn only the first and last portions of the incense-stick;

likewise, having burnt three morsels of jaggery every day, one should allow it to rest. One should burn incense equal to one-eighth part of the substance every day; otherwise, by this [method], it becomes uncooked, while with too much [incense] it becomes burnt-smelling. It is the rule that if it is uncooked, it becomes sour.

"Piṇḍa" refers to *piṇḍadhūpa* (ball-incense), which is as described in the *Kakṣapuṭa*: mixed with camphor and devoid of pungent substances (*ugradravya*). *Piṇḍadhūpa* consists of five substances sweetened with honey and sugar; that very [incense] should be burned in the measure of a conch-shell, which means adding a quarter-part of the [other] substances. In this regard, the "son" (*putraka*) is nutmeg (*jātīphala*), camphor, and *nābhi*. Having added another excellent leaf as prescribed in the *Kakṣapuṭa*, there are three substances joined with these: *malaya* is sandalwood, *laghu* is agallochum (*aguru*), *cala* is musk (*sihnaka*), and *candra* is camphor. Thus, it is the triad of substances combined with that.

In the same manner, one should burn a substance similar to the incense-pellet (piṇḍadhūpa), combined with honey and sugar. Here, "molasses" (guḍa) refers to ball-molasses (vaṭikāguḍa) and not that which is prepared from raw ingredients; this is the rule.

Once cooked, one should spread the fragrance over beautiful flowers for several days, as long as desired; thereafter, one should perform the transmutation (vedha) by one hundredth part using the three fruits (triphalā), mercury (śaśimada), and so forth, along with fermented liquors (sāsava).

One should boil *śikhambu*, goat’s urine, and flower-juices together until the end of the flowering period; after one month, it becomes a grain-matured liquor (*dhānyapaka*) equal to that of deer, provided it has not been pierced at the navel. || 141 ||

Then, having recognized that the fragrance has matured—if, by the scent of this [incense] being rubbed, the palm of the hand becomes red, then it is fully matured; otherwise, it is not matured. Therefore, as long as maturity has not been reached, one should not burn the cold incense. When this matured fragrance is mixed with fragrant flowers such as *campaka* and others for several days—whether for half a fortnight or a full fortnight—until the defects of the incense are abandoned, it then becomes desirable. Afterwards, perform the piercing (*vedha*) in a hundredth part (*satāṃśa*). 1. Bho Pa La Ka (*pālaka*).
2. Bho. *rZas* (substances);
Ka. kha. *grīvāsaṃ*. 4. Bho. *Khu Ba* (semen); Ka. kha. *nijjāsa*.
5. ka. kha. *bala* means [the plant]. 6. ka. kha. *piṇḍadravyadhūpasadhṛśam* [means] similar to incense made from solid substances.

Regarding *phala*: *jātīphala* is nutmeg, and *kakkola*; alternatively, *elā* may take the place of *kakkola*, *latā* is musk (*kastūrikā*), *śaśī* is camphor (*karpūra*), and *mada* is musk (*kastūrī*). Having made these into equal parts, one should cause the perfuming (*vedha*) of the fragrance to be performed with a hundredth part [of the total].
One should provide a piercing (*vedha*) of one hundredth part together with the intoxicants (*āsava*) to be mentioned later, such as *mada*.

The rule for piercing is that all [the intoxicants] are eight times the amount of the piercing. Now, the intoxicant (*āsava*) for the purpose of pleasing the fragrances is described starting with the word "śigru" and so forth. Here, regarding the detailed process of cooking the intoxicants and other substances according to the method prescribed in the treatise on perfumes (*gandhaśāstra*), that should be understood from that very treatise on perfumes.
And here, "Śigru-water" has been mentioned briefly:

one should boil *śigru* juice, goat's urine, and flower-nectar—which is honey—with fire in equal proportions, ending with the flowers (i.e., including honey). Then, having extracted it and placed it in a coconut shell or similar vessel, it becomes cooked after being kept in the midst of a heap of grain for one month.

Regarding "the essence [āsava] equal to deer, not pierced": at the conclusion of the heating by fire, *nābhi* refers to musk; although not explicitly mentioned, camphor is also included. Together with the three fruits (*triphalā*), one should apply a hundredth-part piercing (*vedha*) to it and then place it in grain. Thereafter, one should perform the aforementioned piercing of the fragrance with that [mixture]; this is the rule.

In all treatises on perfumes (*gandhaśāstra*), there are three types of incense-burners (*dhūpayantra*) for the preparation of incense: the flat (*sama*), the shaped like a hand-drum (*ḍamarukākāra*), and the shaped like a shallow bowl (*sarāvākṛti*). The inferior type has a hole two finger-widths wide and six finger-widths high, intended for pungent incense (*ugradhūpa*). The medium type is eight finger-widths high, intended for incense made from resinous lumps (*nakhaguḍapiṇḍa*). The superior type is ten finger-widths high, intended for cold incense (*śītadhūpa*). Having placed a shallow pan (*kharpara*) filled with sand upon the base of this burner and a small hearth (*cūllikā*) on top of it, one should place the incense mass upon the heated sand. Then, placing the burner over that, one should place a clay pot half a finger-width high—smeared with fragrant paste (*gandhakalka*)—on top of the burner. If the paste is very thin, one may use a coconut shell. Having determined the quantity of incense to be one or half a stick (*daṇḍa*), one should burn the incense.

Then, having removed the skull-cup, one should place a cloth upon a wooden board and set it face down, so that the smoke does not escape. Even during the time of cooking, one should wrap the space between the skull-cup and the apparatus with a moist cloth.
This is the rule for the preparation of incense (*dhūpapāka*).

Having extracted the inner grain from a citron (*bījapūraka*) when its fruit has ripened, and having removed the rind, one should place a paste of fragrance (*gandhakalka*) inside. Having wrapped the exterior with bark fibers, one should coat it with clay to a thickness of one finger-breadth. Afterwards, one should cook it using the *puṭapāka* method over a fire of dried cow-dung until the coating becomes the color of fire. Thereafter, the fragrance will vanish; then, having removed it from the fire and once it has cooled, one should pierce the fragrance with the navel and other [mudrās] according to the previously mentioned procedure. This is the rule for the ripening of the fruit.
In the *dalapuṭapāka* method as well, one should make a packet using *ketakī* leaves and place the medicinal paste (*gandhakalka*) inside;
the rest is like the *phalapāka*.

In the *haṃsapāka*, a golden or silver vessel smeared with the medicinal paste inside to a height of one finger-breadth floats in a copper cauldron half-filled with fragrant water; undergoing the process of boiling while floating like a swan, it is called *haṃsapāka*. This is the procedure for the *aṅga*.
8. bho. bDug PahDZin Pa (Skt. dhūpagrāha);
9. ga. nālikeraṃ.
10. Smoke (dhūmaḥ). 11. Fruit (phalam).
12–13. Ka. Kha. Thus, piercing and so forth are as previously described; this is the rule for the ripening of the swan (haṃsapāka), according to the statement "and in the ripening of the swan."

Regarding dolāpāka (swinging-roasting) and so forth: among the nine types of substances mentioned in the science of perfumery (*gandhaśāstra*), there are eight procedures for the purification of the inferior materials—namely, washing (*kṣālana*), sweating (*svedana*), rubbing (*udvartana*), roasting (*bharjana*), impregnation (*bhāvana*), fumigation (*dhūpana*), perfuming (*vāsana*), and binding (*bandhana*).

In that regard, washing is with *kāñjika* (sour gruel); steaming is by means of *dolāpāka* (swinging-pot cooking); rubbing is with scented water; roasting of the ground substances is with molasses-water and the like; infusion is with the urine of children, goats, and so forth; fumigation is with the fire of decoctions (*kaṣāya*); perfuming is with flowers such as *ketakī*; and piercing is with substances such as *nābhi*.
For inferior petals such as *mustaka* and others, one should perform washing, steaming, and so forth within the group of flowers, excluding roasting.

Thus, in the group of barks (*tvaggaṇa*), in the group of middle parts (*madhyamadalānām*), in the group of roots (*mūlagagaṇa*), in the group of wood (*kāṣṭhagaṇa*), in the group of leaves (*patragaṇa*), and in the group of living organisms (*jīvagaṇa*), there is the roasting (*bharjanam*) of nails and the *puṭapāka* (cooking in a sealed vessel) of *putrakeśa*.
The remainder is like the group of flowers (*puṣpagaṇa*).
In the group of fruits (*phalagaṇa*), in the group of exudations (*niryāsagaṇa*), and in the group of liquid substances (*dravadravyagaṇa*), no specific procedure is to be performed.

Having made a powder of these aforementioned substances, one should place the powder upon a cloth at the mouth of the vessel. Having filled the vessel halfway with scented water and placed the powder on top, one should subject it to steam-sudation until the powder becomes moistened. Then, having removed it, one should perform the application of ointment and so forth.

In this manner, there is also the sweating (*sveda*) of *putrakeśa* on a swing; for *nakha*, there is boiling and roasting with cow dung or clay in place of sweating, followed by sprinkling with decoction water. The remainder is as previously stated; such is the rule for the fivefold cooking process. The rest should be understood from the *Gandhaśāstra* by one who desires fragrance. Now, the secret [ingredients] for perfumes and so forth are described, beginning with "the secret": The secret among perfumes is *pūti*; in incense preparations, the secret is *rasanakhacapala*. Likewise, in matters of fumigation, the secret is cold *turuṣka*, as well as *guru* and *śaśin* (camphor), and flowers.

In the process of piercing [the ears], camphor, nutmeg, the three fruits (triphalā), and liquor are used; for the bath, these are properly combined; for the secret [application], cinnamon, granthiparṇa, and vanacarī are used together as a fragrant paste for rubbing the body. 142.
Here, during the time of preparing cool incense from perfumes and other substances, one should apply the secret [ingredient] among the perfumes.
"Trembling with the tip of the tongue" is the secret.
Here, when preparing the incense, one should offer incense made from sour-smelling substances after having prepared the incense formulation.

Regarding the method for incense (*dhūpayoga*): in the context of preparing incense through cooking (*pāka*), one should purify the fragrance, resin, *nakha*, and *sihnaka* with molasses for one or two days, until the acidity is discarded. Thereafter, one should offer it as a ball (*piṇḍa*) or other forms; this is the rule.

Now, if the fragrance is scorched by harsh cooking, one should let the incense be touched by the rays of the moon at night. In the absence of such [moonlight], one should place it on the bank of water until the defect of scorching is pacified.

The causes for the destruction of fragrances are stated here: the mixing of pure and impure substances is a cause of destruction; likewise, oil, a moist location, straw, alkaline substances, excrement and urine, contact with mice, wind, and an excessively hot location. Similarly, cold [conditions] are [causes]; sandalwood, *turuṣka*, *guru*, camphor, and *guhya*—these should be applied as cool incense at the conclusion of the cooking process once the hair of the *putraka* has fallen out; this is the rule. [Chapter on] Alchemy and the Great Instruction on Pediatrics.
Regarding the perfuming of flowers, the secret [ingredient] is to be used until the defects of the incense are neutralized.

Regarding "piercing" (*vedha*), in the context of piercing, camphor, musk, the three fruits (*triphalā*), and *madasure*—that is, musk-liquor—is the secret [ingredient], to be used until the defects of the flower-perfuming are neutralized; such is the rule for the application of fragrances.

And regarding the application for bathing, "properly" means that in the context of bathing, the secret [ingredient] must necessarily be given among the collection of bathing substances, namely, cinnamon bark (*tvak*) and *granthiparṇa*.
"Accompanied by *vanacara*" means accompanied by *putrakeśa*. The rule is that the three parts are to be given within the midst of fifteen parts.
In the preparation for *udvartana*, *granthiparṇa* is to be added; in the bath (*snāna*), it is according to the division. Thus the procedure for the *puṭa* of fragrant substances has been stated.

Now, the fragrance called "the lord of the navel" (*nābhibhartṛ*) is described with the words beginning "pure lotus" (*śuddhābja*) and so forth: pure lotus is devoid of other substances and free from *madhuka*; ground with fragrant water and cooked with incenses consisting of *kaṣāya*, *ugra*, and the pollen of *madhuka*, it is increased in dose gradually.

Two morsels of candied sugar mixed with camphor, benzoin, and liquid storax, along with iron filings and camphor, should be burnt at the beginning and end of the incense offering, starting from the first smoke, while honey and white sugar are also consumed.

In this context, when one wishes to prepare *gandharāja* with a single substance, then "pure lotus" refers to the fingernail; that itself is generally of four kinds: elephant-ear, horse-hoof, lotus-petal, and jujube-leaf (*varada*).
Among these, for a formulation of perfume (*gandhayoga*), the elephant-ear and horse-hoof should be used; for an incense formulation (*dhūpayoga*), the jujube-leaf and lotus-petal should be used.

In this context, the *varuṇa* (badara) leaf is best; in its absence, lotus leaves and the like should be used. It is "pure" when boiled according to the procedure prescribed in the *Gandhaśāstra*, sprinkled with water decocted from molasses and medicinal extracts (*kaṣāya*), powdered, or smeared and perfumed with *triphalā* and other substances—this is what is meant by "pure.
That same substance, when devoid of other ingredients, is called *madhuka*; it is "free from that" when lacking such an *āsava*.

Regarding the phrase "ground with scented water": here, for the purpose of scented water (*gandhodaka*), one should take clear water and place one *karṣa* each of cardamom (*elā*), cinnamon bark (*tvag*), spikenard (*māṃsī*), vetiver (*vālaka*), and sandalwood (*candana*) tied in a cloth pouch into eight *āḍhakas* of water.
Then, one should boil it down until one-fourth remains, at which point it becomes scented water.
With that, one should grind the other fragrant substances; this is the rule.

"Ripened by incenses" means that very same [substance] with pure nails, ground and ripened by the procedure for cooking incenses (*dhūpapāka*). "By increasing the morsels in sequence" means: on the first day, one should take a single morsel of the decoction (*kaṣāya*) together with honey (*madhu*) and sugar (*śarkarā*); at the beginning and end of the morsel, one should also consume *madhuka* and sugar. This is according to the rule: "One should burn [the ingredients] starting from the initial incense."

First, a morsel of honey and sugar should be given; in the middle, of the astringent incense (*kaṣāyadhūpa*); and again at the end, one should burn honey and sugar. On the second day, one should perform the "flower-vow" (*puṣpavāsa*). In this manner, alternating [the days], one should burn two morsels of the fierce incense (*ugradhūpa*) over two days. Then, three morsels of *nakha* over three days; thereafter, two morsels mixed with sugar for *malaya* over two days; and one [morsel] for *capala*.
For iron and camphor as well, at the beginning and end of the morsel, honey (or sugar) is used as before;
thus, cooked with incense at intervals of one day for twenty-four days, it becomes like a jujube fruit (*badara*).

Having placed *Rā* (*badara*) in a vessel of stainless luster, mixed with excellent flowers and scented water for several days, and having sealed the mouth of a clay pot with a firm lid and wrapped it in wax and cloth, one should then place it in a wide container filled with sand on the surface of the earth. Through the practice of six months, it becomes cooked; when immersed in water, the Lord of the Navel (*nābhibhartā*) emerges, fragrant. (144)

Then, having stayed for ten days with excellent flowers until the pacification of the king's afflictions occurs, one should boil fragrant water every day according to the previous procedure, mixed with fragrant water; one must not add cold water.

It becomes sour with cold water; having mixed that fragrance with fragrant water, one should place it in a leak-proof earthen pot whose exterior is wrapped in silk cloth and whose mouth is firmly sealed. This should be placed inside another large vessel—either in a clay jar or on the ground. In the absence of such a vessel, one should throw it into that [other] vessel and pour sand over it until the vessel is filled up to its neck.

In that regard, when the vessel has been filled with *vāluka* (sand), ordinary water heated by the sun should be poured in; one should place that very vessel in the heat of the sun for as long as six months.

Thus, through use over six months, it becomes cooked, and the fragrance residing in the water becomes the "Lord of Scents" (*gandharāja*), which supports the navel [of the body]. This is the rule for the King of Scents.

Now, for the sake of flower-oil and scented oil, the purification of sesame seeds is described, beginning with the words "having performed," and so forth: having performed the purification of the sesame seeds with boiled leaf-water and by means of incense, ointments, and so on, one should afterwards perfume them with *jāti* and other flowers for several days, or until the desired result is achieved.

O King, having extracted the oil from the press, one should skillfully place it in a glass vessel; for this unrefined flower-oil becomes intoxicating when used for bathing or anointing the body. (145)

In this context, having collected fresh, fully ripened sesame seeds, one should grind them with "boiled leaf-water"—where "leaves" refers to mango leaves, as well as the leaves of the five trees, namely the rose-apple (*jambū*), wood-apple (*kapittha*), citron (*mātuluṅga*), and *bilva*. This grinding with the boiled leaf-water constitutes the first purification, which is the removal of the husks from the sesame seeds. Then, having placed a cloth over a winnowing basket (*jālāyantra*) and covered it with the sesame seeds in another vessel, one should fumigate them; this is the second purification.

"With plasters and so forth" means that a plaster made from the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), ground with scented water, should be applied; first, one should dry it with the rays of the sun. Having thus purified the sesame seeds, one should afterwards perfume them for several days, a fortnight, ten days, or continuously with flowers such as jasmine (*jāti*) and others, until the crushed seeds emit the fragrance of the perfumed flowers. Then the desired perfuming is achieved. Thereafter, having extracted the oil by means of a *kolu* (or *klhu*) press—O King, this is the address—one should carefully store it in a glass vessel.
That oil, whether for bathing or for anointing, becomes intoxicating because flower-oil is unrefined.
Now, if one wishes to prepare refined oil, one should boil that same oil with an equal amount of fragrant water until the oil releases its foam;
then, at the time of removing it from the heat, one should add aromatic substances ground with scented water in an eighth part of the quantity, and subsequently remove it once it has become cool.
Then, having applied a penetration (*vedha*) with musk and other substances, one should place it in a glass vessel.
That very [substance], mixed with a quarter-part of *madāsava* liquor, heated for seven days in a lacquer vessel by the heat of the sun, becomes musk-oil (*kastūrikā-taila*).

When cooked in a bamboo tube, it becomes "sun-cooked" (*sūryapāka*); likewise, an ointment and so forth, when cooked in a bamboo tube, becomes a divine ointment when pierced by the navel and other [mystical points].

In this way, one should prepare the various types of incense formulations taught in the treatises on perfumes (*gandhaśāstra*). Here, the Blessed One has spoken briefly regarding the rules for the preparation of incense. Now, for the purpose of facilitating childbirth for pregnant women, the thirty-four-fold diagram (*yantra*) is described starting with the words "bhūbhṛt" and so forth: "The mountains, sun, moon, manas, eyes, Madana, Vasus, Rudras, kings, fires, directions, elements, apertures, the six, lunar days, and oceans are to be placed within the squares."

Having drawn the complete Śrīcakra with four compartments for numbers and [the figures] one and three along the lines, one should show it to pregnant women on the surface of the measuring board at the time of delivery.

In this context, when the obstruction of the fetus occurs for pregnant women at the time of delivery due to the fault of an external *dūtī*, one should then draw this yantra on the back of a measure; "measure" (*māna*) here refers to an *āḍhaka*.

Having made sixteen squares on its back, one should place the following numbers: seven in the first square (the mountains), twelve in the second (the sun), one in the third (Indra), fourteen in the fourth (Manu), two in the fifth (the eyes), thirteen in the sixth (Madana), eight in the seventh (the Vasus), eleven in the eighth (Rudra), sixteen in the ninth (the kings), three in the tenth (the fires), ten in the eleventh (the directions), five in the twelfth (the elements), nine in the thirteenth (the apertures), six in the fourteenth (the seasons), fifteen in the fifteenth (the lunar days), and four in the sixteenth (the oceans); these are to be established in the sixteenth moving square.
The total number of these digits situated within the four squares, when added together as a single sum, is "the ocean and the fire" (34).

Having written this entire *yantra* on the surface of a measuring board, one should show it at the time of delivery to the mother of the disciple; such is the rule for the release of the fetus (*garbhamocana*).

Now, the *tantra* concerning the child from conception onwards is described, beginning with the words "O Yoginīs": "The Yoginīs who are the sixty-four [deities], the Mothers well-known upon the manifest earth, those called 'Womb' (*garbha*) and those called 'Day' (*vāsara*), the others being three, nine, ten, eleven, and fifteen."
Those known as Māsa and Vatsara seize the child upon the entire surface of the earth; they cause colic in the womb and likewise inflict pain during the time of birth in the birth canal. (147)

On this surface of the earth, those sixty-four Yoginīs who are manifest are well known as the Mothers in groups of eight. Among them, twenty-seven are called *garbhā* (womb-born), being nine multiplied by three; ten are called *vāsara* (day-born); eleven are called *māsa* (month-born); and fifteen others, consisting of three times five, are called *vatsara* (year-born). These sixty-three seize the child on the entire surface of the earth, causing colic in the womb and pain even at the time of birth within the vagina.

Here, among those known as the *garbhākhya* (womb-born), for fifteen days starting from the fifteenth day of conception they cause womb-pains; thereafter, until the ninth month, there are nine; at the time of birth, one; and two who suckle the salty breast-milk—such is the rule for the *garbhākhya*. For those born according to the *Vimalaprabhā*, there is the *Bālatantra* (Infant Tantra) based on the division of days, months, and years. [Adhyātma: Five cruel youths are established at the joints of the lunar nodes (*parvasandhi*) by the power of their innate qualities (*prakṛtiguṇa*).

O King, those fools indeed seize [the victim] when he has fallen into fear of his guests, and they do not release him at all; for their pacification, various rites such as fire-oblations are effective within this mandala.

Regarding the statement, "For children who have been born, there is the Bālatantra according to the division of days, months, and years," here "Bālatantra" refers to the medical treatment for children afflicted by the Mothers (*mātṛ*). In that regard, one should offer the oblation (*bali*) to be described later to those known as the "Days" (*vāsara*), starting from the birth day of the newborns up until the tenth day. For each of the Mothers who cause affliction to children on their respective days, there is a sequence of eleven months, lasting for eleven months.

Then, for fifteen years out of the [first] fifteen, there is the state of being a young boy; beyond that, the state of childhood ceases. In the sixteenth year, there is the emission of semen (*śukracyavana*). Now, the five cruel ones are described, beginning with "krūra" and so forth. Here, in the context of worldly experience (*bhukti*), at the junctions of the five lunar days (*tithi*) starting from Nandā, the Kaumāras are situated according to the qualities of the primordial elements (*prakṛti-guṇa*) such as space and so on. At the junction of the lunar festivals (*parva-sandhi*), they seize the child who has fallen into danger during their own respective lunar day. O King—this is the address—they do not release the child at all, even though he possesses general strength.
For their pacification, various rites such as *homakā* (fire offerings) and so forth, which will be described hereafter, are effective within this maṇḍala; such is the rule for cruel [rites].

Now, the medicine for pregnant women afflicted by those known as the "wombs" (*garbha*) is stated, beginning with *kuṣṭha*: Having ground *kuṣṭha*, *uśīra*, *kaseru*, *tagara*, blue lotus (*kuvalaya*), and the filaments (*keśara*) of the lotus with cold water, it should be consecrated with mantras and administered even with *vajra* [medicines] for womb-afflictions.

In the case of a stagnant womb (*garbhastambha*), one should grind the eight feathers of a peacock and administer them. Furthermore, milk, ghee, milk-rice (*pāyasānna*), along with curd and molasses, are given to the women. || 149 ||

In this regard, when pregnant women suffer from uterine pain (*garbha-śūla*), the remedy is as follows: *kuṣṭha*, *uśīra*, *kaseru*, the root of *tagara*, the bulb of *utpala*, and the filaments of the lotus (*padmakeśara*). Having ground these substances with water that has stood overnight and cooled, one should empower them with the mantra "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ, remove, remove the uterine pain of [Name], svāhā"—this is the mantra, "empowered even by the thunderbolts. It is the rule that, having empowered it with this, it should be administered for cases of uterine pain.

Likewise, for the stabilization of the embryo (*garbhastambha*), one should take the eight hairs of a mongoose and a peacock feather, grind them with cold water, and administer them as before after consecrating them with mantras. One should bathe [the woman] at the foot of a milk-tree (*kṣīravṛkṣa*) using seven *mallika* flowers filled with cow’s milk, and offer an oblation (*bali*) of milk-rice; such is the rule for those [rites] called "embryo-stabilization."
[In this] chapter, the *Mahoddeśa* on the *Rasāyana* and other *Bālatantras*, the ritual for the *vāsarīs* is now described, beginning with the word "milk" (*dugdha*).

Here, for the sake of pacifying a child taken [into the world] within ten days, milk, clarified butter, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), curd with molasses, cakes (*polikā*), and sweetmeats (*modaka*), as well as perfume, flowers, and a lamp, are offered as a *bali* to the *vāsarīs*. Bathing and incense are to be performed as will be explained; such is the rule for the three-night *bali* offering to the *vāsarīs*.

Now, the ritual procedure for those known as the *māsa* [spirits] is described, beginning with the word "cooked" (*pakve*) and so forth: For five nights, one should perform the following: cooked food of five kinds, curd combined with jaggery, *polikā* cakes and *modaka* sweets, incense, flowers, lamps, and bathing with petals;
as well as cow-tusk, ram-horn, deer-claw, hair, and snake-skin as incense. This entire offering is prescribed for the sake of nourishing children born under the *māsa* spirits. || 150 ||

In this context, after ten days, for one month, and thereafter for up to eleven months, one should offer a *bali* to the Mothers for the sake of pacifying those born during that month. The "five distinct items" consist of cooked food prepared with ghee—namely *pūrikā* (flattened cakes) and *ghṛtapūra* (ghee-filled pastries); *saumālī* (garlands), *sevāla-vaṭaka* (algal-shaped dumplings); another portion of rice accompanied by curd and molasses; and *polikā-modaka* (sweet cakes).
As for the "fragrance," it is sandalwood; as for the "scented flowers"; and as for the "lamp," it is [fed] with sesame oil or ghee.

Regarding "bathing with leaves" as well: one should bathe the child with slightly boiled water, made warm, using the leaves of the five milk-exuding trees (*pañcakṣīravṛkṣa*), such as the *aśvattha* and others; this should be done for five nights, performing the rite in its entirety.
At the conclusion of the bath, one should offer incense to the child: cow's tooth, ram's horn, human nail, deer hair, human hair, and snake-skin.

Having combined these together, one should offer incense with intense charcoal; during the *devatābali*, the previously mentioned perfumes, incense, and so forth should be offered in the four directions and in the center of the village—this rule for children born within a month has been stated for the sake of nourishment. Now, the offering for those one year old is described by the verse beginning with "five foods" (*pañcānna*): five foods, five edibles, the flesh of aquatic creatures, perfume, flowers, a lamp, liquor, the previously mentioned incense, and likewise the ritual bathing; this is the directional offering (*digbali*) in the various divisions of the directions.

O King, for the sake of the nourishment of children born during the rains who have manifested upon the earth, the worship of the Yoginīs certainly becomes effective after five or three years from conception. 151.

In this context, two months after ten months have passed are taken as one year; therefore, for the sake of pacifying those born in the year who are fifteen years of age and have been oppressed by kings, one should offer the annual *bali* consisting of the "five foods. Having colored these with turmeric and other substances, the five foods—the aforementioned cooked food, the aquatic creature, the fish, the meat, and the flesh—along with the previously mentioned perfumes and so forth, constitute the "five eatables" (*pañcakhādya*). This is the cooked food.

Having placed all the previously mentioned substances, such as liquor, incense, and so forth, into a bamboo basket, one should perform the ritual sprinkling (*nirmarca*) three times with the offering of a lamp and food (*balinā*).

For ten days, offerings should be given in the ten directions—starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna, including below and above—at the crossroads in the center of the village. This is the distribution of the *bali* throughout the ten directions.
For children born in the year, [the title] "O King" is manifested on earth for the sake of their nourishment;
such is the rule for the worship of those who have completed one year.

Thus, from conception up to fifteen years—three times five years—the worship of the sixty-three Yoginīs must certainly be performed; otherwise, the pacification and other rites for children will not take effect. This is the rule for the worship of the Yoginīs.

Now, the symptoms of the defects of those seized by the Mothers (*mātṛ*) are described, beginning with "O limb" (*aṅga*), and so forth: There is wasting of the limbs, pain in the eyes, and the mouth, hands, and feet turn yellowish; there is excessive discharge of a yellow color, fever, vomiting, emaciation, and fainting.

O King, having recognized these signs, one should perform the ritual within the mandala and the fire-oblation (*homa*). Otherwise, the Mothers born of spirits (*bhūta*), acting according to their natural qualities, will not release them. || 152 ||

In this context, when a child is seized by the Mothers (*mātṛ*), then there occurs a wasting away of his limbs, pain in the eyes, and the face, hands, and feet become pale; the urine becomes yellowish and flows copiously; fever arises, vomiting occurs, and emaciation as well as fainting ensue. Having recognized these signs of the Mothers' affliction, one should perform rites such as the *maṇḍala* and *homa* for those children—and by the word "also" (*api*), for those seized by cruel planets. Otherwise, the aforementioned Mothers born of spirits (*bhūta*) will not release them unless an offering (*bali*) is given, due to the influence of their innate nature. Such is the characteristic of the medical treatment.

Now, the signs of death for one seized by the sixty-fourth *Kulikā* are described, beginning with the word "white": "O King, he whose entire body becomes white, who has extremely minute pustules, whose neck is crooked along with his limbs, and from whose mouth, private parts, and anus blood flows—one should not perform worship for him; for there is surely death for that deluded practitioner, and he cannot be protected by gods, men, or serpents. (153)

In this context, the sixty-fourth *kulikā* abides as the pervasive form at every junction (*sandhi*) of all the *yoginīs*. At the junction of the days, months, and years of the womb, the entire body of the child grasped by her becomes white; the eruptions (*sphoṭakāḥ*) are extremely subtle, the size of mustard seeds or *rājikā* grains; the neck becomes crooked; and blood flows from the limbs, or from the mouth, the secret parts, or the anus.
Having observed such a mark, one should not offer worship toward that object;
if one does so, then due to greed, there arises a state of insignificance for deluded practitioners.
Why? Because it is certain that death awaits him, and he cannot be protected by gods, humans, or serpents—such is the rule regarding the signs of death.

In this chapter, the "Great Instruction on Alchemy and the Tantra of Child-Raising," those who are worshipped in the mandala and who bestow happiness are now described, beginning with the words "Nāgas": The Nāgas, Yakṣas, and Grahas; those born of the lineage of Danu, the Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Śākinīs, and the wicked Nāgas;

those who delight in human blood, the Ḍākinīs, Kumbhāṇḍas, Kṣetrapālas, Gaṇapatyas, as well as the Kṣetra-Vetālas, Siddhas, Apasmāras, and Khagendras—when worshipped in the mandala, they shall become the bestowers of supreme happiness. (154)
In this world, for those afflicted by nāgas and other spirits, the worship of the nāgas and others within the mandala to be described hereafter brings about happiness.
Their many characteristics, as taught in the *Bhūtatantra*, are to be understood through the binding of mudrās; however, how many of these will be mentioned right here in what follows?

Now, for the sake of the fierce worship, the mandala and the location of the mandala are described, beginning with "of the fierce ones" and so forth: "O Lord of Men, for the sake of worshipping the fierce ones, the mandala is located outside the village, at a tree site, in a cremation ground, in the abode of the best of gods, or at the confluence of rivers."

In the measurement of the deities, [the dimensions] are one cubit, two, four, three, ten, nine, or eight; in the center, there is an eight-spoked wheel, which, by virtue of its qualities, occupies half the portion of the maṇḍala. || 155 ||

Here, for the purpose of worshipping the cruel deities, the mandala is located outside the village, specifically at a site with a single tree, in a cremation ground, in a temple of a supreme god—that is, an empty shrine—or at the confluence of rivers; it may be one cubit, two, or four.
In this case, according to one's means, the preceptor should construct a mandala starting from one cubit, two cubits, or four cubits, up to as much as a thousand cubits.

Regarding the phrase "by the thirty-three and nine kings": here, the measurement for the nine deities is a mandala of one cubit; for thirteen, it is two cubits; and by the term "king," for sixteen, it is four cubits. Starting from these, one should construct up to the limit of one thousand cubits for sixteen hundred and twenty [deities], according to one's resources.
In the center of all these mandalas, there is either an eight-spoked wheel or a lotus, occupying half the portion of the mandala.

The door shall indeed be one-eighth of the wheel, and the altar (vedī) and the garlands (hārāḥ) shall be half of that; the walls (prākārāḥ) shall be half the size of the altar, while the archway (toraṇa) shall be three times the measure of the door.

One should fashion a circular pit (kuṇḍa), consisting of three parts, filled with white lotuses and colored with white pigments; and in the direction of one's own family (kula), one should place the respective emblems (cihna) of the deities using the five auspicious colors (pañcaraṅga). ||156||

The door is one-eighth of the circumference of the mandala circle; the door, the pedestal (vedikā), and the ground for the hanging garlands (hārabhūmi) consist of five lines for the walls, with the pedestal being half [the height] of those, and the jeweled band (ratnapaṭṭikā) likewise; the turret (niryūha), the side-wing (pakṣaka), and the cheek (kapola) are according to the measurement of the door; and the archway (toraṇa) is three times the size of the door—this is the rule for the characteristics of the mandala.

Now the *śāntika* fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) is described, beginning with the words "circular" (*vṛtta*) and so forth. Here, among the fire-pits to be described, the circular pit is to be taken for pacification (*śānti*). That same [circle] is divided into three parts: two *vitastis* in diameter and one *vitasti* in depth. It is "filled with white powder" (*sitakamalāmaya*), meaning that within the center of the womb (*garbha*) there is a lotus made of white pigment; on the altar (*vedikā*) there is a row of lotuses, and outside, below, there are lotus petals—thus it is filled with white colors.

Then, one should cause the symbols of the deities to be drawn with five colors upon the petals of the pericarp of a white lotus, situated in their respective directions according to the family (*kula*) or according to the five Tathāgatas.

Thus: a *vajra* in the center; a sword in the east according to the family; a red jewel in the south; a white hundred-petaled lotus in the north; a wheel symbol in the west; a curved knife (*kartikā*) resting on a lotus petal in the southeast; a hook (*aṅkuśa*) in the southwest, the corner of the demons; a vajra-noose in the northwest, O Lord of Men; and a trident on a Rudra petal in the northeast. (157)

Regarding the phrase "the vajra in the center": because of the statement to be made here, "or the vajra in all rites" (3.12), there is a blue vajra upon the pericarp of the lotus, representing the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). On the eastern petal is a black sword, representing formative factors (*saṃskāra*); this occurs according to the [respective] family. On the south is a red jewel, representing sensation (*vedanā*). On the left, the northern petal, is a white hundred-petaled lotus, representing perception (*saṃjñā*). On the west is a yellow wheel-mark, representing the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

In the southeastern petal is a black knife, which is the element wind; in the southwestern corner, at the petal of the Daityas, is a red goad, which is fire; in the northwest is a yellow vajra-noose, which is earth; in the northeast, on the petal of Rudra, is a white trident, which is the water element; in the center is a vajra, which is the space element together with consciousness;
and at the eastern gate is a sword resembling a dark cloud, while in the south is a vajra-staff.
In the western direction the glorious mace prevails, and in the north the mallet certainly prevails;

having understood this according to the mind's inclination, perform the many various forms of the Kālacakra for the sake of sons of barren women, for men struck by planetary afflictions, and for the purpose of pacification and nourishment. 158.
At the eastern gate is Khaḍga, black, the Wrathful One who is the Vajra of Envy;
at the southern gate is Vajradaṇḍa, red, the Wrathful One who is the Vajra of Passion;
and at the western gate, in the direction of Varuṇa, is [Śrī]Gadā, yellow, the Wrathful One who is the Vajra of Delusion.
At the northern gate is the white Mudgara, the wrathful Mānavajra;
in the center is the Vajra, the blue Wrathful King Dveṣavajra—
having understood this, and so forth, up to "this is for the sake of nourishment," is easily understood.

Now, the procedure for bathing those afflicted by planetary influences is described, beginning with the word "kumbha": One should perform a bath using eight jars containing gems, with mouths shaped like lotus petals, along with seven unripened *mallaka* vessels, water, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and other substances.

Having performed a diverse worship with mustard seeds and the like, perfumes, incenses, lamps, various fruits and juices, white flowers, and cloths—using a raised platform (*mañcha*)—one should then again offer oblations of pacifying sacrificial materials (*śāntihavya*). || 159 ||
