[In the *Vedikāpadmāvalipaṭala*, within the *Mahoddeśa* on Alchemy and Pediatrics: Here, in the directions of the mandala, there are eight vases endowed with the characteristics to be described, containing gems—that is, accompanied by the five precious gems—and joined with the medicinal herbs and other substances to be described; "with petals" refers to the sprouts of milk-trees, which have lotuses at their openings; "by those" [is meant] by these [vases].

Likewise, "with seven *mallas*" means with seven unbaked earthen bowls (*sarāva*) accompanied by waters such as the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth—namely, water, milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugarcane juice, and scented water.
One should perform the ritual bathing (*snapana*) with these seven bowls filled [with the substances] in their proper order.
Then, [one should do so] with eight jars (*kumbha*), and also with the two jars of Victory (*jaya*) and Triumph (*vijaya*), as indicated by the word "also" (*api*).

One should perform the ritual purification (*nirmārjana*) with mustard seeds and so forth—first with five balls of cow dung, then with burning tufts of grass, mustard seeds and the like, and also with balls of cooked rice and such.

Having performed worship with perfumes and other offerings, and having performed the consecration of the mandala, one should cause [the disciple] to enter the mandala; there, having bestowed the initiation, and having performed the water-initiation and others using the water from the mandala-vase, one should then offer the oblation for pacification (*śāntihavya*).

One should offer milk, grain, sesame and the like, as well as fuel-sticks of five kinds of milky trees by the hundreds; likewise, one should perform the invocation, the sipping of water (ācamana), the worship, and the ritual adoration for the sake of pacification—this is the constant mode of worship for the thirty-six Yoginīs who afflict those on this excellent earth, O Lord of Men. || 160 ||
The passage beginning with "milk" (*dugdham*) and so forth is easily understood.

Furthermore, whatever else has not been stated, all that should be performed by the Master according to the procedure taught in the Chapter on Consecration (*abhiṣeka-paṭala*); this is the rule everywhere.

Thus ends the sixth great chapter, the Mahoddeśa on Alchemy and the Science of Child-rearing (*rasāyanādibālatantra*), in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja*, which follows the *Śrīmūla-tantra*. 6.

(7) The Great Chapter on the Investigation of the Logic of One’s Own and Others’ Views: Selflessness, the ripening of karma, the three realms of existence, the six destinies, the arising of the twelvefold dependent origination, the Vedas, the truths, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the five aggregates, the three bodies, and the innate—likewise, non-inertness and emptiness: that in which they proclaim these things is the teaching of the Vajrī, revealed with certainty. 161.
Having prostrated before the Lord of the World, Kālacakra, the Great Bliss,
I shall set forth somewhat of my own view regarding both our own and other philosophical systems.
1. ka. *bhaṇḍa* 2. ka. kha. *mūla* 3–4. ka. kha. in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the commentary on the *Dvādaśasāhasrikā*.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, that which was spoken by Mañjuśrī from the *Paramādibuddha*—which accords with the tenets of both one's own and other systems of philosophy—is now expanded upon through a commentary, beginning with the words "Selflessness" (*nairātmya*) and so forth.
Here, when examined according to worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*), the established conclusions of all philosophical systems are identical for the sake of worldly accomplishment; as it is said:
"By whatever means the mind of men is joined to an object..."
Through that, he attains identification with it, just as a multiform gem [reflects its surroundings].
The intention regarding the nature of "the empirical" (vyāvahārika) is the same today as it was before;
likewise, the analysis of the elements, the sense organs, and so forth is identical,
and the agent, the instrument, and the rest are also the same.

"There is no difference between the Buddhist and the non-Buddhist [regarding the self]," yet there is a difference concerning the reality of emptiness (*śūnyatā-tattva*), which is [described as] "selflessness" (*nairātmya*) and so forth.
Here, selflessness is twofold: the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
Furthermore, the ripening of karma (*karma-vipāka*) is threefold: physical, vocal, and mental.
The three realms of existence consist of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

The "course according to reality" refers to the six courses of rebirth—namely, those of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, asuras, and gods. The direct origination of these beings through the twelve links of dependent origination is the truth of the Vedas, which is the Four Noble Truths characterized by suffering, its origin, the path, and cessation.
"Doubled nines" refers to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), which will be explained below.
"The five aggregates" refers to form and so forth;
"the three bodies" refers to the Dharma-body and so forth; and the "fourth" is the *sahajakāya* (innate body).

In the same way, that in which the Teacher teaches this selflessness and so forth—namely, that non-inert emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects is like a reflection—within the three vehicles, that is the revealed and definitive teaching of the Vajra-holder; it is by the power of the Buddha’s vision, according to the disposition of sentient beings—such is the fixed rule of the Tathāgata’s doctrine. Now, the doctrine of Brahmā and Viṣṇu is stated, beginning with "in which": that in which the Veda is self-existent, and where for one born from a womb there is no dharma other than the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), that is the teaching of Brahmā.

The self is the agent, as are karma, time, primordial nature, and the qualities; emptiness is the destruction of dharmas. Here, Viṣṇu’s teaching is that the agent is the cause of the fruit, and that this is the manifestation of necessity. 162.

[153a] Here, in this system, the Veda is self-existent, uncreated, and like space; and regarding the "wombs" (*yoni*) of birth, it is held that the mouth of Brahmā is the womb of the Brāhmaṇas, the two arms are the womb of the Kṣatriyas, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the two thighs are the womb of the Vaiśyas, and the two feet are the womb of the Śūdras.

Furthermore, it is taught that there is no other dharma superior to the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*); that is, in this world, for the sake of attaining heaven, there is no other dharma such as giving (*dāna*) that is superior to the horse sacrifice. Such is the teaching of Brahmā; this is the rule of the Brahmā-system.
1. kha. asti; 2. ka. kha. *nairātmyeti*; bho. *Ces Pa La Sogs Pa* (*ityādi*);
3. ka. kha. ga. *sakāśāt*; bho. *dños* (*sākṣāt*).

4. O! [In the] *Kāya* [chapter], the great summary concerning the investigation of the principles of one’s own and others’ philosophical systems (*darśana*). Herein, within that [system], in the *Gītā-dharma* of the Vaiṣṇava school, it is as follows: there is an agent; there is a self (*ātman*); there is auspicious and inauspicious karma; there is time; there is primordial nature (*prakṛti*) consisting of earth and so forth; there are qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* and the rest; and there is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which is the non-perishing nature (*anaṣṭadharmatā*). From the statement, "He does not see, for he has become one," and so forth, it follows that the agent is the cause who bestows the fruit of whatever auspicious or inauspicious deeds have been performed.
The teaching revealed here in the *Kālacakra* as "that of Viṣṇu" is indeed the rule of the Vaiṣṇava system.

Now, the system of Īśvara is stated, beginning with "the six paths," and so forth: "The six paths, the five principles (*pañcatattva*), the supreme state, the entirely other, the mantra-body, the nature of knowledge (*vidyātman*), the state of Śiva-hood, the conjunction through the movement of the three states, the state of renunciation, the piercing of the drop (*bindu*), the state of Śiva pervading all bodies, and the piercing of the twelve knots—all this indeed prevails therein; that is the fixed teaching of Śiva. (163)

In this context, why is the "six paths" (*ṣaṇmārga*) and so forth mentioned alongside the previously stated view of Viṣṇu? [The Ga. manuscript states: "'The three gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—are one form.

[And] 'Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the state of the perished phenomena (*naṣṭadharmatā*),' [but] it does not exist [in the Bho. manuscript]. [However, the Bho. manuscript reads: *chos nyid de* (that very reality/nature), which corresponds to *śūnyatā samadharmatā asti*. Regarding the reading:

in both the root text and the commentary, the reading is either *śūnyatā naṣṭadharmā* or *śūnyatā naṣṭadharmatā asti*. In the Ga. manuscript, instead of the phrase *śūnyatā naṣṭadharmatā asti*, the reading *nāsti* (it does not exist) has been accepted.

In the Tibetan translation of the *Ṭīkā*, however, the term *naṣṭadharmatā* was translated as *samadharmatā*. Nevertheless, the venerable Khedrup Je, expressing his own view while relying upon both the root text and the *Ṭīkā*, accepted the reading *naṣṭadharmatā* exactly as it stands and demonstrated how the statement "emptiness is *naṣṭadharmatā*" is indeed consistent within the Vaiśeṣika position.

Even though the world comes into being through the conjunction of eternal atoms, the material universe derived from them as its material cause must necessarily perish because it is impermanent; therefore, this entire creation is understood to be emptiness (*śūnyatā*) by virtue of its nature of having perished. This is the essence of the opinion of the venerable Kheṅ dba’ rje, which is explained in the Tibetan language as follows: "Emptiness (*stong pa nyid*) is the state of having the property of destruction or cessation, even for an entity that remains for a long duration from the time of its own establishment."
Because, through the process of all entities dissolving into the root and becoming one, they finally vanish and are no longer seen (as stated in the *Vimalaprabhā-ṭīkā*, page 161A).

The Sanskrit translation of the aforementioned Tibetan passage is as follows: There indeed exists emptiness (*śūnyatā*) in the form of the perishability, disintegration, and cessation by nature of things that have remained for a long time since their own origination; for things perish through being dissolved into their own material causes (*upādāna*) via processes such as unification, and they pass into invisibility.

As stated in the *Vimalaprabhā* [in the section on the Inner Science]: "The agent, the self (*ātman*), action, time, the qualities of primordial nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*), emptiness, the dharma of destruction, and nirvāṇa—from these, the ultimate state (*kāṣṭhāvasthā*)."
The rule is that along with these, the six paths and so forth are to be understood.
Here, in this body, the six paths are those that operate within the six sense objects.

"The five principles" refers to the collection of elements beginning with space; "the supreme state" refers to the sixth element, the element of consciousness (*jñānadhātu*); "entirety" means that which has become integrated within all the elements; and by the word "and," there is further the "mantra-body," which is the reality of mantra consisting of the vowels and consonants (*ālikāli*).

"Vidyā" refers to the reality of *ānanda* (bliss) and so forth; "ātman" refers to the eternal reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*); and "Sachivatva" refers to the all-pervading reality of Śiva (*śivatattva*).

For that which is devoid of form, there is a threefold movement of the stages (*pada-gati*)—namely, *piṇḍasthā*, *padasthā*, and *rūpasthā*. These pertain to the nature of the conceptualizations of body, speech, and mind. "Union" (*yojana*) refers to the joining of these three types of stage-movements.
Regarding these six paths and so forth, "union" (*melāpaka*) means their conjunction at the time of arising, while "the state of abandonment" at the time of death means their disintegration.

"The piercing of the *bindu* is Śiva-hood": here, the piercing of the seminal *bindu* (*śukra-bindu*), characterized by the state of bliss at the moment of emission, is itself Śiva-hood. "Pervading all things" means it extends throughout the moving and the unmoving. "The piercing of the twelve knots" (*granthi*): here, the twelve zodiac signs (*rāśi*) inherent in living beings are designated by the word "knots. The piercings of those twelve signs consist of the year, the solstice (*ayana*), time, the age (*yuga*), the season (*ṛtu*), the month, the fortnight, the day, the hour (*ghaṭikā*), the *pāṇīpala*, and the breath (*śvāsa*).
Indeed, that teaching in which all this is established as manifest is the teaching of Śiva.
Thus is the rule of the Śivamata.
Ka. Kha. From the state of the body;
Ka. Kha. Śivatva; Bho. Si Bahi De Nid (Śivatattva).
kha. Varṣāpana: Addressing the question of how the Śaiva system arose from the Vaiṣṇava doctrine, the *Ṭīkā* states: "The three gods are one single form," and so forth.

Elucidating this, the venerable Kheḍrabajē has stated that by asserting there is a creator in the Gītā-Vaiṣṇava doctrine, both the theory of atomic agency and the theory of divine agency as the bestower of fruits are accepted; in accordance with that, the emergence of the Śaiva doctrine is indeed logically consistent with the context.
In Tibet, it is said as follows: "Regarding those gathered here who profess the Dharma through song—the Vaiśeṣikas and Naiyāyikas who follow the tradition of the god Viṣṇu—their position is this:
one must explain that 'there exists a creator' and 'consciousness' as referring to the existence of eternal, partless atoms which are the creators of the entire world.
However, it is not the meaning [of their doctrine] to say that there exists a creator of all things, such as Viṣṇu."

"In these [verses] concerning the refutation of the Self (*ātman*), the authorship of partless atoms (*paramāṇu*) is refuted, but the authorship of the pervasive one (*vyāpin*) is not refuted. (From the *Vimalaprabhā-ṭīkā-vyākhyā*, 'Ga' volume; Sanskrit reconstruction of the cited Tibetan passage: *atra eteṣu saṃgṛhīteṣu gītā-dharmavādeṣu vaiṣṇaveṣu vaiśeṣika-naiyāyikayor yad abhimataṃ tat kartā astīti sarvalokasya racayitā nitya-niravayava-paramāṇur astīty arthakam, na tatra sarvakartā brahmā vā viṣṇur vā astīty abhimatam; ata evāgre tayoḥ khaṇḍanāvasare niravayava-paramāṇoḥ kartṛtvam eva dūṣitam, naiva tat-prasaṅge viṣṇoḥ kartṛtvaṃ khaṇḍitam*). In these Vaiṣṇava discourses on the Dharma contained within the *Bhagavadgītā*, that which is accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas and Naiyāyikas—that there is an agent who is the creator of all worlds, namely a permanent, partless atom—is what is meant [by the opponent's position]. It is not accepted therein that Brahmā or Viṣṇu is the creator of all. For this very reason, when those two [schools] are later refuted, it is specifically the agency of the partless atom that is criticized, and in that context, the agency of Viṣṇu is not refuted at all.

The Great Chapter on the Investigation of the Logic of Our Own and Other Systems: "There is no Lord, nor even the ripening of karma; rather, the multitude of elements experiences the objects of the qualities. In the absence of that [Lord], the fruit is not manifest"—this is to be understood as the teaching of the Teacher of the Immortals (Brahmā).

"The Creator fashioned everything, both moving and unmoving, for the sake of the enjoyment of the Tāyins (Jainas); through his satisfaction, heaven indeed comes to be for men"—this is the teaching of Rahmaṇa (the Muslim God). (164)

Now the Lokāyata doctrine is stated, beginning with "it does not exist" and so forth: Here, for embodied beings, there is no Lord; there is no agent, and thus no ripening of karma either. Regarding "the qualities and objects": the qualities (*guṇas*) are *sattva* and the others; the objects (*viṣayas*) are smell and the rest. "The collection of elements" refers to earth and the other [elements]; one experiences these. Upon the dissolution of that collection of elements at the end of death, there is no fruit of karma.

Just as the power of intoxication arises from the combination of *harītakī*, molasses, and so forth, so too is the power of the elements produced by their conjunction; in the absence of that [power], there is no body for the next world. Thus, it should be understood that the teaching of Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, is clear. This is the established doctrine of the Lokāyata school. Now, the doctrine of the Mleccha Tāyi(nas) is stated, beginning with "the creator," and so on: here, everything—whether moving (*cara*), meaning mobile, or unmoving (*acara*), meaning stationary—is created by the Creator, Brahmā. The term "of the Tāyi(nas)" refers to the Mlecchas who wear white garments (*śvetavāsinaḥ*), for the sake of their livelihood.
Heaven results from the propitiation of that *Rahmaṇa*, while hell indeed comes to men from his non-propitiation;
that aforementioned practice is the rule of the *Tāyi* doctrine.

[154a] Now, the doctrine of the *Kṣapaṇakas* is stated, beginning with "the three times," etc.: there are the three times, the six substances, the nine categories as prescribed, the six classes of living beings, the five other bodies, the vows, the restraints, the states of existence, and the divisions of knowledge and conduct.

The soul is indeed of the same size as the body; through celibacy across immeasurable births, liberation is attained. That teaching in which the measure of liberation is declared above is the teaching of the Jinas. 165.
In this Jain doctrine of Syādvāda, the conventional usage of permanence and impermanence is established through substance (*dravya*) and modification (*paryāya*).

Among these, "the three times" refers to the past, the future, and the present; and "the six substances" are: the soul (*jīva*), matter (*pudgala*), time (*kāla*), space (*ākāśa*), merit (*puṇya*, or *dharma*), and demerit (*pāpa*, or *adharma*).

Among these, the soul (*jīva*) is that which is established by nine categories (*navapada*): namely, soul (*jīva*), non-soul (*ajīva*), influx (*āsrava*), restraint (*saṃvara*), shedding (*nirjarā*), bondage (*bandha*), liberation (*mokṣa*), and movement (*gati*). Space (*ākāśa*) is eternal. [The category of] movement includes the six classes of living beings (*ṣaṭkāya*): the class of earth-beings (*pṛthvīkāya*), the class of water-beings (*apkāya*), the class of fire-beings (*tejaskāya*), the class of air-beings (*vāyukāya*), the class of plant-beings (*vanaspatikāya*), and the class of mobile-beings (*trasakāya*).
The six bodies of living beings are as follows:

there are five other bodies—namely, the assimilative body (*āhārika-kāya*), the luminous body (*jyotiḥ-kāya*), the natural body (*naiḥsargika-kāya*), the spontaneously born body (*upapāduka-kāya*), and the final body (*carama-kāya*)—which together constitute the bodies of living beings.

The vows of the Kṣapaṇakas are fivefold, distinguished as vows, restraints, conducts, cognitions, and characters: first, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*); second, truthfulness (*satya*); third, taking only what is given (*dattādāna*); fourth, celibacy (*brahmacarya*); and fifth, renunciation of all possessions (*sarvaparigrahaparityāga*). The restraints (*samiti*) are five: restraint in movement (*īryā-samiti*), restraint in speech (*bhāṣā-samiti*), restraint in seeking alms (*eṣaṇā-samiti*), restraint in handling objects (*ādāna-nikṣepaṇa-samiti*), and restraint in disposal (*nikṣepa-pratiṣṭhāpana-samiti*, also known as *utsarga-samiti*). The distinctions of destiny (*gati-bheda*) are five: hell-beings, animals, humans, gods, and those destined for liberation (*mokṣa-gati*). The distinctions of cognition (*jñāna-bheda*) are five: sensory perception (*mati*), scriptural knowledge (*śruta*), clairvoyance (*avadhi*), telepathy (*manaḥ-paryeṣaṇa*), and omniscience (*kevalya-jñāna*).

There are thirteen divisions of conduct: the five divisions of vows, the five divisions of carefulness (*samiti*), and the three protections—protection of body, protection of speech, and protection of mind.
This is the path to liberation proclaimed by the Arhats.
The soul (*jīva*) is of the same size as the body.

In that doctrine where liberation is not possible for one whose life is eternal across immeasurable existences—wherein the measure of liberation is declared to be the three worlds, forty-five hundred thousand *yojanas* in extent and shaped like an umbrella—that is the teaching of the Jinas; such is the rule of the Kṣapaṇakas (Jainas). That [Veda] is not self-existent; in the abode of the three worlds, the word "Veda" denotes meaning: in ancient times, Brahmā revealed the meaning through the word "Veda" by means of his four mouths.

If the meaning of a word is also non-different from the word itself, then why does the word "fire" not burn the mouth when it is uttered? Therefore, there must indeed be a teacher even regarding objects that are unknown, as well as those that are yet to come or have already passed.
When investigated here through reasoning, the Veda is not self-existent.
Why?
It is said: because the word "Veda" denotes a meaning.
In this regard, it is established that whatever word denotes an object is produced by the effort of the throat, palate, and so forth; therefore, it is not self-existent (*svayambhū*).

Now, it is established that this [word] is not the Veda; rather, the Veda is something else—an eternal entity that has become merged with the objects of all sounds within the cavity of the ear—and this [word] is its manifestor.

Therefore, he says: If the eternal Veda were here established as being merged (*kalolībhūta*) within the meaning of every word, then when the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) is uttered, there ought to be a clamor within the cavity of one's ears; but this is not the case. Therefore, this proposition is futile: "The eternal word exists as something else, pervasive and non-different from its object.
If there were identity between the word and its object, then why does the word "fire," when uttered, not burn one's own mouth?

Therefore, it is established that the Veda is not eternal, nor is it identical with its meaning. Furthermore, it is heard here: when the absence of the Veda occurs—that is, when the Vedic dharma has been destroyed by barbarians—then Brahmā makes manifest through his four mouths the meaning by means of the ancient Vedic words, such as the recitation beginning with "Indra was the sacrificial animal. Thus, the meaning is one thing and the Veda is another; [this constitutes] the deposits, the emissions, and the ritual fuel-offerings. Knowledge thereafter ascends upwards to the end of the world, [establishing] the vision of self and others and the great exposition on the investigation of logic. This is established.

Therefore, there exists a teacher who is Brahmā; for one who has not known the subject matter, the past, and the future, a teacher is established as having existed through oral recitation—that is, through word-of-mouth transmission. Thus, the Veda is proven to be a product [of human effort] and is not equal to space. Here, it is produced by being uttered from the mouth; due to differences in the vocal organs (*sthāna*), it is established by reasoning as being localized. Recited from the mouths of Brahmins, it is limited in scope, whereas others claim it is all-pervading.

Since this Veda—which is not all-pervasive—is recited and written by those of the Śūdra and other castes, it cannot be an authoritative means of knowledge for wise and learned men. Therefore, the Veda is not equal to space; rather, it is a product here, uttered from the mouth according to the rule of distinct articulatory places. By logic, it is localized when recited by the mouths of the twice-born, whereas others recite it as being all-pervasive.

Because this Veda—which Śūdras and other castes read and write—is not the *asvarga* (heavenly) Veda, therefore it is not a valid authority (*pramāṇa*) for wise and learned men; thus, the Veda is established as being of human origin (*kṛtaka*). This is the summary [of the argument], and it should be understood in detail from the treatises on logic (*pramāṇaśāstra*); such is the rule of Mañjuśrī.

Now, the previously mentioned corruption of the origins (*yonidūṣaṇa*) of the Brāhmaṇas and others is stated: here, indeed, the mouth of Brahmā is the origin of the Brāhmaṇas, because they were born from that.

Thus, the arms are the source of the Kṣatriyas; from the word "and so forth" (ādi), the two thighs are the source of the Vaiśyas, and the two feet are the source of the Śūdras. In this way, there are four castes.
Among these four, the fifth caste is that of the Caṇḍālas; their source is not known by the Brāhmaṇas for the time being.
Furthermore, is it true that here the Brahmins were born from the mouth of Brahmā?
Therefore I ask: were the Brahmin women (*brāhmaṇya*) also born from him? If they were, then they would be sisters, because they would have arisen from the same womb.
In this way, does marriage with a sister also occur for Kṣatriyas and others?
How so?
If it does occur, then the practice of the Mleccha dharma arises.
The logical principle is that by engaging in the dharma of barbarians (mleccha), one's caste is destroyed, and from the destruction of caste comes hell.
Furthermore, another point is considered: if there is here a single creator of all beings, then how do the four castes come to be?
Just as when a man has four sons, they do not have separate and distinct castes, so it is with the castes as well.
Now, if there were a distinction based on the differentiation of Brahmā’s mouth and other parts, then how could that very [distinction] not be logically untenable?
Just as there is no distinction among the roots, middles, and tips of udumbara fruits, so it is with living beings as well.

Furthermore, no distinction is observed based on differences in color—such as white, red, yellow, or black; likewise, no distinction is observed through differences in elements (*dhātu*), faculties (*indriya*), pleasure, pain, knowledge, scriptures, and so forth. Since this is the case, it is established that birth is not determined [by such factors].

Thus, the fruit of sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) has been refuted by Śuka. For example: "Having cut down the sacrificial post, having slaughtered the animal, and having created a mire of blood—if heaven is reached in this manner, by what means is hell reached?"

Thus, the statement of Śuka is well known: "Therefore, the Veda is not self-born; it is not the source of birth for humanity from [Brahmā’s] mouth and other [limbs]; nor is there any dharma superior to the Aśvamedha. Since all such prattle is found to be meaningless upon investigation, the doctrine of Brahmā and the doctrine of Viṣṇu must be refuted along with that of Īśvara.

Now, the refutation of the doctrine of Īśvara is stated, beginning with "If [He] exists," and so forth: "If there exists an Īśvara who is the creator of all, and He alone is the enjoyer of the fruits of the world's actions and no one else; or if there is no Īśvara who is the performer of actions, and if He were not the universal creator; or if the creator, being impelled by another, acts only when prompted—then this would mean the creator is entirely dependent on another. Therefore, the Īśvara cannot be the giver of the auspicious and inauspicious fruits of living beings' actions, apart from their own karma.
In this regard, if there exists an Īśvara who is the creator of all, then how is it that He alone is the enjoyer of the fruits of action and no one else?
One person eats a cake, while another dies of thirst;

yet it is not the case that he who acts is the doer [in the ultimate sense], nor that what is done is the action [itself]. The one who experiences the fruit of that performed action is the "doer of the action" (karmakartṛ).

Furthermore, an agent is not established without action; for according to the logical principle that "one who makes a pot is a potter," so too "he who performs an action is the agent. Thus it is said: nor is the Lord the agent of action, for he is an independent instigator.

In this context, if he were not the agent of action, then the statement that he is the "universal agent" (sarvakartā) in every respect would be meaningless. If, on the other hand, the agent performs an action while being impelled [by another], then the agent is dependent upon another. How could one who is dependent not exercise restraint when a contrary action has been committed by that which he impels? Without independence, there is no such thing as independence; independence is pervaded by God (Īśvara).

Thus, for those who maintain the existence of a creator, the non-existence of the fruit of action is established; yet this is not the case. Therefore, it is established that there is no creator whatsoever—an Īśvara who bestows the fruits of good and evil upon living beings—apart from their own karma; thus, the experience of the fruits of one's own actions is established even without a creator.

Now, the dependence of an independent creator upon other factors is stated, beginning with "the earth": If, at the outset, the earth, water, fire, wind, and ocean do not exist here in space due to the absence of a creator, then in the absence of material substances, how could a creator devoid of objects create the universe?

O Lord of Men, for this agent who is devoid of objects, there is no means of knowledge—neither direct perception nor indirect inference; rather, everything, including the form of action, arises solely from conjunction, not by his own will.

If, in this world, the atoms of earth and the other elements do not exist in space at the beginning, then, in the absence of material substance, how can he who is devoid of objects, partless, and the creator of all, create the universe?

For this agent who is devoid of objects, there is no means of proof—neither perception nor inference—because of which [one might conclude otherwise]; therefore, the entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, arises solely from the conjunction of substances, and not through the will of the agent in the form of action: such is the principle. Thus is the negation of the agent's will.
(Ga. Śukra0 Kha. Praṇidhāna)

[In the chapter] "The Great Summary on the Investigation of the Logic of One's Own and Others' Views" [it is said]: "Without an agent" (*kartāraṃ vinā*). Now, dependent origination is explained, beginning with "from conjunction," etc.: From the conjunction [of light], water arises from the moonstone; the reflection of an object appears in a mirror; from the cause of sourness, saliva flows from the tongue; from a magnet, the other [iron] becomes possessed of sound; and from a pure seed, a sprout shall arise. Even the whirling of an iron rod occurs due to a magnet. Not even a slight bit of these things happens by will; this power of these entities has been fashioned by no one within the abode of the three worlds.

In this world, the production of all things arises from conjunction (*saṃyoga*); having reached this, that arises through conjunction. For example, water arises from the moonstone due to its conjunction with moonbeams; by the word "and" (*ca*), fire arises from the sunstone;
and in a mirror, the reflection of an object arises from the conjunction with the object.
Just as the tongue-tasting of one person occurs due to the contact with another’s consumption of sour food— arising from the cause of that sourness—
and just as an echo arises in a well or similar place due to the contact with sound,
so too would a sprout exist in a pure seed due to the contact with earth, water, and other factors.

"From the magnet" means that from the magnet-stone (*kāntapāṣāṇa*), there occurs the whirling of iron rods; "from conjunction" means that no object among these things comes into being by mere will, but rather this power of objects was fashioned by someone within the abode of the three worlds— thus is the production [of effects] established through perception.

He says: "Since an effect does not exist without a cause, therefore a cause exists; thus, God and so forth are established. To this, he replies: "In this case, regarding the effect that arises from a cause, is that effect existent (*sat*) or non-existent (*asat*)?

An existent effect does not arise from a cause; for instance, clay and other such materials do not become the causes of an already existing jar, because it already exists. Nor does a non-existent effect arise, because of its non-existence, like a tortoise's hair. Likewise, threads, the shuttle, the loom, and so forth, do not become the causes of a cloth."
The effect cannot be of a dual nature because of mutual contradiction:
that which exists does not become non-existent, and that which is non-existent does not become existent, due to contradiction.
Therefore, it is established that the effect is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent at the time of its cause.

He says: "In this case, by the negation of the cause, there is also the negation of the effect; from the negation of both, the non-existence of everything is established. To this he replies: "In this case, the non-existence of everything does not follow, because of their mutual dependence. Here, that which is the causality of a cause is conceptually constructed in dependence upon the effect, and the effect is likewise [constructed] in dependence upon the cause. Thus, because of this mutual dependence, it would follow that both possess the status of being a cause.

Because both [cause and effect] would be causes, there would be an absence of effects; in the absence of those [effects], there would be an absence of causes, because a cause is dependent upon its effect, which leads to the consequence of [the cause] being non-determinative.
Therefore, due to this lack of determinateness, the consequence follows that they are not causes.
Thus, it is established that all supposed causes, such as Īśvara and others, are non-determinative and therefore not causes.
He said: "The establishment [of things] is not relative; for that which is a cause is simply a cause, and that which is an effect is simply an effect—this is established.
[This passage does not appear in manuscript *ga*, as it is beyond the scope of perception in manuscript *kha*.]
ka. kha. ga. the consequence of impermanence;
bho *aniyatatva* (the state of being non-determined);
ka. kha. ga. because of impermanence.

Ka. Kha. Ga. [Regarding] impermanence in the *Vimalaprabhā*, [the section on] the inner [self] says: "In this world, accomplishment comes to you by your own will, but not to me"—this is indeed partiality (*vaiṣamikatva*).
If [the point] were established by mere wish, then by my wish as well, that which is "non-existent" for you would be established as "existent" for me, because it is devoid of logical justification.
To this he says: "This is our tenet based on authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*)."
It is not possible to say that the *samaya* is unestablished, for it has been stated by those learned in the scriptures;
thus he says: "Sometimes reasoning is expressed."

In this regard, [the Sāṃkhya] says: "Because there is no production of everything from every material cause, and because a capable cause produces only that which it is capable of producing, the pre-existence of the effect (*satkārya*) is established. To this he replies: "In this case, how is your reason (*hetu*) futile? If your position (*pakṣa*) possesses the characteristics of a valid proof, then it will prove my position as well."
Now, if your thesis (*pakṣa*) has fallen under the definition of being refuted, then it will refute my thesis as well; just as fire burns both [things], it is not [limited] to one alone.
Here, for example, the proposition (*pratijñā*) of those who maintain that sound is real is: "Sound is eternal. What is the reason (*hetu*)? Because it is formless (*amūrtatvāt*).
What is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)? Like space (*ākāśavat*); just as space is eternal because it is formless, so too is sound. Therefore, sound is established as eternal.

He said: "This is not a mere proposition (*pratijñā*); the opponent will also say: 'Sound is impermanent—what is the reason? Because it is produced (*kṛtakatvāt*)—what is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)? Like a jar; just as a jar is produced from clay, a staff, a wheel, thread, and the exertion of a person's hand, so too sound is produced through effort by means of the throat, palate, and so forth; therefore, it is established that sound is impermanent.'"
Therefore, the establishment of an effect does not occur through the mere statement of a reason;
rather, that which speaks according to reality would be the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and not the statement of a reason—
thus, the reason is useless.
Furthermore: for those who hold the thesis (sādhya), the reason (hetu) does not become a prover because it contradicts the proposition (pratijñā).

At the time when the proposition exists, the reason does not exist; at the time when the reason exists, the proposition does not exist. Therefore, of what would that be the reason? For, being non-simultaneous, they do not share a common substratum (dharmin).
At the time when there is the letter *pra*, at that time there is not the letter *ati* nor the letter *ajña*;

likewise for the letters *pa*, *ra*, and *a*. Just as it is not possible to perform the function of a son by means of a son who is unborn or dead—this being the case even with respect to each individual letter—so it is also with respect to the cause (*hetu*).
Therefore, because the cause is perceived, the effect does not exist [independently], since it is established through non-causality (*ahetutaḥ*).
"Non-causality" (*ahetu*) and "cause" (*hetu*) or "reason" (*kāraṇa*) are indeed synonymous.

Thus, the effect is not in the cause, nor does the effect arise without a cause. Consequently, it is established that the effect does not exist from itself, does not exist from another, does not exist from both, and does not exist without a cause; this constitutes the refutation of the agent and the eternal cause.

Now, the refutation of the self is stated, beginning with "If," and so forth: "If the self were all-pervading, how could it experience the pain of separation from loved ones? And if it were eternal, why does it fall into such a state when struck by the arrows of Love? If it were active [in the past], how does it reach this state of stupor during sleep? Thus, it cannot be all-pervading, nor even omnipresent; furthermore, this self was not active in the past. That [position] is therefore false. 1–2. kha. That which is [stated] there is incorrect.

In this chapter, the Great Exposition on the Investigation of the Logic of One’s Own and Others’ Views: If the self (*ātman*) were omnipresent (*sarvaga*), how could it experience the suffering of separation from loved ones? In this context, that self which is omnipresent would be one; for such a [self], there would be no suffering of separation from loved ones.
Consequently, through the suffering of a single sentient being, all sentient beings would suffer, because the self is omnipresent.
Now, if there were multiple selves, then those multiple selves would lack omnipresence.
Furthermore, if this [self] were eternal, then when it is struck by the arrows of Love (*madana*), what state could it possibly undergo?

For that which is eternal here has no transition to another state, because it is devoid of modification. Therefore, how can one struck by the arrows of Love undergo these ten types of states of passion? Consequently, the self must be non-eternal, due to its association with modification.

"If it were active during [the waking] time, how could it fall into this state of insentience at the time of sleep?"—if, in this context, it were active, characterized by the waking state, and (by the word "ca") eternal, then how could it fall into insentience—that is, become devoid of activity—at the time of sleep?

Thus, when examined with absolute rigor, it follows that [the soul] would be either omnipresent or not the sovereign lord, and neither eternal nor active; therefore, it is established that it is not the Self.

Now, the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is stated as beginning with "there is no self," and so forth: "There is no self, nor is there rebirth; there is the fruit of the unwholesome and the wholesome, yet it is devoid of an agent. There is no goer, yet there is the journey toward liberation. There is bondage in its entirety, yet there is no one bound. There is both existence and non-existence, and there is a state of being that is devoid of momentariness and lacks intrinsic nature. This is my word of truth; this word of truth is not subverted by the words of gods or serpents, even through their collective efforts. (172) In this world, for phenomena arisen dependently, there is arising from cessation, and cessation from arising.
Thus, for things subject to cessation, there is no self because of the absence of anything belonging to a self (*ātmīya*);
however, for things subject to arising, there is occurrence due to the taking up of rebirth.
Their establishment through analogies such as Vedic recitation and so forth will be stated in what follows.

"Because there is the fruit of the impure and the pure," this means that for phenomena subject to arising, there is the fruit of the pure and the impure; "devoid of an agent" (kartrā vinā) refers to those phenomena subject to cessation being devoid of an agent by virtue of their non-existence.

"There is no goer" means that the collection of phenomena subject to cessation has no goer, yet there is a going toward liberation; and "for others, there is another such form"—from such statements, [it follows that] everything is entirely so.
"There is bondage, but no one bound": here, for phenomena characterized by arising, there is bondage; for phenomena characterized by cessation, there is no one who is bound.

Furthermore, there exists both being and non-being; there exists a state that is devoid of momentariness, lacking intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), and free from the conceptualization of substantial entities.

Here, the state that has become a fusion of being and non-being—devoid of intrinsic nature, free from the conceptualization of substance, comparable to a reflection, devoid of momentariness, and free from arising and ceasing—exists for the Buddhas as they turn the wheel of Dharma.
This speech of mine, which is liberated from all conceptual constructs (*graha*), cannot be refuted here by the words of the gods and serpents when they are gathered together;

just as a wrestler seized by a demon cannot defeat a wrestler who is free from that demon, so too those seized by the demon of conceptual construction cannot defeat one who is free from the demon of conceptual construction. Thus, the proof of selflessness and so forth has been stated here in brief; the rule is that the detailed exposition is to be understood from the extensive scriptures.

Now, the refutation of the views of the Vaibhāṣikas, Sautrāntikas, and Yogācāras is stated, beginning with "He who [says] reality," and so forth: "He who asserts that reality called the *pudgala* resides within the body by virtue of its own nature is ruined. Though he speaks of objects conventionally, he is one who does not know the ultimate truth, for he considers what is non-existent to be existent.
1. ka. kha. *madanasara* 2. bho. *Sad Pa* (*jāgrata*) 3. bho. *bGog Pahi Chos rNam La* (*nirodhadharmāṇām*)

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is said: "The proponent of consciousness (*vijñānavādin*), who considers all the three worlds to be nothing but consciousness—he who is not destroyed, though his own position is destroyed—becomes a proponent of the non-duality of compassion and emptiness.

[Adhyātma: Herein lies the grasping at positions by these non-Buddhist outsiders and Buddhists; by that grasping at one's own position, there is also the grasping at the positions of others, whether through their similarity or their dissimilarity. Among those of childish intellect, the Vaibhāṣika here—who asserts that the reality called the "person" (*pudgala*) resides in the body because of its inherent nature—is "destroyed. (173)

In this regard, if there exists a person (*pudgala*) who is internal to the person and constitutes a factor of rebirth, then its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) must be stated: is it of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*) or of the nature of non-knowledge (*ajñāna*)? If it is of the nature of knowledge, then it is impermanent; for here, when the cognition of a jar has ceased, the cognition of a cloth arises, and therefore it is impermanent.
Alternatively, if it is of the nature of knowledge, then there would be an absence of pleasure and pain for one who lacks knowledge;
thus, when examined from the perspective of that nature, that Vaibhāṣika is destroyed.

"In this regard, there is a person who carries the burden; I do not say 'non-existent' (na jñeyam), nor do I say 'existent' (na jñeyam)"—this statement of the Blessed One is to be explained in detail in the *Jñānapaṭala*.
Thus, according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), he speaks purposefully, for one who does not know the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) considers even that which is non-existent to be existent.

In this context, how is it that one who asserts the apprehension of objects such as blue and so forth conventionally is ruined? For he, not having realized the ultimate truth, considers the *jñānakāya* (the body of gnosis) to be non-existent like the son of a barren woman. Thus it has been said: "Space and the two types of cessation—these three unconditioned phenomena are eternal;
all conditioned phenomena are momentary, empty of self, and devoid of an agent. [And: "Sense-born cognition is devoid of form; it directly perceives the collection of atoms."
"The Vaibhāṣika doctrine, which is like an ocean of the Kashmiri school’s thought, holds this view:
those objects of the senses that produce cognitions with their own forms are visible;

cessation and space are like the son of a barren woman and are similar to space; conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) do not exist as insentient entities, nor is there a persistence through the three times."

"The Sautrāntikas know that form is non-existent and non-obstructive. Thus, if non-obstructive form—which is known across the three times—is like the extinguishing of a lamp, then in the absence of non-obstructive form, there would be no Omniscient One; without the four bodies (*kāya*), Buddhahood does not exist through a merely partial body.

In this regard, if there were no non-obstructive body (*apratighakāya*), the Buddha would be unable to manifest all forms of miraculous power (*ṛddhi*); his utterance of all sounds would not occur, his knowledge of the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*) would not function, and all [faculties] such as the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) would be fruitless. Such is the fault in the position of the Sautrāntikas. Now, the fault in the position of the Yogācāras is stated: "The proponent of Consciousness (*vijñānavādin*) considers the entirety of the three worlds to be consciousness alone. He says: "There is no such thing as a composite whole (*avayavin*); atoms (*paramāṇu*) do not exist.
Manifestation is without objective support (*nirālamba*), resembling the experience of a dream."
Because it is devoid of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject, consciousness is ultimately real;
thus it is proclaimed by those who have reached the further shore of the ocean of the Yogācāra doctrine.

[Chapter 1. ka. kha. sākṣādvedāṇu0; Bho. *Phra Rab... Rig* (0 *vettyaṇu0*)] The Great Summary on the Investigation of the Logic of One's Own and Others' Views: Therefore, through the investigation of consciousness by means of its nature as being either one or many, the proponents of consciousness (*vijñānavādin*) are destroyed due to separation.
Here, the triple world is nothing but consciousness.
If there is no external object-form other than cognition, then how is it that for the visual consciousness, which is the grasper, an external form appears with the nature of the grasped?
He said: "It is due to the influence of the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyāvāsanā*).
He asked: "Is there no cessation of this ignorance within consciousness?
Does ignorance not have the characteristic of being a constituent element (*dhātu*)?"

If ignorance (*avidyā*) were not characterized by the three realms (*traidhātuka*), then it would be characterized as transcending cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); such is this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). But it is not so. Therefore, this ignorance is the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) for cyclic existence, and cyclic existence is characterized by the three worlds (*tribhava*). The three worlds are the triple realm (*tredhātuka*), and the triple realm is consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Thus, ignorance is consciousness-only; consciousness-only is its very nature. Because it is of that nature, there is no removal of ignorance, since consciousness is nothing but ignorance.
If, then, the triple world were merely consciousness, there would be a loss of your own proposition; thus, the state of being "merely the triple world" is unestablished.
In this context, regarding the destruction and arising of phenomena that occurs from a single moment, does that occur without stability?
If destruction and arising occurred without stability, then it would also occur for a rabbit's horn.

Now, if from arising comes duration, from duration comes destruction, and from destruction comes arising—thus, there is no unity among duration, destruction, and arising; they must possess distinct characteristics.

Here, at the time when there is duration, there is neither arising nor destruction; at the time when there is destruction, there is neither arising nor duration; and at the time when there is arising, there is neither duration nor destruction! "Time" here means a moment (*kṣaṇa*); thus, while existing at a single moment, there would be the identity of birth, aging, and death.
Furthermore:

here, regarding the destruction and arising of a phenomenon (*dharma*) in a single moment, does that arising of a subsequent phenomenon occur from a preceding phenomenon that has ceased, or from one that has not ceased? If the arising occurs from a ceased phenomenon, then it would be like the arising of a subsequent lamp from a lamp that has already been extinguished. If, however, the arising occurs from one that has not ceased, then it would be like the arising of a lamp from a lamp that has not yet ceased; thus, from that [preceding] one, there is the arising of another. In this way, through arising after arising, there is a series of consciousnesses (*vijñāna-mālā*), just like a garland of lamps.

Therefore, it cannot be said that another consciousness arises from the cessation of a preceding one; nor can it arise from one that has not ceased, because they are mutually exclusive and thus lack identity.

Consequently, the Mādhyamika says: "Even that consciousness is not accepted by the wise as ultimately real, because it is devoid of a nature that is either unitary or manifold, like a lotus in the sky."
“The Madhyamikas know reality to be neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor even of the nature of neither; it is liberated from the four alternatives.
Thus, he who has not lost the position of non-destruction becomes such.
Who is he?
He is the proponent of the non-duality of compassion and emptiness.

Herein lies the established rule of the Buddhist tenets: for him, compassion is without objective support and free from conceptual construction, while emptiness is endowed with the excellence of all aspects and pertains to the three times for the sake of thoroughly knowing the three times.
ka. kha. external form;
ka. kha. bho. in these texts, the phrase "the departure of ignorance" is absent;
[this] is not present in the ka. kha. bho. texts.
[This passage] is not in manuscript *ga*.
In manuscripts *ka* and *kha*, it reads *tatpā*.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, [in the section on] the Inner [Science], the refutation of the experience of past karma and the accumulation of present karma is now stated, beginning with the words "the living being" (*jantu*), etc.: "If a living being experiences past karmas performed here in this life through another birth, then there would be no destruction of karma for humans across various births."
Departure from saṃsāra may occur through immeasurable births, yet there is no entry into liberation; for this is indeed the doctrine of the Protectors, which has abandoned other [inferior] views.
In this regard, for those who hold the view that a living being experiences in this life the actions performed in a previous birth and those performed in another birth,

if this were so, then there would be no destruction of karma for men through successive births, because of the continued enjoyment of the fruits of karma. Thus, there would be no exit from saṃsāra through immeasurable existences, and there would be no entry into liberation.
This is indeed the doctrine of the Tāyi(n)s; however, it is devoid of other births—such is the doctrine of the Mleccha Tāyi(n)s.
A human being, upon death, experiences pleasure or pain in heaven or hell in this very human form by the decree of Rahmaṇa.
Therefore, the rule is that it is devoid of other births.

Now, the refutation of the Cārvāka doctrine is stated, beginning with "by the elements" (*bhūtaiḥ*), and so forth: If the witnessing consciousness arises from the elements alone, just as the power of intoxication arises [from fermented ingredients], why indeed would it not exist in trees, given their conjunction with earth, water, fire, air, and space? If you say that these [trees] lack the capacity for being a sentient being, then the power of the combination of the elements must be utterly false. This statement of the Cārvākas does not yield the fruit of happiness for men who have lost their way.

If it is established here that the minds of humans possess the senses because they are composed of the previously mentioned elements—earth and so forth—in conjunction with harītakī, molasses, and dhātakī, like the potency of wine, then why does the mind of trees, which are likewise composed of earth and the other elements, not also possess the senses? This follows from the combination of the elements. If you argue that these stationary beings lack the capacity for sentient life, then the power of the combination of elements is utterly false. Therefore, this statement of the Cārvākas does not yield the fruit of happiness; it is a lost path for men. Such is the rule for the refutation of the Lokāyata doctrine.

Now, the refutation of the Kṣapaṇaka doctrine is stated, beginning with "The soul" (*jīva*), and so forth: If the soul is of the same size as the body, would it not be destroyed when the hands and feet are cut off? Is it eternal? Or, by the power of the body, would even an atom become gross? When liberated from karma, does it go from saṃsāra to the state of bliss situated at the summit of the world? Furthermore, that which is composed of atoms—the three worlds—is always eternal; it does not perish due to time.
ka. kha. eṣām | kha. 0bhoga | This is not found in manuscript ka.
O Tagzig!
O Kāvaṇa! O Rāmaṇa!

This is the great chapter on the investigation of the logic of one's own and others' philosophical systems. Here, if it is argued that in the doctrine of the Kṣapaṇakas it is established that the soul (*jīva*) is eternal and its size is equal to the body, then when a limb such as a hand or foot is severed from the body, does the soul perish? For [if it were so], there would be an absence of the soul due to the absence of the physical form whose limbs have been severed.
The body might be eternal due to its power, yet it could also be atomic because of its capacity to assume a subtle body and its capacity to assume a gross body; why, then, would it undergo grossness?
In this regard, that which is eternal is unchanging, and that which is changing is established as non-eternal.
[The opponent] says: [This is resolved by] the doctrine of manifold predication (*syādvāda*), according to which [the self] is both eternal and non-eternal by way of substance and modification.

He said: "In this world, just as gold is both eternal and non-eternal in relation to its earrings, so too the substance of the soul (*jīvadravya*) is eternal in relation to its substance and non-eternal in relation to its modifications (*vikāra*); such is the doctrine of manifold aspects (*syādvāda*).
For it is said: 'In some respects the soul is powerful, and in some respects the karmas are powerful;
these enmities of the soul and the karma have been bound since beginningless time.'"
He explains the meaning of this verse with the words "in some cases":
in the matter of liberation, the soul (*jīva*) is powerful by virtue of the power of the knowledge of absolute isolation (*kaivalya-jñāna*);

in some cases, namely in the matter of the cycle of existence consisting of the four states of birth (*caturgati-saṃsāra*), karma is powerful by virtue of the power of ignorance (*ajñāna*). Thus it is established that there are mutual enmities between the soul and karma, bound from beginningless time in the past.
Thus, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that a substance consists of origination and destruction while being endowed with its own qualities, and not otherwise.
An objection is raised: Are substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*) identical or different?

If they are identical here, then there is no distinction between substance and mode; if they are different, then a mode would exist without a substance, yet this is not observed, just as a cloth does not exist without threads.
In this way, there is also the fault of the conjunction of the eternal and the non-eternal regarding both the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*).
There is no identity between the eternal and the non-eternal because they are mutually contradictory, just as, for example, the dissimilar and the similar cannot be one.
Therefore, it is established that the substance consisting of the genus of living beings and so forth is non-eternal.
Thus, liberated from karma, one proceeds from saṃsāra to the state of bliss situated at the summit of the world.

Here, in the Siddhānta of the Kṣapaṇakas, there is only one triple-world (*tribhuvana*); there is no second. Therefore, this triple-world is without beginning or end, devoid of arising or passing away, entirely composed of *vajra*, and shall never undergo destruction.
If there were destruction of this world, then, due to the absence of another triple-world, where would all living beings abide?

For that reason, this is eternal; the *jīva* (living soul) is also eternal, for having been liberated from karma through the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), it goes to the state of liberation (*mokṣa*), the "Good Place" (*sukapada*) measuring four million five hundred thousand *yojanas*, which is devoid of matter (*pudgala*). This is established. An objection is raised: "In this world, the three realms (*trailokya*) are produced by atoms (*aṇu*); they do not exist without atoms. Furthermore, because of the word 'and' (*ca*) [in the verse], liberation also [is composed of them]. Therefore, how can it be eternal? For even that which is constructed of atoms, though it may be permanent, is not eternal at all times—for all time—since it will go to destruction under the power of the time of dissolution (*saṃhāra-kāla*). Due to its destruction, there will also be the destruction of the established doctrines (*siddhānta*)."
This is established by the principle of "siddham" (it is proven).
Furthermore,
among the aforementioned six classes of living beings and their respective tints (*leśyā*), the life-principle (*jīva*) of plants is as follows:

Does each individual plant-body experience pleasure or pain alone by the power of karma, or do many do so? To this he says: A single *jīva* grasps a single *pudgala*, by whose influence plants, crops, and the like possess the designation of "life.

If there were no *jīva*, how could it be established that they are "trees"? Furthermore, it is established that non-living things such as wood do not drink water and produce flowers and the like according to the seasons.

He said: "If, in this world, there were a single individual soul (*jīva*) in each individual person, then when a stalk of sugarcane is cut into pieces and becomes many fragments, that eternal soul would have entered one of those fragments, contracting under the influence of karma.

Which [parts] would have been abandoned by it? Moreover, this is not logically tenable, for upon examination, when those [pieces] are planted back in the earth, sprouts and so forth are seen from every single fragment."
Therefore, it is established that the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of trees consists in their capacity for sprouts and so forth. This concludes the refutation of the Jain doctrine.
The extensive and manifold tenets of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) must be rejected by means of the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*), which is the science of multiple valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*).

"Whatever is equal to the word of the Perfect Buddha, whether by way of convention (*saṃvṛti*) or ultimate reality (*vivṛti*), that is not to be criticized; such is the rule of the Blessed One, the *Ādibuddha*, in the *Kālacakra*.

For example: 'For the sake of primordial wisdom, Kālacakra reveals the great teaching according to the mental dispositions of men—whether soft or hard—by the power of their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Since the mind indeed becomes colored by the passions of objects like a crystal due to external conditions, therefore no teaching whatsoever, whether belonging to one's own or another's family, should be criticized by a yogi. (177)
It is established that this refers to one's own power (*svaśakti*).

What is the intended meaning of these two statements in the *Kālacakra-tantra* and its commentary, the *Vimalaprabhā*: "Whoever, whether by way of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) or the ultimate (*vivṛti*), is equal to the word of the Perfectly Awakened One, he is not to be criticized; such is the rule of the Blessed One, the *Ādibuddha*, in the *Kālacakra*"; and "Therefore, no doctrine whatsoever belonging to one's own or another's family (*kula*) is to be criticized by a yogin"? From these two statements, it appears at first glance that the Kālacakra practitioner must never criticize the views of others.

This being the case, while this great introductory exposition (*mahoddeśa*) on the method of investigating self and other is currently proceeding, how is it that the refutation of the views of others (*paramatākhaṇḍana*) has been performed both in the root text and in the commentary? Furthermore, at the conclusion of this great exposition, the commentary states: "The tenets of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) are to be rejected by the Madhyamaka. The resolution of this apparent contradiction is achieved through the elucidation of his own intention by the illustrious Kheṅdrup Je.

They said: "Dharma is the great instruction on the investigation of the logic of one's own and others' views; it is the benefit of sentient beings and is free from sense objects. Adharma, even when causing harm, is not a source of suffering at all times, for violence is not validated by the Vedas as yielding the fruit of happiness. Friendship with the good, arising from the words of the wise, brings supreme bliss and is affectionate toward all beings. Therefore, O King, for the sake of sentient beings, cultivate in your mind the single realization that they are devoid of intrinsic nature. (178)

In the heavenly realm I am Indra; on earth I am the preceptor of the thirty gods; in Pātāla I am the King of Serpents, bowed to by the race of *phaṇi*s; I am the all-pervading and supreme one. I am knowledge; I am the Buddha, the Lord of Sages; I am the imperishable, supreme Sovereign; I am the Vajrayoga of yogis; I am the Veda, the sacred syllable *Oṃ*. O King, take refuge in me with your whole being! (179)

Thus concludes the rule for taking refuge. Now follows the homage to Sūryaratha: "You are my mother, you are my father; you are the teacher in the world, and you are my kinsman and good friend. You are my lord, you are the creator, you are the benefactor who removes misfortune, and you are the abode of all prosperity. You are the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*), you are the repository of excellent qualities, you alone are the one whose faults are destroyed. You are the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) for the poor and the helpless; O Lord of Jinas, I have come to you for refuge. (180)
Thus ends the second chapter, the Determination of the Inner Self, in the glorious Mahākālacakra extracted from the glorious Ādibuddha. ||2||

Thus, Sūryaratha, having praised the Blessed Mañjuśrī with a salutation to his guru, placed [the Blessed One’s] two feet upon his head and sat down again on his own seat. Thus ends the seventh great chapter, "The Investigation of the Logic of One's Own and Others' Views," in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja* following the *Śrī-mūla-tantra*. 7.
